PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One-Hundred Seventy First Report on the subject “Working of All India 
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi and Problems Faced by Patients in availing 
healthcare and treatment”. 
 
2. In exercise of its constitutional mandate, the Committee, in its meeting held on 18th 
November, 2024 identified the subject "Working of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
(AIIMS), New Delhi and Problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment" and 
decided to undertake a detailed study on the Subject. The primary objective behind identifying 
the subject Committee is to examine the organizational structure of the Institute alongwith its 
governing structure, foundational mandate for delivery of top tier medical education, ground 
breaking research, patient care besides ongoing infrastructure projects, faculty, staff position vis 
a vis sanctioned strength alongwith overall human resource management, issue of overcrowding 
and managerial steps taken to overcome the said problem comparative SWOT analysis of the 
institute vis a vis leading global healthcare institute, etc.  Through this study, the Committee 
intends to identify areas of structural or procedural bottlenecks and recommend reforms that 
would enhance both the quality and inclusiveness of care. 
 
3. The Committee in its meeting held on 13th May, 2025 heard the representative of 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and top management of AIIMS, New Delhi to take into 
account the routine functioning of AIIMS, New Delhi, medical education both graduate and 
under graduate, medical services and healthcare treatment facilities available, status of allied 
professionals and nursing, implementation of master plan, key concern areas alongwith steps, 
policy intervention, organisational development, innovation and changes required to address the 
issues, etc. 
 
4. The Committee undertook a visit to AIIMS, New Delhi on 13th June, 2025 to take stock 
of ground realities on the actual working of the AIIMS, New Delhi and problems faced by 
patients in availing healthcare and treatment. During the course of the visit, the Committee 
interacted with the representatives of various associations that inter-alia included Faculty 
Association, Nurses Association, SC/ST Association, Karamchari Union, Officers Association 
and Resident Doctors Association and gathered detailed information pertaining to Master Plan, 
Basic Infrastructure & On-going and future projects, Various departments imparting UG and PG 
Courses alongwith faculty and non-faculty Staff in-position against the sanctioned position, Beds 
occupancy rate, Functional OTs, Governing Structures, Health Research Ecosystem, undertaken 
Research Projects alongwith its key areas, Human Resource Management, Strategic steps taken 
to extend Patient Care and Comforts, including Grievance Redressal Mechanism, global standing 
of AIIMS, New Delhi vis-a-vis leading healthcare institutes of developed countries. The

Committee also interacted with the representative of AIIMS Administration & Management and 
sought details of steps taken to combat the challenges being faced by the Administration as well 
as the patients seeking treatment in the Institute.   
 
5. During the finalization of its Report, the Committee relied upon the following 
documents/ papers:- 
(i) Background Note on “Working of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), 
New Delhi and Problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment" as 
received from the Department of Health and Family Welfare; 
(ii) Action Taken Notes on Committee’s 87th Report on “The Functioning of All India 
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) presented/laid on 11th August, 2015; 
(iii) Annual Report (2025-26) of the Department of Health & Family Welfare; 
(iv) Research Publications (2016-24) Centre for Integrative Medicine and Research 
(CIMR), AIIMS, New Delhi; 
(v) Oral Evidences tendered by Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare; 
(vi) Oral evidences tendered by stakeholders and their written submissions; 
(vii) Written submissions of various Organizations/Associations of AIIMS; 
(viii) Response of the Department of Health and Family Welfare on the issues raised in 
memoranda received by the Committee; 
(ix) Replies to the questionnaires received from the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare; and 
(x) Other relevant documents pertaining to the subject. 
 
6. The Committee, in its meeting held on 18th March, 2026, considered the draft Report and 
adopted the same. 
7. For facility of reference and convenience, the observations and recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report and also reproduced at the 
end of the Report at ‘Observations/Recommendations -at a Glance’ . 
8. On behalf of the Committee and on my own behalf, I extend special thanks to (i) 
Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare and officers concerned with the subject 
matter (ii) Director of AIIMS, New Delhi.  I also acknowledge the contribution of the 
stakeholders for their deep insight and valuable suggestions during the course of interactions. I 
further extend special appreciation to the officers of the Committee Secretariat for their valuable 
efforts in assimilating all relevant information and enabling the Committee in producing such 
quality Report.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
1.0 AIIMS, New Delhi, created in 1956 as an autonomous Institute through an Act of 
Parliament is an Institute of National Importance (INI) and globally known to deliver top-tier 
medical education, ground breaking research, exceptional patient care and good governance 
for innovative implementation of healthcare national policies and programmes besides 
serving as a nucleus for nurturing excellence in all aspects of healthcare. 
 
1.1 Over the decades, AIIMS, New Delhi has expanded in scale, capacity, complexity and 
has attained reputation and status, however, despite its outstanding contributions in academic 
and clinical domains, there remain persistent challenges in service delivery that directly affect 
patient comforts and access to care. Long waiting times, overcrowded outpatient departments, 
pressure on emergency services, shortage of beds and limited infrastructure for attendants and 
patients continue to impede the full realization of the institution’s potential. There is also an 
evident need to assess systemic issues related to patient grievance redressal, appointment 
scheduling, interdepartmental referrals, diagnostics bottlenecks and cost barriers. 
 
1.1.1 The Parliamentary Committee, through its mandate, plays a critical role in ensuring 
institutional accountability, transparency in public service delivery and aligning the 
performance of institutions like AIIMS with national health priorities and citizen 
expectations.  The Committee through detailed study of “Working of All India Institute of 
Medical Sciences (AIIMS)” intends to understand the following issues pertaining to the 
institutes:– 
(i) Problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment; 
(ii) Problems being faced in the routine functioning of the AIIMS, Delhi; 
(iii) Medical services and other facilities available in the institutes; 
(iv) Availability of opportunity for medical education at both under-graduate and post-
graduate levels; 
(v) Status of skilled development of Allied Professionals; 
(vi) Standard and clinical exposure to Nursing personnel; 
(vii) Progress of ongoing infrastructural projects; 
(viii) Implementation status of Master Plan; 
(ix) Availability of faculty and non-faculty against the sanctioned strength; 
(x) Key Areas of Concerns including SWOT analysis of the institute; 
(xi) Comparative study of the institute with leading hospitals of the world; 
(xii) Strategy required to overcome the overload of patients and consideration of 
overall suggestions for improvement in the working of the Institute; 
(xiii) Problems faced by patients while availing healthcare and treatment at AIIMS, 
Delhi; 
(xiv) The steps, policy interventions, design and organizational changes that being 
carried out to address the complex issues; 
(xv) Exploring the possibility of the setting up of another AIIMS like institution in 
NCR to overcome the problems of work overload in AIIMS, New Delhi. 
 

 
2 
 
1.1.2 The Committee believes that a close scrutiny of AIIMS, New Delhi, thus, is crucial to 
strengthen governance, equity and outcomes not only within the institution but across the 
national tertiary healthcare system.  
 
1.1.3 The erstwhile Committee on Health and Family Welfare had earlier presented/laid its 
87th Report on “The Functioning of All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS)” to both 
Houses of Parliament on 11th August, 2015 and the same was forwarded to the Ministry for 
furnishing Action Taken Notes on the recommendations contained in that Report. The 
Ministry, in response to that furnished the Action Taken Notes, thereon, however the 
Committee could not present Action Taken Report on the 87th Report due to paucity of time.  
 
1.1.4 The previous Committee in its meeting held on 13th May, 2025 heard the 
representative of Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and top management of AIIMS, 
New Delhi. The Committee undertook a study visit to AIIMS, New Delhi on 13th June, 2025 
to take stock of ground realities on the actual working of the AIIMS, New Delhi and 
problems faced by patients in availing healthcare and treatment. During the course of the 
visit, the Committee interacted with the representatives of various associations that inter-alia 
included Faculty Association, Nurses Association, SC/ST Association, Karamchari Union, 
Officers Association and Resident Doctors Association and gathered detailed information 
pertaining to Master Plan, Basic Infrastructure & On-going and future projects, Various 
departments imparting UG and PG Courses alongwith faculty and non-faculty Staff in-
position against the sanctioned position, Beds occupancy rate, Functional OTs, Governing 
Structures, Health Research Ecosystem, undertaken Research Projects alongwith its key 
areas, Human Resource Management, Strategic steps taken to extend Patient Care and 
Comforts, including Grievance Redressal Mechanism, global standing of AIIMS, New Delhi 
vis-a-vis leading healthcare institutes of developed countries. The Committee also interacted 
with the representative of AIIMS Administration & Management and sought details of steps 
taken to combat the challenges being faced by the Administration as well as the patients 
seeking treatment in the Institute.   
 
1.2 HISTORICAL BACKGROUND  
 
1.2.1 The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) was originally conceived by the 
Advisory Committee on Professional Education, established to implement the 
recommendations of the Bhore Committee (1943), which laid the groundwork for modern 
India's health policy and infrastructure. Chaired by Dr. A. L. Mudaliar and including eminent 
members such as Dr. B. C. Roy, the Committee proposed the creation of a premier medical 
institute that would serve as a hub for training medical educators, provide state-of-the-art 
hospital facilities for medical education and promote comprehensive research essential for 
effective teaching and training. 
 
1.2.2 The vision of the Advisory Committee was translated to reality through the dedication 
and leadership of Ms. Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the first Health Minister of the country, who 
introduced the AIIMS Bill in Parliament on 18th February 1956, which was eventually passed 
as the AIIMS Act, 1956. She not only secured the necessary funding and selected the 

 
3 
 
founding faculty but also became the first President of the Institute in 1957. Her aim was to 
establish an institution that would allow Indian students to pursue world-class postgraduate 
medical education within the country.  
 
1.3 VISION AND SPECIAL CHARACTERS  
 
1.3.1 The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi is an Institute of 
National Importance (INI) which functions under a trinity of mission - medical education, 
research and patient care and later on added the fourth vision of Good Governance- each 
reinforcing and strengthening the other. The vision of AIIMS, New Delhi is rooted in its 
foundational mandate to function not merely as a medical college or hospital, but as an 
Institution of National Importance empowered with the status and responsibilities of a 
University. 
 
1.3.2 During the course of the interaction the Committee was apprised of the four pillars of 
vision of AIIMS, New Delhi as enumerated below:-

1.3.3 Such unique vision enables AIIMS to bring about revolutionary changes in medical 
education through innovative curricula and modern modes of teaching that break away from 
traditional patterns. By integrating academic excellence with practical clinical exposure, the 
Institute envisions to set new benchmarks in the training of healthcare professionals.  
1.4 Aims and Objectives of AIIMS 
1.4.1 As informed by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the following are the aims 
and objectives of AIIMS:- 
 
(i) To develop pattern of teaching in under-graduate and post-graduate medical 
education in all its branches so as to demonstrate a high standard of medical 
education to all medical colleges and other allied institutions in India. 
(ii) To bring together in one place educational facilities of the highest order for the 
training of personnel in all branches of health activities. 
(iii) To attain self-sufficiency in post-graduate medical education. 
 
1.4.2 Responding to the Committee’s query regarding the larger vision of AIIMS Delhi that 
got transformed over the years with the scientific and technological advancement upto now-a-

 
4 
 
days along with the paradigm shift in vision alongwith modification and administrative and 
governing landscape to cover the activities to change in mission and objectives of the  
AIIMS, the AIIMS management informed the Committee, in its written submission that the 
historical and original vision of AIIMS in the field of education envisage to trained top tier 
medical professionals through rigorous undergraduate and postgraduate programmes while in 
the field of research the mission indicates advance medical science through pioneering 
research in clinical and basic sciences and healthcare facilities intends to serve as a referral 
centre for complex medical cases. The paradigm shifts over the decades envisage shift 
towards patient care due to absence of a robust national referral system that led to AIIMS 
becoming the first point of contact for millions of patients. The resultant is overwhelming 
footfall diverting focus from academic and research priorities to managing daily clinical 
loads. 
  
1.4.3 Although faculty and resident doctors spend disproportionate time on clinical duties 
and research output and teaching quality, thereby face challenges due to time constraints and 
administrative overload but the administrative and governance structure moved towards 
autonomy of AIIMS operating under the AIIMS Act and now AIIMS Delhi mentor newer 
AIIMS institutions across India and digital governance adopted e-Hospital systems, bio-
metric attendance and centralized procurements. Despite the Shift in focus, AIIMS has 
maintained a delicate balance between clinical excellence and public trust, besides remarkable 
resilience during health crisis during Covid-19. The Challenges faced inter-alia include 
infrastructural strength and long waiting time, besides dilution of academic and research 
focus, therefore there is rising demand for tertiary care, need for equitable access and 
decentralization, integration of AI genomics, and digital health. 
 
1.4.4 The Committee understands that in order to realize the vision set out for the 
Institute, AIIMS, New Delhi has been granted a high degree of academic, administrative 
and financial autonomy allowing it to chart its own path in pursuit of excellence. The 
Committee believes that strict adherence to level of autonomy granted to the Institute 
will certainly ensure that AIIMS, New Delhi will remain dynamic, responsive and 
forward-thinking in addressing the ever-evolving healthcare needs of the nation. The 
Committee recommends that the Government will remain committed to providing the 
necessary financial support to maintain and advance its operations, ensuring that 
AIIMS continues to serve as a world-class hub for patient care, medical education, 
cutting-edge research and Good Governance. 
 
1.4.5 The Committee believes that since the vision of AIIMS, New Delhi originates 
from its foundational mandate to function as a medical college or hospital as well as an 
institution of national importance empowered with the status and responsibility of 
university, therefore, all activities/efforts at each level of structural arrangement 
entrusted with specific functional behaviour must be made on the principle of 
Management By Objectives (MBO) rather than mere Management By Activities (MBA) 
so that the enshrined objectives/goals are achieved within the stipulated time-frame. In 
this regard, the Committee also recommends that the AIIMS, New Delhi must continue 
to serve as the apex referral center all over the country, a think-tank for national policy 
formation and a nerve center for healthcare innovation and reforms.

3.0 INFRASTRUCTURE AND EXPANSION PLANS OF AIIMS, NEW DELHI 
3.1 Since, the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, is a premier 
institution in India that serves as a national centre of excellence in patient care, education and 
research, therefore, its extensive infrastructure comprises a wide network of specialized 
centres and departments that provide comprehensive healthcare across disciplines.

decongest the OPD, recommends that the Ministry should undertake time-bound

3.3.3 Upon enquiring about the reason for non-functionality of beds, the Committee was 
informed that 520 posts for the Mother and Child Block and 720 posts for the National 
Cancer Institute (NCI), Jhajjar, have recently been sanctioned by the Department of 
Expenditure. The process of recruitment for these sanctioned posts is presently underway and 
it is expected that upon joining of the new faculty and staff, all the currently non-functional 
beds will be made operational. Additionally, 328 beds in the Main Hospital remain non-
functional owing to the ongoing renovation of a dilapidated building—one of the oldest 
structures in the Institute, constructed over half a century ago—which had to be vacated in the 
interest of patient safety. 
 
3.3.4 The Committee was further informed that the operationalization of beds in the newly 
commissioned blocks and centres would be significantly enhanced upon completion of the 
ongoing recruitment drive and approval of additional manpower proposals. Renovation work 
is actively underway in various areas of the Main Hospital, including AB1, AB5, C3 and D7 
blocks. The Institute has taken steps to rationally redistribute patients to functional wards to 

 
10 
 
ensure continuity of care and frequent coordination meetings are held between clinical 
departments, engineering divisions and manpower units to expedite restoration of full 
functionality. 
 
3.3.5 With regard to the non-functional status of operation theatres, the Committee was 
apprised that the primary cause is the shortage of faculty in the Department of Anesthesiology 
and associated support staff. Similarly, the shortfall in functional ICU beds has been 
attributed to inadequate availability of qualified faculty and support personnel. However, the 
Committee was assured that with the recent sanctioning of approximately 1,400 posts across 
various cadres, the Institute is actively engaged in recruitment efforts to operationalize all 
non-functional ICU beds and OTs at the earliest possible time. 
 
3.3.6 The Committee expresses concern that despite having 112 Major OTs, 44 Minor 
OTs and 433 ICU beds, a significant portion of infrastructure remains underutilized, 
with 26 Major OTs and 81 ICU beds non-functional and 843 hospital beds lying 
unutilized. This is an alarming situation and sheer apathy in view of the fact that 
thousands of patients look up to AIIMS for healthcare needs. The AIIMS management 
should overcome its lethargy and address the contradiction wherein on one hand 
patients are made to wait for long periods for surgical interventions whereas on the 
other hand the OTs are lying non-functional. Such non-functionality not only 
undermines patient care but also reflects gaps in maintenance, resource utilization and 
management failure to ensure timely operationalization of critical facilities. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Institute to take immediate corrective measures 
to operationalize the non-functional OTs and hospital beds.  The Committee is of the 
considered view that there is urgent need to enhance the number of beds in cardiology, 
neurology and trauma departments as cardiac disorders and brain strokes account for 
large number of death (almost 30%) in India, therefore, time is a crucial factor in the 
treatment of heart attacks, brain strokes and road accidents, therefore, optimal 
treatment in time within the golden hour is required to save the life. The Committee is 
of the view that department of cardiology must fulfil the sanctioned strength vis-à-vis in-
position strength (teaching and non-teaching) so as to capacitate the department to 
handle current patient load keeping in view the rising cases of heart diseases across the 
country. The Committee is of the considered view that the department of cardiology 
must strengthen in terms of manpower, research and infrastructure to be fully equipped 
to tackle the increasing incidence of heart attack. The Committee strongly recommends 
for an indepth analysis as to why experienced cardiologists leave AIIMS or are not 
allowed to function independently. 
 
3.3.7 The Committee also recommends for a time-bound action plan for repair, up-
gradation and staffing, along with periodic monitoring mechanisms to ensure 
sustainability of operations. The Committee further recommends that AIIMS should 
strengthen its maintenance and infrastructure planning mechanisms to minimize service 
disruption and ensure that all sanctioned beds and operation theatres are made fully 
functional at the earliest. 
 

 
11 
 
3.3.8 The Committee notes that a significant number of ICU beds and operation 
theatres at AIIMS, New Delhi, remain non-functional primarily due to shortage of 
faculty and support staff, as well as ongoing renovation of old hospital blocks. The 
Committee, in this regard, recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi, should accord the 
highest priority to expediting the recruitment process to fill up the sanctioned faculty 
and technical positions within a defined timeframe. The Committee also recommends 
that the Institute, in consultation with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 
prepare a comprehensive manpower deployment plan to ensure optimal utilization of 
available infrastructure and prevent recurrence of such functional shortfalls. The 
Committee recommends that wherever feasible the manpower gaps be filled by 
appointing Resident Doctors on a large scale.  
 
3.4 Status of ongoing and proposed expansion plans, present and proposed 
infrastructure for patients and faculty/officials of the hospital. 
  
3.4.1 AIIMS New Delhi currently has over 3300 operational beds and provides advanced 
medical care to over 12000 patients daily. To overcome the shortage of beds for 
emergency/in-patients and those waiting for procedures and surgeries, continuous expansion 
of various facilities is underway. The ongoing and proposed expansion plans for AIIMS-
Delhi are as under:- 
  
(A) AIIMS MASTER PLAN 
3.4.2 The Union Cabinet in its meeting held on 28th February, 2019 accorded in-principle 
approval for the implementation of a Master Plan to transform AIIMS, New Delhi into a 
world-class Medical University. The integrated Master Plan, covering nearly 190 acres across 
five land parcels with phased development over seven years at an estimated cost of 
₹15,558.37 crore.  The Committee was informed that AIIMS had submitted the Expenditure 
Finance Committee (EFC) memorandum with the Detailed Project Report (DPR) to the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) on 23rd March, 2022 and subsequently 
provided responses to queries from the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change and NITI Aayog on 27th February 2023. On 23rd October 2024, 
the MoHFW advised AIIMS to submit a revised EFC/PIB memorandum, de-linking the two 
projects, viz. construction of the new OPD Block at Masjid Moth (₹484.51 crore) and hostel 
accommodation at the Trauma Centre Extension (₹876 crore) as independent proposals. 
Given the time elapsed since the original costing, the DPR is being updated based on current 
Plinth Area Rates and the revised EFC memorandum for the Master Plan was to be submitted 
to MoHFW. 
 
3.4.3 The Officers Association of AIIMS, in its submission to the Committee, highlighted 
that although the Institute has invested considerable effort and resources in preparing this 
comprehensive Master Plan, funding constraints have prevented timely execution. The 
Association emphasized that full implementation would substantially enhance infrastructure, 
expand institutional capacity and strengthen AIIMS’s academic, research and clinical outputs, 
ultimately improving patient care. 
 

 
12 
 
3.4.4 The Committee, while appreciating the vision of transforming AIIMS Delhi into 
a world-class Medical University through its integrated Master Plan, expresses concern 
over the slow pace of implementation despite the Cabinet’s in-principle approval being 
granted as early as 2019. The Committee is of the view that further delays are 
unwarranted and risk enshrined thereto, thus undermining the objectives of this 
ambitious initiative. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare, in coordination with all concerned agencies, to expedite the 
implementation of the Master Plan through strict adherence to timelines, robust 
monitoring mechanisms and prioritization of critical infrastructure. The Committee 
also recommends the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to extend adequate 
financial and administrative support and also provide financial and administrative 
flexibility to AIIMS to address evolving functional requirements during the seven-year 
implementation period, thereby ensuring that the vision of establishing AIIMS as a 
world-class Medical University is realized as per stipulated time-frame. 
 
3.4.5 The Committee also recommends that the Master Plan should adopt a holistic 
approach by ensuring the comprehensive development of hospital, research, academic 
and residential zones. In addition, the Plan should provide for the establishment of 
integrated 24×7 operational zones that will facilitate uninterrupted patient care, foster 
advanced research and enable continuous academic collaboration.

repeated delays due to prolonged approval processes with civic bodies, environmental

of AIIMS, various independent blocks proposed in the Masjid Moth area like Mother &

cost overruns.

3.4.10 The proposal for construction of a Super Specialty OPD Block at the Masjid Moth 
campus of AIIMS, New Delhi, was recommended by the Standing Finance Committee in its 
meeting held on 2nd December 2022 and ratified by the Governing Body in its meeting on 6th

(E) Expansion of National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), Ghaziabad 
3.4.11 The expansion of NDDTC to include women and adolescent treatment facilities and a 
private ward represents a vital step in addressing the growing public health challenge of

beds each. Clinical care is provided through outpatient, inpatient settings and community 
clinics. NDDTC runs an outpatient clinic for women and other adolescent substance users.  
To expand services to provide inpatient care for women and adolescent substance users, a 
project for construction of additional 50-bedded facility has been undertaken for which MoU 
between CPWD and AIIMS has been signed on 18.03.2024. The project, budgeted at ₹43.67 
crore, is at in the tendering stage subsequent to signing of the MoU process with CPWD and 
is.

3.4.13 The ward block in CRHSP Ballabgarh is more than 70 years old and is in a

3.4.14 The Committee, while recognizing the importance of the ongoing and proposed

robust centralized monitoring mechanism to track both physical and financial progress

among AIIMS, CPWD, HSCC and other civic and regulatory authorities through 
periodic high-level review meetings to ensure timely resolution of bottlenecks.  
 
3.4.15 The Committee also recommends that proactive steps be taken in securing time-
bound approvals from civic bodies, pollution control boards and environmental

Committee emphasizes that AIIMS and the executing agencies must strictly adhere to

actively pursue matters with regard to project delayed due to external factors such as 
litigation or regulatory clearances with the competent authorities and submit a status 
report to the Committee.

(H) RESIDENTIAL AND HOSTEL ACCOMMODATIONS 
  
Redevelopment of Residential Colonies at AIIMS, New Delhi 
3.4.16 The Cabinet had approved the redevelopment of residential colonies at West Ansari 
Nagar (WAN) and Ayur Vigyan Nagar (AVN) Campuses of AIIMS, New Delhi, at a cost of 
₹4,441 crore to construct 3928 residential quarters along with social and commercial 
infrastructure, on a self-financing basis and with no cost to the exchequer. NBCC (India) 
Limited was appointed as the Project Management Consultant. The project suffered initial 
delays due to prolonged statutory approvals, including restrictions on tree felling imposed by 
the Hon’ble Delhi High Court, as well as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Financing 
challenges also emerged, as the sale of commercial spaces at WAN was disallowed by the 
DDA on account of land use restrictions, reducing the anticipated revenue. Consequently, 
AIIMS sought revised Cabinet approval for monetization through the sale of residential 
apartments at AVN, which was not agreed to by the Empowered Committee. Meanwhile, 
NBCC proceeded with the sale of commercial space at AVN as per the original Cabinet 
decision, generating ₹236.03 crore from the e-auction of a local shopping complex. These 
funds are now being utilized for the construction of three towers (117 Type-IV S) at the 
WAN campus, marking visible progress in the project. 
 
3.4.17 The Committee received submissions from various associations of AIIMS, New 
Delhi, highlighting the acute housing crisis across different cadres. The Faculty Association 
(FAIMS) pointed out that out of more than 850 faculty members, only around 250 are 
provided on-campus housing. This shortage not only affects faculty well-being but also 
undermines the Gurukul Model of immersive learning, hampers UG and PG training and 
weakens preparedness for night-time emergency care. The AIIMS Nurses Union submitted 
that less than 4 percent of the nursing cadre have access to housing, a factor contributing to 
attrition and migration abroad. Similarly, the Karamchari Union and Officers Association 
reported that less than 10 percent of employees are accommodated in government quarters.  
 
3.4.18 The Committee is disappointed over the inordinate delays in the redevelopment 
of residential colonies at West Ansari Nagar and Ayur Vigyan Nagar campuses which 
were expected to provide modern housing and supporting facilities for AIIMS staff. The 
inability to monetize commercial space at WAN due to land-use restrictions and the 
prolonged procedural hurdles has slowed the pace of implementation, leaving a large 
gap between the original financing model and current progress. The Committee 
emphasizes that such slow pace of progress has created a situation where the acute 
shortage of accommodation for faculty, students, nurses and other employees has 
become unsustainable.  
 
3.4.19 The Committee understands that such shortage of housing accommodation not 
only affects well being but also undermines the Gurukul Model of immersive learning, 
hampers UG and PG training and weakens preparedness for night-time emergency 
care. The Committee expresses concern that out of more than 850 faculty members only 
around 250 faculty members, less than 4 per cent of nursing cadres and less than 10% of 
employees of AIIMS, New Delhi have been provided campus accommodation. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, in 

 
16 
 
coordination with DDA and NBCC, urgently devise a viable financing mechanism that 
ensures project continuity without further reliance on piecemeal monetization. The 
Committee further stresses the need for time-bound resolution of statutory clearances, 
so that the housing requirements of AIIMS employees are met at the earliest. 
 
3.4.20 The Committee further recommends that the redevelopment should be designed 
and executed with a clear prioritization of residential allocation to faculty, students, 
nurses and staff in a fair and proportionate manner so that the housing deficit across all 
categories is effectively addressed. The Committee is of the view that the successful and 
timely completion of residential project is not merely a matter of infrastructure 
development but an essential requirement for sustaining AIIMS’s national stature as a 
centre of excellence in patient care, education and research. 
 
Hostel Accommodation of Resident Doctors 
3.4.21 AIIMS, New Delhi, in their written submission, informed the Committee that it 
currently has 20 hostels for students and resident doctors, accommodating around 2,700 
individuals across married, single and shared units. To address growing demand, construction 
of new hostels with 2,277 units, at an estimated cost of ₹876.17 crore, has been approved by 
the Standing Finance Committee in its meeting held on 16th April 2024 and ratified by the 
Governing Body, with the appraisal and approval process currently underway. 
 
3.4.22 The Resident Doctors Association, in their written submission to the Committee, 
highlighted the inadequacy of hostel facilities in light of the Central Residency Scheme, 1992, 
which mandates provision of adequate accommodation and amenities for resident doctors. 
With the expansion of specialty departments and increased postgraduate intake, demand has 
far outstripped supply. The situation is particularly acute for female residents and those 
requiring married accommodation, many of whom face long waiting periods. The conversion 
of a postgraduate hostel into one for undergraduates has further strained capacity. The 
Association emphasized the urgent need for expanded hostel infrastructure, with a focus on 
safety, convenience and proximity to duty areas, to ensure doctors remain efficient, well-
rested and able to provide high-quality patient care. 
 
3.4.23 The Committee expresses deep concern over the acute shortage of hostel 
accommodation for resident doctors, students and trainees at AIIMS, New Delhi, which 
has resulted in prolonged waiting periods, especially for female and married residents. 
Such ugly situation undermines the intent of the Central Residency Scheme, 1992 and 
directly impacts the efficiency, preparedness and well-being of resident doctors who are 
required to perform round-the-clock duties. 
 
3.4.24 The Committee also notes that approval has already been granted for the 
construction of new hostels with 2,277 units at estimated cost of Rs. 876.17 crore on 16th 
April, 2024. The Committee strongly recommends that the housing accommodation of 
residential doctors project be expedited on priority so as to bridge the current gap 
between demand and availability. The Committee further recommends that the 
allocation of new hostel facilities must give due consideration to the requirements of 
female residents and those in need of married accommodation, with appropriate focus 

 
17 
 
on safety, convenience and proximity to duty area to ensure that doctors remain 
efficient, well rested thereby able to provide best quality patient care. The Committee is 
of the view that timely implementation of Hostel Accommodation for doctors will not 
only ease the pressure on existing infrastructure but will also ensure a conducive 
environment for medical education, research and patient care, thereby upholding the 
standards of excellence for which AIIMS is renowned. 
 
3.4.25 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends for construction of quarters on 
fast track mode for doctors, allied services and other staff and allotment of 
accommodation as per entitlement to enable them to lead hassle-free life so that they can 
devote their time for treatment of patients with peaceful state of mind and careful 
attention. In this regard, AIIMS, New Delhi management may seek all sorts of 
assistance and guidance including financial assistance. The Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry must have track of implementation of projects on 
construction of residential accommodation.

4.1.1 AIIMS, New Delhi operates through a structured management hierarchy designed to 
balance autonomy with accountability. This framework comprises several statutory and 
standing bodies, each entrusted with defined roles in governance, academics, finance, 
infrastructure and hospital services. Together, they ensure that AIIMS functions not only as a 
premier healthcare institution but also as a leader in medical education and research. The

4.2 The AIIMS governance structure is multi-tiered and consists of the following entities:- 
 
Institute Body
Governing Body
Academic Committee
Standing Finance Committee
Standing Selection Committee
Estimate Committee
Hospital Affairs Committee

 
18 
 
Institute Body (IB) 
 
4.2.1 The Institute Body is the apex decision-making authority of AIIMS and functions as 
the highest governing organ under the AIIMS Act, 1956. The IB is chaired by the Union 
Minister of Health and Family Welfare and includes representatives from Parliament, eminent 
scientists, medical experts, and senior officials from the Government of India. It provides the 
broad vision and direction for the Institute. The IB formulates policies, approves long-term 
development plans, ratifies major initiatives and ensures that the Institute adheres to statutory 
and regulatory obligations. Its decisions form the foundation for the governance and growth 
of AIIMS. 
 
Governing Body (GB) 
 
4.2.2 The Governing Body is the executive arm of the Institute Body and is chaired by the 
Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare. It consists of senior officials from the Ministry 
of Health & Family Welfare, Ministry of Human Resource Development, the Director of 
AIIMS as Member-Secretary, faculty representatives and other nominated members. It 
translates the broad policies of the Institute Body into actionable measures. The GB oversees 
implementation of institutional policies, allocates resources, monitors academic and hospital 
development, and approves key administrative and academic appointments. It acts as the 
principal supervisory authority for day-to-day governance, bridging vision with execution. 
 
Standing Finance Committee (SFC) 
 
4.2.3 The Standing Finance Committee ensures the financial integrity of AIIMS. It 
scrutinizes annual budgets, expenditure plans, audit reports and funding proposals before they 
are placed before the Governing Body or Institute Body. The SFC also recommends financial 
allocations for new projects, ensures adherence to fiscal discipline and monitors utilization of 
grants. By maintaining financial prudence, the SFC safeguards the economic sustainability of 
AIIMS. 
 
Standing Academic Committee 
 
4.2.4 The Academic Committee regulates the entire academic and research ecosystem of the 
Institute. Chaired by the Director and comprising senior Deans and faculty, it reviews and 
updates curricula, introduces new courses, frames policies for teaching and training and 
promotes faculty development. It also ensures that academic programs align with the evolving 
needs of healthcare and global standards of medical education. The Academic Committee 
plays a critical role in sustaining AIIMS’ reputation as a centre of academic excellence. 
 
 
 
Standing Estate Committee 
 
4.2.5 The Estate Committee oversees the planning, development and maintenance of 
AIIMS’ physical infrastructure spread across its multiple campuses. Its responsibilities 
include managing land use, accommodation policies for staff and students, upkeep of 

 
19 
 
buildings and development of new facilities. By ensuring efficient use of land and 
infrastructure, the Estate Committee supports the Institute’s growing academic and healthcare 
needs. 
 
Standing Hospital Affairs Committee 
 
4.2.6 The Standing Hospital Affairs Committee supervises and guides hospital operations at 
AIIMS. It addresses patient care services, formulates hospital policies, monitors quality 
standards and manages regulatory compliance in clinical operations. This committee plays a 
vital role in ensuring that the hospital side of AIIMS meets its mandate of delivering 
affordable and high-quality healthcare to patients from across the country. 
 
Standing Selection Committee 
 
4.2.7 The Selection Committee is entrusted with the recruitment, appointment and 
promotion of faculty and academic staff. It ensures merit-based and transparent processes, 
maintaining the highest standards in faculty selection. Through this role, the Committee 
upholds the quality of human resources, which directly impacts the teaching, research, and 
clinical services provided by AIIMS.

CORE FUNCTIONS OF AIIMS, NEW DELHI 
5.0 MEDICAL EDUCATION 
5.1 The All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi stands at the 
forefront of medical education in India, offering a comprehensive and evolving academic 
ecosystem that nurtures excellence in healthcare training, research and innovation. With a 
distinguished faculty, diverse programs ranging from undergraduate to super-specialty and 
paramedical courses and a strong emphasis on competency-based learning, the institute 
equips students with the skills and knowledge required to meet modern healthcare challenges. 
By blending rigorous academic training with hands-on clinical exposure and cutting-edge 
research opportunities, AIIMS continues to shape the next generation of highly skilled 
healthcare professionals and leaders. 
5.2 Training of Healthcare Professionals 
 
5.2.1 AIIMS, New Delhi stands as a premier institution in India, dedicated not only to 
excellence in healthcare but also to pioneering and evolving medical education. Since 1987, 
the institute has trained over 17,000 students, contributing significantly to the country’s 
skilled healthcare workforce. With distinguished faculty strength of 825 and a robust 
academic ecosystem comprising 56 teaching departments and centers, AIIMS currently hosts 
2,491 academic students, residents and scholars, along with 1,756 non-academic residents, 
making it a vibrant hub of medical education and research. 
 
5.3 Academic Programs and Courses Offered 
 
5.3.1 The institute offers an extensive array of academic programs designed to cater to the 
diverse needs of modern healthcare. These include undergraduate and postgraduate courses 
such as MBBS, MD, MS, DM, M.Ch, specialized fellowships and PhD programs. In addition, 
the institute offers Bachelor of Science programs in Nursing and Post-Basic Nursing, Master 
of Science degrees and several paramedical courses. The academic framework also embraces 
a significant cohort of research scholars, reflecting the emphasis of the institute on innovation 
and evidence-based learning. 
 
5.4 Curriculum Evolution and Competency-Based Learning 
 
5.4.1 Central to the educational mission of the Institute is the commitment to maintaining a 
curriculum that evolves with the dynamic landscape of Global Healthcare Standard. The 

 
22 
 
MBBS program is overseen by a dedicated Curriculum Upgradation Committee, which 
operates independently to review and revise the curriculum periodically. The Committee is 
task with the responsibilities to introduce competency-based modules, aligning educational 
content with national and international medical standards and ensuring responsiveness to 
educational trends and public health priorities.  
 
5.4.2 The postgraduate programs, including MD, MS, MDS, DM, M.Ch and fellowship 
courses, are regularly reviewed to keep them aligned with contemporary medical practices 
and emerging health priorities. The Academic Section plays a pivotal role in this process by 
periodically inviting departments to suggest updates or amendments to the curriculum. Once 
received, these proposals are carefully evaluated by the departments, drawing upon the latest 
research evidence, clinical advancements and national health needs. Each recommendation 
then undergoes rigorous peer review and academic scrutiny, ensuring that only the most 
relevant and evidence-based changes are adopted.  
 
5.5 Introduction of Specialized Courses 
 
5.5.1 The academic innovations introduced between 2015 and 2025 underscore the 
commitment of the Institute to pioneering specialized medical education. New DM courses 
introduced during this period include Critical Care Medicine, Cardiac Radiology and 
Endovascular Interventions, Infectious Disease, Therapeutic Nuclear Medicine, Onco-
Anesthesiology, Addiction Psychiatry, Pediatric Cardiology, Reproductive Medicine, Medical 
Genetics, Pediatric Nephrology and Pediatric Oncology. These courses are tailored to address 
contemporary healthcare challenges.  
 
5.5.2 The Committee sought to know the reasons for substantial number of vacancies of 
Seats at Senior resident/ junior resident/ Senior resident (DM/MCh)/ Junior 
resident(MD/MS/MDS) that remained unfilled during the last three years which must have 
affected the quality adversely affected the quality of service delivery to patients. Responding 
to that the AIIMS Management submitted in writing that Admission of academic residents 
(Junior Residents as well as Senior Residents) are done every 6 months. After admission 
process is over in any session (i.e. on 28th Feb/31 Aug for January & July sessions) any seats 
which remain vacant or any vacancies which arise because of resignation are filled in next 
session. It implies that vacancies which arise after 28th Feb/31 Aug (for January/July session 
respectively) are filled in next session i.e. within 6 months. When somebody has joined in a 
specialty at AIIMS which is not his/her first choice and he or she gets selected at some other 
place in the subject of his/her choice, then these residents resign to join at the new places. 
Junior Resident (Academic) and Senior Resident (DM/M.Ch) admission in various courses 
done twice a year.  Some of the residents join residency courses (MD/MS/MDS) in some 
non-clinical branches and prepare for PF entrance resign from MD/MS courses in non-
clinical branches to sit and prepare for entrance examination.  
 
5.5.3 For Senior Resident (DM/M.Ch) admission in various courses is done twice a year.  
Which is a position of 3 years duration and this position is joined by doctors after completing 
MD/MS/MDS in the respective specialty. In this position doctors get teaching and clinical 

 
23 
 
experience before they join as specialists/faculty in other/same institutions. While pursuing 
Senior Residency some of these residents keep on applying for faculty/consultants position 
and leave residency when they get a suitable position. Some Senior Residents leave to start 
their own practice or go abroad. Recruitment for Senior Resident are done every year twice 
by regular selection and special recruitment drives. Junior Resident is a tenure post for 6 
months. The fresh MBBS are eligible for these positions, MBBS doctors join these positions 
to learn clinical medicine in the subject of their choice before they are able to qualify in 
entrance examination and join PG course. Therefore, some of them who happen to get

5.5.4 Counseling/ Selection Process for all seats/posts which will be falling vacant due to 
completion of course/tenure or resignation etc. during January & July session are done 
accordingly.  In order to fill vacancies special recruitment drives and walk-in-Interviews are 
also held as and when required from time to time. 
 
5.5.5 The Committee observes that AIIMS, New Delhi has established itself as a 
premier institution of national importance, excelling in both healthcare delivery and 
medical education. The Committee appreciates the wide range of academic programs of 
UG and PG courses viz. MBBS, MD, MS, DM, M.Ch and periodic curriculum

new specialized medical education courses viz. Critical Care Medicine, Cardiac

address contemporary healthcare challenges and to nurture a cadre of highly skilled

5.5.7 The Committee is of the firm view that AIIMS will continue to shape the next

5.6 Ideal working hours of junior and senior residents 
 
5.6.1 Pertaining to the Committee’s query regarding the ideal vis-à-vis the actual status of 
the working hours and training programmes of the junior residents, senior residents and 
faculty of the Institute and the quantum of workload on the senior residents in the Institute, 
the Department inform the Committee that AIIMS, New Delhi strictly adhered to the 
Government of India Residency Scheme which is as under:– 
 
a. Working hours for Junior Resident: 
As per residency scheme, continuous active duty for resident doctors will not 
normally exceed 12 hours per day.  Subject to exigencies of work the resident 
doctors will be allowed on weekly holiday on call duty not exceeding 12 hours at a 
time.  The Junior Residents should ordinarily work for 48 hours per week and not 
more than 12 hours at a stretch subject to the condition that the working hours will 
be flexible as may decided by the Medical Superintendant concerned keeping in 
view of the workload and availability of doctors for clinical work. 
 
b. Working hours for Senior Resident: 
As per residency scheme, continuous active duty for resident doctors will not 
normally exceed 12 hours, Subject to exigencies of work, the resident doctors will 
be allowed on weekly holiday by rotation.  The resident doctors will also be 
required to be on call duty not exceeding 12 hours at a time. 
The Department informed the Committee that quantum of workload varies from 
department to department. 
 
5.6.2 The Committee understands heavy workload on the Senior Residents and the 
Junior Residents due to overall workload on AIIMS, New Delhi.  The Committee is 
please to note that normally the quantum of workload varies from department to 
department and is as per Government of India Residency Scheme.  Nevertheless, the 
Committee is of the considered view that the working hours for senior residence/junior 
residence should not exceed beyond 12 hours at a stretch to avoid fatigue syndrome 
among the senior/junior residence so that they can treat the patients with careful and 
cautious state of mind. 
 
5.6.3 The Committee is of the considered view that the patient should be treated in the 
first instance by the Sr. Residents supported by auxiliary staff to ensure the treatment in 
right direction.

to fill up the advertised seats for Senior Residents, Junior Residents and DM/M.Ch 
programmes despite conducting recruitments twice a year that indicates a growing 
challenge in attracting and retaining candidates, which directly impacts the availability 
of trained specialists. The Committee observes that a substantial number of posts, 
especially in the Senior Resident category and the Sponsored/Foreign National quotas, 
remain consistently vacant. Undoubtedly such shortfall adversely must have affecting 
both patient care and academic training, given the critical role residents doctors play in 
the Institute’s daily functioning. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that 
AIIMS, in consultation with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, undertake a 
comprehensive review of the Sponsored and Foreign National categories that remain 
consistently unfilled and consider reallocation of unfilled seats to the open category to 
ensure full utilization of capacity.

colleges, health institutions and international partners. The Committee is of the view 
that incentives such as financial benefits, structured career progression and enhanced 
research opportunities should be introduced to make Senior Residency more attractive.

administration must focus on aligning with the nation’s healthcare needs by identifying 
and prioritizing high-demand specialties. The existing practice of carrying forward 
unfilled seats to the next session should be made time-bound with provisions for re-
advertisement or reallocation to avoid prolonged vacancy. The Committee desires that a 
monitoring mechanism be institutionalized to review recruitment/admission outcomes 
session by session, identify the reasons for unfilled seats and take corrective measures 
promptly. The Committee believes that steps so undertaken will strengthen the 
Institute’s capacity to deliver both high-quality medical care and advanced training, 
thereby ensuring that its critical role in the national healthcare system is better 
delivered in time.

Medical Innovation and Entrepreneurship (CMIE)/BioNEST nurtures innovation by

6.9 Research Achievements and Impact of AIIMS New Delhi  
 
6.9.1 Over the five-year period from 2020 to 2025, AIIMS New Delhi has made substantial 
contributions to medical research and public health, emerging as one of the foremost centres 
for innovation in diagnostics, therapeutics and healthcare systems research. Supported by a 
wide range of national and international extramural grants, the Institute’s work has advanced 
critical areas including oncology, neurology, infectious diseases and digital health 
technologies. A major part of this period was defined by the COVID-19 pandemic, during 
which AIIMS played a central role in shaping India’s national response. Experts from the 
Institute were integral to government advisory bodies such as the National Task Force, where 
they contributed to the formulation of treatment protocols, testing strategies, clinical 
management guidelines and telemedicine policies. AIIMS also guided oxygen allocation 

 
32 
 
during the national crisis and participated in vaccine trials while contributing significantly to 
vaccine safety datasets. The Institute operated major vaccination centres that inoculated over 
five lakh beneficiaries, including healthcare workers and the general public. Through 
initiatives such as the AIIMS COVID Portal, dedicated helplines, media engagements and 
community outreach, the Institute undertook extensive public communication efforts aimed at 
addressing misinformation, providing mental health support and enhancing public awareness. 
 
6.9.2 Between 2022 and 2025, AIIMS researchers achieved several notable breakthroughs 
across clinical and translational research. Collaborative projects with Wadhwani AI led to the 
development of artificial intelligence–based screening tools for diabetic retinopathy, 
pulmonary tuberculosis and skin cancers. These Smartphone-enabled applications achieved 
diagnostic accuracies exceeding 90 percent, offering scalable, cost-effective solutions for 
early detection, particularly in low-resource environments. In 2024, researchers developed a 
blood-based biomarker test for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease, providing a 
significantly more affordable alternative to high-cost imaging techniques. In the same period, 
a new CAR-T cell therapy targeting the BCMA antigen was developed for the treatment of 
multiple myeloma, demonstrating promising preclinical outcomes in reducing tumour burden. 
Most recently, in 2025, the Institute introduced a diagnostic platform using transmission 
electron microscopy for rare genetic disorders such as Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, enabling 
more precise identification of ultra-structural ciliary defects and improving timely clinical 
intervention. 
 
6.9.3 The Committee notes the research contributions made by AIIMS New Delhi 
between 2020 and 2025, particularly in the areas of diagnostics, oncology, neurology, 
artificial intelligence and infectious disease management. While these achievements have 
strengthened India’s healthcare capacity, the Committee observes that sustained 
advancement in such high-impact research will require dedicated institutional support, 
enhanced infrastructure and structured collaborations. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that AIIMS New Delhi institutionalize a minimum of 20 percent protected 
time for faculty engaged in research, ensuring that clinical responsibilities do not 
impede scientific productivity. The Committee further recommends the establishment of 
Institute-wide innovation and incubation centres to promote translational research, 
foster start-ups and accelerate the development of technologies with public health 
relevance. 
 
6.9.4 The Committee observes that AIIMS, New Delhi has established a vibrant 
research ecosystem supported by substantial extramural and intramural funding, 
advanced facilities and strong national and international collaborations. The Committee 
recommends that the Institute’s research wing must make notable contributions to 
national health programs and policies. The Committee is of the considered view that 
AIIMS research, in addition to pure research must become part and parcel of doing the 
research having implications for the policy and advocacy of national healthcare 
priorities and plans.  
 
6.9.5 AIIMS has also made important contributions through the creation of standardised 
best-practice guidelines for research across diverse domains. Technical resource centres 

 
33 
 
established at the Institute have developed evidence-based frameworks to enhance 
methodological rigour, ethical compliance and reproducibility in basic science, as well as to 
support structured, high-quality clinical research. These research achievements have had a 
far-reaching impact on the Indian healthcare landscape. Advances in diagnostics have reduced 
dependence on expensive imaging modalities and significantly shortened diagnostic timelines 
for conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia, enabling wider 
access and timely care. Innovations in cancer treatment, particularly affordable CAR-T 
therapy, have expanded access to advanced care for low-income patients and improved 
survival outcomes in multiple myeloma. AI-driven diagnostic tools have substantially 
increased screening coverage in a country managing approximately 1.4 million new cancer 
cases annually. In the realm of infectious diseases, AIIMS’ contributions during the COVID-
19 pandemic accelerated vaccine deployment, strengthened variant surveillance and informed 
national policies that helped reduce mortality among high-risk populations. 
 
6.9.6 The Committee observes that the creation of standardised best practices 
guidelines for medical research across diverse domain in AIIMS have generated 
broader systemic benefits. The Committee believes that AI-led healthcare solutions 
would contribute to more efficient diagnostics nationwide, expanded telemedicine 
adoption and reduced disparities between urban and rural health system through 
proliferation of research outcome at peripheral ground level. Moreover, the growth of 
medical technology innovation linked to the modern and scientific advanced initiatives 
would produce additional economic and employment benefits in the healthcare sector. 
The Committee recommends for an outcome based analysis of the research outcomes by 
AIIMS. The Committee also recommends that AIIMS should actively collaborate with 
other Scientific Institutions like CSIR, DBT, IITs, ICMR etc to develop an integrated 
approach along with optimal utilisation of common facilities. 
 
6.9.7 Looking ahead, the Committee, however, recommends for further augment 
academic and research activities at AIIMS New Delhi that inter-alia include instituting 
protected research time, establishing innovation incubators across the Institute and 
expanding partnerships with private-sector and industry stakeholders through 
performance-linked research grants. The Committee understands that there is urgent 
need for further strengthening of research infrastructure, including the creation of AI-
enabled laboratories and recruitment of additional research-focused faculty. 
Additionally, deeper international collaborations through joint PhD programmes, long-
term research fellowships, student and faculty exchange initiatives are expected to 
enhance the Institute’s global engagement and research output. 
 
6.9.8 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that AIIMS strengthen its 
research infrastructure by setting up new laboratories equipped with artificial 
intelligence–enabled systems and by undertaking targeted recruitment of research-
focused faculty and technical personnel. The Committee is of the view that expanding 
international partnerships through joint doctoral programmes and exchange 
fellowships will enhance the Institute’s global engagement and contribute to capacity 
building.

6.10 Key Concern Areas and Opportunities of Research Wing 
 
6.10.1 The Research Wing at AIIMS New Delhi serves as the central coordinating body for 
fostering and managing biomedical research across all departments of the Institute. Its 
responsibilities span a wide range of functions that are essential for maintaining scientific 
quality and supporting the advancement of medical knowledge.  
 
6.10.2 Another major area of attention is the development of infrastructure and capacity 
building. This includes upgrading laboratory facilities, expanding the use of digital research 
platforms such as REDCap and strengthening training resources for faculty, residents and 
research staff. The Research Wing also prioritizes collaboration and networking, working to 
strengthen institutional ties with national and international research organizations to promote 
joint academic and scientific initiatives. 
 
6.10.3 Maintaining high standards of research quality and integrity is an overarching priority. 
The Wing actively promotes principles of reproducibility, methodological transparency and 
adherence to ethical standards in both basic and clinical research. Alongside this, improving 
digital data management, meta-analysis capabilities and systematic review methodologies has 
emerged as a critical need to support evidence-based practice and robust scientific output. The 
Wing also seeks to enhance the visibility of AIIMS research through increased publication in 
high-impact journals and strengthened dissemination mechanisms. 
6.10.4  To further strengthen the Research Wing and enhance the Institute’s overall 
research output, several measures have been identified. Encouraging multidisciplinary and 
cross-institutional research collaborations can broaden scientific perspectives and accelerate 
innovation. Leveraging artificial intelligence and big data analytics will support advances in 
predictive modelling, diagnostics, and personalized medicine. Regular training workshops in 
research methodology, ethics and publication strategies can improve the competence and 
confidence of early-career researchers. Streamlining grant application and approval processes 
through centralized digital platforms will reduce administrative burden and improve 
efficiency. 
 
6.10.5 In addition, promoting open access to global scientific literature, particularly through 
national initiatives such as One Nation One Subscription, can democratize knowledge and 
improve the quality of research. Strengthening partnerships with biotechnology and 
pharmaceutical industries will facilitate translational research and foster innovation in 
therapeutics and diagnostics.  
 
6.10.6 The Committee notes the wide-ranging responsibilities of the Research Wing at 
AIIMS New Delhi and the critical role it plays in managing research funding, ensuring 
regulatory compliance, maintaining research quality and supporting collaborative 
scientific work. While the Institute has made commendable progress, the Committee is 
of the view that further strengthening of the Research Wing is essential to enhance 
research productivity and promote innovation at par with global standards. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS New Delhi expand and institutionalize 
multidisciplinary and cross-institutional research programmes, particularly in emerging 
areas such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics and personalized medicine. The

7.3.2 The Committee was informed that 22 new AIIMS have been set up under the Pradhan 
Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojna in various States and are in different stages of operation, 
which will considerably help in easing the patient load in AIIMS, New Delhi. 
 
7.3.3 The Committee notes with concern the disproportionately high patient load at 
the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi leading to 
congestion/long waiting time for patients not just inside the hospital but wobbling 
queues outside too. The OPD data for the period January to December 2024 reveals that 
a significant proportion of patients hailed from neighbouring and distant States viz. 
Delhi (39.72%), UP (23.45%), Haryana (13.29%), Bihar (12.64%), Uttrakhand (3.45%) 
and remaining from other States.  The Committee observes that such overwhelming 
reliance on AIIMS, New Delhi indicates not only the pre-eminent status of the Institute 
but also the lack of comparable facilities in other parts of the country. Such excessive 
concentration of patients in one institution has led to overburdened facilities, longer 
waiting times and strains on both infrastructure and manpower, ultimately 
compromising the quality of patient care and academic training. 
 
7.3.4 Under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY), 22 new 
AIIMS, established in various States across the country are at different stages of 
operationalisation. The Committee understands that these institutions were envisioned 
precisely to reduce the patient load at AIIMS Delhi by providing high-quality tertiary 
care closer to the population in their respective regions. The Committee, in this 
connection, recommends that urgent steps be taken to strengthen the infrastructure, 
faculty, diagnostic facilities and overall patient care standards in all 22 new AIIMS so 
that the AIIMS like other Institutes  may emerge as credible and reliable alternatives to 
AIIMS, New Delhi. Additionally, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should 
ensure time-bound recruitment of faculty and non-faculty staff, expedite the 
commissioning of super-specialty departments and provide adequate budgetary support 
for state-of-the-art diagnostic and treatment facilities in such institutes. The Committee 
desires that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should furnish the details of 
updated status of the operations of these 22 AIIMS to enable the Committee to obtain a 
real picture and to assess the time by when the problem of overcrowding in AIIMS, 
Delhi will be resolved.  The Committee also recommends for setting up of AIIMS like 
institution in each state, including Karnataka, as patients from all over the country 
cannot make access for treatment of diseases from far flung areas.  The Committee 
further recommends for strengthening of all AIIMS like institutions in the states, like 
Telangana and Andhra Pradesh to be strengthened, as well equipped and manpowered 
as AIIMS, New Delhi to seek treatment of diseases at par to reduce the dependency of 
patients on AIIMS, New Delhi and thus reducing the overcrowding. 
 
7.3.5 The Committee further recommends that effective referral mechanisms be 
developed in coordination with other AIIMS like institutions in various States, so that 
patients requiring tertiary care can be guided towards the nearest functional AIIMS 
rather than converging disproportionately on AIIMS, New Delhi. Public awareness 
campaigns should also be undertaken to build confidence in the quality of services being 
provided at these new AIIMS in various States.

7.4 STEPS TO ADDRESS OVERCROWDING AND LONG WAITING TIME  
 
7.4.1 Upon enquiring about the measures taken to address overcrowding and long waiting 
time, the Committee was informed that the appointment system at AIIMS, New Delhi permits 
patients to book appointments with a maximum waiting period of one month for new cases 
and three months for follow-up consultations. It was further stated that, in order to reduce 
waiting time, the Institute has expanded its facilities through the commissioning of new 
specialty centres and blocks such as the National Cancer Institute, the Surgical Block, the 
New RAK OPD Block, the Mother & Child Block and the National Centre for Ageing. These 
additions, inter alia, had contributed to a substantial increase in the number of OPD 
consultations. 
 
7.4.2 The Committee took into consideration the action taken by AIIMS, New Delhi to 
reduce overcrowding and long waiting times through the new specialty centres, the 
Online Registration System (ORS) and token-based walk-ins. The Committee 
appreciates the introduction of online appointments through the Online Registration 
System (ORS) portal, along with a token system designed to regulate walk-in patients on 
a first-come, first-served basis. The distribution of OPD slots as 50 per cent allocated for 
online appointments, 30 per cent reserved for walk-ins and the remaining 20 per cent 
earmarked for cross-referrals is a rational approach. However, the Committee is of the 
view that despite these measures, the demand for services at AIIMS continues to exceed 
its capacity. The Committee therefore recommends that AIIMS, New Delhi further 
strengthen its digital appointment management system by making it mobile-friendly, 
multilingual and integrated with centralized electronic medical records, real-time 
updates, automated reminders and referral linkages with other AIIMS and regional 
institutions. These measures, along with physical patient-support mechanisms, would 
streamline patient flow, reduce unnecessary congestion from routine follow-ups and 
ensure equitable access. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare replicate the ORS and token-based model across all AIIMS 
and major central hospitals for greater efficiency and transparency nationwide. 
 
7.4.3 The Committee also recommends that a structured two-way referral system be 
established between AIIMS institutions and other medical colleges in order to ensure 
effective distribution of patients across healthcare facilities. The Committee is of the 
considered view that the adoption of a hub-and-spoke model, linking Primary Health 
Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), district hospitals, medical colleges 
and AIIMS institutions, would facilitate seamless integration of services across different 
levels of care. The Committee also strongly recommends that the Government should 
seriously consider setting up the ‘Hub and Spoke’ model to address the problem of 
overcrowding in the hospitals in metropolitan cities. Such a system would enable 
patients to be directed to the most appropriate facility based on the nature and severity 
of their medical needs, thereby enhancing efficiency, reducing overcrowding at apex 
centres and improving outcomes.  
 

 
47 
 
7.4.4 The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare, in consultation with AIIMS, explore the possibility of establishment of satellite 
centres of AIIMS around Delhi for all time given treatment and emergency, particularly 
in four part of Delhi viz. East Delhi, West Delhi, North Delhi and South Delhi and other 
suitable locations in the National Capital Region with just 100 to 150 bedded centres 
with estimated cost of Rs. 150 crore to Rs. 200 crore and search centres may be called as 
AIIMS Satellite Centre.   The Committee thinks once these satellite centres are tagged 
with AIIMS, there would be a lot of public acceptability.  Since in Delhi, the travel 
radius is almost 50-60 KM there is also the need to have cardiology, neurology and 
trauma centres of AIIMS, New Delhi in different parts of Delhi/NCR viz. Gurugram, 
Sonipat, Baghpat, Faridabad, Ghaziabad/Noida or at other suitable location because 
time is a crucial factor in the treatment of the heart attack, brain stroke and road 
accidents where the medical treatment is to be given within the golden hour.  Resident 
doctors may be posted on rotation basis in these centres, functioning as extensions of 
AIIMS, New Delhi, could provide outpatient consultations, diagnostics and follow-up 
care, thereby decongesting the main campus and ensuring easier access to patients 
residing in surrounding regions. Such decentralisation would not only improve patient 
convenience & timely treatment but also allow AIIMS, New Delhi to focus its core 
capacity on complex tertiary care, research and advanced training.
