4.1.7 The Committee notes that the National Health Mission (NHM) has played a 
pivotal role in strengthening India‘s public health system and advancing progress 
towards the targets set under the National Health Policy, 2017 and Sustain able 
Development Goal -3. Significant improvements have been recorded in several health 
indicators, including an increase in life expectancy to 70.3 years, reduction in Infant 
Mortality Rate to 25 per thousand, Maternal Mortality Ratio to 88 per lakh live b irths, 
and high levels of immunisation coverage and antenatal care. The Committee 
appreciates the progress made in elimination of diseases such as Kala -Azar and 
sustained control of leprosy, along with improved TB treatment coverage. However, the 
Committee observes that certain targets, such as further reduction in under -five 
mortality, neonatal mortality, and improvement in family planning coverage, still 
require sustained attention. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department 
strengthen targeted interventions under NHM, particularly in States and districts that 
continue to lag behind national averages, through enhanced monitoring, data -driven 
planning, and focused support under Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs). Greater 
emphasis may also be placed on preventive healthcare, early detection of diseases, and 
behavioural change communication to consolidate the gains already achieved and 
accelerate progress towards remaining health targets. 
 
4.1.8 The Committee observe s the steady expansion of ser vices under the National 
Urban Health Mission (NUHM), with a significant increase in the number of Urban 
Primary Health Centres, polyclinics, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, and healthcare 
personnel over the last three years, which has contributed to rising OPD a ttendance and 
improved service delivery in urban areas. While these developments indicate progress in 
strengthening urban health infrastructure, the Committee emphasises that rapid 
urbanisation, migration, and the growth of informal settlements continue to  place 
considerable pressure on urban public health systems. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Department should strengthen the NUHM framework by ensuring 
adequate human resources, improving urban health infrastructure, and enhancing 
coordination with Urban Local Bodies to effectively address the healthcare needs of 

162 
 
vulnerable populations, including urban poor and migrant workers. The Committee also 
suggests expanding community participation through Mahila Arogya Samitis and 
ASHAs, and strengtheni ng initiatives such as free diagnostics, free drug services, and 
mobile medical units to ensure equitable and accessible healthcare services in urban 
areas.

4.1.15 The Committee notes tha t the expenditure under the National Health Mission 
(NHM) for FY 2024 –25 exceeded the Revised Estimates, indicating strong demand for 
financial resources and the critical role of the Mission in supporting public health 
systems across the country. However, the Committee also observes that in FY 2025 –26, 
the utilisation of funds up to 31.01.2026 stands at about 72.41 per cent of the Revised 
Estimates, which appears relatively low considering that only two months remain in the 
financial year. The Committee is of the view that such variations between allocation, 
utilisation, and actual expenditure point towards issues relating to financial planning, 
timely release of funds, and absorption capacity at the State/UT level. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Department must strengthen monitoring and 
coordination mechanisms with States/UTs to ensure timely submission of Programme 
Implementation Plans (PIPs), faster approval of Record of Proceedings (RoPs), and 
more efficient utilisation of allocated funds. The Committee also desires that the 
Department put in place a robust system for periodic review of expenditure trends so 
that mid -year corrections can be undertaken to avoid both underutilisation and 
overshooting of allocations.

allocation. Given the expanding scope of services under the Ayushman Arogya Mandirs

underserved populations in both rural and urban areas.

4.2.8 On being asked about the response of the Department to the proposal of centralized 
system of drug regulatory system to prevent the manufacturing of spurious medicine and 
ensure production of quality drugs for treatment of various diseases, the Department stated 
that t he subject 'drugs' falls under the Concurrent List of the Constitution and under the 
present legislation, the powers of the Centre and states are  clearly demarcated. State Drugs 
Authorities regulate sale, distribution, and manufacture of drugs and Class A and B Medical 
Devices. CDSCO governs the import of all drugs, cosmetics and medical devices, approves 
new drugs in the country and high-risk medical devices. Further, Central regulator coordinates 
activities of State Drug Control Organisations and provides expert advice through the Drugs 
Consultative Committee (DCC) meetings held with State Drugs Controllers for uniformity in 
administration of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. This collaborative approach enables effective 
regulation and enforcement, leveraging both central and state expertise to ensure drug safety 
and quality in India. 
4.2.9 On a query related to the steps that are being taken to de -centralise CDSCO approvals 
to State Government regulators to serve in time and speed up the setting up of Medical 
Devices Industry, the Department stated that t he Medical Device Rules, 2017, categorize 

173 
 
medical devices into four classes (A, B, C, and D) based o n risk, with 'A' being low -risk and 
'D' being high-risk. The regulatory framework is as follows: 
4.2.10 Class A & B devices: Regulated by State Drugs Authorities while Class C & D 
devices are regulated by Central Drugs Authorities (CDSCO), while import of all medical 
devices is regulated by CDSCO.  
4.2.11 This risk -based approach ensures that CDSCO focuses on medium - to high -risk 
devices (C & D), leveraging its expertise and resources. The online portal (MD Online) 
facilitates transparent, predictable, and timely processing of applications, promoting

4.2.13 On a specific query related to functioning of Central Drugs Standard Control 
Organisation (CDSCO), the Department stated that a s per information obtained from CDAC, 
during the last financial year, total number of manufacturing and import applications 
processed for Class C and Class D Medical Device are 2999 and out of these in approx. 62 
percent of applications queries were raised more than twice. Further, out of 1677 import 
applications, 1060 applications belong to Class -C and Class D Medical Devices having 
USFDA/CE certificate. In this, 253 such applications are under process for more than 90 
days. Most of these applications are pending at the applicants end for submission of r equisite 
documents as per MDR-2017.  
 
4.2.14 The Committee notes with concern the significant administrative bottlenecks 
hindering the swift clearance of medical devices, particularly the Class C and Class D 
categories regulated by the Central Drugs Standa rd Control Organisation (CDSCO). 
The Committee observes that out of 2,999 manufacturing and import applications 
processed, approximately 62% were subjected to queries more than twice, and 253 
import applications, even those possessing USFDA/CE certificatio ns, have been pending 
for over 90 days. The Committee believes that such repetitive query cycles indicate a 
systemic lack of clarity in the initial submission guidelines and point toward an 
inefficient, iterative assessment process. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department immediately overhaul the 'MD Online' portal to include a mandatory, AI -
assisted pre-submission validation checklist to ensure applications are complete before 
formal submission. The Committee is of the view that CDSCO must  adopt a "single 
comprehensive query" policy, wherein all deficiencies in an application are identified 
and communicated to the applicant in a single instance, rather than in piece -meal 
fashion. The Committee, furthermore, recommends the establishment of a  dedicated 

174 
 
facilitation cell within CDSCO to assist domestic manufacturers in navigating the 
Medical Device Rules (MDR) 2017, thereby reducing the delays currently attributed to 
pending applicant responses. 
 
4.2.15 The Committee acknowledges the constituti onally mandated decentralized 
framework where State Authorities regulate drugs and Class A/B devices, while the 
Centre oversees imports and Class C/D devices. The Committee recommends for a 
decentralized framework for imports and Class  C/D devices . The Com mittee strongly 
recommends that CDSCO approval for imports be completely decentralized to the State 
Authorities. Centralization with the DGCI  at the Central level has created major 
bottlenecks and is the biggest hurdle in India being at the forefront of Me dical devices 
manufacturing. The Committee recommends for decentralization of approval for all 
Medical Devices with the State Drug Authorities to reduce pendency. In this current 
phase when we are competing with China, Vietnam, Malaysia giving CDSCO approv als 
for even already approved devices/ technologies beyond a period of 45 days in resulting 
in India losing its competitive edge.  
 
4.2.16 The Committee further observes that CDSCO has generated substantial revenue 
from medical device licensing, collecting  between ₹87.18 crore and ₹118.69 crore 
annually over the last three financial years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the revenue earned should be used for self -financing of the Institution. A designated 
percentage of the revenue collected by CDS CO be ring -fenced and directly reinvested 
into upgrading the digital and technical infrastructure of both the Central and State 
regulatory bodies. The Committee is of the view that the Department must utilize these 
funds to develop a unified, real -time Nat ional Regulatory Dashboard that seamlessly 
integrates CDSCO‘s 'MD Online' portal with State -level licensing databases. This will 
ensure that intelligence regarding non -compliant manufacturers, suspended licenses, 
and spurious drug trails is instantly share d across jurisdictions, leveraging both central 
and state expertise to guarantee uniform enforcement of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 
nationwide. 
 
4.2.17 In respect of Drugs Inspector (Regulatory), the Committee has been informed that due 
to a court case reg arding the experience, the post of Drugs Inspector could not be filled. The 
Recruitment Rules (RRs) have been revised and notified on 11.11.2025. Subsequently, a 
proposal for filling up 186 vacant posts of Drugs Inspector (Regulatory) has been forwarded 
to UPSC for initiating recruitment. Further, in respect of Drugs Inspector (Medical Devices), 
the Committee has been informed that RRs of the post of DI (Medical Devices) was notified 
on 06.11.2024. Subsequently, a proposal for recruitment of 20 posts of Dru gs Inspector 
(Medical Devices) was also sent to UPSC. The UPSC conducted the examination on 
02.11.2025, however, final list of selected candidates is still awaited from UPSC. 
Furthermore, in respect of Addl. DC (I), JDC (I) and DDC (I) in Medical Devices V ertical, an 
advertisement was published to fill up these posts through Deputation basis. Some, applicants 
were received and the same are under examination. Moreover, a requisition for filling up the 
22 posts of ADC (I), Medical Devices has already been sub mitted to UPSC. Recognizing the 
complexity of high -tech medical devices, the Ministry has strategically recruited Drug 
Inspectors (Medical Devices) with dedicated Engineering backgrounds (such as Biomedical, 

175 
 
Mechanical, and Electronics). Further to bridge the knowledge gap, the department deputes 
the officers from time to time for specialized training programs tailored for technical devices. 
4.2.18 The Committee finds significant vacancy position in the regulatory workforce 
under the Drugs and Medical Devic es verticals, particularly at the level of Drugs 
Inspectors and Assistant Drugs Inspectors. While the sanctioned strength under the 
Drugs Vertical stands at 613 posts, as many as 257 posts remain vacant, including 186 
vacancies of Drugs Inspectors. In the Medical Devices Vertical, only 24 personnel are in 
position against a sanctioned strength of 249 posts. The Committee notes that delays in 
recruitment were partly due to litigation and pending revision of Recruitment Rules, 
and that proposals for filling a  number of posts have now been forwarded to the Union 
Public Service Commission. The Committee is of the view that such a large number of 
vacancies could adversely affect regulatory efficiency, quality surveillance and 
enforcement activities. The Committee , therefore, recommends that the Department 
take urgent and time -bound measures, in coordination with the Union Public Service 
Commission, to expedite the recruitment process and fill the vacant posts. The 
Committee also urges the Department to review the overall human resource framework 
of the regulatory system and consider strengthening technical capacity through 
specialised recruitment, structured training programmes and career progression 
mechanisms so that the regulatory apparatus keeps pace with the r apid growth and 
technological advancement of the pharmaceutical and medical devices sectors in the 
country.

4.3.8 The Committee notes that the T ertiary Care Programmes under the National 
Health framework support a number of critical public health initiatives such as the 
National Mental Health Programme, National Programme for Prevention and Control 
of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke, Trauma Care, Health Care 
for the Elderly, Telemedicine and Tobacco Control. The Committee , however, observes 
a recurring pattern of reduction in allocations at the Revised Estimates stage however 
partial utilisation of funds across several componen ts. In 2024 –25, the actual 
expenditure of ₹287.72 crore fell short of the Revised Estimates of ₹322.90 crore, and in 
2025–26, only ₹167.10 crore (about 57 per cent of the reduced RE) had been utilised up 
to 17.02.2026. The Committee observes with serious c oncern that the shortfall is largely 
attributed to delays at the State level in fulfilling procedural requirements such as 
utilisation of earlier instalments, creation of Single Nodal Accounts, submission of 
utilisation certificates, and compliance with fi nancial reporting norms. The Committee 
is of the view that these procedural and administrative constraints are adversely 
affecting the timely implementation of important tertiary healthcare programmes. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Departme nt strengthen coordination and 
capacity-building mechanisms with States/UTs to ensure timely compliance with 
financial procedures, faster on boarding of institutions under the SNA -SPARSH system, 
and prompt submission of utilisation certificates and procure ment proposals so that the 
allocated funds are effectively utilised for strengthening tertiary healthcare services. 
 
4.3.9 The Committee expresses dissatisfaction to find that several critical components 
such as the National Mental Health Programme and the  National Programme for 
Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke have 
witnessed substantial reductions in allocations at the Revised Estimates stage due to 
delays in project proposals, procurement processes and institu tional readiness. 
Considering the rising burden of non -communicable diseases, mental health issues and 
trauma-related cases in the country, the Committee is of the view that sustained and 
predictable funding for these programmes is essential for strengthen ing specialised 
healthcare services. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should 
adopt a more proactive planning and monitoring framework to ensure timely 
submission of proposals by States/UTs, expeditious approval of projects, and impr oved 

178 
 
utilisation of funds under these programmes. The Committee also desires that special 
attention be given to expanding telemedicine infrastructure, strengthening trauma and 
emergency care facilities, and enhancing institutional capacities for cancer and  mental 
health care so that tertiary healthcare services become more accessible and responsive to 
the growing healthcare needs of the population.

Under the revised SNA -SPARSH system, the Central s hare is released directly to the State 
Government‘s SNA account maintained in the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Conditions for 
release of funds: 
a) State/UT must sign MoU with Ministry of Health & Family Welfare committing land 
provision, faculty appointment, recurring expenses and state share for infrastructure 
and operations.  
b) Central assistance shared with States 90:10 for North Eastern and Special Category 
States and 60:40 for other states. 
c) Funds are released in instalments tied to release of state share, p rogress of 
construction, equipment, and submission of Utilization Certificates. 
4.4.6 The Committee understand s that the Human Resource for Health and Medical 
Education (HRH & ME) scheme plays a crucial role in addressing the shortage of 
medical professionals and reducing regional imbalances in access to medical education 
and healthcare services. The Committee points out that although substantial allocations 
have been made under the Head, there has been a significant reduction at the Revised 
Estimates stage. A Budget Estimate of ₹1,274.79 crore was provided in 2024 –25, which 
was reduced to ₹579.12 crore at the Revised Estimates stage (indicating substantial 
reduction at RE stage). Against this, the actual expenditure during the year amounted to 
₹549.33 crore. For the year 2025 –26, an amount of ₹1,675.00 crore was provided at the 
Budget Estimates stage and revised to ₹1,630.00 crore at the Revised Estimates stage, 
against which an expenditure of ₹779.48 crore had been incurred up to 31.01.2026 
(which is about 48% of reduced RE allocation). 
 
4.4.7 The Committee finds that under the scheme, a total of 157 new medical colleges 
have been approved but out of that 137 Medical College s are functional, with expansion 
of MBBS seats in existing institutions, and the creatio n of postgraduate medical seats 
across the country. While appreciating the initiatives, the Committee is of the view that 
timely completion and operationalisation of approved institutions are essential for 
translating financial allocations into tangible im provements in healthcare manpower. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department strengthen monitoring and 
coordination with States/UTs to ensure timely submission of DPRs, completion of 
infrastructure projects, recruitment of faculty and adhere nce to funding conditions 
under the SNA -SPARSH framework so that the approved medical colleges and 
expanded seats become fully functional within the stipulated timelines.  There is need to 

185 
 
strengthen infrastructure in medical college and maintain quality of  Medical education 
to produce professionals of global quality instead of below -average mass production of 
bunch of incompetent medical professionals who will definitely prove threat to human 
life and safety due to lack of clinical exposure and quality education.  
 
4.4.8 The Committee further notes that under the scheme for augmenting nursing 
education, the construction of six Colleges of Nursing in Rajasthan has been completed 
but none of them had commenced operations during the academic year 2025 –26. 
Considering the critical shortage of trained nursing professionals in the healthcare 
system, the Committee is of the view that such delays undermine the objective of 
strengthening the health workforce. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department wo rk closely with the concerned State Government to ensure early 
operationalisation of the completed Colleges of Nursing and to expedite similar projects 
across other States. The Committee also urges the Department to adopt a 
comprehensive approach towards s trengthening the entire healthcare workforce by 
simultaneously expanding medical, nursing and allied health education capacities, 
particularly in underserved regions, so that the growing demand for skilled health 
professionals in the country can be effectively met. 
 
4.4.9 The Committee strongly recommends for adoption of nearby Primary Health 
Care (PHC), CHC and sub centers hospitals by medical colleges both government and 
private can significantly strengthen healthcare delivery at the grassroots level. It can 
improve the availability of doctors and ensure a steady presence of interns, postgraduate 
trainees, and other healthcare personnel. This additional manpower can enhance service 
delivery, support preventive and promotive health activities, and improve c ontinuity of 
care. Such collaboration would particularly benefit maternal and child health services 
by ensuring better antenatal care, safe deliveries, immunization coverage, and early 
identification and management of high -risk cases, while also providing valuable 
community-based training opportunities for medical students. 
 
4.5 PRADHAN MANTRI AYUSHMAN BHARAT HEALTH INFRASTRUCTURE 
MISSION (PM-ABHIM) 
4.5.1 The PM-Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM -ABHIM) was launched 
on 25th October, 2021 with an outlay of Rs.64,180 Cr to be implemented over five years from 
2021-22 to 2025-26, with the aim to strengthen the public health infrastructure to fill critical 
gaps in health infrastructure, surveillance and health research - spanning both the urban and  
rural areas. The objectives of the scheme are as follows: 
i. To develop capacities of health systems and institutions across the continuum of 
care at all levels viz. primary, secondary and tertiary. 
ii. To strengthen grass root public health institutions to deli ver universal 
comprehensive primary health care and governance capacities for comprehensive 
diagnostic and treatment including for critical care services.  

186 
 
iii. To expand and build an IT enabled disease surveillance system by developing a 
network of surveillanc e laboratories for effectively detecting, investigating, 
preventing and combating Public Health Emergencies and Disease Outbreaks. 
 
4.5.2 PM-ABHIM is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with Central Sector Components. The 
envisaged targets under the CSS component s (including XV -FC share) of the scheme 
includes: 
i. Infrastructure Support for 17,788 Rural building -less Sub Health Centers -Health 
and Wellness Centers, now renamed as Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM). 
ii. Establishment of 11,024 Urban Health and Wellness Centers ( Ayushman Arogya 
Mandir) in all the States with a focus on slum and slum like areas. 
iii. Establishment of 3382 Block Public Health Units at block levels. 
iv. Setting up of 730 Integrated Public Health Labs in all districts across the Country. 
v. Establishment of 602 Critical Care Blocks in all the districts with population more 
than 5 lakhs and referral linkages in other districts.  
 
4.5.3 The Committee notes that the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health 
Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) was launched with a substantia l outlay of ₹64,180 
crore for the period 2021 –22 to 2025 –26 with the objective of strengthening public 
health infrastructure across primary, secondary and tertiary levels of care. The Mission 
envisages a wide range of infrastructure interventions including  construction of 
building-less Sub -Health Centres as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, establishment of 
Urban Health and Wellness Centres, Block Public Health Units, Integrated Public 
Health Laboratories and Critical Care Hospital Blocks across districts. While 
appreciating the comprehensive design of the Mission aimed at strengthening health 
systems, surveillance networks and emergency preparedness, the Committee is of the 
view that the success of such a large -scale initiative depends on timely completion of 
infrastructure, operationalisation of facilities and adequate human resources and 
equipment support. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
strengthen coordination and monitoring mechanisms with States/UTs to ensure timely 
completion of sanctio ned infrastructure, adherence to project timelines and optimal 
utilisation of funds so that the envisaged public health facilities become fully functional 
at the earliest to facilitate healthcare of the global standard. 

187

Estimate of ₹3,200.00 crore was provided in 2024 –25, which was revised to ₹3,000.00 crore 
at the Revised Estimates stage. Against this, the actual expenditure during the year amounted 
to ₹2,086.34 crore (just about 70% of the already reduced RE). For the year 2025 –26, an 
amount of ₹4,200.00 crore was provided at the Budget Estimates stage and revised to 
₹2,442.50 crore (reduced to about 58% of the allocated BE) at the Revised Estimates stage, 
against which an expendi ture of ₹1,444.52 crore (about 59% of the reduced RE) had been 
incurred up to 31.01.2026. For 2026–27, an allocation of ₹4,200.00 crore has been proposed.

construction of new facilities, upgradation of existing institutions, procurement of 
equipment, and establishment of public health units across States/UTs. Such activities 
inherently entail gestation periods, including preparation of Detailed Project Reports 
(DPRs), obtaining technical approvals, ensuring land availability, completing 
tendering processes, and complying with State -specific procedur al requirements. 
These factors collectively influence the pace of expenditure. 
 
b) The scheme experienced a relatively slow pace of expenditure during the initial years 
of implementation due to systemic and operational challenges. The SNA -SPARSH

4.5.6 On being asked for the reasons for reduction of budget from ₹ 4,200 crore (BE) to ₹ 
2,442.50 crore (RE) in 2025-26, the Department stated that:  
a) PM-ABHIM is a capital -intensive infrastructure scheme involving construction, 
renovation, procurement of equipment, and establishment of facilities across 
States/UTs. Such activities are subject to procedural requirements, tendering timelines, 
site readiness, and State -specific implementation capacities, which can lead to 
variations between projected and actual expenditure within a financial year.  
b) In addition, during the year, all 31 States/UTs were onboarded onto the SNA SPARSH 
platform under PM -ABHIM. The transition to the SNA SPARSH system —including 
opening of Single Nodal Accounts, mapping of implementing agencies, and alignment 
of financial reporting processes initiall y moderated the pace of fund releases and 
expenditure.  
c) Further, funds under PM -ABHIM are released to States/UTs on a lump -sum basis, 
based on approved proposals and fulfilment of requisite conditions. Consequently, 
actual expenditure in a given year depen ds on the pace at which States/UTs utilize 
previously released funds and meet conditions for subsequent releases, which may not 
always align evenly with annual budget estimates. 
d) The adjustment was not attributable to any single component alone. Variations were 
observed across multiple infrastructure components including Urban Health & 
Wellness Centres, Block Public Health Units, Integrated Public Health Laboratories, 
and Critical Care Hospital Blocks, depending on the stage of tendering, construction 
progress, and procurement processes in different States/UTs. The reduction reflects 
timing and implementation related factors rather than any curtailment of the approved 
scope or objectives of the scheme. 

189 
 
4.5.7 The Committee is displeased to observe the persiste nt and drastic under -
utilization of funds under the PM -ABHIM scheme, evidenced by the severe reduction of 
the 2025–26 Budget Estimate from ₹4,200.00 crore to a Revised Estimate of ₹2,442.50 
crore, of which only 59% had been utilized by January 2026. The Co mmittee believes 
that while the onboarding of all 31 States and UTs onto the SNA -SPARSH platform is a 
necessary financial reform for transparency, but such transition should not become a 
perennial bottleneck that stalls the rollout of critical health infra structure. The 
Committee, therefore, desires that the Department should immediately deploy dedicated 
Task Forces. These task forces must move beyond basic capacity building and actively 
assist state treasuries in mapping implementing agencies, reconciling unspent balances, 
and expediting the fulfillment of conditions required for subsequent lump -sum releases. 
The Committee is of the view that until the SNA -SPARSH system is fully stabilized, the 
Department should conditionally ease procedural rigidities to e nsure that fund flows for 
life-saving infrastructure are not artificially constricted. 
4.5.8 The Committee observes that the fundamental delays in executing PM -ABHIM 
are consistently attributed to the gestation periods inherent in capital -intensive projects, 
including the preparation of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), land acquisition, and 
state-specific tendering processes across various components like Integrated Public 
Health Laboratories (IPHLs) and Critical Care Hospital Blocks (CCHBs). The 
Committee believes that leaving States entirely to their own administrative capacities to 
navigate these complex pre -construction phases inevitably leads to the highly uneven 
physical and financial progress currently observed. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends th at the Department establish a centralized 'Infrastructure Project 
Management Unit' (IPMU) strictly dedicated to PM -ABHIM. This unit should provide 
States with pre -approved, standardized DPR templates, centralized architectural 
blueprints, and model tenderi ng documents to bypass local bureaucratic inertia. 
Furthermore, the Committee is of the view that future fund releases must be linked to 
centrally monitored timelines for land allotment and human resource recruitment, 
ensuring that once physical infrastruc ture is erected, it does not lie dormant due to a 
lack of specialized medical personnel. 
4.5.9 On a query regarding the allocation of ₹4,200 crore at the BE stage for 2026 –27 under 
the scheme, despite the PM -ABHIM being originally envisaged for implementation over a 
five-year period from 2021–22 to 2025–26, the Department stated that: 
a) PM-ABHIM is  a capital -intensive infrastructure initiative aimed at strengthening 
public health facilities up to the block level. Given the nature of construction, 
procurement, and upgradation activities, the scheme entails inherent gestation periods, 
which resulted i n relatively lower expenditure during the initial years of 
implementation. As the scheme has now reached at an advanced stage, with a 
substantial number of projects under execution and nearing completion, expenditure is 
expected to accelerate in line with implementation progress.  
b) The allocation of Rs. 4,200 crore in BE 2026 -27 has been made keeping in view the 
scheme‘s committed liabilities, and the anticipated scale -up and completion of 

190 
 
ongoing projects, rather than past expenditure trends alone. The prov ision is intended 
to ensure continuity of works already approved and to meet financial requirements 
arising from physical progress on the ground. Further, EFC document for extension of 
the scheme has been circulated & proposal is under consideration. 
c) The Ministry continuously reviews State/UT-wise physical and financial progress, the 
pipeline of approved projects, utilization patterns, and implementation readiness 
through regular review meetings and Common Review Missions. Budgetary 
projections are aligned with realistic absorptive capacity and the requirement to 
complete approved deliverables within the approved framework of the scheme.

4.5.11 The Committee is displeased to find the stark disparity between the initiation of

Public Health Laboratories (IPHLs) and Block Public Health Units (BPHUs) languish at

Committee believes that the ultimate metric of a healthcare scheme's success is not 
merely the progression of civil works, but the actual delivery of accessible services to the 
public. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department immediately pivot 
its primary monitoring focus from 'work started' milestones to 'functional status' 
outcomes. This must be achieved by strictly synchronizing the procurement of essential 
medical equipment and the recruitment of specialized human resources with the 
ongoing civil construction timelines. The Committee is of the view that the national 
Program Management Unit must mandate that states initiate hiring and procurement 
processes well before the physical completion of the buildings, ensuring that newly 
constructed facilities do not sit idle due to administrative delays.

intensive schemes involve inherent gestation periods, however projecting estimates 
should calculate the ground -level executio n capacity , otherwise vagabo nd budgeting 
with distorts broader financial planning. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department formulate realistic, milestone -based budgetary demand intricately tied 
to the actual absorptive capacity of implementing agencies of States and UTs.  
 
4.6 AYUSHMAN BHARAT -PRADHAN MANTRI JAN AROGYA YOJANA (AB -
PMJAY) 
 
4.6.1 Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri – Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM -JAY) is the world‘s 
largest health assurance scheme that intends to reduce the out -of-pocket expenditure arising 
due to catastrophic expenditure on healthcare. AB PM-JAY was launched on 23rd September, 
2018 as recommended by the National Health Policy 2017, to achieve the SDGs vision of 
Universal Health Coverage (UHC), subsuming the erstwhile Ras htriya Swasthya Bima 
Yojana (RSBY). The scheme provides health cover of ₹ 5 lakhs per family per year for 
secondary and tertiary care hospitalization to bottom 40% of the India‘s poor and vulnerable 
population.  

192 
 
 
4.6.2 Initially, 10.74 crore eligible households were identified under the scheme from SECC 
2011 based on certain deprivation and occupational criteria in rural and urban areas 
respectively. Further, in January 2022, the Cabinet to the Government of India revised the 
beneficiary based to 12 crore f amilies, considering the decadal population growth rate of 
11.7% and gave the flexibility to States/UTs to use other State scheme databases.  
 
4.6.3 In March 2024, 37 lakh families of Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), 
Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) and  Anganwadi Helpers (AWHs) were also included in the 
scheme. Further, on 29th October 2024, the Government has expanded AB PM -JAY to 
provide free treatment benefits of up to ₹5 lakh per year to all senior citizens aged 70 years 
and above along with their families, irrespective of their socio-economic status. 
 
Salient Features of AB PM-JAY  
a) Health Cover of ₹5 Lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care 
b) Completely paperless and cashless services  
c) No cap on family size, age or gender to ensure that  all members of the beneficiary 
families are covered.  
d) Provides healthcare services across 27 specialties covering 1961 procedures.   
e) Includes 3 days of pre-hospitalisation and 15 days of post-hospitalisation expenses.  
f) All pre–existing conditions are covered from day one. 
g) The benefits under the scheme are portable across the country i.e., benefits can be 
availed at any Empanelled Healthcare Providers across the Country 
h) 35 States/UTs are currently implementing Ayushman Bharat PM -JAY except West 
Bengal.

4.6.7 On being asked for the reasons of increasing allocation ₹ 9,500 crore in BE 2026 -27, 
the Department stated that u nder AB PMJA Y, the budget requirement is estimated based on 
the number of eligible beneficiary families and fixed annual premium of ₹1,052 per family 
per year. As the AB PMJAY is a Centrally Sponsore d Scheme, the cost is shared between the 
Centre and the States. Accordingly, the budget for the core AB PMJAY beneficiary family 
base for 12 crore families remains a committed and largely fixed liability. Further, in FY 
2024-25, coverage under AB PM -JAY wa s expanded to include approximately 37 lakh 
families of ASHA, AWW and AWH workers, as well as about 4.5 crore senior citizen 
families aged 70 years and above.  
4.6.8 During FY 2025–26, a total central share of ₹ 7,093.51 crore has been released so far

during FY 2025-26. However, several States/UTs have not yet raised demands for the central  
share under Ayushman Vay Vandana and ASHA/AWW/AWH category due to various 
implementation related challenges.  It is expected that the pending demands for FY 2025 –26, 
along with the regular demands for FY 2026 –27, will be raised in the subsequent financial 
year. Further, the expansion of beneficiary groups under Ayushman Vay Vandana and 
ASHA/AWW/AWH has led to an increase in Ayushman Card creation, hospital admissions, 
and claims submission. In view of this rising utilisation and expanded beneficiary base, 
demands from States/UTs are expected to increase in FY 2026 –27, and th erefore the 
enhanced Budget Estimate of ₹ 9,500 crore is expected to be fully utilised.

utilization in FY 2024-25.

5.4 FOOD SAFETY AND STANDARDS AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
5.4.1 On a query on the issue that ch ronic kidney diseases are increasing due to misuse of 
preservatives in packaged food and action taken by FSSAI in this regard, the Department 
stated that FSSAI is taking the following measures to address the issues raised: 
 
a) FSSAI has limited the presence of additives (including preservatives) in food 
products by notifying the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and 
Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 which are in harmonization with global 
standards like Codex.  
b) Additives permitted in various food categories along with their usage limi ts are 
prescribed in the Appendix A of the above -mentioned regulations. Risk assessment 
is carried out at international level by bodies like Joint FAO Expert Committee on 
Food Additives (JECFA) and European Food Safety Authority (EFSA).  Additives 
are permitted in food by FSSAI only when risk assessments establish the safety of 
the additives.  
c) FSSAI through State/ UTs and its regional offices has stepped up enforcement that is 
primarily done through the state government and conduct regular surveillance, 

211 
 
monitoring, inspection and random sampling of food products to check compliance of 
the standards laid down under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, Rules and 
Regulations made thereunder. 
d) Annual mandatory inspections and Third -Party Audits are mandatory for FBOs 
dealing in high-risk product categories. 
5.4.2 The Committee recommends that the Department, through FSSAI, intensify 
efforts to curb the misuse of preservatives in packaged food, given the rising incidence of 
chronic kidney diseases. While regulatory  limits on additives are already harmonised 
with Codex standards and enforcement mechanisms such as surveillance, random 
sampling, and third -party audits are in place, the Committee urges the Department to 
strengthen risk -based monitoring and targeted enfo rcement drives for high -risk food 
categories. Additionally, the Committee recommends enhancing public awareness 
campaigns on the health risks of excessive preservative consumption, coupled with 
stricter penalties for non-compliance by Food Business Operators. 
5.5 REGULATION OF QUACKS PRACTICING MEDICINE 
 
5.5.1 On a query to control the rising number of quacks practicing medicine, particularly in 
North India,  the Department submitted that t he Clinical Establishments (Registration and 
Regulation) Act, 2010 (C EA, 2010) provides for mandatory registration and regulation of all 
clinical establishments, including private hospitals, clinics and diagnostic centres, in the 
States and Union Territories which have adopted the Act. Under the Act, no person can run a 
clinical establishment without valid registration, and only qualified and duly registered 
medical practitioners are permitted to practice. The Act empowers the State/UT Governments 
to enforce compliance through designated authorities. At the district level, t he District 
Collector/District Magistrate, who functions as the District Registering Authority (DRA) 
under the Act in many States/UTs, is responsible for monitoring implementation, ensuring 
registration of establishments, conducting inspections, and initia ting action against 
unregistered or illegally operating entities including quacks.  
 
5.5.2 The Committee is of considered view that the Department must strengthen 
enforcement against quack practitioners by ensuring strict implementation of the 
Clinical Establishments Act, 2010 in States and Union Territories, particularly in North 
India where the problem is acute. The Committee recommends the Department to 
institute regular inspections, coordinated drives, and public reporting mechanisms to 
identify and pen alize unauthorized practitioners. Further, the Committee recommends 
enhancing coordination between State Medical Councils, District Authorities, and law 
enforcement agencies to ensure that only duly qualified and registered medical 
professionals are permitted to practice.  
 
5.6 STRENGTHENING PREVENTIVE CARE 
 
5.6.1 On the issue of strengthening preventive public health systems to manage seasonal 
outbreaks like malaria, especially in high -risk urban areas, the Department submitted that in 
2015, a total of 155 districts were High Burden Districts with Annual Parasite Incidence (API: 

212 
 
cases per 1000 population per year) of more than 1, which declined to 32 in 2025. National 
Malaria Elimination Programme under National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control 
focuses on  strengthening of surveillance, early diagnosis & complete treatment, Integrated 
Vector Management and IEC/BCC activities, across the country including the high burden 
districts.  In urban areas, inter -sectoral convergence and involvement of Municipa lity is 
ensured for effective control of Malaria.  Malaria transmission intensifies during the monsoon 
season, which creates favourable conditions for vector breeding. Awareness campaigns are 
organized on World Malaria Day (25 th April) to strengthen IEC/BC C activities and review 
preparedness for the upcoming transmission season. Additionally, Anti -Malaria Month is 
observed in June to sustain the momentum of awareness campaigns and reinforce preventive 
and control measures during the peak transmission period. 
 
5.6.2 The Committee is of the firm view that the Department must strengthen 
preventive public health systems to proactively manage seasonal outbreaks of diseases 
like malaria, particularly in high -risk urban areas and undertake immediate measure s 
to contain and eliminate the outbreak then and there. The Committee, therefore , urges 
the Department to institutionalise year -round surveillance, rapid diagnostic capacity, 
and integrated vector management with special focus on urban slums and densely 
populated areas. Further, the Committee recommends scaling up community awareness 
drives beyond seasonal observances, ensuring sustained behavioural change in 
sanitation and mosquito-control practices.  
5.6.3 On a query regarding efforts taken for immunization for m igrants, the Department 
stated that the MoHFW has taken several steps for nationwide scaling up of the Universal 
Immunization Programme for beneficiaries including the migrant community. The Universal 
Immunization Programme is an equitable vaccination prog ram for all categories of the 
population irrespective of socio -economic status, providing 11 vaccines for 12 vaccine 
preventable diseases, free of cost to all eligible beneficiaries. The sessions sites are held in 
fixed health facilities like in the primary health centre, sub health centre and outreach sessions 
in areas such as urban slums, remote areas, migrant settlements etc. Various outreach 
programs are held at the migrant habitations like brick kilns, agricultural farms, construction 
sites and VHSND in villages for providing routine immunization to migrant beneficiaries.  
5.6.4 The Universal Immunization Program is supported by a single digital platform UWIN, 
which is a national repository of immunization services on a single digital platform, replacin g 
paper formats with digitized records, recording all vaccination events of eligible beneficiaries, 
including migrants and can be accessed anywhere in India, ensuring continuity of the 
vaccination schedule (due doses) where the migrant families have relocated.  
5.6.5 The Committee recommends that the Department intensify efforts to ensure 
equitable immunization coverage for migrant populations, who often face 
mobility-related barriers in accessing routine services. While the Universal 
Immunization Programme  already provides free vaccines nationwide, the Committee 
urges the Department to strengthen micro -planning, targeted outreach at high -density 
migrant habitations, and real -time tracking through the U -WIN digital platform. The 

213 
 
Committee also recommends enh ancing inter -state coordination and portability of 
immunization records, so that migrant families can seamlessly continue vaccination 
schedules after relocation.  
5.6.6 On being asked about the STEMI -based Heart Attack Management Programme under 
NHM and an y plan to introduce a similar structured programme for stroke management, the 
Department stated that STEMI -based heart attack management is implemented under  the 
CVD component of NP -NCD through a hub -and-spoke model to ensure timely diagnosis, 
stabilization and referral of acute cardiac emergencies. The programme supports 
strengthening of infrastructure including operationalisation of Cardiac Care Units (CCUs) at 
District Hospitals and strengthening of referral linkages with higher centres. Peripheral 
facilities such as PHCs, CHCs and Sub -District Hospitals are equipped for early recognition 
through ECG, initial stabilization and thrombolysis (where indicated), followed by referral to 
designated hubs such as District Hospitals and Medical Colleges with advan ced cardiac care 
facilities.  
5.6.7 Stroke is covered under the CVD component of NP -NCD through a comprehensive 
approach encompassing prevention, early detection, acute management and long -term care. 
The programme provides population -based screening of ind ividuals aged 30 years and above 
for hypertension and diabetes at Ayushman Bharat – Health and Wellness Centres to reduce 
stroke risk, along with IEC activities promoting tobacco cessation, salt reduction, healthy diet, 
physical activity and control of blo od pressure and blood sugar. Stroke care is delivered 
through a hub -and-spoke model wherein PHCs, CHCs and District Hospitals ensure early 
recognition, stabilization, CT-based diagnosis and thrombolysis (where available), and timely 
referral, while Medical  Colleges and tertiary centres provide advanced diagnostics including 
24×7 CT/MRI facilities, mechanical thrombectomy (where available), dedicated stroke units, 
multidisciplinary management and comprehensive rehabilitation services. Follow-up of stroke 
patients for secondary prevention and long-term risk factor control is undertaken through NP -
NCD clinics.  
5.6.8 The Committee emphasizes that the Department must strengthen nationwide 
implementation of the STEMI -based Heart Attack Management Programme under 
NHM while ensuring uniform standards of care across States through the 
hub-and-spoke model. The Committee further urges the Department to develop a 
structured, nationwide stroke management programme on similar lines, with dedicated 
stroke units, 24×7 imagi ng facilities, and referral linkages for advanced interventions, 
and the setting up of Mobile Stroke Units at District Hospitals to ensure timely diagnosis 
and treatment in underserved areas. This dual approach, consolidating STEMI care and 
institutionalising structured stroke management, will enhance early diagnosis, timely 
stabilization, and equitable access to advanced emergency care, thereby reducing 
mortality and long-term disability from acute cardiac and cerebrovascular events. 
5.6.9 On being asked t hat given rising longevity and pneumonia burden among elderly 
populations, whether the Government considering introducing an Adult Immunization 
Programme e.g. pneumococcal Vaccine for citizens aged 70+ with comorbidities, the 

214 
 
Department replied that respiratory diseases remain significant contributors for morbidity and 
mortality among older persons in India. Findings from the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India 
(LASI)7, which is first nationwide population -based survey in India to assess lung function, 
highlight the declining respiratory health associated with ageing. The survey indicates that 
nearly 49% of individuals aged 45 years and above have either restrictive or obstructive lung 
disease. Approximately 40% have restrictive lung disease, while about 9% h ave obstructive 
lung disease (including mild and moderate -severe forms). The findings underscore the high 
prevalence of compromised lung function among older adults, which increases susceptibility 
to respiratory infections, including pneumonia, particularl y in those with comorbid 
conditions. 
5.6.10 At present, a universal Adult Immunization Programme for elderly persons has not 
been introduced under the public health system. Inclusion  of any vaccine in the national 
immunization schedule requires comprehensive evaluation of epidemiological evidence, cost -
effectiveness, financial sustainability, operational feasibility, and recommendations/approval 
by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) under the regulatory 
framework of the Drugs and Cosmet ics Act and the National Technical Advisory Group on 
Immunization (NTAGI). As of now, adequate policy approvals for nationwide public rollout 
of routine pneumococcal vaccination for all persons aged 70 years and above have not been 
accorded. The Government  of India continues to address pneumonia prevention and 
respiratory health among the elderly through existing public health programmes. The National 
Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) provides preventive, promotive, curative 
and rehabilitativ e services for older persons at various levels of healthcare delivery. 
Additionally, under Ayushman Bharat Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC) through 
Health & Wellness Centres, a continuum of care is provided for non-communicable diseases. 
5.6.11 The Committee recommends  that the Department evaluate the feasibility of 
introducing a structured Adult Immunization Programme targeting elderly populations, 
particularly citizens aged 60+ with comorbidities, in view of the rising pneumonia 
burden and declini ng respiratory health highlighted by Longitudinal Ageing Study in 
India (LASI) findings. While elderly care is currently addressed through NPHCE and 
Ayushman Bharat CPHC, the Committee urges the Department to initiate expert 
consultations with National Technical Advisory Group on Immunization (NTAGI)  and 
CDSCO to assess epidemiological evidence, cost-effectiveness, and operational feasibility 
of pneumococcal vaccination for high-risk groups. 
 
5.6.12 On being asked about the reason for the delay in approval of indigenous cervical 
cancer vaccines by Drug Controller General of India despite their potential affordability, the 
Department submitted that the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has

Serum Institute of India Pvt. Ltd., Pune for prevention of the disease caused by Human 
Papilloma Virus types 6, 11, 16 and 18. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 under 
                                                           
 

215 
 
which vaccines are regulated, contains provisions for accelerated/ expedited approval process 
in certain situations.  
 
5.6.13 The Committee recommends that the Department  to expedite the rollout and 
public ava ilability of indigenous cervical cancer vaccines, given their potential 
affordability and impact on reducing disease burden. While CDSCO has already 
granted approval for manufacturing and marketing of the quadrivalent HPV vaccine

Standard Treatment Guidelines for Trauma care management and Standard Treatment 
Guidelines for Management of Burns have been developed. Emergency and trauma care 
services is under expansion to other district hospitals as per the budget announcement para 88 
of Budget 2026 -27: Emergencies expose families, particularly the poor and vulnerable, to 
unexpected expenditure. We will strengthen and increase these capacities by 50%  in District 
capacities by establishing Emergency and Trauma Care Centres. 
5.8.5 The Committee recommends that the Department accelerate the establishment of 
trauma centres in every district to reduce the burden on major city hospitals. While 196 
Trauma Care Facilities and 14 Centres of Excellence have already been sanctioned, and 
expansion is planned under Budget 2026 -27 to increase district capacities by 50%, the 
Committee urges the Department to lay down a clear phased implementation timeline 
with annual  targets to ensure timely coverage across all districts. The Committee 
recommends leveraging Centres of Excellence for capacity building, standardized 
treatment protocols, and referral linkages so that district -level trauma centres are fully 
equipped to ha ndle emergencies. Th e structured expansion, backed by monitoring and 
accountability mechanisms, will strengthen emergency care nationwide and reduce 
preventable mortality from trauma and burn injuries. 
5.8.6 On a specific query related to address service g aps at Community Health Centres, 
particularly the shifting of gynaecologists and paediatricians, the Department relied that under 
NHM, support is provided for engagement of contractual workers. More than 5 lakhs health 
workers like MPW, Staff Nurse, Lab Te chnicians, Medical Officers, Specialists and CHOs 
are supported under NHM. The supply of Human Resources for Health (HRH) has shown 

218 
 
significant improvement over the past  decade. This expansion in pre -service education 
capacity has gradually translated into  better availability of health workforce in public health 
facilities. With the expansion of infrastructure across States/ UTs, NHM has continued to 
support filling up of HR gaps against IPHS norms. Overall availability of these key HRH has 
increased over the years, especially in the regular cadre. The number of UG and PG seats also 
has increased in the past few years. Also, under NHM, support is also provided for creation of 
DNB seats, to increase the availability of doctors. Specilaized training programs l ike LSAS 
training, BEmONC (Basic Emergency Obstetric and New Born Care) and CEmONC 
(Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care including C Sections) are provided 
through NHM to address specialist shortages. Further, some States are providing reserv ation 
to in -service candidates who have mandatorily served for defined number of years in rural 
areas under the State Quota Seats in NEET PG.   
5.8.7 On an another query related to strengthening ambulance services (102/108) and 
establishing blood storage u nits at Rural Hospitals, the Department replied that u nder the 
National Health Mission (NHM), the Government of India has undertaken various initiative to 
strengthen health facilities and service delivery to reduce the maternal mortality across States 
and Union Territories, including in rural and tribal areas which are as follows: 
a) Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a demand  promotion and conditional cash transfer 
scheme for promoting institutional delivery. 
 
b) Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK)  entitles all pregnant woman delivering in 
public health institutions to have absolutely free and no expense delivery, including 
caesarean section. The entitlements include free drugs, consumables, free diet during 
stay, free diagnostics, free transportation (to and fr o) (102/108) and free blood 
transfusion, if required. Similar entitlements are also in place for sick infants up to one 
year of age.  
 
c) The Government of India also facilitates alternative modes of ambulance 
transportation in hard -to-reach tribal areas, inc luding boat ambulances, bike 
ambulances, air ambulances, palkis and other locally appropriate transport 
mechanisms to ensure timely access to care. 
 
d) Further, under the National Ambulance Services (NAS) the Government of India 
provides free, 24×7 emergency and patient transport services across States and Union 
Territories. Operated primarily through the toll -free numbers 102 (for pregnant 
women, mothers and sick infants) and 108 (for medical, trauma and other 
emergencies), the service ensures timely access t o public health facilities, particularly 
in rural, remote and tribal areas. These ambulances are equipped with essential life -
saving equipment and trained personnel to provide basic emergency care during 
transit, thereby reducing delays in accessing critic al maternal and emergency health 
services.

The Committee recommends integrating DCCCs more closely with the broader

5.9 DISEASE CONTROL 
5.9.1 On certain queries related to malaria elimination programme to strengthen targeted 
interventions in high -burden districts of Tripura, strengthen critical areas such as deng ue 
control, rare disease research, the Department stated that Tripura is a Category -3 State in 
respect of Malaria disease burden, with Annual Parasite Incidence (API: cases per 1000 
population per year) of 1.54 in 2025 which is 37.65% decline as compared to 2024 where API 
was 2.47. The state maintains adequate surveillance in terms of ABER (Annual Blood 
Examination Rate) of >10% (21.65%). Malaria cases have decreased in the state by 37.45% in 
2025 (6091 cases) as compared to 2024 (9738 cases) due to strengt hening of surveillance, 
early diagnosis & complete treatment, Integrated Vector Management and IEC/BCC 
activities. High burden districts in the State of Tripura have decreased to 1 (Dhalai) in 2025 as 
compared to 4 in 2024 (Dhalai, South Tripura, Khowai and Gomati). 
5.9.2 Dengue is a mosquito borne viral disease , mostly self-limiting, but in its severe form 
due to vascular permeability results in hemorrhagic manifestation leads to shock and causes 
deaths. Dengue virus has four serotypes ( DENV 1, 2, 3, 4). All can cause the disease and 
infection by one serotype do not confer protection to the other. Individuals who are infected 
for the second time or more are at greater risk of severe dengue.  There is no specific 
treatment/drug available for Dengue, cases ar e managed symptomatically. Trainings of 
Trainers were conducted for States/UTs to strengthen clinical management and reduce 
deaths. As a result of the cascading trainings, the CFR for Dengue is sustained below 1% 
(National target), which was 0.09% in 2025.  

221 
 
5.9.3 Health is a State subject and the Centre provides support based on the proposals 
submitted by States/UTs in their annual Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs), and funds 
are released in accordance with approved plans. States are encouraged to raise  appropriate 
demands in their PIPs to further expand dialysis services as per needs. T he Government of 
India, through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), provides structured 
technical leadership, national surveillance standards, and conti nuous monitoring support to 
States and Union Territories for disease surveillance, outbreak preparedness, and rapid 
response.  
5.9.4 The Committee believes that while the Department has achieved significant 
epidemiological milestones, evidenced by the stee p decline in malaria cases in Tripura and 
the sustained dengue case fatality rate of 0.09% nationally, the existing framework's 
reliance on state -initiated Programme Implementation Plans (PIPs) for critical 
infrastructure risks creating regional disparitie s in healthcare access. The Committee is of 
the view that passive central support is insufficient for addressing acute rural gaps, even 
with the commendable expansions under the Integrated Health Information Platform 
(IHIP). The Committee, therefore, recom mends that the Department immediately 
transition from a responsive to a proactive national mandate, directly standardizing the 
deployment of advanced diagnostic laboratories, Rapid Response Teams (RRTs),  critical 
care units , ambulance services and blood st orage units  across all high -burden and rural 
districts, ensuring that inter -sectoral coordination under the One Health approach is 
uniformly operationalized rather than contingent upon individual state proposals. 
5.9.5 On being asked about the targeted strategies being adopted to address drug -resistant 
TB, the Department stated that u nder TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan, the Government , to address 
TB, including drug -resistant TB among the vulnerable population across the country, 
implements key strategies like mappi ng of congregate settings & vulnerable population 
including asymptomatic, pro -active screening of vulnerable population by chest x -ray for 
early detection, upfront nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for all presumptive TB cases, 
timely treatment initia tion & completion, differentiated TB care for managing high -risk TB 
cases, nutrition support and preventive treatment to eligible vulnerable population. Further, 
the Government, has provided 1,191 portable AI -enabled handheld X-ray machines covering 
all districts of the country & an additional 2,247 more handheld X -ray machines are under 
supply. 9,826 molecular laboratories for conducting NAAT tests across the country have been 
established. These portable equipment‘s have contributed to the scaling up of sc reening of 
vulnerable population for early detection of TB & drug -resistant TB across the country. As 
per the World Health Organization‘s Global TB Report 2025, the incidence rate of TB in 
India has shown a 21% decline from 2015 to 2024, while the mortalit y rate has reduced by 
25% during the same period.  
 
5.9.6 The Committee appreciates the targeted strategies under the TB Mukt Bharat 
Abhiyan to address drug -resistant TB, particularly at the rural hospital level. While 
significant progress has been made th rough universal drug susceptibility testing, 
availability of newer drugs, and decentralized DR -TB centres, the Committee urges the 
Department to ensure full deployment and optimal utilization of portable AI -enabled 

222 
 
diagnostic technologies, such as handheld  X-ray machines and NAAT facilities, across 
all districts. The Committee also recommends greater involvement of private healthcare 
partners in TB detection, diagnosis, notification, and treatment under a strengthened 
public–private partnership framework. Further, integration of portable diagnostics with 
Nikshay tracking, nutrition support, curbing illicit liquor consumption and treatment 
adherence mechanisms should be strengthened, alongside capacity building and training 
of frontline health workers for early detection, diagnosis, and timely referral. 
5.9.7 The Committee notes that portable X -ray systems are being used for rapid and 
accessible chest imaging for early detection of Tuberculosis. The Committee is, however, 
concerned about the influx of cheap de vices, reportedly sourced from countries 
bordering India and marketed as ―Make in India‖, emitting high radiation exposure. 
Considering the high patient load in Government healthcare facilities, the Committee 
recommends that all deployed portable X -Ray sys tems adhere to the highest available  
global safety and precision standards of 0.4mm or smaller focal spot of X- Ray tube with 
adjustable tube current of minimum 5 mA to a maximum of 8 mA so as to ensure 
responsible use of diagnostic radiation for improved patient safety.

5.11.1 On a specific query on strategy of the Government to ensure quality training and avoid 
future unemployment or under -skilled surgical specialists, as India rapidly increases MBBS 
and PG seats under the oversight of the National Medical Commission, the Department stated 
that the Govern ment of India is systematically expanding medical education to keep pace. 
Over the  past 11 years, the Government of India made gains in making quality medical 
education more accessible. There are now 23 publicly funded and leading All India Institute 
of Me dical Sciences institutes, including the first -ever AIIMS in the northeastern area in 
Assam. There are 2,086 medical colleges, including 818 allopathy, 323 dental and 942 
AYUSH institutions. Medical education seats for the MBBS (Bachelor of Medicine and 
Bachelor of Surgery) increased by 151% (from 51,348 to 128976), and postgraduate seats 
grew by 173% (from 31,185 to 85020). DNB qualification has been recognized for 
appointment as teaching faculty to take care of shortage of faculty. 
5.11.2 The Committee st rongly recommends that the Department must ensure that the 
rapid expansion of MBBS and PG seats under the oversight of the National Medical 
Commission is matched with robust quality assurance mechanisms to safeguard training 
standards and prevent future un employment or under -skilled specialists. In parallel to 
the establishment of new medical colleges, seat expansion, and recognition of DNB 
qualifications, the Committee urges the Department to strengthen faculty development, 
clinical exposure, and skill -based training modules  across institutions. Further, the 
Committee recommends instituting periodic accreditation, competency -based 
assessments, and structured career planning  to align medical education output with 
national health system needs. By balancing ex pansion with quality and workforce 
planning, the Department can ensure that the growing pool of medical graduates and 
specialists are well -trained, employable, and capable of delivering high -quality 
healthcare services nationwide.

multi-skilling and continuous professional development programmes to enhance career

medical professionals in rural hospitals.

through regulatory functions are transparently monitored and effectively aligned with 
the broader objectives of strengthening medical education and he althcare regulation in 
the country. 
 
5.11.15 The Committee believes that it is financially imprudent and contrary to 
the principles of parliamentary accountability for statutory bodies generating hundreds 
of crores in regulatory charges to evade legislativ e scrutiny. Specifically, the Pharmacy 
Council of India (PCI) generates upwards of ₹300 crore annually through Pharmacy 
Education Regulatory Charges (PERC) but bypasses parliamentary presentation by 
exploiting General Financial Rule (GFR) 238 (5) and (6), citing that its direct 
government grant for salaries is only ₹20 lakh. Similarly, the Dental Council of India 
(DCI) retains its annual revenue of approximately ₹36 crore entirely as internal receipts 
under the provisions of the Dentists Act, 1948. 
 
5.11.16 The Committee is of the view that revenue generated by statutory 
regulatory bodies through mandatory fees, inspections, and licensing is inherently public 
money. Permitting these funds to be retained autonomously as internal receipts or 
parked indefinitely in Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDRs) without mandatory parliamentary 
oversight creates a severe accountability vacuum and contravenes Government‘s 
standard financial propriety.

5.14 MEDICINE 
 
5.14.1 On being asked about plans to regulate drug pricing to minimize the gap between 
MRP and actual prices, and to extend duty exemptions to essential post -transplant

immunosuppressant drugs, the Department stated that National P harmaceutical Pricing 
Authority (NPPA) under Department of Pharmaceuticals fixes the ceiling prices of scheduled 
drugs as listed in Schedule -I of DPCO, 2013 which is based on the National List of Essential 
Medicines (NLEM) published by Ministry of Health a nd Family Welfare. No manufacturer 
(whether generic or branded) of scheduled medicines can sell such drug above the ceiling 
price (plus applicable Goods and Service Tax) fixed by the NPPA whether in urban or rural 
area. As per the provisions of DPCO, 2013,  ceiling prices of scheduled formulations are 
revised every year as per annual Wholesale Price Index (WPI) (all commodities) for 
preceding calendar year on or before 1st April of every year, which is notified by the 
Government on the 1st day of April every  year. In case of non -scheduled formulation, 
manufacturers are required not to increase MRP by more than 10% of the MRP during 
preceding 12 months. 
5.14.2 The Committee is of the considered opinion  that the Department, in coordination 
with the Department o f Pharmaceuticals and NPPA, must undertake  measures to 
minimize the gap between MRP and actual sale prices of medicines  by ensuring stricter 
enforcement of ceiling prices under DPCO, 2013 and enhancing transparency in retail 
pricing across States. Uniform monitoring mechanisms should be instituted to prevent 
regional disparities and ensure affordability for patients nationwide. Further, the 
Committee recommends that the Department examine the proposal to extend duty 
exemptions to essential post -transplant i mmunosuppressant drugs , given their critical 
role in patient survival and long-term care.
