justified projections is the reason for the Department securing the Projected Demands.

recommends the Department to continue with the judicious utilisation of enhanced 
funds and build confidence in its capacity to deploy and absorb resources effectively for 
nationwide research infrastructure. 
 
3.3.7 The Committee, further observes a thrust towards the funding of MRUs at Rs 
100.27 crores in comparison to that of MRHRUs at Rs 71.08 crores for the FY 2026-

health research and multi-disciplinary research in medical colleges. But, when more 
thrust is being given to MRUs, it by default leads to rural areas being left out as these 
areas lack in government medical colleges compared to urban areas. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends more or at least equal thrust for both areas and to ensure apt 
push is given under MRUs to government medical colleges in rural areas. This would be 
in alignment with National Health Policy goals for more research in underserved areas. 
 
3.3.8 The Committee, keeping in mind the increasing life span of the Indian 
population, has highlighted the arising need for attention towards the problems related 
to ageing and geriatrics. In this regard, it is curious to know about the 
recommendations of the Performance Evaluation Committee (PEC) constituted vide 
order dated 19th December, 2022 by DHR on the establishment of a new institute- 
National Institute of Ageing and Healthy Longevity. National Centre for Ageing, 
AIIMS, is one of the government institutions which are currently dedicated for the 
cause. The Committee wants to be appraised on the progress made on this 
recommendation of the PEC. The Committee recommends that proactive steps shall be 
taken for the establishment of the National Institute of Ageing and Healthy Longevity

collaborate with AIIMS to create protocol of treatment to address the problems related

i. Multi-Disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) 
3.3.9 Originally conceptualized during the 12th Plan Period (2012–17) under the umbrella 
scheme Development of Infrastructure for Promotion of Health Research, the MRU initiative 
aims to bridge longstanding gaps in research capacity, laboratory infrastructure, and 
scientific output across medical institutions in India. Following successful implementation 
during previous plan periods—including an interim extension aligned with the 14th Finance 
Commission, the continuation of the scheme for the 15th Finance Commission cycle (2021–
22 to 2025–26) was approved. As of now, 123 MRUs including 5 MRUs in Private Medical 
Colleges have been established across various States and Union Territories. These units 
primarily focus on Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs), while also addressing emerging 
public health challenges through clinical trials, multi-centre research, and capacity-building 
initiatives. The key objectives of MRUs are:- 
i. To strengthen the research environment within medical colleges by establishing 
dedicated, state-of-the-art MRUs. 
ii. To bridge infrastructural gaps that hinder the conduct of quality health research by 
creating well-equipped research facilities. 
iii. To build research capacity and human resources in the field of health research 
through training, mentorship, and hands-on project involvement. 
iv. To ensure equitable geographical distribution of health research infrastructure by 
establishing MRUs across underserved and underrepresented regions. 
v. To contribute to improved public health outcomes through the generation of 
evidence-based diagnostic methods, processes, and scientific knowledge. 
vi. To undertake clinical trials in accordance with the Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government of India. 
vii To promote multi-centric research projects involving MRUs, medical colleges, and 
research institutions for addressing national and regional health priorities. 
3.3.10 Monitoring of MRUs is carried out at both the institutional and central level to ensure 
effective functioning, accountability, and alignment with the objectives of the sub-scheme. 
The Local Research Advisory Committee (LRAC)considers and approves research proposals. 
The Executive Committee ensures broad participation of all Departments in submitting 
research proposals to the MRU. At the central level, DHR administers and monitors the 
progress of MRUs through a structured framework, supported by the Programme Monitoring 
and Implementation Unit (PMIU) comprising of Project Manager, Finance Manager, 
Scientists, and other support staff.

the contention may contain merit but, in its opinion, to ensure even ground, the varying 
constraints under which different beneficiary institutions operate has to be 
appropriately factored in while deciding upon the parameters to assess the 
performance. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Department create a 
dedicated MRU monitoring cell under DHR with real-time tracking for both physical 
and financial progress for evaluating performance/requirement-based funding beyond 
uniform allocations.

3.4 C. Development of tools/support to prevent outbreaks of epidemics 
 
3.4.1 The scheme Development of tools/support to prevent outbreaks of epidemics operated 
as a separate central sector scheme with a small budget to the tune of Rs.50.71 cr. for five

contingent needs during public health emergencies. This scheme is complementary to the 
VRDL scheme i.e. Setting up and strengthening of nation-wide network of laboratories for 
managing epidemics and national calamities” which runs concurrent in emergent situation.

3.2.6 Further, the Department has conducted a third-party evaluation through the National 
Productivity Council in the Financial Year 2025–26 to assess the reasons for poor proposal 
quality and low participation from young faculty and researchers in medical colleges. 
 
Major Key Findings: 
(i) Limited Awareness and Outreach: Many young faculty members were not 
adequately aware of the schemes and opportunities available under DHR; 
(ii) Capacity Constraints: Lack of structured mentorship and limited exposure to 
proposal writing and project management skills resulted in weak technical quality 
of submissions; and 
(iii) Time Constraints: Heavy teaching and clinical responsibilities left limited time for 
young faculty to engage in research activities.

(i) Enhanced Awareness Campaigns: Wider dissemination of scheme details through 
workshops, webinars, and social media outreach to enhance the participation; 
(ii) Capacity Building: Training programmes on proposal writing, research 
methodology, and project management targeted at young faculty and early-career 
researchers; 
(iii) Streamlined Processes: Increasing the frequency of Technical Evaluation 
Committee (TEC) meetings and simplifying application procedures to reduce 
delays; and

3.5.8 DHR through its Fellowships abroad programme under HRD scheme supports 
advanced trainings of Indian scientists and researchers in foreign countries, with condition 
that they serve back in India utilizing the skills gained. To counter the challenge of “brain 
drain” and to retain skilled researchers in India, the DHR, has undertaken several specific 
initiatives aimed at providing better facilities and competitive career prospects comparable to 
international standards. The key initiatives include: 
 
(i) NRI/PIO/OCI Research Support Programme: This programme has been launched to 
encourage Indian-origin scientists working abroad to return and contribute to 
biomedical and health research in India. It provides contractual research positions and 
financial assistance, thereby leveraging the expertise of highly trained professionals 
with exposure to advanced technologies and methodologies. 
 
(ii) Training Fellowships: Researchers are supported through various training workshops 
and travel grants programmes for international exposure, enabling them to strengthen 
their skills and contribute effectively to national research priorities. 
 
(iii) Foreign Training and Repatriation Support: Faculties and researchers are facilitated 
for foreign training opportunities and are supported upon their return to India, 
ensuring knowledge transfer and capacity building.

three years, along with a research grant of up to Rs. Twenty lakhs per year to support

3.5.24 The Committee thereafter wanted to be updated on the status of Anti-cancer vaccine. 
In response ICMR submitted that the interest in the development of cancer is ever growing 
from a public health perspective. Efforts and scientific progress are being made globally in 
this field. At present, the availability of personalized mRNA-based vaccines for specific 
cancers and its clinical use will depend on the completion of ongoing trials and subsequent 
regulatory approvals. A generalised or universal “anti‑cancer vaccine” is unlikely to be 
introduced for public use in the coming year. It is important to distinguish these emerging 
therapeutic vaccines from preventive anti‑cancer vaccines, which are already established and 
in public health use. In this domain, the Government of India has taken a significant step 
through the planned national HPV vaccination campaign, which directly contributes to 
cancer prevention. The Government on 28 February 2026, has launched the HPV vaccination 
programme wherein all 14‑year‑old girls across the country will be offered a single dose of 
the HPV vaccine through government health facilities. This national initiative aims to 
substantially reduce the future burden of cervical cancer. 
3.5.25 The Committee takes cognisance of the work being undertaken by DHR/ICMR 
through the DIAMOnDSR scheme. According to the Department, the DIAMOnDS

3.5.26 On the Uniform Cancer Treatment Protocol, the Committee acquiesce with the 
submission of ICMR, being the field experts, that it does not recommend “uniform 
cancer treatment protocol”. Having said that the Committee observes that the 
treatment procedures and cost involved in a particular type of cancer in the country 
have wide gaps between a government institution and a private institution. While the 
Committee acknowledges that DHR does not have any say in the cost involved in 
treatment procedures, the Committee recommends the ICMR’s National Cancer 
Registry Programme (NCRP) along with the D/o H&FW should undertake a study to 
identify a way to address the issue of wide gaps in treatment procedures for a particular 
type of cancer between a government institution and a private institution. The 
Committee, however, is of the considered view that as a beginning, DHR should 
formulate treatment protocol for common cancers like oral, cervical and breast cancers 
and come up with a broad based for its treatment procedures and guidelines. Like the 
submission of ICMR, since National Institute of Cancer Prevention & research 
(NICPR)‑ICMR updates are directly linked to national clinical guidelines, the 
Committee perceives such a study would help to lessen the gaps. 
 
3.5.27 Regarding anti-cancer vaccine, the Committee has been impressed upon that 
efforts and scientific progress is being made in this field globally. The availability of 
personalized mRNA-based vaccines for specific cancers and its clinical use depends on 
the completion of ongoing trials and subsequent regulatory framework. The only anti-
cancer vaccination as of now available, both globally as well as in India, is the HPV 
vaccine. The Committee hopes that India, through ICMR, enters this field as the rising 
incidence of cancer among the population, especially among the youth, in recent times is 
alarmingly high. Accordingly, the Committee recommends ICMR should make efforts 
to make itself a part of on-going anti- cancer vaccination research projects globally in 
coordination with international entities like WHO and come forward for regulatory 
approval for clinical use.

INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR) 
 
4.1 The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), headquartered in New Delhi, is 
India's apex organization for formulating, coordinating, and promoting biomedical research. 
As one of the world's oldest medical research institutions, ICMR operates under the 
Department of Health Research (DHR) within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 
Government of India. Its research agenda aligns closely with national health priorities, 
focusing on communicable diseases, fertility control, maternal and child health, nutritional 
disorders, environmental and occupational health issues, and non-communicable diseases 
such as cancer, cardiovascular conditions, diabetes, blindness, and mental health disorders. 
 
4.2 The Secretary, DHR in his oral evidence related to the examination of Demand 2026-
27of DHR submitted that in BE 2026-27, the Department has got a budgetary allocation from 
the Government of Rs.4,821 crore. Out of which, on the allocation of Rs.4,000 crores for 
ICMR, he stated that this does not include any money from revenue or from any other source 
from within the ICMR.  This is the funding from the Government to the ICMR 
 
4.3 While explaining the ICMR budgetary system, the Secretary submitted that major 
portion is Grants-in-Aid General which is basically the money spent on research i.e. research 
projects and research institutions. The remaining amount is for the salary of ICMR scientists, 
technical staff and administrative staff, capital assets, etc.  He also informed that ICMR 
pensions are not paid out of salaries head but out of the Grants-in-Aid General. Under the 
research budget, there is intramural research, which means research in ICMR institutions, 
and there is extramural research, where ICMR funds more than 300 institutions in the

things in its attempt to make India a developed country. Viskit Bharat@47, which is a

young population as well as a healthy population. The Committee therefore

comparable to leading Asian economies such as China, South Korea, Japan, etc. Efforts 
to be made to choke out a road map to bridge the research and investment gap by 
extracting measurable outcome from intramural and extramural project, especially in

recommends for adequate budgetary support towards theoretic development advanced 
trails and indigenous innovations. Action plans should be chalked out for PPP based 
funding on mission mode to reduce long term dependency on expensive imported 
therapies.  
4.7.10 Every health scheme/program/research/study should be conceived as a step 
towards creating a healthy population who would directly/indirectly contribute to the 
GDP of the country. The Committee feels that at 0.02% of its GDP, India is at a very 
lower position compared to developed countries in the field of Health Research 
expenditure. As of now, India’s representation and contribution to the global health 
forums is not much remarkable. The Committee feels that India has no dearth of

4.8 Physical outcomes of ICMR projects 
 
4.8.1 Subsequently, the Committee wanted to know the physical outcomes of ICMR 
projects during 2025-2026. DHR gave the details as under:- 
 
 
 
 

83 
 
Disease wise outcomes-  
 
A. Nipah Virus: During the Nipah outbreaks in Kerala, rapid containment and timely 
public health interventions have been facilitated due to the deployment of mobile BSL-
3 laboratories. A colorimetric isothermal (RT-LAMP) assay for rapid detection of 
Nipah virus has been developed and the technology has been transferred for 
commercialisation through Patent Mitra. Finally, monoclonal antibodies that can be 
utilised for treatment have been developed.  
 
B. Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD): The KFD Virus Clinical Management Protocol that 
would provide a standardised framework for clinical management, diagnostic 
approaches, and therapeutic decision-making has been developed and finalised. Risk 
mapping of KFD using species distribution modelling that supports the implementation 
of targeted prevention strategies has been developed. An inactivated KFD vaccine 
candidate, which shows promising potential in preclinical studies has been developed. 
 
C. Leptospirosis: The identification of Leptospira as a major contributor to mortality 
associated with Acute Febrile Illness and Acute Encephalitis Syndrome in eastern Uttar 
Pradesh has led to the inclusion of leptospirosis testing within the diagnostic protocols. 
 
D. HIV: Results from Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) retention studies highlighted 
programme redesign with a focus on early engagement and integrated TB-HIV care 
aligns with national efforts to achieve the 95-95-95 benchmarks.  
 
E. Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis: To support ophthalmological monitoring in 
PKDL, ICMR developed national and global databases. Field validation of three 
platforms for visceral leishmaniasis and PKDL, including qPCR-based test-of-cure, 
RPA suitcase laboratory, and cell-free DNA-based diagnostics have been completed. 
Finally, Infectious Diseases Data Observatory (IDDO)-Oxford database has been 
developed for VL, PKDL and VL-Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) for data 
sharing and reuse. 
 
F. Dengue: Development of a molecular point-of-care pan-Dengue assay that can detect 
all four Dengue Virus serotypes using RT-RNA amplification with CRISPR/Cas12a 
fluorescence detection has completed. A paper-based dengue type-2 detection kit using 
77 blinded clinical samples has been validated. Results from the school-led dengue 
prevention under the Dengue Reduction through Education, Awareness, and 
Monitoring in Schools (DREAMS) programme has showed potential for scalability 
through community engagement and policy alignment.  
 
G. Tuberculosis: ICMR has validated and deployed three indigenous handheld x-ray 
technologies which supports TB screening among the underserved populations of the 
country. Various other diagnostic technologies like the Quantiplus® MTB kit, the 
UniAMP MTB Card, the PathoDetect™ and the CyTB skin test are in various stages of 
validation. DeepCXR has been integrated into the National TB elimination Programme 
(NTEP), to provide rapid, standardised and scalable interpretation of chest x-rays. An 
ICMR clinical trial on a modified BPaL (mBPaL) regimen established that optimisation 

84 
 
of the Linezolid dose improved tolerability while maintaining efficacy and enhancing 
treatment adherence among Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB) patients. The findings 
of the Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutritional Status 
(RATIONS) trial reinforced the correlation between nutrition and TB prevention and 
care. In Tamil Nadu, the Tamil Nadu KasanoiErappilaThittam(TN-KET) care model, 
using a severe illness triage tool, utilised five clinical indicators to identify high-risk 
patients which led to 20% reduction in early TB deaths and 10% reduction in overall 
TB-related mortality. ICMR-NIRT has entered collaborations with national and 
international partners for paediatric TB clinical trials, drug-resistance surveillance, 
diagnostic innovation, vaccine immunology, and TB innovation hubs. 
 
H. Malaria: Two CRISPR-based ultra-sensitive platforms for simultaneous detection of 
Plasmodium falciparum and artemisinin resistance has been developed. The first 
recombinant multi-stage malaria vaccine (AdFalciVax) has entered the technology 
transfer phase, and industry engagement has been initiated. A MoA have been executed 
for malaria elimination research and Phase III long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN) 
trials.  
 
I. Enteric Diseases: A multiplex two-tube real-time RT-PCR kit (En-ViroQPlex) for 
enteric viruses has been developed. A broad-spectrum glycoconjugate vaccine effective 
against typhoidal and non-typhoidal Salmonella, and an outer membrane vesicle-based 
vaccine against Shigella, have progressed to the technology transfer stage. Adjunctive 
strategies have been evaluated to test the potential of existing antibiotics, including the 
enhancement of ciprofloxacin activity against Shigella flexneri. Preclinical evaluation 
in BALB/c mouse models demonstrated the therapeutic potential of a newly 
characterised Shigella bacteriophage.A patent has been filed for a multiplex PCR assay 
that differentiates hypervirulent and classical Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Tests (RTD). A hydroxyurea dose-optimisation trial comparing 10 mg/kg/day and 20 
mg/kg/day which optimises treatment has been completed. To address stigma-related 
barriers to care among the tribal populations, a sickle cell disease stigma scale was 
developed. The BHARAT CARES initiative has been launched as a five-year national 
cohort to track SCD progression, treatment outcomes and long-term impact of the 
disease across the country. 
 
K. Cancer: National cancer surveillance has been expanded through a network of over 600 
cancer registry sites. Drone-based medical logistics has been deployed to support the 
rapid transport of corneal grafts and oncology samples. 
 
L. Cardiovascular Disease: Under the India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI), 
standard treatment protocols have been established in 157 districts across the country. 
A tele-ECG enabled ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) care model that 
demonstrated the feasibility of thrombolysis at district and community health centres 
has by the Uttar Pradesh Government as HridaySetu, which is operational in 12 hubs 
across 46 districts.  

85 
 
 
M. Stroke: A public-sector Mobile Stroke Unit integrating CT-enabled ambulances with

N. Poly-Cystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS): Evidence from 75 high-impact publications 
informed updates to clinical guidance and lifestyle recommendations for the national 
PCOS cohort.

validated.

4.9.17 The Committee reckons that to regulate clinical trials, DHR registers Ethics 
Committees (EC) to review Biomedical and Health Research which also involves human 
participants through the NAITIK portal. Further, the Committee also acknowledges 
the reforms undertaken by DHR to facilitate public access to necessary trial 
information, like introduction of multilingual interface, mobile friendly platforms, 
mandatory registration tied to funding/publication, awareness campaigns for public, 
researchers & institutions, etc. In this regard, the Committee holds the view that 
regulatory reforms and ease of doing research, while maintaining ethical standards, 
needs to be encouraged. Maintaining ethical standards itself is a challenge viz. hurdles 
include uneven Ethics Committees quality, delays, and vulnerability in multicentric 
trials, etc. Hence, the Committee recommends further strengthening of the role of DHR 
as a regulatory entity through frequent trainings for Ethics Committees members and 
participants, introduction of digital tools for monitoring and timely review of 
guidelines. ICMR should ensure that participation in clinical trials is based on genuine 
informed consent and all measures to ensure this shall be taken by DHR.

4.10.1 When the Committee enquired about the measures taken by ICMR to translate its

Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS), etc. DHR furnished the 
following domain wise details: - 
 

92 
 
a) Oncology

for oral suspension (PFOS) of 6-mercaptopurine (PREVALL), which helps in 
accurate dosing for children undergoing treatment for Acute Lymphoblastic 
Leukaemia (ALL).  
 
(ii) ICMR’s CARE-Clinical Pharmacology initiative focuses on therapeutic 
monitoring of anti-cancer drugs like sunitinib and docetaxel, which demonstrates 
that drug monitoring improves patients' quality of life (QOL) and reduces 
treatment costs.  
 
(iii) ICMR’s pilot project on screening and early detection of cervical, breast, and oral 
cancers in Cachar, Assam demonstrated the effectiveness of frontline health

(v) The pattern of care and survival studies (POCSS) provided information on 
improved care strategies and early detection measures.

history of other cancers, age at menopause, and physical activity are considered 
important risk factors.  
 
(vii) ICMR evaluated the efficacy of multiple point-of-care systems for detection of oral 
potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and to develop a prognostic model 
combining clinical/ auto-fluorescence images, saliva markers, cytology, histology,

(i) The Centre for Advanced Research (CAR) for cardiovascular disease (St. John’s, 
Bengaluru) has developed a synergistic, low-cost Intervention Package (IP) for 
CVD burden reduction. A key translation measure is the “task shifting” model, 
where Non-Physician Health Workers (NPHWs) are trained to deliver protocol-
based care.  

93

f) Stroke 
 
ICMR established a population-based stroke registry at Dibrugarh and 
observed that stroke incidence rate was 160 /100000 population in this region. An 
unusually higher rates of haemorrhagic stroke (65-70%) were observed in the stroke 
patients in this population. In view of this, ICMR with support from the Govt. of 
Assam, had initiated a research project to establish a clinical stroke care pathway for 
management of acute stroke cases at Dibrugarh and Tezpur. MSU (Mobile Stroke

leading cause of death.

ICMR’s CKD program integrates discovery, population surveillance and service 
innovations, with emphasis on CKDu hotspots. 
(i) Discovery & diagnostics: CAR at SGPGIMS Lucknow with two patents on urinary 
exosome miRNA biomarkers for early CKD and diabetic nephropathy differentiation. 
 
(ii) Burden & care: multicentric urban CKD study (2018) across 7 cities, n=15,372 →

(iii) Genomics & precision care (ongoing): FSGS genetic panel standardization;

ICMR has informed that the rapid shift towards urbanization, sedentary lifestyles, and 
unhealthy dietary habits has led to a significant rise in risk factors for CKD and liver 
diseases. Both diabetes and hypertension are leading causes of CKD, particularly through 
mechanisms like diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephrosclerosis. Environmental 
factors, including contaminated water and exposure to heavy metals, pesticides, and 
pollutants, have become significant contributors to CKD. The ICMR HEAL-CKDu project in 
Andhra Pradesh highlighted how occupational heat exposure, particularly in industries like 
agriculture, brick kilns, and construction, increases the risk of kidney damage, especially in 
areas with poor water quality. Additionally, studies on Chronic Kidney Disease of Unknown 
Etiology (CKDu) in areas like Uddanam and the microplastics research have shown how 
environmental toxins are linked to kidney dysfunction and disease progression. Preventive 
strategies like healthier diets, regular exercise, better control of diabetes and hypertension, 

96 
 
and addressing environmental toxins are crucial to reducing the growing burden of these 
diseases. 
 
i) Fetal anomalies 
 
ICMR has informed that under the National Health Research Priority (NHRP) on

clinical settings. Also, the National Action Plan (NAP)-AMR 2.0 (2025-2029) emphasizes

(iii) HPV Vaccine 
 
4.10.17  The Committee desired to know the primary objectives & scope of the study titled 
"Antibody Response following One Dose of Cervavac® as compared to One Dose of 
Gardasil Vaccine in Healthy Girls Aged 9-14 Years: A Non-inferiority, Multicentre, Double-
blind, Randomized Controlled Trial" under ICMR.  
 
4.10.18  Replying to the queries of the Committee, DHR submitted that the primary objective 
of the study was to determine whether the antibody response elicited by one dose of 
Cervavac® (study product) is non-inferior to one dose of Gardasil® (comparator) against 
HPV types 16 and 18 among healthy girls in the age group of 9-14 years, 24 months post-
vaccination. Scope of the study are generation of evidence to aid in adoption of WHO’s 
single dose HPV vaccination strategy as a public health initiative by India and having an 
understating about the utilisation of a Make-In-India vaccine for the same adolescent age 
group.  
 
4.10.19 DHR added that Gardasil® was selected as the reference vaccine because it is a 
vaccine with robust clinical trial and real-world data, including evidence supporting 
immunogenicity following reduced-dose schedules. The vaccine is one of those 
recommended by WHO-Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE) for one dose schedule 
for girls aged 9-14 years, and thus has a well-established immunogenicity, safety and 
extensive global clinical use. Finally, both Gardasil® and Cervavac® contain virus-like 
particles targeting HPV genotypes 16 and 18, enabling a scientifically valid comparison of 
antibody responses based on similar antigenic composition and mechanism of action. 
Therefore, it was an appropriate reference for a non-inferiority design and allows rigorous 
assessment of whether a single dose of Cervavac® elicits a non-inferior antibody response in 
healthy girls aged 9–14 years. 

102 
 
 
4.10.20  Further, the Committee asked about how the results of this trial could potentially 
impact India’s national HPV vaccination program, especially regarding the use of the 
indigenous vaccine Cervavac®. Besides this, the cost and availability of Cervavac® 
(developed by Serum Institute of India) compare with Gardasil®, possibility of positive non-
inferiority results accelerating its inclusion in public health programs, etc were also areas of 
interest to the Committee. DHR submitted in this regard that the National Technical 
Advisory Group on Immunisation had requested ICMR to conduct this study as data 
regarding single dose of Cervavac® was not available in the public domain. If the results are 
positive, then this indigenously developed vaccine could be deployed in public health 
programmes. 
 
4.10.21 As informed by DHR, Gardasil® is available as a single dose of prefilled syringes 
and needs to be imported. As per the submission of DHR, the current market rate of 
Gardasil® single dose pre-filled syringe is around ₹3000- ₹4000. On the other hand, 
Cervavac® a “Make in India product”, is available in single as well as multidose vials. The 
current market rate of single dose vials of Cervavac® is around ₹1400 to ₹1800 with 
additional syringe and needles cost of ₹10 to ₹15 per dose. The Committee are however not 
sure of the exactness of the price of Gardasil®single dose pre-filled syringe vaccine available 
in India as on date.  
4.10.22 Regarding the economic benefits arising from developing a home-grown single-dose 
HPV vaccine and how it could reduce the price of the HPV vaccine and accelerate its 
integration into India's Universal   Programme, DHR submitted that Home-grown single dose 
vaccines, if proven to be non-inferior, would save import costs and duties, thus rendering the 
vaccination more affordable. These lower prices would make universal public rollout 
financially possible. If the country purchases the vaccine for the Universal Immunisation 
Programme, price negotiation would ensure that the costs are much lower for larger scale 
vaccination. Single dose strategy will help achieve coverage of greater than 80% which 
would make it cost effective. Additionally, internal transport costs are reduced if the 
manufacturer could deliver the vaccines to the major vaccination sites in the country while 
maintaining a cold chain. All girls between 9 and 14 years can be vaccinated in a campaign 
mode to achieve near complete coverage in this age group.  
4.10.23  Delving deeper into the matter the Committee sought to know how single-dose HPV 
vaccine impact cancer incidence among women in India. DHR informed the Committee in 
this connection that girls who are vaccinated before their sexual debut are less likely to 
develop precancers or cervical cancer that are due to oncogenic HPV type 16/18 after 30 
years of age. Provided >80% vaccination coverage is achieved in girls between 9-14 years of 
age, the impact of this vaccination programme can be observed one and half decades after the 
vaccination, when they have grown into the age group at risk. Globally, focus is placed in the 
use of nonvalent vaccines because of the identification of cancer-causing HPV that are not 
covered with the current quadrivalent vaccine in use.  
 
4.10.24 The Committee reckons the importance of national HPV vaccination 
programme. The Committee understands that ICMR is engaged in the "Antibody 
Response following One Dose of Cervavac® as compared to One Dose of Gardasil 

103 
 
Vaccine in Healthy Girls Aged 9-14 Years: A Non-inferiority, Multicentre, Double-
blind, Randomized Controlled Trial" to determine whether the antibody response 
elicited by one dose of Cervavac® (study product) is non-inferior to one dose of 
Gardasil®. The result of the trial would to aid in adoption of WHO’s single dose HPV 
vaccination strategy as a public health initiative by India. Further, the Home-grown 
single dose vaccines, if proven to be non-inferior, would save import costs and duties, 
thus rendering the vaccination more affordable as well as effective. The Committee 
feels that to make the trial result oriented, a transparent narration of the facts related

believes that HPV vaccination is a corrective and a way forward step. The delay in the 
roll out of the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) maybe due to lack of 
information among the public. Hence, the Committee strongly recommends publishing 
of a detailed fact sheet on the ICMR/DHR website outlining the primary objectives and

transparency and community involvement, the programme would emerge as a 
consequential public health achievement in protecting next generation of women from

4.10.25 The Committee further recognises the fact that if the trial could demonstrate 
Cervavac®’s single-dose non-inferiority, it would be a "major fillip" by enabling faster

(iv) Oral Health 
4.10.26 Anant Muskaan, ICMR's National Health Research Priority Program, is aimed at 
promoting awareness of the importance of oral health in school children. According to DHR, 
these interventions are much more affordable than out of pocket expenditure for expensive 
oral diseases treatment in the country. 
 
4.10.27  As per the study conducted by Sharda et al., it was observed that the per capita cost 
of the School-Based Toothbrushing programme is lower than the out-of-pocket expenditure 
in real- scenarios in India. The per capita cost of the STB programme is ₹29,339 (95% CI: 
26,487-32,381) and lifetime caries experience with the programme is 2.72 teeth (95% CI: 
2.69–2.76) while the lifetime caries experience without the programme is 3.74 teeth (95% CI: 
3.69-3.78). Out of pocket expenditure studies reveal that ₹44,874 is saved per person with 
30% public treatment while ₹26,160 is saved per person with 100% public treatment. Thus, it 
has been observed that in real-world scenarios in India, the STB programme is expected to be 

104 
 
a cost-effective strategy for reducing the burden of dental caries and the associated treatment 
costs. 
 
4.10.28 According to DHR, the data collection process is still undergoing. The costing data 
will be collected at the end of one year of full-scale implementation (February 2026) and 
again at the end of two-year of full-scale implementation phase (February 2027). As per the 
data collected till date, the average estimated per-child annual running cost of the Anant

4.10.29 Anant Muskaan, ICMR's National Health Research Priority Program, is aimed 
at promoting awareness of the importance of oral health in school children. The project 
focus on primary school-based toothbrushing and oral health education to prevent 
costly oral diseases and reduce out-of-pocket expenditure. It is a cost-effective 
preventive intervention. The Committee perceives that the extension of the Anant 
Muskaan Project beyond the current seven districts would be considered upon

(v) Food safety 
 
4.10.30 ICMR, through its 100 years of existence, has contributed significantly to nutrition 
science and policy in the country along with food safety. The following are some of them: 
 
1. Early studies on nutrient deficiency disorders: The studies on parboiled and milled 
rice helped to explain the incidence of beriberi among rice eaters in the east coast of 
Andhra region where milled rice was consumed largely and no incidence in Madras 
where parboiled rice was consumed more. 
2. Stomatitis associated with the deficiency of B group of vitamins, particularly 
riboflavin, was described for the first time in India, and a treatment with yeast and 
skimmed milk was found to be effective. 
 
3. Nutritive values of Indian foods:  The Nutritive Value of Indian Foods and Planing 
of Satisfactory Diets was published in 1937, which turned out to be a very popular 
contribution. Apart from this, the nutritive values of fruits and vegetables were also 
determined during 1960s. This publication was thoroughly revised and rewritten 

105 
 
with data obtained after updating some methods of nutrient estimation and was 
published as 'Nutritive Value of Indian Foods' in 1970s. More recently, the database 
profiling the nutritive values of Indian foods has been readied in 2017. The new 
'Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT) 2017 is the compilation of nutritional 
information on 151 discrete food components for 528 key foods. 
 
4. Formulation of recommended dietary allowances (RDAs): The first 
recommendations on Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA) were made for the 
Indian context in 1944. Later, the RDAs were modified in the early 1960s, and then 
in the early 1970s, 1980, 1991 and last in 2010. These are the recommendations of 
how much of the nutrients should be ideally consumed by people of different age 
and physiological groups based on their activity 
 
5. Dietary guidelines for Indians: A manual with information on the key practicable 
points for diets and physical activity for Indians to ensure optimal health and 
freedom from disease was proposed for the first time in 1998. In 2011, after the 
RDAs were revised and the guidelines were redrafted, the revised version was 
released. 
 
6. Studies on protein-energy malnutrition (PEM):  The institutes research paved way 
for a new hypothesis that malnutrition among underprivileged children was due to 
energy deficiency and not solely due to protein deficiency. 
 
7. Contribution to national programmes and policies:  ICMR-NIN’s research was also 
the basis for the Government of India in the 1970s, to launch a supplementary 
feeding programme to provide 300 Kcal/day to improve the nutritional status of 
children in rural areas and in urban slums, which was operated under the Integrated 
Child Development Scheme (ICDS). 
 
8. Contribution to the National Prophylaxis Programme against nutritional blindness 
due to vitamin A deficiency: ICMR-NIN studies paved the way for a nationwide 
vitamin A prophylaxis programme with its inclusion in the Fourth Five-year plan in 
1969. Based on the recommendations of the ICMR-NIN, it became a national 
programme and is being implemented throughout India. 
 
9. Supplementation of iron and folic acid to pregnant women: ICMR-NIN 
recommended that a programme of iron folate supplementation be taken up for 
pregnant women and preschool children as a prophylactic measure. The government 
introduced the National Nutritional Anaemia Prophylaxis Programme aimed at 
pregnant women and young children in 1970. 
 
10. Operational research to strengthen nutrition programmes: The Institute carried out 
operational research studies on Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) to 
assess its impact on the nutritional status of children, including process and input 
evaluation. The study results helped in strengthening of the programme and 
subsequently, it was expanded in all the villages by universalizing ICDS services. 
 

106 
 
11. Development of Nutrition Surveillance System (NSS): In order to promote effective 
functioning of ICDS and nutritional well-being of the beneficiaries, the ICMR-NIN 
developed 'AAA' (triple A) approach covering Assessment, Analysis and Action 
involving the entire ICDS mechanism from the grassroots level to the supervisory 
level. This involved 'Assessment' of health and nutritional status on a continuous 
basis amongst vulnerable population groups, identifying area-specific determinants 
(Analysis) of nutrition problems and food insecurity and integrating various 
departments to take appropriate 'Action' in the prevention and control of 
undernutrition. 
 
12. Regular nutritional surveys: The National Nutrition Monitoring Bureau (NNMB) 
under ICMR-NIN carried out regular surveys in 10 to 16 States and generated a 
dynamic database on diet and nutritional status of the communities. Many surveys 
were regularly conducted among rural, tribal and urban populations. The most recent 
survey was the 'Diet and nutritional status of urban population in India and 
prevalence of obesity, hypertension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia in urban men and 
women' released in 2017 
 
13. Balamrutham: ICMR-NIN in collaboration with State governments has developed 
micronutrient-fortified (iron, folic acid, B1, B2, B12, niacin, zinc, vitamin A, 
vitamin C, calcium) take-home ration called Balamrutham for 6-36 month old 
children, which is being implemented in all districts of Andhra Pradesh and 
Telangana. Earlier, the integrated State of Andhra Pradesh used to provide Modified 
Therapeutic Food (MTF) to children (aged 6-35 months) under Supplementary 
Nutrition Programme of ICDS. The ICMR-NIN conducted a study comparing the 
new ready-to-eat (RTE) formulation with the existing MTF and proved that it was a 
superior food supplement. This led to the introduction of Balamrutham, which 
reached the mothers and caregivers of over 10 lakh children in Telangana State. 
 
14. Food safety and toxicology: Studies on food toxins explored some major areas such 
as neurolathyrism, aflatoxicosis, argemone toxicity and epidemic dropsy and erucic 
acid toxicity in edible oil. Significant contributions have been made by the Institute 
in identifying the nature of the toxic factors and in providing solutions for prevention 
and control. 
 
15. Investigations on epidemic dropsy: In 1998, epidemic dropsy was reported from 
several States such as West Bengal, Bihar, Orissa (now Odisha), Madhya Pradesh, 
Haryana, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Delhi and 
Maharashtra, mainly due to consumption of food cooked in argemone oil mixed with 
mustard oil. The ICRM-ICMR-NIN carried out a study on epidemic dropsy 
prevalent in the areas of State of Madhya Pradesh and recommended to the 
government to stop the unauthorised use of adulterated oil. Selective cultivation of 
yellow mustard, strict enforcement of regulation and exemplary punishment to 
unscrupulous traders were followed as preventive measures. 
 
16. Knowledge, attitude, belief and practice (KABP) study on food safety: ICMR-NIN 
spearheaded the knowledge, attitude, belief and practice study on food safety in 
2005-06 which was conducted among households and other stakeholders such as 
doctors, regulators and teachers in 28 States of the country. 

107 
 
 
17. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs): Most recently, in 2017, the ICMR-NIN has 
generated data on the prevalence of overweight/obesity and non-communicable 
diseases (NCDs) in urban and rural areas from 16 States of India. The urban survey 
alone covered as many as 1, 71, 928 individuals from over 52,500 households of 
1097 wards of 16 States. 
 
18. Fenugreek seeds in the management of diabetes: It was found out that fenugreek 
seeds could improve the glucose tolerance and ameliorate other symptoms of 
diabetes mellitus (type 2). It was reported that the mechanism of action of fenugreek 
seeds on improving glucose tolerance in diabetes was due to improvement in glucose 
utilization at the cellular level.  
 
19. Research on edible oils: In the 1980s when there was a concern about the inadequate 
production of edible oil in India, the Government of India's policy of looking at 
promoting the use of unconventional edible oils got attention. Systematic studies on 
the nutritional quality and safety evaluations of unconventional edible oils such as 
rice bran oil were carried out at the ICMR-NIN. 
 
20. Recommended use of multiple oils: The relative role of n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated 
fatty acids (PUFAs) in regulating the plasma profile was studied, and the desirable 
ratio of these fatty acids in Indian diets was worked out. Based on these studies, it 
was advocated to blend or use a combination of oils to reap the benefits of n-3 and n-
6 fatty acid form of different oils.ICMR- ICMR-NIN recommended the use of more 
than one oil as diverse sources of oils confer the additional advantage of providing a 
variety of minor components (present in non-glyceride fraction of oils). 
 
21. Health effects of trans fats: Based on the studies of the ICMR-NIN  the Food Safety 
and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) fixed the norms for trans fatty acid 
content of vanaspati, limiting to 10 per cent, and proposes to bring it down to five 
per cent and to two per cent or lesser than that in the next couple of years. 
 
22. Double-fortified salt (DFS): ICMR-NIN's research efforts focused on developing a 
technology for double fortification of salt with both iodine and iron to combat both 
IDD and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) led to the development of a successful 
formula after exploring several stabilizers to ensure the stability of iodine on storage, 
no discolouration and bioavailability of both micronutrients when taken with food. 
The technology of DFS has been transferred to the industry. The ICMR-NIN also 
contributed to the preparation of the regulatory specifications for FSSAI for DFS. 
 
4.10.31 The Committee is impressed with the number of programmes/studies 
undertaken by ICMR in the country in the field of nutrition science and policy along 
with food safety. The Committee notes that majority of the studies undertaken by 
ICMR are hinged on the biomedical aspect. The Committee feels ICMR would be the 
ideal forum to initiate studies on India's diverse food ecosystem. For this, ICMR should 
include experts from agriculture (ICAR), environment (MoEFCC), and FSSAI while 
identifying the subjects of study to address real-world problems. The Committee 
strongly recommends a Multi-Disciplinary Food Safety Research Panel for this. 

108 
 
Another recommendation of the Committee is that due attention shall be given to 
changing food habits of the population across the societal strata keeping in mind 
aspects like easier access to fast food with the advent of fast food delivery at door steps 
primarily through platform-based services. At the same time, there is also an emerging 
cross section of population who is very health conscious. The Committee strongly feels 
that if the gist of findings in this field can be communicated in lay man’s language, it

medical devices. MedTech MITRA, an ICMR-CDSCO initiative with guidance from 
Niti Aayog, supports MedTech innovators including those of medical devices. Further, 
ICMR’s Indian Clinical Trial and Education Network (INTENT) and Centre for

facilitates the clinical validation of such devices already approved by Atomic Energy 
Regulatory Board (AERB) and Central Drugs Standard Control 
Organisation (CDSCO), resulting in regulatory overlap creating an uneven protocol for 

111 
 
development of medical devices. The Committee observes that the current medical 
device registration process involves multiple organizations and ICMR has no role after 
AERB approval. Hence, the Committee strongly recommends a more simplified, single-
window system which would reduce timelines and improve transparency. 
 
4.11.10 The Committee observes that ICMR, in collaboration with Institute of Plasma 
Research (IPR), has developed and validated an indigenous AI-based tool (DeepCXR) 
for automated interpretation of chest X-rays. The Committee recommends that ICMR 
make such indigenous technology available throughout the country free of cost which 
would be a step towards accessible and affordable healthcare. Even while making 
progress towards developing indigenous technology, the Committee opines that our 
country still relies heavily on imported medical technologies and equipment such as 
MRI, CT scans, PET-CT, and LINAC systems, which are procured from international 
companies like Philips and Siemens. ICMR has acquiesces that certain component such 
as the X-ray tube (a part of the X-ray source) and the detector, which are integral to the 
handheld X-ray system developed by them were imported substantiates this fact. If the 
core component like, X-ray tube, HV tank, etc is being imported ICMR should refrain 
from claiming it as their own technology. The better way for ICMR would be to engage 
itself in depth research for indigenous production, design, and development of medical 
devices. The medical devices developed viz the portable x-ray should be completely 
indigenous including X-ray tube, HV tank. Medical innovation and products should not 
be an assembly of components to be cited as ‘Made in India’. In this context, the 
Committee recommends that ICMR should set up a benchmark for ‘Made in India’ 
initiatives and derive a protocol wherein ‘Atmanirbhar Bharat’ is encompassed on a 
true scale. In case ICMR has to go for compilation of medical devices, the protocol 
should be clearly highlighted on the dashboard. Having said that the Committee also 
recommends that ICMR should make maximum efforts to develop some mechanism to 
manufacture these machines in our medical device parks with 100 % percentage of 
indigenous value addition which is essential for regaining public trust in the field of AI. 
 
4.12 ICMR and Young Researchers 
 
4.12.1 ICMR has developed Impact of Research and Innovation Scale (ICMR-IRIS), which 
provides a standardized framework for multidimensional impact assessment. This approach 
converts diverse research outputs into a single metric termed Publication-Equivalent (PE). 
Impact is measured across indicators including peer-reviewed publications, highly cited 
research, contributions to clinical or public health guidelines, granted patents, development 
and commercialization of health technologies and evaluation studies supporting regulatory 
approval or procurement. Aggregated PE scores are further normalized as PE per year, per 
unit of funding, and per scientist-year to enable benchmarking.  
 
4.12.2 This framework ensures comprehensive evaluation of scientific, translational, 
technological, and policy outcomes of publicly funded research. Improving research 
indicators in the country requires sustained investment in skilled human resources and 
enhanced participation of young researchers. Under the HRD Scheme, the DHR places 
special focus on the youth pursuing undergraduate/postgraduate medicine and Ph.D. 

112 
 
programmes, as well as young faculty and women scientists with career breaks to build a 
strong pipeline of biomedical researchers comparable to global standards. 
 
4.12.3 To promote health research in the country, particularly among the youth, DHR has 
undertaken the following initiatives: 
 
(i) Targeted Support for Young Researchers: The HRD Scheme is primarily designed 
to benefit early-career biomedical researchers across medical colleges and research 
institutions, enabling them to develop research skills and scientific thinking at an 
early stage. 
(ii) Fellowships and International Exposure: DHR provides overseas fellowships and 
travel grant support to young scientists and researchers for short-term training 
abroad and participation in international conferences. This exposure helps them 
gain insights into cutting-edge global research practices. 
(iii) Encouraging Research Culture Among Students: By focusing on undergraduate, 
postgraduate, and doctoral students, the Scheme aims to inculcate scientific 
curiosity, promote hands-on research experience, and motivate youth to pursue 
long-term careers in biomedical research. 
4.12.4 Also, the new ICMR–AcSIR PhD Programme is expected to strengthen India’s 
clinical research ecosystem and foster indigenous innovation in medical devices and 
therapeutics by integrating clinicians into structured PhD training alongside biomedical and 
public health researchers. Following the ICMR–AcSIR MoU, all 27 ICMR Institutes and the 
Headquarters became affiliated academic centres, enabling 376 ICMR scientists to be 
recognised as faculty and nearly 298 medical scientists and biomedical students enrolled in 
PhD programmes, with an additional fifty clinical scientists from 11 ICMR CCoEs under the 
DHR–Young Faculty Scheme joined the programme. This initiative will build a cadre of 
clinician-scientists, enhance translational research capacity, and support technology 
development, contributing to self-reliance in health innovation. 
 
4.12.5 Further, ICMR is addressing gaps in structured mentorship by introducing formal 
coursework in research methodology, biostatistics, and publication ethics through ICMR-NIE 
(Chennai) and ICMR-NIMR (New Delhi) as part of the AcSIR PhD curriculum, with 
centralised annual examinations ensuring uniform standards. Additionally, protocol 
development workshops and related training programmes are being conducted to improve 
study design, ethical conduct, and scientific rigor, thereby shifting the academic culture from 
quantity-based outputs to quality-driven research. 
 
4.12.6 The Committee notes with appreciation the measures adopted by ICMR to

research institutions, Fellowships & International Exposure to support young scientists 
and researchers for short-term training abroad and participation in international 
conferences; and Encouraging Research Culture Among Students focusing on

DHR places special focus on the youth pursuing undergraduate/postgraduate medicine

4.13.1 The Committee wanted to know about the latest health research trends around the

Latest Global Health Research Trends 
 
1. AI-Driven Health Innovation: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are 
now central to epidemic surveillance, diagnostics, drug discovery, and 
personalized medicine. AI algorithms increasingly power real-time outbreak 
detection, predictive models, and health systems planning.  
2. Digital Health and Health Data Integration: Telemedicine, wearable sensors, 
digital health records, and secure interoperable data platforms are transforming 
care delivery, improving chronic disease monitoring and enabling decentralized 
clinical research models.

surveillance and predictive models aim to detect novel pathogens early and 
accelerate countermeasure development.

stewardship programs, alternative therapies, and global collaboration to slow 
resistance trends. 
Role of DHR/ICMR 
1. AI and Digital Health: Indian Council of Medical Research is validating AI-
based tools for TB chest X-ray interpretation, diabetic retinopathy screening, and

5.1 Strategic Plan of DHR (2024–29) 
 
5.1.1 DHR has formulated a comprehensive Strategic Plan 2024–29 aligned with the 
national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047. The strategic goals for the next 5–10 years for 
advancing health research in the country are outlined as follows: 
 
1. Promotion of Indigenous, Affordable, and Globally Competitive Health 
Technologies DHR aims to significantly enhance India’s capability in developing frontier 
health technologies through the following initiatives: 
 
(i) ‘First in the World’ Challenge: Funding support for 100 high-risk, high-reward 
research ideas to encourage disruptive innovations. 
(ii) Frontier Technologies: Advancing work in areas such as cell and gene therapy, 
synthetic organs, therapeutic vaccines, advanced robotics, and other emerging 
medical technologies. 
(iii) Section-8 Company (MIDAC): Establishment of the Medical Innovation 
Development and Assessment Corporation (MIDAC) to facilitate industry 
partnerships, development of clinical trial batches, technology transfer, and 
validation processes. 
(iv) Med-Tech Mitra: Providing end-to-end support to start-ups and MSMEs for 
medical device innovation and development. 
(v) Centres of Excellence (CoEs) at IITs: Strengthening research and innovation

I. Cost Effectiveness of Medical Technologies through Health Technology 
Assessment 
A defining contribution of DHR to UHC lies in institutionalizing priority setting 
through Health Technology Assessment in India. By generating cost-effectiveness and 
budget impact analyses, HTA informs decisions on which technologies, drugs, and 
procedures should be financed through publicly funded schemes such as Ayushman Bharat - 
Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana. HTAIn provided cost evidence for 1573 Health benefit 
packages and supported revision and rationalization of 857 Health Benefit Packages under 
the AB-PMJAY. HTA also recommended that the cost of these packages may be utilized by 
CGHS and other insurance companies. This ensures that limited public resources are directed 
toward interventions that deliver maximum health gains and financial risk protection. The 
development of standardized HTA methods and the creation of Regional Resource Centres 
have further strengthened transparent and evidence-based decision-making at both national 
and state levels. 
Taken together, DHR’s role in India’s UHC agenda is not that of a service delivery 
agency, but of an enabler and steward of evidence. By generating robust scientific data, 

121 
 
strengthening infrastructure and human capital, standardizing care, and institutionalizing 
economic evaluation, DHR ensures that the expansion of health coverage in India is not only 
broader but also smarter, more equitable, and financially sustainable. 
II. Strengthening Public Health Research Infrastructure 
Beyond knowledge generation, DHR invests in strengthening research infrastructure 
within Government Medical Colleges and public institutions. The establishment of advanced 
diagnostic laboratories, genomics facilities, biorepositories, and clinical research units 
improves access to quality diagnostics and supports translational research. These investments 
enhance the public sector’s ability to respond to emerging health challenges while improving 
service delivery capacity. Through Human Resource Development (HRD) Scheme, DHR 
builds indigenous capacity in biomedical research, clinical trials, epidemiology, and health 
systems research, ensuring sustained availability of technical expertise required for evidence-
informed governance of UHC. 
III. Development of Evidence-Based Clinical Guidelines 
DHR also strengthens the quality dimension of UHC through evidence-based 
guidelines developed in collaboration with experts across the country. These guidelines aim 
to reduce unwarranted variation in care, promote rational drug use, and support uniform 
standards across public facilities. Standardization is essential in a large and diverse health 
system, particularly when financial protection schemes depend on clearly defined packages 
of care.

5.2 Research on Traditional and Integrative Medicine Practices  
 
5.2.1 Even when the nation is turning towards AI for finding solutions in healthcare and 
research, traditional and alternative medicines hold its sacred place in the sphere of 
medicines. Accordingly, measures have to be taken to ensure that research on traditional and 
integrative medicine practices is conducted with rigorous scientific standards, allowing for 
evidence-based integration with modern medicine. DHR have taken many steps towards this 
like signing of the Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) with the Ministry of AYUSH on May 
11, 2023, ICMR and the Ministry of AYUSH established various joint working groups 
consisting of scientists and heads of institutions from both sides (ICMR and CCRAS, 
Ministry of AYUSH). All major decisions and any modifications to programs are made with 
approval during meetings co-chaired by the two Secretaries. The progress of programmes, as 
well as the planning and execution of studies, are collaboratively managed in working group 
meetings overseen by the heads of ICMR divisions and the Deputy Director General (DDG) 
of the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS) from the Ministry of 
AYUSH. 
 
5.2.2  Subsequently, DHR also submitted to the Committee that a collaboration has been 
made with Ministry of AYUSH and Five AYUSH-ICMR Advanced Centres for Integrative 
Health Research have been setup at four AIIMS. ICMR also has dedicated National Institute 
of Traditional Medicine (NITM) in Belagavi to advancing the research of traditional 
medicine in India. Established with the vision of integrating traditional knowledge systems 
with modern scientific approaches, ICMR-NITM has undertaken various cutting-edge 
research projects fostering innovation and promoting evidence-based practices in traditional 
medicine for the benefit of public health. The following measures are employed by ICMR to 
encourage scientific rigour in research on traditional and integrative medicine: 
 
a) Investigators and staff are well-trained and knowledgeable in Good Clinical Practices 
(GCP).  
b) Study plans are supported by a clear and appropriate rationale, with well- defined and 
clearly articulated study objectives.  
c) To account for confounders and effect modifiers related to the Traditional (Ayush) 
interventions being evaluated, the study population is selected using stringent inclusion 
and exclusion criteria.  

125 
 
d) Sample size calculations are performed using appropriate statistical methods to ensure 
that the study has sufficient power.  
e) A comparative or control group is included, utilising either standard care treatment or a 
placebo. 
f) All subjects are randomised to prevent selection and treatment bias. 
g) Whenever possible, double blinding is implemented for both patients and investigators, 
or single blinding for patients. 
h) A third treatment arm, which combines standard treatment with traditional medicine, is 
maintained for integration when necessary. 
i) For the evaluation of efficacy and safety of interventions, standard modern tools that are 
objective in nature are used as outcome parameters. 
j) Comprehensive methodological details for each study parameter are provided to support 
transparency and reproducibility in research on traditional and integrative medicine. 
k) All adverse events are meticulously recorded, including their intensity, type, and 
frequency, to ensure safety and enhance confidence in the integrity of the study. 
l) Protocols are reviewed and modified by the Protocol Development and Selection 
Committee, which comprises a team of subject experts from relevant areas. 
m) Studies are initiated only after obtaining IRB/EC approval and in strict accordance with 
applicable regulatory guidelines to ensure adherence to scientific and regulatory 
standards. 
n) Ayush products under study are of standard quality, accompanied by a certificate of 
analysis, and are prepared in a GMP-certified manufacturing facility. 
o) Investigators and staff are thoroughly trained in GCP. 
p) Sample handling and analysis are conducted in either NABL-accredited laboratories or 
according to good laboratory practice guidelines. 
q) Data recording, data capture, and record keeping are done using standard software or 
digital tools. 
r) Study sites are equipped with all necessary infrastructure and facilities to ensure the 
smooth completion of the study. 
s) A statistical plan is provided for data analysis.

5.3 AI in Health 
5.3.1 With the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), digital health platforms and 
data-driven research into healthcare delivery and public health programmes, the Department 
of Health Research (DHR) considers digital health research to be a priority area requiring 
sustained and predictable financial support. AI-enabled healthcare technologies such as 
clinical decision-support systems, digital diagnostics, digital screening and surveillance tools, 
disease prediction models, population surveillance analytics and real-world evidence 
platforms are increasingly essential for improving efficiency of national health programmes 
and early disease detection and optimisation of healthcare expenditure. Accordingly, DHR 
expects that the Ministry of Finance may support a structured expansion of budgetary 
allocations specifically earmarked for digital and AI-enabled health research. 
5.3.2 DHR has already planned strengthening of national digital and translational research 
capacity through programmes such as establishment of Infectious Disease Research & 
Diagnostic Laboratories for surveillance and outbreak response, the NIRMAN network for 
indigenous medical device development and clinical evaluation, creation of a national-grade 
data centre with AI/ML and cybersecurity infrastructure across ICMR institutes through PM-
ABHIM and a National Virus Resource Facility to support vaccine, diagnostic and 
therapeutic research; accordingly, the Department seeks sustained and dedicated budgetary 
support from the Ministry of Finance to scale such digital, AI-enabled and preparedness-
oriented research initiatives. 
5.3.3 Requirements for ICMR-NIRDHDS: To attain its objectives of accelerating research 
for development and evaluation of Digital and AI based solutions in health, the institute will 
benefit from a state of the art building infrastructure with high performance/ super computing 
facilities. Currently, the institute is actively exploring options for enhanced space and 
infrastructure to expand its scientific and technical workforce, thereby enabling the uptake of 
large-scale collaborative studies in digital health research. Digital health research is an 
emerging yet rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field that demands a diverse array of 
specialized skills. To strengthen its scientific capacity and address this expanding domain, 
the institute plans to recruit approximately 20 additional scientists over the next few years. 
Currently, the institute has three Scientists on board, with two more expected to join in the 
near future. 
5.3.4 Therefore, DHR’s considered expectation from the Ministry of Finance is not merely 
incremental increases in routine funding, but a mission-mode, ring-fenced financial support 
framework for AI and digital health research covering infrastructure, validation, regulatory 
evaluation, human resource development and implementation research. Such support would 

129 
 
enable evidence-based adoption of emerging technologies, promote indigenous innovation 
and ultimately improve efficiency, accessibility and affordability of healthcare delivery in the 
country. 
5.3.5 Further, the Committee’s query DHR on its plan to integrate emerging technologies 
like AI, genomics, and big data into its research framework. In reply, DHR stated that DHR/ 
ICMR plans to integrate AI, genomics, and big data into its research framework by (i) 
strengthening dedicated institutional capacity for digital health and data science, (ii) building 
enabling platforms and standards for trustworthy data use, and (iii) accelerating translation 
through targeted funding, regulatory handholding, and structured Intellectual Property (IP) 
support. 
5.3.6 A key step is the establishment of ICMR–National Institute for Research in Digital 
Health and Data Science (ICMR-NIRDHDS), which was repurposed from the erstwhile 
National Institute for Research in Medical Statistics (NIMS) in April 2024. The institute is 
mandated with research in development, evaluation and implementation of high impact and 
affordable digital and AI based health solutions. Development of India-specific, accurate AI 
algorithms, which depend on robust, secure, and representative health data systems that 
safeguard privacy while enabling responsible innovation. To address this need, the Indian 
Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has established the Health Research Data Repository, 
providing researchers with access to standardized, interoperable, and ethically governed 
health research data. Equally critical is rigorous evaluation and evidence generation to ensure 
that AI solutions demonstrate real-world effectiveness, safety, and equity. In this regard, 
ICMR’s National Institute for Research in Digital Health and Data Science (NIRDHDS) is 
collaborating with clinical, technical, and governmental partners to build a network for 
systematic technical, clinical, economic, and implementation evaluations of AI health 
technologies. ICMR has further strengthened the translational research ecosystem through 
initiatives such as MedTech Mitra and Patent Mitra, which support innovators from 
validation to regulatory and intellectual property guidance. 
5.3.7 For genomics and high-dimensional biomedical data, ICMR is strengthening compute 
and analytic capacity to support rapid processing of large sequencing datasets and 
downstream applications such as outbreak investigation and AI-enabled discovery. For 
example, ICMR’s NAKSHATRA high-performance computing cluster for virological 
research is intended to enable faster analysis of complex genomic and bioinformatics data 
and support more efficient outbreak response and preparedness. 
5.3.8 ICMR is pushing emerging technologies into the translational pipeline through 
structured intramural and extramural funding mechanisms, including dedicated MedTech 
development grant calls.To ensure that innovations are protected and transferred effectively, 
ICMR has also operationalized “Medical Innovations Patent Mitra,” which offers services 
such as patentability assessment, patent filing support, prosecution assistance, and facilitation 
of technology transfer to industry partners. 
5.3.9 The Committee, thereafter, wished to know about the assessment of Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) penetration in diagnostics in India. DHR submitted that AI is being 
integrated into various diagnostic processes, particularly in medical imaging (radiology, 
pathology), to enhance speed, accuracy, and efficiency. Government initiatives like the 
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and the National Health Mission are creating the 

130 
 
digital infrastructure and regulatory frameworks to support the integration of AI. ICMR has 
also released ethical guidelines for AI use in healthcare.  
 
5.3.10 As part of understanding emerging technologies, the Committee asked about the steps

submission and monitoring of projects under its schemes like HRD, VRDLs (Epidemic

5.3.12 VRDL Scheme: The e-PMS portal has been developed and operationalized to enable

Submission: 
- Integration of new components with existing databases to maintain seamless

Integration of new portals into the DHR ePMS:

(iii) Post Doctoral Fellowship 
(iv) UC/SOE and report uploading functionality, enabling applicants to upload

Monitoring:

5.3.14 Further, DHR submitted before the Committee the major challenges in AI and Digital 
Health Integration which are as follows:  
 
(i) Data Quality, Privacy, and Security: AI models require vast amounts of high-
quality, diverse, and representative data for training and validation.  
(ii) Regulatory and Ethical Concerns: The rapidly evolving nature of AI technology 
outpaces traditional regulatory frameworks for medical devices.  
(iii) Interoperability and Integration: A lack of standardised data protocols hinders 
effective data exchange between different systems and providers. 
(iv) Clinical Validation and Reliability: Rigorous, real-world validation through 
prospective studies and randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is needed to 
demonstrate a tool's clinical and economic utility and ensure it is safe and reliable 
for diverse populations. 
(v) Workforce Skills and Acceptance: There is a significant shortage of healthcare 
professionals with expertise in AI and data science.  
(vi) DHR, often in collaboration with the National Health Authority (NHA) and ICMR, 
is addressing these challenges through initiatives:  
(vii) Establishing Regulatory and Ethical Frameworks: DHR adheres to existing national 
digital and data protection frameworks, including the ICMR's ethical guidance for 
biomedical AI, the IT Act 2000, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.  
(viii) Developing an Interoperable Digital Ecosystem: Through the Ayushman Bharat 
Digital Mission (ABDM), the government is building a national digital health 
infrastructure that uses a unique Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) ID for 
citizens to link and access their digital health records across various facilities. 
 
5.3.15 The Committee is seized of the importance of Artificial Intelligence in health 
research and notes that DHR has plans to integrate emerging technologies like AI, 
genomics, and big data into its research framework. AI is being integrated into various

speed, accuracy, and efficiency. Government initiatives like the Ayushman Bharat 
Digital Mission (ABDM) and the National Health Mission are creating the digital 
infrastructure and regulatory frameworks to support the integration of AI. ICMR has 
also released ethical guidelines for AI use in healthcare.

clinical decision-support systems, digital diagnostics, digital screening and surveillance 
tools, disease prediction models, population surveillance analytics and real-world 

132 
 
evidence platforms are increasingly essential for improving efficiency of national health

5.3.17 A few of the remarkable steps by DHR that the Committee takes note of are (i)

across ICMR institutes through PM-ABHIM, (ii) establishment of ICMR–National

performance computing cluster for virological research is intended to enable faster

5.3.18 The Committee notes that DHR understandably expects that the Ministry of
