12.1   The Committee notes that monitoring and evaluation of the performance of the Family Welfare Programme is
conducted by eight Regional Evaluation Teams located at Delhi, Bangalore, Bhopal, Pune, Patna, Lucknow, Kolkata
and Chennai. Each evaluation team undertakes tour of 20 days every month and covers two adjoining districts selected
randomly covering an average of 700 acceptors of family planning.
The Committee would like to be apprised about the feedback received regarding U.P., Bihar, Orissa, M.P. and NE
States.
12.2   The Committee feels that availability of funds is therefor carrying out Family Welfare Programmes. However,
problem lies in their effective implementation. The Committee is of the view that a number of initiatives need to be
taken by the Department in this regard. Instead of routine publicity campaigns on the need of family planning, the
Department should have a publicity programme which is region-specific. Mass leaders, leading actors etc. need to be
involved for popularizing positive aspects of family planning methods. Surrogate advertisements in the form of
dialogues in films can be another measure. The Department may coordinate with Ministry of Information &
Broadcasting in this regard. Similarly Panchayati Raj Institutions and Community at large can play an effective role in
this field. The Committee is of the view that the Department should evolve a mechanism where under Panchayati Raj
Institutions as well as Anganwadi Centres are actively involved in Family Planning measures. A beginning can be made
by ensuring availability of condoms etc. in Anganwadi Centres/Panchayats. Cooperation of the Department of
Panchayati Raj /Women & Child Development may be sought in this regard. Another effective initiative can be about
the NGOs who are actively involved in the implementation of family welfare measures. The Committee feels that in
order to make them more accountable and also to assess the work being done by them, it would prove to be very fruitful
if a list of NGOs working in a particular area/district is given to the local MP. The Committee is of the view that instead
of depending only on the State reports indicating achievement in implementation of different programmes, the
Department should evolve a strategy where under all the agencies as indicated above make useful and far-reaching
contributions in an area which is of prime importance for the growth and development of the country.

        The Committee would like to be apprised about the feedback received regarding UP, Bihar, Orissa, MP and
NE States.                                                                                                                         (Para 12.1)
        The Committee feels that availability of funds is there for carrying out Family Welfare Programmes. However,
problem lies in their effective implementation. The Committee is of the view that a number of initiatives need to be
taken by the Department in this regard. Instead of routine publicity campaigns on the need of family planning, the
Department should have a publicity programme which is region-specific. Mass leaders, leading actors etc. need to be
involved for popularizing positive aspects of family planning methods. Surrogate advertisements in the form of
dialogues in films can be another measure. The Department may coordinate with Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting in this regard. Similarly Panchayati Raj Institutions and community at large can play an effective role in
this field. The Committee is of the view that the Department should evolve a mechanism where under Panchayati Raj
institutions as well as Anganwadi Centres are actively involved in Family Planning measures. A beginning can be made
by ensuring availability of condoms etc. in Anganwadi Centres/Panchayats. Co-operation of the Department of
Panchayati Raj /Women & Child Development may be sought in this regard. Another effective initiative can be about
the NGOs who are actively involved in the implementation of family welfare measures. The Committee feels that in
order to make them more accountable and also to assess the work being done by them, it would prove to be very fruitful
if a list of NGOs working in a particular area/district is given to the local MP. The Committee is of the view that instead
of depending only on the State reports indicating achievement in implementation of different programmes, the
Department should evolve a strategy where under all the agencies as indicated above make useful and far-reaching
contributions in an area which is of prime importance for the growth and development of the country.        (Para 12.2)

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED 
BY THE GOVERNMENT 
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL  
Recommendations/Observations 
4.2 The Committee, while appreciating the level of utiliz ation of plan funds allocated for Sufdarjung Hospital 
during 2005-06, also notes that as compared to Rs. 12. 88 crores worth equipment purchased in 2005-06, it is 
proposed to purchase equipment costin g Rs. 15.00 crores during 2006-07. The Committee, therefore is of the view 
that required funds for procurement of equipments in Sa fdarjung Hospital need to be provided in 2006-07. The 
Committee also observes that against 153 number of eq uipments to be purchased during 2005-06, number of 
equipments purchased was only 98. Additional efforts should, therefore, be made to expedite the proposed 
formalities so that targets set for 2006-07 are achievable. 
Action Taken 
 A schedule has already been prepared  to procure the equipments worth Rs .15 crores in the current financial 
year. Rs. 12.79 crores have been allocated in the B.E. fo r the purchase of equipments in this year 2006-07. Every 
effort is being made and process of procurement is regula rly monitored to get the equipments as per the targeted 
schedule. Funds requirement, if any above Rs. 12.79 crores will be projected at the RE stage. 
V. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL 
Recommendations/Observations 
5.2 The Committee notes that sixteen projects/schemes were  approved under the Tenth Plan. Their latest status 
report, however, does not seem to be very encouraging. Setting up of the Post Graduate Institute of Medical 
Education and Research at the hospital is the most ambitio ns project. The Committee is constrained to observe that 
this project seems to have been entangled in the numer ous procedural formalities. Designated plot was handed over 
to M/s HSCC (India) Ltd. on the 14th June, 2005 for demo lition of old barracks and co nstruction of the institute 
building. Although about one year has passed since then but only around 65 per cent of the demolition work has been 
completed. The Committee is not satisfied by the reply of th e Ministry that the tendering work is in process and 
actual construction is likely to commence shortly. The Comm ittee feels that the present pace of construction clearly 
gives an indication that it may perhaps take another plan period (Eleventh Plan commences from 2007-08) to get the 
building of PGIMER ready and functional. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the construction project 
may be completed under ‘a prescribed time-schedule closely monitored by a designated group of authorities. 
Action Taken 
 After following the prescribed tendering process, th e construction project for building of PGIMER at Dr. 
R.M.L. Hospital has been awarded to L-l tenderer for tota l estimated contract price of Rs. 44, 96, 11, 318. The 
contractor has already started the work in May, 06 and the entire work shall be completed within twelve months. As 
regards demolition work, about 80 per cent work is comple ted and remaining demolition will be carried as per 
requirements for construction of the PGIMER building. The project is being monitored by a Project Management 
Committee headed by Secretary (Health and FW). Cost and time schedule for the project are reasonably firmed up. 
VI. CENTRAL INSTITUTE OF PSYCHIATRY, RANCHI  
Recommendations/Observations 
6.1 Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi is a premier inst itute in the field of mental health in India. It offers 
clinical services to mentally ill, trains manpower in th e field of mental health and carries out various research 
programmes. Committee has been observing that this premier institute has not been taking the benefit of plan funds 
earmarked for it for one reason or the other for the past few years. Details regarding the last three years are self-
revealing:- 

(Rs. in crores) 
2003-04 2004-05 2005-06 
Approved outlay AE Approved outlay AE Approved outlay RE 
8.00 4.33 9.00 2.83 18.50 10.26 
 Achievement level of financial targets has been very disappointing. Approved outlay of Rs. 18.50 crore in 
2005-06 had to be reduced to Rs. 10.26 crore at the RE stage and actual utilization figures are not known to the 
Committee. The Committee is not optimistic  about full utilization of Rs. 10.65 crore plan funds allocated for the 
institute for 2006-07 in view of its past track record. 
6.2 Progress made in the procurement of some medical equipments during 2005-06 supports Committee’s 
apprehension. In respect of equipment like Colour Doppler and Campus Server although approved by SFC in 2001-
02 (February, 2002), orders could be placed at the end of th e fourth year (last quarter of financial year 2005-06). In 
the case of procurement of another equipment, Spiral CT Scan also cleared by SFC in February, 2002, advice of 
Ministry of Law has been sought on some procedural matter on 1st March, 2006. The Committee takes a serious 
view of this. The Committee reiterates that there is an urgent need for streamlining the procurement procedure so that 
premier institutes like CIP, Ranchi do not continue to suffer. 
Action Taken  
Para 6.1 and 6.2 
 The allocation in respect of C.I.P. Ranchi for the year 2005-06 was Rs. 10.26 crores under Revenue Budget 
and Rs.8.24 Crores under Capital Budget, making a total of Rs.l8.50crores. 
 The allocation of Rs. 10.26 crores under Revenue was retain ed at RE stage. It may be seen that during 2005-06 
utilization of funds was Rs.7.69 crores and equipments procured include the Colour Doppler and Campus Server. The 
major reason for shortfall in meeting of targets was non procurement of Spiral CT Scan due to revision of technical 
specifications. The Spiral CT Scan same is being procured during 2006-07. 
 As regards utilization of funds under Capital head during 2005-06, as against an allocation of Rs.8.24 crores 
expenditure of only Rs.0.87 crores coul d be incurred. The non-ut ilization of funds under Ca pital was because of the 
fact that the funds allotted for CIP Ranchi under M/o Urban Development were not made available in time to the 
Chief Engineer for executing the works of the institute. 
 During 2006-07, as against the provision of Rs. 10.65 crores under Revenue, Rs.7.36 crores has already been 
utilized as on 30.11.2006. All efforts are being made to utilize funds allocated during 2006-07. 
VII. JIPMER, PONDICHERRY  
Recommendations/Observations 
7.1 Plan allocation for JIPMER, Pondicherry during BE 2005-06 was Rs. 62.00 crore which was substantially 
reduced to Rs. 42.00 crore at the RE stage. Explaining the reasons for the reduced allocation, the Department 
submitted that besides the ongoing activities, the plan allo cation for 2005-06 was meant for the establishment of a 
Super Specialty Centre and Trauma Care Centre. These new proposals involving financial implication worth Rs. 
118.00 crore although cleared by the C.C.E.A had to go through a number of procedural formalities. As these 
activities would take considerable time, the provision in RE   was made to the tune of Rs. 42.00 crore. The latest 
position indicated by the Department was that selection of executing agency was going on which is expected to be 
finalized by early April, 2006. The Committee appreciates the preparedness shown by the Department in fixing a 
time schedule for completion of Super Speciality and Trauma Centre. The Committee, however, recommends that the 
Department should closely monitor the progress in this regard so that the projects can be completed on time. 
Action Taken 
 It is stated that the price bids su bmitted have been opened and action is under way to award the work to EPC 
Developer on turnkey basis and efforts will’ be made to complete the projects relating to establishing the Super-
Speciality Center and the Trauma Care Center at JIPMER, Pondicherry well in time. 
Recommendations/Observations 

7.2 On a specific query, the Committee was informed that against the sanctioned faculty strength of 175, there 
were 89 vacancies at present. Not only this, as per the information made available in the Performance Budget (2006-
07), against the original sanctioned strength of total posts of 3185, the, existing strength is only 2465. The Committee 
has been given to understand that sinc e its inception in April, 1956, the Ins titute has grown to become a premier 
institute providing most modern allopathic treatment for all diseases and disorders. Through its Regional Cancer 
Centre status and also Cardiac Cath Laboratory, the institute has been serving the cause of poor and downtrodden 
patients by providing free but quality medical care to  them. During 2005-06, 221 major operations including 120 
open-heart operations were conducted totally free of cost . Its status as the leading teaching institute is well-
established. An institute of such a high standard continui ng with a depleted staff streng th is however, a cause of 
serious concern. The Committee, accordingly, observes that the Department should take immediate steps for 
providing the necessary infrastructure and required faculty. If need be, a review of both recruitment and procurement 
procedure may also be made by the Department. 
Action Taken 
 It is stated that action is taken expeditiously by the Institution and all concerned for procuring the equipments 
required for the Institution as early as possible. During  last financial year two hi-tech equipments namely MRI 
scanner and whole body spiral CT Scanner were procur ed and during this financial year another Cardiac 
Catherization laboratory and 1000. A X-ray machine are being procured. With these new hi-tech equipments the 
patient care services will improve rema rkably. Besides, regarding the recruitm ent of vacant posts of faculty on 
contract basis was advertised twice a nd about 21 Assistant Professors were appointed on contract basis pending 
regular appointments through UPSC and one Assistant Professor of Anesthesiology and one Lecturer in Radiology 
(Medical Physics) were appointed on regular basis after selection by UPSC. Similarly, 77 numbers of Group ‘C’ 
posts is going on and will be completed in another two months time. This will also improve the patient care services. 
VIII. POST GRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL EDUCATION AND RESEARCH, CHANDIGARH  
Recommendations/Observations 
8.1 PGI Chandigarh, an institute of ‘National Importance’ as declared way back in April, 1967, has been 
providing exemplary service to the coun try, both in the field of health car e and medical education. The Committee 
observes that the Institute continues to make optimum and judicious utilization of allocated plan funds. However, the 
Committee has been given to understand that plan funds al located to the Institute  are not in accordance with its 
requirements. Against the proposed Tenth Plan outlay of Rs . 401.50 crore, an outlay of only Rs. 200.00 crore was 
approved. The Committee has its own doubts about the actual re lease of these approved funds to the Institute. As per 
the details available about the last four years of Tenth Pl an (2003-07), only Rs. 133.00 crore have been allocated 
during this period. It cannot be that in the very first year of the plan period, an amount of Rs. 67.00 crore were placed 
at the disposal of the Institute. As many as 11 project works have been proposed for 2006-07 by the Institute. The 
Committee hopes that plan funds of Rs. 40.00 crore for 2006-0 7 will prove to be adequate for these projects. If not, 
required funds at the RE stage may be provided to the institute. 
8.2 With regard to non-plan funds, the Committee observes th at there is only a marginal increase of Rs. 1.00 crore 
in 2006-07 when compared with the non-plan provision of Rs. 121.00 crore in 2005-06. As per the data regarding 
patient care and other cost indices, 10 per cent increase ha s to be added in the expenditure incurred during 2005-06. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should not be any mismatch between the requirement and 
allocation of non-plan funds for the Institute. 
Action Taken 
 In the Tenth Five Year Plan Rs. 200 crores were a pproved under Plan for the PGIMER. Out of the sanctioned 
Rs. 200 crores, Rs.133 crores have been  allocated to PGI and the same have b een utilized. In the first year, Rs.67 
crores was placed at the disposal to attend to the carry over projects of the 9th Plan. The Institute has also submitted 
that against the balance amount of Rs.67 cores, out of s. 200 crores of the Tenth Plan, only Rs.40.00 crores have been 
allocated to the Institute for the current financial year 200 6-07under Plan and Rs.25.00 cror es have been released. If 
additional amount is required for completion of projects, provisions would be made at R.E. stage. 
 Against the demand of PGI for Rs. 145.72 crores in BE. 2006-07 only Rs.122 crores were approved. On 
account of the following reasons, PGI have requested additional amount of Rs.23.72 crores. 

 (i) For salary and pension additional funds to the tu ne of Rs.1600 lakhs are required due to increase in 
DA and basic pay of employees and due to retirement of about 150 official in the financial year 2006-
07. 
 (ii) An additional amount of Rs.72 lakhs is required due to hike in air-fare, petrol, diesel and in the cost of 
other transport services. 
 (iii) In material and supplies an additional amount of Rs .300 lakhs is required due to increase in the cost of 
prices of various consumables items needed for the essential services being provided by the hospital. 
Also, the new centres like Advanced Urology Ce nter, Bone Marrow Transplant Center (BMTC), 
Advanced Eye Center have started working and their requirement of consumables is also being met 
out of the current allocation. 
 (iv) For maintenance of hospital buildings, campus and equipment, additional funds amounting to Rs.200 
lakhs are required. 
 (v) For replacement of old equipment funds amounting to Rs.200 lakhs are required. 
 To avoid any mismatch between the requirement and allocation of Non Plan funds the additional amount of 
Rs.23.72 crores requested by PGI may be sought at R.E. stage. 
X. SHORTAGE OF REQUIRED MANPOWER AT CENTRAL GOVERNMENT  HOSPITALS/ 
INSTITUTES  
Recommendations/Observations 
10.1 For the last two-three years, the Committee has been monitoring the ever-increasing shortage of manpower-
both medical and para-medical at Premier Institutes/Cen tral Government Hospitals. The Committee observes that 
significant development has taken place in this crucial area during 2005-06. Applicability of Department of 
Personnel and Training O.M. dated 16.05.2001 would no longer be there on technical posts lying vacant for more 
than three years. As per the revised decision of the Cabi net, these technical posts could not be filled up without 
referring them to the Screening Committee. Not only this , future vacancies of scientific and technical posts can 
remain unfilled for a period of three years, instead of the earlier period of one year. The Committee feels that this was 
a step in the right direction. The Committee notes that 69  vacant technical (para-medi cal) posts were advertised 
during the last year. Selection process in respect of some posts has been completed and in respect of the remaining 
posts also, the selection process is expected to be completed very soon. The Committee is of the view that the process 
of filling up of all the vacant technical posts should be closely monitored so as to get the desired result at the earliest. 
Action Taken  
ME.III 
 As regards Lady Hardinge Medical Co llege and Associated Hospitals, it is stated that the action for filling up 
the post is taken as per relevant rules and instructions. However, in order to speed up the action for filling up the post 
in these institutions, directions have been issued to the Directorate General of Health Services also to evolve an 
effective regulating mechanism. 
 As regards JIPMER, Pondicherry, it is stated that the ac tion for filling up the post is taken as per relevant rules 
and instructions. The action for filling up the posts in this institution is also being monitored. 
CHS 
 Owing to the Instructions issued by DoPT regarding optimization of direct recruitment, the posts of CHS 
could not be filled for almost 4 years from 2001 to February 2005 when approval of Cabinet was accorded to the 
exemption from the said instructions. Thereafter, all the po sts have been reported to UPSC. Since its takes almost 1

XI. SETTING UP OF AIIMS LIKE INSTITUTIONS (PRADHAN MANTRI  SWASTHYA SURAKSHA 
YOJANA) PMSSY 
Recommendations/Observations 
11.3 The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier reco mmendation that a scheme should be launched only after 
completing all the ground work and preparatory exercise. It has taken almost four years in getting the CCEA 
approval for PMSSY. The Committee now apprehends that mana gement of such a big project may prove to be too 
difficult to be handled effectively by the Ministry in spite  of their having set-up a designated Cell for the same. The 
Committee is not inclined to agree with the Department’s contention that in view of the track record of State 
Government not being able to manage their own institutio ns, the scheme needs to be implemented by the Centre 
directly. The Committee is of the firm view that the conc erned State Govts. should be  involved in the setting 
up/upgrading of institutes in their States. The Committe e appreciated the PMSSY. This needs to be started

 The CCEA approved the proposals relating to setting up of six AIIMS-like hospital and upgradation of 13 
existing Government Medical College Institutions on 16.3.2006 and 22.6.2006, respectively. The overall 
implementation of the PMSSY including the construction of AIIMS-like institutions will be supervised directly by 
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through the Project Management Committee. The setting up of 6 AIIMS-
like institutions will be executed on  turnkey basis selected th rough a competitive bidding process. The process of 
selection of Project Consultant for implementation of six AI IMS-like Institutions has been expedited and is likely to 
be selected by October, 2006. Likewise, the process of se lection of Architectural concept/Design has been expedited

up for monitoring of construction activities and proper lia isoning with the State Governments. State Governments

existing 13 medical institutions is being undertaken in consultation and above co-ordination with the concerned State 
Governments. Out of Rs.120 crores outlay sanctioned for u pgradation of each institute, the Central Government will 
invest Rs.100 crores as a one time measure and remaining cap ital expenditure of Rs.20 crores will have to be borne 
by the respective State Governments. The State Government s will also need to bear the recurring expenditure in 
terms of man-power, maintenance and further replacement of all the upgraded facilities. The concerned State 
Governments have been asked to contribute Rs. 20 crores as part of their share to the upgradation proposal. 
 Preliminary Project proposals are being prepared by the institutions. Expert teams from Government of India 
Institutions visit the sites. These proposals are now being fi nalized by discussions by Stat es and Institutions. It is 
hoped that DPR’s will be made between December, 06 and December, 07. A mee ting of Health Secretaries/Director 
of Medical Education/Principals of Me dical Colleges identified for up-gradatio n was being held in New Delhi, on 
29th-30th August, 2006 for working out the commonality of approach an d strategy for freezing of specifications and 

procurement of medical equipments. Experts will be involved in this process. States will also spend themselves their 
earmarked funds on procurement of equipments as identified under the Project. 
Recommendations/Observations 
11.4 The Committee is concerned about on e crucial financial aspect of PMSSY. There is a ceiling of Rs. 330 crore 
per institute, out of which Rs. 110 crore will be the contribution from Centre and States pooling Rs. 20 crores. 
Remaining Rs. 200 crore are to come from other sources.  The Committee feels that this  is a grey area and every

raiser, there is a distinct possibility of management slip ping into their hands. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Centre should be more generous by increasing its share and respective State Govts. should also be pursued to

proposed institutes should also begin at the earliest. If th at does not happen, the Comm ittee has little hope of these

 There are two components of the PMSSY setting up of 6 AIIMS like institutions and upgradation of 13 
medical institutions in 10 States. The estimated cost of setting up of each AIIMS like institution is Rs.332 crores.

XIII. RASHTRIYA AROGYA NIDHI  
Recommendations/Observations 
13. Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi was launched in 1996-97 and has been constituted with the objective of providing 
financial assistance to the BPL population for meeting the ex penses on treatment for life threatening diseases in the 
Government hospitals. At the state level, similar societie s have been constituted in the various States/UTs which 
provide the financial assistan ce to BPL patients upto Rs. 1.50 lakh. The Central Government provides the funds to 
these societies to the extent of 50 per cent of the amoun t contributed by the respective State Government and subject 
to a maximum of Rs. 5.00 crore for bigger States and Rs. 2.00 crore for smaller states. The Committee notes that 21 
States have been the beneficiaries of the Nidhi with Ka rnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and 
Rajasthan getting the maximum funds. The Committee notes th at although the scheme was launched in 1997, all the 
N.E States with the exception of Tripura and Mizoram have  remained outside the ambit of the scheme so far. The

position of such States. The Committee feels that the Depart ment has to make vigorous efforts to prevail upon these 
states to join the scheme.

 Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi (RAN) is a Re gistered Society under the Societies Registration Act, with the objective 
to provide much needed financial assistance to the poor for whom expensive but essential treatment is out of reach in 
the present system. The RAN has its Managing Committee comp rising Secretary (H and FW), Director General of 
Health Services, Joint Secretary and Chief Controller of Accounts (CCA) and HFM as Chairman. 
 All State Governments and Union Territories (except Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya,

 Such Societies in some States like Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan are operating

 In so far as North Eastern States are concerned, ex cept Tripura and Mizoram no other State has set up such

Recommendations/Observations 
17.1 Cancer is an important public health problem in In dia with nearly 7-9 lakh new cases occurring every year in 
the country. It is estimated that there are 20-25 lakh cases of cancer in the country at any given point of time. With 
the objectives of prevention, early diagnosis and treatm ent, the National Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) was 
launched in 1975-76. The Programme was revised in 1984-85 and subsequently in December 2004. There are 5 
schemes under the revised Programme. 
 (i) Recognition of New Regional Cancer Centres (RCCs) 
  In order to augment comprehensive cancer care f acilities in regions of the country lacking them, New 
RCCs afre being recognized. A one-time grant of Rs. 5.00 crores is being provided for New RCCs. 
  For the year 2006-07 four new Regional Can cer Centres have been recognized . They are: 
  • Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate Institute, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh 
  • Post Graduate Institute of Medi cal Education and Research, Chandigarh 
  • Sher-I-Kashmir Institute of Medica l Sciences, Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir 
  • Arignar Anna Memorial Cancer Research In stitute and Hospital, Kancheepuram, Tamil Nadu. 
 (ii) Strengthening of Existing RCCs 
  A one time grant of Rs. 3.00 crores is provided to  the existing RCCs in order to further strengthen the 
cancer treatment facilities in the existing centres. 
 (iii) Development of Oncology Wing 
  The scheme aims to correct the geographical  imbalance by providing financial assistance to 
Government institutions (Medical Colleges as well as Government hospitals) for enhancing the cancer 
care facilities. The one-time grant has been enhan ced from Rs. 2.00 crores to Rs. 3.00 crores. Under 
the Oncology Wing scheme 13 proposals worth Rs. 26.46 crores have been cleared for financial 
assistance till date for the year 2005-06. 
 (iv) Decentralized NGO Scheme: 
  This scheme has been devised to promote preventi on and early detection of cancers. Non-government 
organizations (NGOs) will implement these activi ties under the coordination of the Nodal Agency, 
which will be an RCC or an Oncology Wing. A grant of Rs. 8000/- per camp will be provided for 
organizing camps for IEC and early detection activities. 
 (v) This scheme lays focus on presentation, scre ening, early detection and treatment of Cancer. The 
programme would be managed and operationalized by nodal instituti ons, e.g. RCCs or Government 
Medical Colleges and Government Hospitals wh ich have well developed radiotherapy/oncology 
facilities. The districts would be selected on the recommendation of the State Government and a 
financial assistance of Rs. 22.00 lakhs in the first year and Rs. 17.00 lakhs in each of the next four

years, whereafter it is expected that the project would be taken over by the Government. It is proposed 
that the activities will be carried out in two or three districts congruent to the district selected for 
DCCP. The nodal institutions would carry out traini ng of health workers, ANMs, self-help groups etc. 
Under the DCCP IEC activities would also be carried out for promoting prevention, awareness, self-
breast examination, early detection of cancer, anti- tobacco activities etc, in which NGOs would be

XXV. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME  
Japanese Encephalitis 
Recommendations/Observations 
25.4.3 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by media re ports saying that about 3.4 crore children between the 
age of 1 and 15 need to be vaccinated. The Committee has been informed that vaccine worth Rs. 50.00 crore has 
been imported from China and a massive immunization programme has been planned. The Committee has been 
given to understand that an inexpensive vaccine for Japanese  Encephalitis (JE) is availa ble which other JE affected 
countries are currently using to contro l the disease. The Secretary assured th e Committee that appropriate measures 
have been taken by the Centre to effectively control any ep idemic outbreak of JE in any part of the country. The 
Committee would like to be informed about the vaccine that is available in the internat ional market and what has 
been its success rate in controlling JE in the user countries. The Committee hopes that all preventive measures will 
continue to be made on a sustained basis so that epidemic of J.E. which occurred in UP in 2005 may not recur. 
Action Taken 
 JE vaccination programme has been made an integral component of Universal Immunization Programme in a 
phased manner using single dose live attenuated AS-14-14-2 vaccine. During 2006, 135 lakhs doses of live 
attenuated JE vaccine (SA-14-14-2) were  imported from China by Gol. Total co st of vaccine including delivery at 
site is Rs. 12.83 crores and unit cost is Rs.9.50 per dose. 
 Three types of JE vaccine are curren tly in use in JE endemic countries of Asia-Pacific Region as detailed 
below: 
 (i)  Mouse brain-derived inactivated vaccine: The mouse brain-derived in activated JE vaccine is 
produced in several Asian countries such as India, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. So 
far, this is the only type of JE vaccine that is co mmercially available in the international market. In 
Thailand, JE vaccination has been successfully incorporated into the national immunization 
programme. Studies in Korea and Japan showed > 99 per cent reduction in JE cases after 
immunization. In India, inactivated vaccine is being manufactured at the Central Research Institute 
(CRI), Kasauli and the cost per dose is about Rs.50/-. 
  The mouse brain-derived JE vaccine is administered in 3 doses of 0.5 ml or 1 ml (days 0, 7, 30) and 
booster doses at the intervals of every 3 years. In several Asian trials, primary immunization has a 
disease-preventing efficacy of > 95 per cent. Howeve r, the production capacity of CRI, Kasauli is 
limited and do not meet the requirements of endemic States. 
 (ii) Cell culture-derived live attenuated vaccine: This Chinese vaccine is based on a stable neuro-
attenuated strain of the JE virus (SA-14-14-2). In non-endemic areas, 1 single dose of this vaccine 
induced an antibody response in 83 per cent-100 per cent of children aged 6-7 years and in older 
children immunized twice a t intervals of 1-3 mont hs, 94 per cent-100 per cen t showed a serological 
response. Apart from hundreds of m illions of doses used in China, In dia began introduction of this 
vaccine in eleven high endemic districts in four St ates during 2006. This vaccine is also in use in 
Nepal and South Korea. 
 (iii) Cell culture-derived inactivated vaccine: This vaccine is being manufactured in China. Primary 
immunization of infants with this fo rmalin-inactivated vaccine results in about 85 per cent protection. 

The vaccine is inexpensive, and upto 90 million doses are distributed for use in China every year. 
However, in China the cell culture-derived live attenuated vaccine is gradually replacing this vaccine. 
  Besides vaccination in highly endemic district s for prevention and contro l of JE, guidelines and 
advisories have been sent for planning and implementation of district-wise specific action plan. Efforts 
are on to strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnost ic facility, treatment centres at periphery in JE 
endemic areas. Training is being conducted in case management for Clinicians and Nurses.

25.5 Chicken Guinea 
25.5.1 The Committee then drew the atte ntion of the Secretary towards the outbreak of Chicken Guinea epidemic in 
some parts of the country that was widely spreading. The Committee was informed that three States, Andhra Pradesh, 
Karnataka and Maharashtra were affected. Nearly 25,000 pe ople were suspected to be affected by Chicken Guinea 
virus. Nearly 50 per cent positivity has been confirme d by NICD, Delhi and 35 per cent by NIV, Pune. The 
Committee was given to understand that State Government was taking appropriate steps. 
25.5.2 The Committee is however, not inclined to agree with the reported cases of Chicken Guinea disease in 
Andhra Pradesh. The Committee’s apprehensions are based on first-hand information reports being received from the 
affected districts of Andhra Pradesh as  per which the disease has already affected a very large number of people and 
spreading fast. The Committee is of the firm opinion that required steps need to be initiated by the Centre on an 
urgent basis. 
Action Taken 
 The Government of India has already initiated requisite  action for effective cont rol of Chikungunya in the 
State of Andhra Pradesh. The following measures have b een taken to tackle the problem of Chikungunya in the 
affected States including Andhra Pradesh: 
 • States have been provided detailed guidelines for prevention and control of Chikungunya fever. 
 • The teams from National Institute of Communicabl e Diseases and NVBDCP undertook investigations 
in Andhra Pradesh from 13-17th Feb., 2006. The Director, NVBDCP reviewed the Chikungunya 
situation of Andhra Pradesh on 26th June, 2006 and on 29th July, 2006. 
 • The State has been provided with 7,700 It. of Temephos and 4,500 It. of Pyrethrum extract (2 per 
cent). 
 States have been authorized to utilize funds ma de available under NVBDCP for awareness campaigns. 
Recommendations/Observations 
25.5.3 The Committee was informed by th e Director of ICMR that a research team has been sent to the affected 
district, which will be sending its reports about the actual nu mber of cases in Chittoor district and adjoining areas in 
Andhra Pradesh. The Committee would like to point out th at alongwith the assessment of epidemic outbreak, 
preventive measures were required to be initiated without any further delay. Health education and water management 
system are the two priority areas which need to be attended to, to prevent the ongoing epidemic as well as such 
outbreaks in future. The Committee woul d, therefore, recommend that the Department now take, a pro-active 
approach towards preventive measures in active co-ordin ation with state and local authorities. Otherwise such 
outbreaks of epidemic would continue to occur. 
Action Taken 
 Two teams from the National Institute of Epidemiolo gy (ME), Chennai and Centre for Research in Medical 
Entomology (CRME), Madurai, carried out investigation in Tirupati during 8- 12 April, 2006. Earlier a team from 
NIE had visited Kadapa for investigating the outbreak in the district. 
 The team in Tirupati interacted with District Health Authorities and with some of private practitioners in 
Tirupati who had treated several cases of Chikungunya. The team carried out repeated sample survey in urban 
ward/villages affected by Chikungunya in and around Tiru pati to establish the proportion of individuals having 
symptoms indicative of Chikungunya fever. Rapid environmental survey was done to assess water storage and usage 
in the area and mosquitogenic conditions. The team carried out the survey in Bramhagunta, Nehru Nagar at Tirupati, 

Vinayak Nagar, Bogga Street at Reningunta and Ambedkar Nagar at Chittur. A total of 219 individuals from 44 
households were interviewed for the presence of symptoms indicative of Chikungunya ( i.e. fever and joint plain). 76 
(34.7 per cent) of the individuals were having symptoms suggestive of Chikungunya fever. The clinical 
manifestations of the disease included fever that was short lasting (for about 1-3 days) and joint pains. A few of the 
patients also had macuto-papular rash especially on trunk . Swelling of the affected joint was also a common feature 
among the affected individuals. In the localities surveyed, people used to store water in cement tanks, big earthen 
vessels, plastic drums and pitchers. Of the 44 houses survey ed, 29 (65.9 per cent) showed presence of Aedes larva in 
these containers. 
 In district Kadapa, the team carried out house-to-hou se survey in Mallela village in Thondur PHC having a 
population of 1965 to identify suspected cases of Chikungunya. A total of 243 (12.4 per cent) suspected cases of 
Chikungunya fever were identified during the survey. 58.4 per cent of the cases were females. No deaths were 
reported due to Chikungunya in the village surveyed. All age groups are affected but incidence was high in the age 
group of 15 years and above. Cases of Chikungunya were occurring in the village since first week of December 2005 
and reached the peak in the third week of March, 2006. Of the 8 areas of villa ges surveyed, the prevalence of disease 
ranged between 0 to 20.6 per cent. 
 Environmental survey was carried out in Sarpanch B azar, Sivalyam Street, Muslim area and BC colony. A 
total of 56 households were surveyed for presence of larvae  in various clean water containers. The type of containers 
included cement tanks, earthen pots, plastic drums and pitc hers. 22 of the 108 (20.4 per cent) containers were having 
mosquito larvae. 17 of 56 (30.4 per cent) houses were having containers with mosquito larvae. 
 The team visited 34 of the 57 affected PHCs in the di strict and collected information regarding the number of 
suspected cases of Chikungunya attending the outpatient clin ics (defined as fever with joint pains). The team also 
collected information regarding the number of suspected cases identified through various medical camps that were 
conducted in different villages in th e affected PHCs. Analysis of the data  from these sources revealed that the 
outbreak is still ongoing and indications are that it is likely to continue and spre ad further. Estimates available at the 
district were mainly based on the figures of medical camp s carried out in various affected villages. Based on the 
investigations carried out in Tirupati and Kadapa, the ICMR teams recommended the following: 
 (i) Anti-larval activities 
 (ii) Strengthening of disease surveillance 
 (iii) Rational use of medications 
 (iv) Community awareness

XVIII. AVIAN INFLUENZA  
Recommendations/Observations 
18.3 The Committee has been informed that the Ministry has spent a large amount of money to procure medicine 
for bird flu from one particular firm namely - Hetro Drug s. This medicine, however, has an expiry period of six 
months after which it will be unfit for human consumption. Although no human case of bird flu has been reported so 
far, it is understood that an order for 1 lakh vials of vaccine (one vial costing about 12 dollars) has been placed. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly feels that an enquiry may be carried out by the Department. Committee may be 
apprised about the outcome thereof. 
18.4 The Committee has been informed about an advertisement in the media which promotes the consumption of 
Indian Chicken. The advertisement shows popular cine stars vouchsafing that there is no health hazard involved in 
eating chicken. This advertisement was sponsored by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee 
understands that the promotion of any general food item doe s not fall within the domain of Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare whose mandate is to regulate the medical sector and not the cause of some other agency. This, the 
Committee feels is sheer wastage of money. 
Action Taken 
 Government of India over the last 1½ years has b een preparing itself for handling any outbreak of avian 
influenza in the country. As per the WHO guidelines, Pandemic Preparedness plan, Contingency Plan and State 
Action Plan have been duly prepared. 
 As a part of the Contingency Plan, it was decided by  a Committee of Secretaries headed by Cabinet Secretary 
to create a national stock pile of anti viral drugs of 1 la kh courses. This was in accordance with WHO guidelines and 
considered to be a necessary preventive measure. 
 The quantity of one lakh courses was procured at an approximate cost of  Rs.7.00 crores (Rupees seven crores 
only) from M/s Roche and from M/s Hetero Drugs Ltd. 
 These purchases were processed by an Inter Ministerial Task Force that had been set up with the following 
terms of reference: 
 (i) To assess the drugs and vaccines required for managing the Avian Flu virus including their 
availability/non-availability in India; 
 (ii) To examine the possibility of manufacturing these drugs/vaccines in India including: 
 (a) the possibility of resorting to the provisions of public health emergency under the patents law;  
 (b) the possibility of compulsory licensing of Indian companies to manufacture the required 
drugs/vaccines.  
 The members of the Task Force are - 

 (i) Secretary, Ministry of  Health and Family Welfare 
 (ii) Secretary, Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying 
 (iii) Secretary, Chemicals and Petrochemicals 
 (iv) Secretary, Industrial Policy and Promotion 
 (v) Secretary, Department of Biotechnology 
 (vi) Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research 
 (vii) DG, ICMR 
 (viii) Drug Controller of India 
 (ix) Director General of Health Services, Government of India. 
 This Committee contacted Indian Pharma Companies like Hetero Drugs, Ranbaxy and Cipla in a meeting held 
on 18.11.2005. Only Hetero Drugs offered to supply the drug in quantities required by the Government of India. 
 It was decided to procure 50,000 courses of Oseltamivi r Phosphate from Hetero Drugs Limited at Rs.600.00 + 
Excise Duty + Sales Tax, total cost for Rs.724/- per pack of 10 capsules. Hetero Drugs gave an additional discount of 
2 per cent on their quoted price. An order for 30,000 courses of Tami flu was placed with Roche for delivery by 
March/April,2006. When the outbreak of Avian Influenza was announced at Navapur in February this year, another 
20,000 courses were purchased from Hetero Drugs Limited. This drug has a shelf life of three to five years and not 
six months. Therefore, this drug will remain available for use. This drug is necessary not only for the treatment of 
human cases of avian influenza but also as a prophylactic for health and animal husbandry workers who are deployed 
for surveillance, culling and clean up ope rations in the area of infection amongst  poultry. During the outbreaks at 
Navapur, Jalagaon, Surat and Burhanpur, this drug was administered to Rapid Response Teams, Cullers, Clean up 
labour, surveillance workers and patients suspected to have been in close contact with infected poultry. More than 
3000 courses have already been used in the field. Additionally, this drug has also been provided to HSABL Bhopal 
and NICD for cover to workers testing samples. During the outbreak in Turkey, this dr ug was also supplied to the 
Indian Mission there. 
 It would be evident from the facts narrated above that  Government of India have followed a very transparent 
procedure in procuring anti viral drugs for Avian Influenza.  Had this prophylactic cover not been available, it would 
not have been possible to undertake the massive culling and clean up operations. The workers had first to be 
reassured about their personal security. 
 In so far as advertisements in media are concerned, it is clarified that this Ministry has not issued nor 
sponsored any advertisement that shows popular cine stars promoting the consumption of Indian Poultry. This 
advertisement was reportedly released by the National Eg g Co-ordination Committee. Other press advertisements 
promoting consumption of well-cooked chicken were released and paid for by the Department of Animal Husbandry 
and Dairying. This Ministry has only released Press Advert isements about Do’s and Don’s and FAQs pertaining to 
Avian Flu.

indicates that in a few High Focus States, NRHM is yet to take off. Status of activities in Uttar Pradesh, the most 
crucial State under the Mission reveals a very discouraging scenario. Neither the Departments of Health and Family 
Welfare have been merged nor merger of  Societies and registration of Rogi Kalyan Samitis have taken place. Even 
MoU with GoI has not been signed. Status of selection process of ASHA, the most innovative component of the 
Mission is yet another non-starter in the State. Against 65,000 ASHAs to be selected, only 9548 ASHAs could be 
selected, with not even a single ASHA getting trained. Position is more or less the same in respect of other 
components. Jharkhand, Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh are the other States where preparatory exercise has barely 
started. Status of NRHM is equally worrying. Out of total 2,28,327 ASHAs proposed to be selected, only 1,45,546 
ASHAs have been selected as on 21.3.2006 with Rajasthan, Bihar, Orissa and Chhattisgarh almost meeting the target 
and U.P. and M.P. remaining way behind their target. In the case of NE States, H.P. and J and K, Assam is the only 
State which is almost touching its target, in respect of othe r States, selection of ASHAs is not even envisaged. What 
is more striking is that training of selected ASHAs is simply missing. Out of 1,45,546 selected ASHAs, only 32,000 
could be trained and these 32,000 are from one single Stat e of Chhattisgarh. In the case of NE States, HP and J and 
K, nobody seems to have given a thought to the most important aspect of training of ASHA under NRHM. The 
Committee observes that preparatory activities have take n place in most of seventeen Non High Focus States. 
However, in Delhi, the capital of th e country and nearest to the Department, it seems that the message has not 
reached so far. 
Action Taken 
 The first year of the Mission was the preparator y phase during which the States were setting up the 
institutional framework of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). 
 The Selection of Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) is one of th e key strategies under NRHM. During 
2005-06, 40 per cent ASHAs out of the total of 2.5 lakh originally envisaged under the Mission were expected to be 
selected. This has been far exceeded. Th ere are however some delay in starting the selection process in some States 
due to administrative reasons. The State of Uttar Pradesh was expected to select 27,000 ASHAs during 2005-06 
(there was no target allocated to the States as the pr ocess of selection of ASHA is a community based process 
wherein progress was a function of multiple factors including community participation and availability of appropriate 
voluntary workers). Against this, the State of U.P. has reported selection of 19,887 ASHAs during the period. 
 Till date 1.94 lakh ASHAs have already been selected in ten States out of which 78,174 ASHAs have also 
been trained, Mentoring Group for ASHA has been set up and various training modules have been finalized. 
 NRHM has taken off even though the pace of implementation of the Mission is not uniform throughout the 
country. The overall progress of the Mission, however, has been as per the expected schedule. A copy of status of the 
implementation of NRHM is enclosed. 

Recommendations/Observations 
24.5 The Committee understands that the State and District Health Missions are envisaged to be the central players 
in the monitoring of the performance le vel of the various initiatives under the Mission. Both State and District 
Missions have been set up in all the States with a few ex ceptions. However, with only six State Action Plans and 151 
District Action Plans prepared so far, one cannot say that  any monitoring is being done so far. The Committee is of 
the firm opinion that the Department should continue making persistent efforts with all the concerned States so that 
NRHM takes off in the real sense. The Committee would al so like to point out that NRHM is a well-conceived 
Programme but the fact remains that it is the State Gove rnments that would be the im plementing agencies. Not only 
the flagship programmes of Family We lfare but also some of the major Disease Control programmes have been 
brought under one Umbrella Programme. Experience with re gard to implementation of National Health Programmes 
and Family Welfare Programmes on individual programme basi s has varied so far from State to State. Status of 
various Health Indicators and availability of unspent balanc es with the implementing agencies clearly indicates lack 
of effective monitoring mechanism. The Committee is not very convinced especially in view of so many 
programmes. Another complex dimension of the Mission will be inter-sectoral convergence, with the concerned 
Ministries. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that  a highly dedicated team at the Centre alongwith its 
counterparts in States can only be effective. 
Action Taken 
 The framework of the Mission provides for regular monitoring and evaluation of the implementation of the 
various strategies under the NRHM. This is done through regu lar review meetings, data collection, visits to States by 
officers of the GoI and interaction with  the State officials etc. To ensure the compliance with overall NRHM goals, 
the institutional framework in the State including State and District health Mi ssions are also monitoring the progress 
of implementation of the Mission. The Mission also envisages a proactive role for the community in monitoring the 
service delivery in the Health facilities. As part of this initiative, Rogi Kalyan Samitis have been envisaged under the 
Mission and over 6000 Samitis have already been operatio nalized in various States. The detailed multilevel 
monitoring protocols under the NRHM are being made full y operational and the progress of the Mission activities 
including the utilization of funds at various levels is expected to show substantial improvement over the coming 
years. 
 The significant role of Inter-Sectoral Convergence in ensuring the delivery of preventive, promotive and 
curative health care in a holistic manner  is fully articulated in th e strategies of the Mission. The Integrated district 
Health Action Plan is envisaged to be comprehensive docu ment which provides the framework for integrating all the 
related determinants of health into a common plan of Action. 
 The State Plans and Integrated  District Health Action Plans are envisaged to be finalized by all the Districts by 
December, 2006. The funds for this activity have already be en released along with deta iled guidelines and several 
districts are in final stages of preparation of the plans. 
XXV. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME  
Recommendations/Observations 
25.5.5 The Committee observes that the National Institute of Communicable Diseases (NICD) is an apex referral 
organisation meant for prevention and control of communicabl e diseases in the country. Its most important mandate 
is to evolve an integrated approach for early warning si gnals and surveillance of diseases of major public health 
importance. Government has also initiated the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme since 2004-05. The 
Committee feels that with such an effe ctive mechanism in place, instances like  recent outbreak of chickengunya in 
Andhra Pradesh and other adjoin ing States should not be a llowed to reach such a serious dimension. The Committee 
hopes that all possible measures would be affected prom ptly. The Committee strongly feels that a suitable amount 
may be allotted for the total eradication of chickengunya fever in districts of Chittoor of Andhra Pradesh and 
Bangalore city. 
Action Taken 
 The GoI has already initiated action for effective prevention and control of chikungunya including supply of 
logistics and funds for awareness activities as indicated in Para 25.5.3. 

 The NICD is an apex organisation under Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, Government of India. The Institute functions with following mandates: 
 (i) Trained Manpower Development for Disease Control. 
 (ii) Operational Research 
 (iii) Referral Diagnostic and Specialized Services 
 The institute extends support to States in carrying out epidemiological investigations and provides feedback 
for appropriate remedial measures. Surveillance is the key activity for generating early warning signals of impending 
outbreaks and to strengthen the same, Government of India initiated National Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases (NSPDS) as a p ilot project during 1997-98 with NICD as the nodal agency and program 
covered 101 districts in a phased manner. Subsequently a World Bank funded Integrated Disease Surveillance Project 
was launched in November 2004 for decentralized State based surveillance of communicable and non-communicable 
diseases. Advanced Information Technology set up under IDSP is currently being established across the country and 
all districts in the country are being interconnected us ing satellite/broadband technology. Regular collection of 
syndromic and presumptive surveillance data on weekly basis ha s also been started. This data would get analyzed at 
the district level itself and the IDSP software would genera te the early warning signals ba sed on the trigger levels of 
different diseases being covered. The di strict and the State would start getting the early warning signals that would 
evolve with the complete data collection and data analysis ac tivity at district level. The project also has a component 
of upgradation of the State/District Public Health labs. The project was being implemented from MOH and FW and 
has recently been shifted to NICD. 
XXVIII. INFRASTRUCTURE  
Recommendations/Observations 
28.4 The Committee understands that a Task Force has been  set up on review of population norms for setting up of 
Health Centre. The Committee would like to be informed about the major recommendations of this Task Force as and 
when made. 
Action Taken 
 Since the position of ANMs is linked to the number of Sub-Centres, it has resulted in inadequate availability 
of health services, taking into account the population norms as followed presently. It would, therefore, proposed to 
revisit the population norm and effort be made to link the number of ANMs at any Sub-Centre to caseload and the 
distance of village/habitation which comprise the Sub-Cent re. The same logic applies to the number of PHCs and 
CHCs taking into account the staff number at these ins titutions.. Framework for Implementation (2005-2012) of 
NRHM has incorporated the necessity of reconsidering and revising the norms for setting up of health centres. 
Steering Committee in the Planning Commission on Primary He alth Care (Eleventh Five Year Plan) is also looking 
into the issue of review of population norms for setting up  of health centres. The major recommendations of this 
committee will be intimated as soon as they are available. 
Recommendations/Observations 
28.8 The Committee understands that a Task Force constit uted under NRHM has given a number of very crucial 
recommendations to ensure availability of doctors in rural areas. The Committee would appreciate if follow-up action 
is initiated both at the Central and State level at the earli est. The Committee is happy to learn that number of States 
like Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh, Tripura, Sikkim, Himachal Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Orissa and Gujarat have come 
forward in formulating strategic policies to attract and pe rsuade doctors to serve in rural areas. The Committee hopes 
that such initiatives will result in marked improvement in  quality of Primary Health Care. The Committee finds that 
Tamil Nadu is the only State which has provided residentia l accommodation to doctors in most of the PHCs. While 
making the stay of doctors compulsory, strict action is also required to be taken against the erring doctors. The 
Committee is of the view that similar action needs to be taken by other States also. The Committee would appreciate 
if the Centre takes a pro-active approach in this regard by  taking up with other States to follow the above example. 
Another initiative that has come to the notice of the Comm ittee is handing over of PHCs to selected NGOs by States 
like Orissa, Bihar, Uttaranchal, Delhi, Jharkhand and Karn ataka. The Committee is of the view that performance of 
such PHCs needs to be monitored to assess the outc ome of such experiments for further improvement and 
diversification, if necessary. The Committee would like to be apprised about the performance level of such NGOs 
during the year 2005-06. 

 As per the census of 2001, due to increase of popu lation, proportionate new Primary Health Centres and Sub-
centres need to be started all over the country. This ne eds budget allocation. The Committee therefore recommends 
that budget allocation should be suitably enhanced. 
Action Taken 
 A number of States have taken various initiatives to ensure the presence of doctors in rural areas such as 
follows:  
 The Government of Punjab has taken following measures: 
 • First posting in Rural/Difficult areas for three years. 
 • Three years rural posting essential for applying for PG courses. 
 • The State is actively considering the appointment of doctors on contract basis. 
 The Steps taken by Government of Arunachal Pradesh include: 
 • Mandatory three years service in rural areas to re gulate the nomination of serving doctors to various 
post-graduate and in-service training courses. 
 • Identification of certain station as “soft and ur ban” posting places for the purpose of selecting in-
service candidates for post-graduate and in-service training courses. 
 • Classification of the locations of  posting of doctors as category A, B and C and compulsory rotation of 
doctors on completion of prescribed tenure as per classification of locations. 
 • Introduction of contractual appointment of doctors. 
 The steps taken by the State Government of Tripura are: 
 • First posting of medical officers is essential in ru ral/interior areas for three years. The period does not 
include any kind of leave enjoyed. 
 • Three years rural service is a pre-condition for nomination to undertake Post-Graduate study. 
 • Availing of the facility of forgoing non-pra cticing allowance and undertaking practice without 
compromising on assigned duties, as per the service rules. 
 • Attempts are being made to work out details for of fering choice posting after tenure in rural/interior 
areas. 
 • Medical officers were appointed on contract basi s and posted near their home places, to make the 
package attractive. 
 • The State Government is not considering any in centive in the form of allowance etc. to medical 
officers during their posting in rural/interior areas  since this will have a cascading effect on other 
categories of Government employees also. 
 The Government of Sikkim has taken the following measures: 
 • It is mandatory for all MOs to complete 3 years of rural posting in PHCs to enable them to qualify for 
nomination for PG studies by the State. 
 • The MOs posted in the PHCs are given Rural Ar ea allowances of Rs. 1000/-pm which is an added 
incentive for them to opt for rural posting. 
 The following measures have been taken by the State Government of Himachal Pradesh: 
 • First posting in rural/difficult area for 3 years 
 • Tenure of posting in the rural/difficult area is a pre-requisite for promotion, foreign assignment or 
training abroad 
 • Three years rural posting essential for applying for PG Courses. 
 • Choice of posting after rural/difficult area tenure. 
 • Appointment of doctors on contract basis. 
 • Rural/difficult area incentive in form of allowance, retention of Government accommodation in the 
place of last posting for family. 

 The details of steps taken by the Government of Tamil Nadu are: 
 • Persons selected by direct recruitment through the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission are being 
posted in the Primary Health Centres that are rural an d difficult areas. They should serve compulsorily 
for a minimum period of 3 years in the PHCs. 
 • Three years of rural service ha s been made compulsory for applyi ng for Post-Graduate Course as a 
service candidate. 50 per cent of the total seats ar e reserved for the service candidates and the post-
graduate study period is being treated as duty period, countable for pension. 
 • After completing 3 years of rural service, Post-G raduate qualified candidates are being released to 
Government Hospitals/Government Medical Colleges according to the requirement. 
 • Orders were issued appointing 186 doctors to the 93 upgraded PHCs on contract basis for a period of 
one year on a consolidated pay of Rs. 8000/- per mensem. 
 • Doctors working in rura l areas are granted incentives such as rural allowance for serving in rural areas. 
They are also provided with quarters in most of the PHCs. Stay at the HQ’s  of the PHCs has been 
made compulsory and strict action is being taken against erring Medical Officers. Further, those who 
stay in the HQs alone are allowed for Post Gradua te Courses. Weightage marks are given for rural 
service for selection to Post Graduate Courses. 
 The Government of Mizoram has informed that they have not framed transfer and posting norms for their 
doctors, as they do not have much prob lem in posting their doctors in the rural areas. Doctors are normally posted in 
the rural area and hard places on rotation. 
 The Action Taken Report of the Government of Orissa includes: 
 • Introduction of modified internship in the State for Undergraduate students under which three months 
are set aside for compulsory rural service. 
 • It has been decided that a candidate who has worked  as Medical Officer for three years or more in any 
rural area/tribal area/backward area shall be entitled to get 5 per cent of marks added to his qualifying 
marks. 
 • Before going for PG study, the selected PG candidates do one-year mandatory rural services. 
 • The candidate selected for the first recruitment posting of the Orissa Medical Service shall have to 
serve the initial period of minimum 3 years of services in backward areas and next three years in rural 
areas. 
 • In order to be eligible for promotion to the rank of Specialist/Junior Class-I, an Assistant Surgeon shall 
have to render not less than 7 years of services as such inclusive 3 years of rural service. 
 The Government of Gujarat gives a doctor an additional Rs.500 for working in the tribal and remote areas. The 
following steps are under consideration of the Government: 
 • Reservation of 10 per cent of seats for Post-graduation in Obs. and Gyne., PSM, Paediatrics, 
Anaesthesia for doctors who have worked in remote and inaccessible areas continuously for 5 years. 
 • Enhancing incentive pay of Rs.500 to 20 per cent of the pay in the remote and tribal areas. 
  Monitoring of PHCs to selected NGOs is done by concerned State Government. Their monitoring 
reports and performance level during the year 2005 -06 will be obtained to be placed before the 
Committee. Visits to the concerned States would also  be undertaken by the officers of the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare. 
 Under NRHM, it is proposed to set up Sub-Centres as  per 2001 population norms all over the country and 
upgrading existing Sub-Centres including building for Sub-Centres functioning in rented premises. The funds for 
setting up of PHCs are provided by Planning Commission un der PMGY. However, under NRHM, it is proposed to 
provide funds for improving physical infrastructure of PHCs. The recommendation of the Committee for enhancing 
the budget allocation is noted for compliance.

29.3 The Committee understands that a provision of Rs. 23 5 crores was kept under World Bank assisted RCH-II 
project during 2005-06 for procurement of supplies and material including medicines for sub centre, PHCs and CHCs 
could not be utilized as M/s HSCC agency of the Departme nt could not float tenders due to delayed receipt of No 
Objection from the World Bank. The Committee takes a serious  view of this. It seems delay in receipt of NOC from 
World Bank must have occurred due to want of some re quired information by the World Bank. If that be so, the

Action Taken 
 The World Bank assisted RCH-I programme ended in March, 2005. Just before the 2006, negotiation with the 
World Bank for RCH-II, which was due in April, 2005, the Bank submitted a confidential interim report based on the

 During the negotiation with the World Bank, the procurement issues were discussed extensively. As an

the weakness of the procurement system. One of the important features of GAAP is to set up a Centralized 

Procurement Unit in the Deptt. Consequently, the Deptt.  of Health and Family Welfare established Empowered 
Procurement Wing (EWP) to consolidate,  streamline and strengthen  the procurement activity and to professionalize 
the procurement of Health Sector Goods. The negotiations with the World Bank have since been successfully 
completed on 15 July, 2006.
