XXXI. FOREIGN FUNDING  
Recommendation/Observations 
31.5 The Committee observes that damage-control exercise  has been started by the Department in the matter of 
World Bank funding for various projects being put on hold . The Committee is of the view that the very fact that 
instances of corruption and fraud in a number of projects during a prolonged time-frame being noticed by World 
Bank and its funding being put on hold establishes that th ere were inherent flaws in the procurement system which 
went unnoticed for a considerable period of time. Quantum of World Bank funding being too small or Government 
ability to manage in the absence of the same cannot bring back the loss of prestige of the country world over and 
setback to various projects in Health and Family Welfar e sector. The Committee is of the opinion that a thorough 
assessment of procurement procedure in respect of all pr ojects whether foreign funded or otherwise needs to be 
made. This task can be entrusted to the Empowered Proc urement Committee of the Ministry and some independent 
experts should also be involved in this exercise. The Committee would also like to reiterate that monitoring 
mechanism needs to be further strengthened and activated . The Committee would like to be apprised about the final 
outcome of ongoing CBI investigation in the matter of World Bank funding. 
Action Taken 
 Under Empowered Procurement Wing (EPW), the Department of Health and Family Welfare has engaged the 
services of a Consultant Organizatio n to strengthen the procurement process in the Department. The Consultant 
Organization will conduct a comprehensive review of existi ng procurement system, resources, procedure etc. in the 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to identify the ar eas that need further strengthening. The Team Leader of 
Consultant Organization to strengthen the EPW is review ing the existing system of procurement. Consultant 
organization will also assist the Department to establis h a system for procurement m onitoring, reporting, supplier 

performance and complaint database and to develop detailed complaint redressal procedure. CBI is investigating the 
matter and yet to submit its report. 
XXXII. DECLINING SEX RATIO 
Recommendations/Observations 
32.1 Declining trend in the child sex ra tio has been a matter of serious concern. Child sex ratio in the age group of 
0-6 years has been show ing a continuous decline over the decades, fr om 976 in 1961 to 927 in 2001. Specially 
vulnerable States have been Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh and Himachal Pradesh showing more than 50 points 
decline during the decade 1991-2001. 
Recommendations/Observations 
32.2 The Committee observes that besides th e age-old factors responsible for this dismal situation, easy availability 
of sex determination tests across the country can be consid ered as a reason behind the declining sex ratio. Coming 
into force of the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act in 1996 and subsequent 
amendments made to remove the inherent inadequacies has so far failed to make any impact in checking this malaise. 
Action Taken 
 To give special focus to the States of Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan, Gujarat etc., a ‘National Support and 
Monitoring Cell’ with external assistance for effective implementation of the Act by appointing professionals from 
police, law and social sciences as consultants has been set up. The major exception is that the cell will help in putting 
a mechanism in place so that actual wrong doers who are committing female foeticide/abetting female foeticide are 
apprehended by the Appropriate Authorities. They are expected to network with the Appropriate Authorities/medical 
officers in the State and help in stepping up successful "sting/decoy operations" by the Appropriate Authorities to nab 
the actual wrong doers. 

CHAPTER-III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT 
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE COMMITTEE 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION  
Recommendations/Observations 
2.1 Total allocation for the Department of Health and Fami ly Welfare for the year 2006-07 is  Rs. 12545.88 crores 
against the provision of Rs. 10307.30 crores in 2005-06. Th e Committee notes that year wise trend of both allocation 
and expenditure during Ninth and Tenth Plan shows a steady enhancement. Expenditure reported in 1997-98 (first 
year of Ninth Plan) was Rs. 3476.12 crores which has reached to Rs. 9210.46 crores in 2005-06 (Fourth year of the 
Tenth Plan). Committee’s attention has, however, been constantly drawn by one disturbing factor. Over the years, the 
Department has not been able to keep pace with the enha nced allocation of plan funds. Every year, invariably, BE 
allocation gets reduced at the RE stage and expenditure reported is even lesser. Year 2005-06 was no exception. Plan 
allocation of Rs. 9332.00 crore was brought down by almost Rs. 1000.00 crores (Rs. 8500.00 crores) at the RE stage 
and the actual expenditure reported was only Rs. 8076.76 cr ores. The Committee, however, notes that the position is 
entirely different with regard to the trend of allocat ion and utilization of non-plan  funds. Against a non-plan 
allocation of Rs. 943.09 crores in 2004-05, expenditure reported was Rs. 1227.81 crores. Similarly in 2005-06, there 
was an expenditure of Rs. 1133.70 crores against BE provision of  Rs. 975.36 crores. What is more worrisome is that 
shortfall of non-plan allocation has been made good by appropriating funds from plan allocation. Details made 
available to the Committee clearly indicate that position has deteriorated over the years. Diversion of plan funds 
under health schemes of Rs. 68.43 crores to non-plan in 2002-03, has reached the figure of Rs. 289.13 crores in 2005-
06. The Committee finds that premier institutions like AIIMS continue to be deprived of required non-plan funds. 
Position was the same with CGHS. The Committee apprehends that position may be the same more or less in respect 
of other institutions and schemes. The Committee fails to  comprehend the reasons for non-provision of required non-
plan funds. The Committee understands that as a result of concerted efforts made at th e Secretary and Ministerial 
level by the Department, there has been some increase in  the allocation of non-plan funds in 2005-06 which however 
proved to be inadequate. The Committee w ould like to emphasize that there is an  urgent need to curb the trend of 
diversion of plan funds to non-plan side. Such a position cannot be considered advisable for the successful 
implementation of any plan scheme. 
Action Taken 
 We agree with the committee’s observation that diversio n of funds from Plan to Non-plan is not a healthy 
trend. However, this apparently has been resorted to by the Ministry on account of shortage of funds under the non-
plan in respect of certain major health institutions like AIIMS.  It is felt that an internal exercise is necessary to look 
into the non-plan budget particularly of institutions like AIIMS and a strategy be drawn up for the same so that we 
may avoid such transfer of funds from Plan to non-plan side. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is surprised by the response of the Department to such an im portant issue. Instead of 
taking any corrective measures, the Department is simp ly reiterating the observat ion of the Committee made 
last year. The Committee can only conclude that status of diversion of plan funds to non-plan side would be 
the same this year too. The Commi ttee views with serious concern the la ck of action on the part of the 
Department.  
Recommendations/Observations 
2.2 To ensure optimum and judicious utilization of allocated funds, for any scheme, prescribed financial norms 
need to be strictly adhered to. Non-existence of pending  utilization certificates and non-availability of unspent 
balances are the two visible symptoms thereof. The Committe e is, however, constrained to observe that both pending 
UCs and unspent balances continue to persist. This clearly  indicates the failure of im plementing agencies both in the 
private and Government Sector to successfully handle the schemes and also likelihood of inherent flaws in the 
schemes/projects. The Committee has been  given to understand that level of pendency of UCs/unspent balances has 
been reduced due to the constant efforts made by the De partment. However, UCs amounting to Rs. 1675.00 crores as 
on 31st March, 2006 and availability of unspent balanc es of Rs. 15.35 crores as on 1st January, 2006 cannot be 
considered a negligible amount. The Committee is of the vi ew that the Department need s to make all conceivable 

efforts to eliminate such pendency, by  making the monitoring mechanism at all levels more effective and result 
oriented. 
Action Taken 
 The directions of the Hon’ble Comm ittee has been noted for compliance.  
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is not happy with th e evasive reply of the Department. In stead of giving specific details 
about the various steps taken for reducing the pendency le vel of unspent balances and Utilization Certificates, 
simply noting the directions of the Committee for compliance cannot be considered an Action Taken Note.  
Recommendations/Observations 
2.3 The Committee would like to recall its observation made in the 7th Report that ''to meet the target contained in 
the National Health Policy, 2002, health sector needs manifold increase in budgetary support and recommended that 
external grant should be taken over and above the budgetary support''. The Committee, however, finds that the past 
practice of including external assistan ce in the gross Budget of the Departme nt is still continuing. In the domestic 
Budget for the year 2006-07, an external aid component of Rs. 1299.07 crores has been included. The Committee in 
this connection is constrained to observe that if the practice  of including external aid in domestic Budget continues, 
then the commitment of the Government to raise the allo cation in the health sector to 2-3 per cent of GDP will 
remain only on paper and not be realized in actual prac tice. Moreover, the Committee also feels that financing the 
non-plan expenditure by external aid is not a healthy pr actice. The Committee therefore, again recommends that the 
matter must be vigorously pursued with the Planning Comm ission and the Ministry of Finance to consider the 
external assistance over and above the gross budgetary support. 
Action Taken 
 The matter regarding External Assistance over and abov e the Gross Budgetary Support is being taken up with 
the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The matter of inclusion of external aid component in  domestic Budget has been engaging the attention 
of the Committee for quite some time. The Committee, ho wever, is surprised to note that instead of there 
being any positive development in this direction, the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance are yet 
to be approached. It seems that the Department is eith er not interested in additional funding or does not have 
the capacity to utilize the same. 
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME  
Recommendations/Observations 
3.4 The Committee expresses its deep sense of concern on the status of implementation of SIU Report on CGHS. 
This exercise has been going on for the last so many ye ars. The Committee finds that it was only after a fresh SIU 
study conducted on the orders of CAT that a final decision with regard to the posts of Safaiwala, Chowkidar, Lab 
technician, Lab Assistant and Lab Attendant could be arrive d at which was accepted by the Central Government in 
January, 2003. The Committee is, however, given to understand  that as in August, 2004, 453 posts of Safaiwala and 
284 posts of Chowkidar are to be progressively outsourced. Latest feedback in this regard as well as in respect of Lab 
staff still remains unavailable to the Committee. Not only th is, SIU Report may lead to another dispute. It has been 
informed that a number of posts are likely to be declared surplus on the basis of SIU Report. Accordingly, 
information on existing strength in the dispensaries ha ve been sought from CGHS units. The Committee takes a 
strong exception to this appr oach. The Committee is of the view that had there been regular interaction between the 
Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Health and Family We lfare, this kind of uncertainty would not have prevailed 
for so long. The Committee, therefor e, recommends that the Department should complete the exercise of 
implementation of SIU Report without any further delay. 
Action Taken 
 The directions of the Hon’ble Committee has been noted for compliance. 
Comments of the Committee 

 The Committee is constrained to observe that no pr ogress whatsoever seems to have been made in the 
implementation of SIU Report on CGHS. The Committee re iterates that a final view needs to be taken in the 
matter without any further delay. 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.6 The Committee was informed that a Committee has been set up on the 6t h May, 2005 under the Chairmanship 
of Shri P.K. Kaul, former Cabinet Secretary to review  the functioning of CGHS and make recommendations for 
making it more user-friendly. The Committee will also look into and suggest changes with  respect to the financial 
viability of the scheme in view of the rapidly incr easing expenditure in CGHS. The Committee may suggest 
alternative cost effective models of he alth care provisioning to Government employees as well as alternative source 
of financing the CGHS. The Committee notes that the Euro pean Commission is also funding a separate study of 
CGHS functioning to be conducted by the A.E Ferguson and Company. As per the Performance Budget (2006-07) of 
the Ministry, the report was expected in  the next three weeks. The Committee w ould, like to be apprised about the 
findings of EC study of CGHS which must have been received by the Ministry by now. 
Action Taken 
 The report prepared by M/s Ferguson and Company sponsored by European Commission has been received in 
1st week of July which is being examined. Broadly the report has suggested sweeping changes on the following 
subjects. 
 (a) Financial — CGHS is an open ended scheme providing unlimited OPD/IPD coverage with limited 
contribution and any attempt to increase the employee contribution or restrict the scheme coverage is a 
policy decision which the Government must take keeping in view the entire compassionate package 
that it would like to provide its employees. 
 (b) Procurement and supply chain — To prefer procurement structure suggestions are as  
under:- 
 (i) Rate Contract system 
 (ii) Formulation of procurement policy 
 (iii) Procurement Cell to be set up at the Central level for procurement etc. 
 (iv) Strengthen the tendering and rate fixation process  
 (v) Design an Integrated Materials Planning System  
 (vi) Strengthen Internal controls related with receipt and issue 
 (vii) Training of manpower on rele vant aspects of material management. 
 (c) Claims settlement — Suggestions are as under:- 
 (i) Better budgeting to counter delay in bill processing.  
 (ii) Preparation of claims settlement manual. 
 (iii) Monthly reporting. 
 (iv) Track and Analyze Refusal of Cred it and Deviation from Package rates. 
 (v) Claim Tracking Mechanism. A unique serial number to every claim for tracking to CGHS 
Website. 
 (vi) Low value claims say below Rs.500 be disposed off the dispensary level. 
 (d) Service delivery — This chapter provides over view of various service delivery points in the CGHS 
system and suggestions are as under:- 
 (i) Complete data base of CGHS beneficiaries. 
 (ii) Convenient timings for service employees.  
 (iii) Cut down waiting time at the dispensaries.  
 (iv) Re-designing of CGHS cards having data base of beneficiaries. 

 (v) Provision of better emergency services.  
 (vi) Behavioral aspects of the staff. 
 (vii) Specialists consultation.  
 (viii) Laboratory services . 
 (ix) In patient treatment. 
 (e) Hospital Recognition — A schedule may be prepared for the hospital recognition with set dates for 
initiation and completion of each activities. Differential rates may be considered. 
 (f) Grievance Handling — Suggestions are as under:- 
 (i) Set up standard guidelines for addressing grievances  
 (ii) Data base grievances received at all levels  
 (iii) Computerization for records  
 (iv) Monthly MIS on Grievances 
 (g) Utilization of Human resources and infrastructure — Suggestions are as under:- 
 (i) Consolidation of the dispensary 
 (ii) Manpower Utilization continuing CAB, Pharmacists and Nurses to be trained and 
Rationalization of class IV staff as per the workload assessment. 
 (iii) Utilization of Laboratories suggest optimum utilization of the facilities by relax timings, 
reducing the cost of service delivery and to improve beneficiaries satisfactorily. 
 (iv) This chapter focuses on strategic option available to CGHS for outsourcing its operation for 
example Insurance Scheme, TPAs etc.  
 (h) Governance and Autonomy — Suggestions are as under:- 
 (i) Convert CGHS into an autonomous Organization with a well defined framework for 
governance. 
 In this regard it is stated that the above recommend ations of the Committee are being examined and decision 
taken by the Government on the recommendation will be communicated in due course. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been informed that report of the European Commission sponsored study of CGHS 
has been received in the 1st week of July and is at present under examination in the Ministry. The Committee 
fails to understand the reason for undue delay in taking  a view on the report on the part of the Department. 
The Committee would once again emphasize that the De partment needs to take co rrective measures based on 
the study reports of both European Commission and Kaul Committee, but within the parameters of the 
existing system. Recommendations/Observations 
3.7 The Committee fails to understand the rationale for having two studies on the fu nctioning of CGHS being 
conducted simultaneously specially in view of the mand ate of the Kaul Committee covering all aspects of CGHS 
functioning. The Committee is surprised to note that alth ough almost a year has passed since the setting up of the 
Kaul Committee, it has met only on three occasions. It seems only preliminary exerci se has been done by this 
Committee so far. What is more surpri sing is that no time-frame has been fixed for this Committee. The Committee 
views this with serious concern. This does not leave any hope for any significant improvement in the functioning of 
CGHS providing medical services to Central Government employees in the near future. 
Action Taken 
 The Kaul Committee which has been mandated to look in to the functioning of CGHS and to suggest measures 
for improvement by making it user friendly. The Committee so far has had 12 meetings and the proceeding of the 
Committee are still continuing and certain actions have alr eady been initiated as per the decisions taken in the 
Committee proceedings e.g. computeriza tion of Laxmi Nagar Dispensary as a pilot project which is now fully 

operational. A trial run of dispensaries of North Avenue, South Avenue and Medical Centre at Parliament House has 
also started. Digitalization of index cards of CGHS beneficiaries of East Zone, Central Zone and South Zone of Delhi 
has been completed. Proposal for computerization of remainin g dispensaries at an estimated cost of Rs.8.70 crores is 
under process. 
 Computerized processing of all Hospital bills and bills  of local chemists has been outsourced on a pilot basis 
in respect of two dispensaries under CGHS Delhi to Third Party Administrators (TPA) recognized by the Insurance 
Regulatory Development Authority. The pilot project has already started for two dispensaries under CGHS East 
Zone, Delhi. The TPA has to do the following:- 
 (i) Computerizing the receipt, processing and sanction of all claims received by CGHS 
Delhi so as to ensure settlement of claims/bills within five working days. 
 (ii) Placing the entire processing movement on a web-site. 
 (iii) Attending to all queries about bills/claims. 
 (iv) Enabling claimants to track the progress of their claim on the web. 
 (v) Advising the claimants about the disposal of their claim and if sanctioned to confirm 
receipt of payment by them. 
 (vi) From the claims to capture data about disease profiles, course of treatment, drugs 
prescribed etc. 
 (vii) Create an appropriate MIS for future planning. 
 Computerization will help in reducing waiting time of  patient at dispensaries, fast delivery of indented 
medicines to the beneficiaries, processing of all records relating to reimbursement indents reports will be handled 
efficiently, data for MIS would be generated for future planning. 
 Local Advisory Committees have been constituted in the dispensaries to address grievances of beneficiaries, 
with CMOP-in-charge as Chairman and Members from Pensioners Welfar e Associations, Residents Welfare 
Associations and Area Welfare Officers. Local chemists are also required to attend these meetings. 
 Empanelment of private hospitals/dia gnostic centres has now been converted into a continuous process. No 
tenders are henceforth to be floated for empanelment. Hosp itals/Diagnostic centres that fulfil CGHS norms for such 
empanelment can now apply anytime provided they are w illing to accept the rates approved by CGHS. This will 
eliminate the periodicity in the empanelment process. Th e eligible Private Hospitals and Diagnostic centres can 
submit their applications electronically also. The final report of the Kaul Committee will be submitted on the analysis 
of the pilot project and measures initiated.  
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been given to understand that the final report of the Kaul Committee would be 
submitted on the analysis of the pilot project and measures taken based on its initial recommendations. The 
Committee fails to comprehend the basi s for this approach. Whenever a Commit tee is constituted, it has to be 
give a report in accordance with it s mandate within a specified period of time. The Committee is of the view 
that this should have been the case with the Kaul Committee also. 
Recommendations/Observations 
3.8 The Committee finds that in view of the st udy being conducted by the Kaul Committee, all 
expansion/strengthening of infrastructure work of CGHS dispensaries has been brought to virtually a stand-still. The 
Committee would like to quote two instances in this re gard. Proposal for construc tion of building of CGHS 
Dispensary No. 73 in Gurgaon, Haryana for which land has already been purchased will be taken up only after the 
receipt of report of the Kaul Committee and reaction of the Department thereon. Same is the fate of the proposal 
initiated in 2005 for construction of a new building for CGHS headquarter at Kidwai Nagar, New Delhi. The 
Committee would like to emphasize that basic purpose of an y study can only be achieved if it is conducted within a 
prescribed time-frame. The Department should ensure that the report of the Kaul Committee is received at the earliest 
and action initiated immediately thereafter. 

Action Taken 
 As mentioned at para 3.6, rapid strides are being taken to improve and strengthen the functioning of CGHS 
like computerization, constitution of advisory committees , improvement in delivery system etc. As regards 
construction of the buildings for CGHS at Gurgaon and Ki dwai Nagar the Planning Commission has observed that it 
is time to restructure, reform and rejuvenate this contribu tory health scheme. Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
is already examining the shortcomings reported, and could consider several options. Ex isting subscribers to the 
CGHS could exercise an option of continuing with the current arrangement, or alternately, subscribing to a new 
system developed within the CGHS. At the beginning of 2005, the Planning Commission had intimated that keeping 
in view the outcome of exercise for ra tionalization during the review of the Plan schemes they were of the view that 
CGHS as a Plan Scheme being administered by Health Ministry also need not continue and hence no provision 
should be kept w.e.f. Annual Plan 2005-06. However, after persuasion by this Ministry during last financial year an 
amount of Rs.31 crores was allocated for CGHS under Plan head. As Planning Commission has allowed CGHS to 
continue as Plan Scheme, the expansion of CGHS will be taken up with them. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is deeply disturbed to note that th e Central Government Health Scheme is undergoing a 
very confusing phase. On the one hand the Government has appointed Kaul Committee to suggest ways and 
means to improve the existing CGHS system, on the other hand Planning Commission in its Mid-Term 
Appraisal of Tenth Plan has come out with the opinion that CGHS need not continue as a plan scheme and 
accordingly no provision on the plan side should be kept for 2005-06 budget. As a result, projects for 
construction of new CGHS buildings have been put on hold. 
 The Committee would like to point out that Centra l Government Health Sche me is a welfare scheme 
aimed to cater to the health needs of a large nu mber of beneficiaries incl uding Central Government 
employees, pensioners and VIPs like Members of Parlia ment, Judges of the Supreme and the High Courts, 
freedom fighters etc. Any attempt to tinker with the sc heme to the disadvantage of its beneficiaries cannot be 
appreciated. The Committee would like to  emphasize that this state of ind ecisiveness should not be allowed to 
continue. The Committee is of the view that there is a need to further improve and strengthen the facilities 
under the existing system. Introducing another parallel system does not seem to be an appropriate move.

Recommendations/Observations

Safdarjung Hospital from Rs. 72.42 crores in 2005-06 to Rs. 74.58 crores in 2006-07. The Committee has been 
observing that every year, pressure on Safdarjung Hospital has been growing. Following indicators in respect of 
different services are self-revealing:-

4.4 The Committee strongly feels that in view of overall an ticipated increase in the various medical services being 
provided by Safdarjung Hospital, proportionate increase in the non-plan funds also needs to be made. The Committee 
observes that whereas patient load and resultant pressure on various services being provided by the hospital has been 
steadily increasing, bed strength remains stuck at 1531 for the last so many years. It has not been possible to add even 
a single bed so far. The Committee wonders whether anybody has given a thought in this direction. The Committee is 
of the firm opinion that there is an urgent need to provide more beds so that better health care may be provided to the 
patients at Safdarjung Hospital. 
Action Taken 
 At this stage it is not feasible to increase the bed strength in view of the constraint of existing infrastructure. A 
comprehensive re-development plan for Safdarjung Hospital is being drawn up. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee notes that the reply of the Ministry is deafenin gly silent about making proportionate 
increase in the Non-Plan funds for Safdarjung Hospital, as recommended by the Committee. The Committee 
would, therefore, like the Ministry to make all out efforts for enhancement of non-plan funds. 
 The Committee, however, welcomes the comprehen sive redevelopment plan being drawn up by the 
Ministry for Safdarjung Hospital. Safarjung Hospital is one of the biggest tertiary care hospitals in Delhi 
where admissions, emergency attendance, total operations,  general OPD attendance etc.  have been increasing 
year after year. Consequently, there is an urgent ne ed for increasing bed stre ngth and enhancing other 
infrastructure facilities in the hospital. The Committee hopes that all the constraints hindering the capacity 
expansion of the Safdarjung Hospital will be taken ca re of in the redevelopment plan. The Committee would, 
however, like to emphasize that the implementation of the redevelopment plan should be carried out in a time 
bound manner. Recommendations/Observations 
4.5 The Committee understands that evening OPDs are also being run at Safdarjung Hospital for quite some time. 
The Committee would, however, like to point out that pub lic at large is perhaps not aware about evening OPDs. The 
Committee is of the view that adequate publicity needs to be given to such services. 
Action Taken 
 The functioning of the evening OPDs running at Safdarjung Hospital was periodically reviewed and it was 
observed that the number of patients attending evening OPDs have shown a decline over the past few years as low as 
average 2 to 3 patients per day in a Speciality. There is already emergency services running in casualty where the 
small number of patients attending the evening OPDs have to be again called in the morning hours for various 
investigations which defeats the very purpose of running evening OPDs. It was also observed that the majority of 
patients seen in the evening OPDs are either spill over from the morni ng OPD or known to hospital staff. The 
Specialist services at Safdarjung Hospit al are already overstretched due to s hortage of doctors/staff, increasing 
patients load in the emergency/I.P.D./O.P.D. and posting of doctors/staff for various VIP, VVIP and disaster 
management duties etc. There is also  no willingness of the staff/doctors for coming to run the evening OPDs due to 
their already overstretched routine workload. During the Resident Doctors strike in May, 2006 evening O.P.Ds were 
suspended to strengthen the strike contingency plan. The periodic reviews shows that the services in evening OPDs 
has not proved useful to the patients. Hence, after getti ng the overall review of the circumstances, evening OPDs 
have been suspended. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is not convinced by the justifications  given for the closure of evening OPD services at 
Safdarjung Hospital. Working conditions were the same  when decision to start evening OPD services was 
taken. Fact remains that wide publicity was never given to  this initiative. Had it be done, patients would have 
definitely availed of such a service.  Heavy patient load in th e morning OPDs would also have been some what 

less. The Committee would also like to emphasize that any new facility should be introduced only after making 
a proper assessment of the ground realities and the effective mechanism, so as to ensure its maximum reach.

 The Committee is not happy with the snail’s pace of the progress made in the matter of setting up of

VIII. POST GRADUATE INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL EDUCATION AND  RESEARCH, CHANDIGARH  
Recommendations/Observations 
8.3 The Committee is surprised to note that against the total sanctioned 5585  posts for the Institute, there are only 
4805 posts filled up as on 31st Marc h, 2005. The Committee is of the view that as many as 780 posts lying unfilled 
cannot be considered a healthy sign. The Committee would like to be apprised about the category-wise status of these 
vacant posts and efforts made for filling them up. 
Action Taken 
 The Government of India, on 24th May and 31st August, 2001 had issued instructions regarding optimization 
of direct recruitment of civilian posts. As per the instructions each Ministry/department including autonomous bodies 
are required to prepare their Annual Direct Recruitment Plans in respect of non technical posts and l/3rd of the 
vacancies arising in a year could be fille d up subject to the condition that this  does not exceed 1 per cent of the total 
sanctioned strength of the department. For this purp ose, a Screening Committee ha s been constituted in each 
Ministry, which clears the Annual Recruitment Plans of the Organization falling under their administrative control. 
 Due to increasing workload, the Institute had requested the Ministry on 23.2.2002 to exempt them from the 
above mentioned instructions. But PGI was instructed to follow the said instructions of the Government. In the 
meeting of Screening Committee held on 14.10.2003 the matter was discusse d and it was decided that all the 
technical posts may be filled up. However in respect of non technical posts, the said instructions on optimization of 
direct recruitment will be effective i.e. 2/3rd of the direct recruitment vacancie s occurring in a year shall have to be 
surrendered. Accordingly, the Institut e has surrendered 48 posts of Class IV in lieu of 73 non technical posts. 
However, in the minutes of the meeting it was mentione d that Screening Committee is  not competent to grant 
exemption to technical posts from the provisions of the DOPT orders. Also there was no clarity on the number of 
posts cleared for the PGIMER though there was a reference of number of vacancies. The Institute requested the status 
of non technical posts to be filled up. The Institute had sent updated information regarding vacant non technical posts 
to the Ministry on 20.6.2006, approval of Screening Committe e is still awaited. All the non technical posts are lying 
vacant since 2001-02 as the vacant non technical posts have not been approved by the Screening Committee. 
 In view of the recommendations of the Parliamentar y Standing Committee, approval of the Screening for 
filling up all the vacant non technical posts without any cut may be requested for so that the Institute may able to 
ensure deliverance of quality services at every outlet to the ailing humanity and optimal utilization of resources. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is deeply disturbed by the casual approach of the Department in a matter connected 
with a premier institute of the country . Instead of taking the required acti on and giving the feedback in its 
Action Taken Note, the Department is simply indicating th e line of action required to be taken by it. Taking a 
serious view of this, the Committee would also like to point out that the Screening Committee of the Ministry, 
not taking any decision inspite of the Institute sending the requisite information on the 20th June, 2006, 
confirms lack of action/initiative for reasons best known to the Department.

XV. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME  
Recommendations/Observations 
15.6 The Committee also takes note of the fact that the is sue of revealing of HIV status  to donors was discussed in 
the 16th Governing Body meeting of National Blood Transfusion Council. The Co mmittee has been given to 
understand that the Council was of the opinion that all out e fforts should be made to ensure  provision of facilities in 
terms of pre-testing, counseling and HIV testing so that more and more donors will come forward to know their HIV 
status and can access these services as and when required. The Department has also accepted that revealing of HIV 
status can follow the effective preventi on practices by the individual found to be  positive. On a specific query in this 
regard, officials of NACO informed the Committee that its  suggestion has been agreed to. The Committee hopes that 
this change in the policy must have been conveyed to a ll the implementing authorities across the country. If not, 
action should be taken at the earliest. 
Action Taken 
 On the recommendation made by the Parliament Standing  Committee, this matter was placed as an agenda in 
the 16' G.B. meeting of National Blood Transfusion Coun cil (NBTC) to discuss and take the opinion of all the 
members regarding the implication of the policy. The members of NBTC suggested that the sero-reactive donors may 
be called upon to the blood bank concerned for their counse ling and confirmatory test instead of referring them to 

various counseling and testing centres. Th ey opined that Blood Bank, particularly the Major Blood banks should be 
equipped with the facilities for counseling and confirmatory  testing for the sero-reactiv e donors, as Blood Banks are 
already conducting HIV tests on donated units by trained sta ff. The members also expressed other alternatives that 
the blood banks collecting blood from blood donors directly or through camps, should send the sero-reactive samples 
at their own initiative to government recognized diagnostic laboratories for confirmatory tests. 
 As per the recommendations made by the members of NBTC, one post of counselor may be created for all the 
Major Blood Banks in the Government sector supported by NACO. These couns elors will be providing the pre and 
post test counseling to the HIV sero-reactive blood donors along with confirmatory testing for HIV. 
 This will be placed as an agenda  for approval by next National AIDS Control Board (NACB) meeting. Once 
NACB approval is received all the implementing authorities across the country will be informed. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee has been pursuing the implementati on of its recommendation regarding revealing of 
HIV status to blood donors. Last year itself the Commi ttee was informed that the matter was discussed at the 
16th General Body meeting of the National Blood Transf usion Council. Action Taken Note of the Department 
also gives the same details. The Committee finds that the proposal is yet to get the formal approval of the 
National AIDS Control Board. The Committee would like to emphasize that the meeting of the Board, if not 
held so far, should be  convened without any further delay so also  to expeditiously implement the proposal, 
vital for prevention of HIV/AIDS. 
XVI. NATIONAL MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME  
Recommendations/Observations 
16.2 Tenth Plan outlay of Rs. 139 crore was approved fo r the National Ment al Health Programme. However, the 
Committee notes that although funds were released every year during the Plan period, utilization figures reveal a very 
discouraging picture. During the first three years of the Plan period, against an allocation of Rs. 90.00 crore, 
expenditure reported is only Rs. 33.55 crore. The Committee apprehends that expenditure would not have shown any 
increasing trend in 2005-06 in spite of there being an enhanced allocation of Rs. 40.00 crore. The main factor 
responsible for this state of affairs was the delay in approva l of the revised District Mental Health Programme. As a 
result, against a target of up gradation of 37 Government Mental Hospitals and 75 medical colleges during the Tenth 
Plan period, only 18 Government Mental Hospitals and 13 medical colleges could be funded, as per the latest reports. 
The Committee hopes that during the last  year of the Tenth Plan, the programme would ultimately take off and 
implemented as envisaged. The Committee is also of the view that shortage of trained psychiatric manpower and lack 
of awareness regarding treatment, the two major constrai nts of the programme need to be addressed without any 
further delay. 
Action Taken 
 During the Tenth Five Year Plan it is envisaged to expand District Mental Health Programme to cover 100 
districts in the country, strengthen the 37 Government me ntal health institutes and also psychiatric wings of 75 
medical colleges, undertake IEC activities and research and training. So far 94 districts have been covered under the 
District Mental Health Programme; funds have been rele ased for up-gradation of psychiatric wings of 24 medical 
colleges and 19 Mental Hospitals. Further, funds have also  been released for undertaking research and IEC activities. 
In fact, during the year 2005-06, under National Mental  Health Programme Rs.46.00 crores has been released 
(Rs.40.00 crores from the NMHP Programme and Rs.6.00 cr ores under North East Funds). As regards shortage of 
trained psychiatric manpower, there are over 3000 qualified ps ychiatrists, 500 clinical psychiatrists, 300 psychiatric 
social workers and about 400 trained psychiatric nurses in th e country. The effort of the Government is to diagnose 
the mentally ill patients at an early stage and treat them th rough the general health delivery system. For this purpose 
under the National Mental Health Programme, the General Duty Medical Officers are given short-term training in the 
field of psychiatry for handling cases of mental illness. The Government is also providing primary treatment to the 
common man through the District Mental Health Programme (DMHP). 
Comments of the Committee 

 The Committee is pleased to note that under the Dist rict Mental Health Programme, out of 100 districts 
to be covered during the Tenth Five Year Plan, 94 distri cts have been covered. However, in respect of the 
target of upgradation of 75 medical colleges and 37 Government mental hospitals, during the same period, the  
achievement figures so far are only 24 and 19 respectiv ely. Therefore, the performance of the Department in 
this regard has fallen woefully short of its target. With only a few months left for the completion of the Tenth 
Plan, the Committee has serious doubts whether these target s will ever be achieved. The Committee feels that 
up-gradation of these medical hospitals and mental hospital s is required to be carried out on an urgent basis 
as it will help in curing the patients at the initial stage and save him or her from the agony of being sent to the 
mental asylum.

 Global Funds for AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (G FATM) supported Intensified Malaria Control Project 
(IMCP) is being implemented in seven NE St ates and West Bengal, Orissa and Jharkhand w.e.f. 1st July, 2005 for 
enhanced support. GFATM grants are being released to the State Societies. 
 Due to large number of vacancies of male health work ers in States, early detection of malaria cases through 
active surveillance and prompt treatment get delayed. Gol has requested the State Govts to fill the vacant positions to 
improve surveillance and treatment of malaria cases. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that situ ation continues to remain grim so far as malaria 
cases/deaths reported in NE States, Orissa and West  Bengal is concerned. Situation in Assam has rather 
deteriorated further with maximum number of deaths reported from that State alone. The Committee would 
like to point out that mere release of massive funds through the Glob al Funds for AIDS, TB and Malaria 
(GFATM) to these badly affected States is not showin g any visible improvement. The Committee reiterates its 
apprehensions that funds are not reaching the district s. This is borne out by the statement made by the 
Department that GFATM funds are being released to State Societies. The Committee can only conclude that 
there is no mechanism to confirm wh ether the districts are receiving the funds in time. Another disturbing 
trend noticed by the Committee last ye ar was the acute shortage of male health workers in these vulnerable 
States. Taking a serious note of the nonchalant attitude shown by the chronically malaria-endemic States of 
Assam and Orissa, the Committee would like to point out that non-filling of vacancies by States is a serious 
drawback that is eventually going to affect the Global Funds for  AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (GFATM) 
supported Intensified Malaria Control Project (IMCP). The Committee is disturbed to note that the only 
initiative taken by the Department is making a request  to the State Governments to fill up the vacancies. The 
Committee would also like to impress upon the fact that a more pro-active role is required on the part of the 
Department in the prevailing situation. The very first action which can be taken by the Department 

immediately is to impress upon the NE  States, Assam and Orissa to first zer o in on the underlying causes of 
vacancies and take prompt remedial measures accordingly. 
 The Committee would like to be informed about steps taken and also progress made by the NE States, 
Orissa and West Bengal regarding the filling up of the vacant posts. 
Recommendation/Observation 
25.2.4 The Committee understands that us e of Insecticide Treated Bed Nets is an alternative and cost effective 
vector control measure which is being supplied free or at highly subsidized rates to the high risk areas of endemic 
States. Committee has made a specific query about adverse Report of CAG abou t allotment of 5.20 lakh mosquito 
nets to Assam by the Centre in 2000. These nets were handed over to the State Government between 7th February 
and 7th April, 2000. As per CAG Report, out of 5.20 lakh  mosquito nets, 4,86,133 nets were distributed to 22 
districts from 7th to 11 April, 2001. The Committee, however,  notes that instead of being distributed, these nets had 
to be kept in the health department stores and godowns of the State Warehouse Corporation till February 2005 at a 
monthly rent of Rs. 82,500 since February, 2001. 
Recommendation/Observation 
25.2.5 From the detailed note submitted by the Department , the Committee could infer that prescribed norms were 
not adhered to while negotiating the procurement of 8 lakh single bed nets and 2 lakh double bed nets. The 
Committee notes that supply or ders were placed with three different fi rms based in Guwahati, Kolkata and Delhi. 
During the process, a complaint abou t the sub-standard quality of bed ne ts was received from CVC. After 
preliminary inspection by the central team, distribution of  bed nets was stopped till further directions from the 
Centre. Analysis of samples of bed nets was got done by IIT, Delhi that confirmed the bad quality of nets. On being 
asked to lift the bed nets, the concerned firm went to court. Subsequently, one of the firms went to the Indian Council 
of Arbitration and the matter hangs there. The Committee not es that only one Delhi based firm has received the 
payment. The Committee takes a serious view of this deve lopment. The Department has chosen not to reply to the 
specific query about the rent being paid for storage of be d nets in the State warehouse and godowns. The Committee 
strongly feels that the Department has to be very cautious while entering into any procurement procedure involving 
such big amount of funds. Non-adherence to procurement procedure has resulted not only in financial losses but also 
depriving the most vulnerable class of society. Payment of rent to godowns for keeping sa fe mosquito nets certified 
and fit for use is a classic case of mismanagement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should make all conceivable efforts for settlement of case so as to stop incurring of unnecessary expenditures. 
Action Taken 
 The Department has not mentioned anything in the Action Taken Note.  
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is deeply disturbed by the indifferent approach adopted by the Department to such a 
serious issue reported upon by the Co mmittee. The Committee would like to impress upon the fact that 
through Action Taken Notes, the concerned Department  is expected to apprise the Committee about the 
specific action taken after submission of the Report. Non-committal approach of the Department confirms the 
apprehension of the Committee that the CAG case about Insecticide Treated Bed nets in Assam remains 
unresolved and the likely beneficiaries continue to suffer. 
25.3 Kala-Azar  
Recommendations/Observations 
25.3.2 The Committee is constrained to note that in spite  of funds being made availa ble to the states, they are 
somehow not making an optimum and judicious utilization of allocated funds. Result is that provision of Rs. 58.86 
crores in 2005-06 had to be brought down to Rs. 17.62 crore at the RE stage. What is more worrying is that cash 
assistance could not be released to Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal for want of Utilization Certificates for the 
previous years. The Committee understands that Rs. 20.00 crore have been provided under the programmes for the 
four endemic states. The Committee hopes that Bihar, Jh arkhand and West Bengal must have submitted Utilization 
Certificates by now. The Committee is of the view that in  order to achieve the elimination of Kala-azar by 2010 
vigorous efforts need to be made with special focus on endemic States. 
Action Taken 

 During 2005-06, against the allocated budget of Rs.58. 86 crores, Rs.40.00 crores w as kept for procurement of 
DDT and medicines and Rs. 18.86 crores as cash assistance to  States. The allocated budget could not be utilized by 
third quarter due to late receipt of DDT consignee instructions from the States particularly from the State of Bihar for 
supply of allocated quantity of DDT. The consignee instruct ion from Bihar received in the fag end of financial year 
(February2006) resulting to reduce the budget from Rs.58.86 crores to Rs. 17.62 crores in RE 2005-06. 
 In current financial year 2006-07, Rs.20.00 crores has been kept under BE which includes  
Rs. 15.00 crores for DDT and Kala-azar medicines and Rs.5 .00 crores approved as cash assistance for meeting 
operational costs. 
 The utilization certificates (UCs) of previous years are mandatory for release of next instalment of cash grant. 
Due to non-submission/partial submission of UCs from the States, the cash assistance for the current year could not 
be released yet. The issue has been taken up with the four endemic States for early submission of UCs. 
Comments of the Committee 
 Kala-azar has a history of taking a heavy toll on human lives in the four endemic States. Though, of 
late, its incidence has registered a decrease, its total er adication is still a far cry, which is why the Ministry 
should not lower its guard against Kala-azar. Timely submission of UCs assumes added significance in view of 
the fact that timely release and utilization of funds wo uld play a crucial role in co mbating Kala-azar. Merely 
informing the Committee that “the issue has been taken up with the four States for early submission of UCs” 
without specifying the efforts made and the level of correspondence entered into with the defaulting States is 
not sufficient. The Committee, would therefore, like to be enlightened about the precise steps taken 
subsequent to the Committee’s recommendation on making vigorous efforts for early submission of Utilization 
Certificates and subsequent judicious utilization of allocated funds. 
25.4 JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS  
Recommendations/Observations 
25.4.1 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has been reported 
repeatedly from 15 States. During the year 2004, 1714 case s and 367 deaths due to suspected JE were reported from 
the States. In 2005 (up to 5.12.2005), 6550 cases and 1645 deat hs have been reported due to  outbreak in eastern part 
of Uttar Pradesh. The strategy for control includes stre ngthening the surveillance activ ities and integrated vector 
control, capacity building and Behavior Change communication. 
25.4.2 The Committee is constrained to note that despite  continuous efforts made by the Department, number of 
cases of JE infection is on the rise. Year 2005 was exceptionally bad. Upto December 2005, as many as 6550 cases 
were already reported with 1645 cases of deaths. In UP, major outbreak of JE was reported with number of 
cases/deaths being 5978 and 1458 respectively. The Committee observes that UP has been the most endemic state for 
quite a few years. The Committe e is not aware whether any special drive has been launched in UP to contain the 
spread of disease. The Committee also observes that Haryan a seems to be poised for increase in the number of cases 
reported. 
Action Taken 
 For effective prevention and control of JE and implementation of advance action plan to prevent any outbreak, 
the Dte of National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme  (NVBDCP), Gol is regularly  monitoring the situation 
through continuous interaction with State Government In addition, the Dte is convening review meetings; organizing 
trainings for capacity building, awareness campaigns for co mmunity involvement and field visits for supervision and 
monitoring and providing technical guidance to States. 
 During the year 2006, Gol has initiated JE vaccinat ion programme as an integral component of Universal 
Immunization Programme (UIP) with single dose live attenuated JE vaccine (SA-14-14-2) in 4 States - Uttar Pradesh, 
Assam, West Bengal and Karnataka. JE  vaccination campaign was completed su ccessfully in 7 districts of Uttar 
Pradesh for children between 1 and 15 years of age (in Dist ricts Gorakhpur, Kushinagar, Maharajganj, Kheri, Deoria, 
Siddharth Nagar; Sant Kabir Nagar) with coverage of above 95 per cent of estimated target. 
 The State of Haryana is endemic for JE; the most af fected districts are Karnal , Kurukshetra, Kaithal and 
Panipat. The JE situation of Haryana during the last three years is given below:

Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is happy to note that steps have  been initiated to contain the spread of Japanese 
Encephalitis, in U.P, Assam, West Bengal and Karnataka. However, the Department has been silent as to 
whether any steps have been initiated to contain the disease in Haryana. The figures given by the Department 
for the year 2005 already show a rise in the number of reported cases as well as deaths in Haryana.

 The Committee notes that the Depa rtment’s reply does not address the concerns raised by it with

Department to focus their attentio n on vulnerable states under RNTCP.  The Committee hopes that with

XXVIII. INFRASTRUCTURE 
Recommendations/Observations 
28.2 The Committee notes that out of the Tenth Plan target of setting up of 8669 Sub-Centres in the Country, only 
6552 Sub-Centres have been opened so far. The Committee is  constrained to observe that Bihar, Meghalaya, Tripura 
and Delhi are the four States which have failed to set up  even one Sub-Centre against the targetted 1218, 5140 and 
148 respectively. The Committee has been observing that inspite of Central funding available for Sub-Centres, States 
continue to fail miserably on this accoun t. The Committee strongly feels that drastic action is required to be taken at 
the earliest to improve at least the qua ntity aspect of Primary health infrastructure. The Committee finds that the 
position is equally discouraging in respect of PHCs. Against the Tenth Plan target of 1714 PHCs in different states, 
only 81 PHCs could be set up, that too, by two states, Andhra Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. CHCs also continue to fall 
way behind the required/targeted number. 
Action Taken 
 Under NRHM, it is proposed to sanction new Sub-Ce ntres as per 2001 population norm including buildings 
for Sub-Centres functioning in rented premises. It is also proposed to create new Community Health Centres (30-50 
beds) to meet the population norms as per census 2001 and bearing their recurring cost for the Mission period. 
28.3 The Committee observes that one of the goals of NRHM  is to consider setting up of new CHCs to meet the 
population norms of Census 2001. This seems to be an am bitious plan in view of the ground realities. This is 
corroborated by the fact that out of 720 districts of the 18 High Focus States and 426 of 17 Non High Focus States 
selected for up-gradation to Indian Public Health Standards during 2005-06 under NRHM, facility survey could be 
done only in 11 and 6 districts respectively. The Committee fails to comprehend the constraints being faced by 
respective State Governments to initiate preparatory exercises inspite of Rs. 20 lakhs per CHC duly released by the 
Centre to all States/UTs. They have also been sent the formats for facility survey. It seems that either the State Govts. 
are not interested or there are too many complexities invo lved in conducting a facility survey. Whatever may be the 
situation, the Committee is of the stro ng opinion that it is time that defaulti ng States are held accountable. The 
Committee strongly feels that different key activities under NRHM cannot be carried out in a mission mode in a fixed 
time frame, if even the preparatory exercises cannot be accomplished timely. 
Action Taken 

 The States have been reminded often to carry out facility survey of the CHCs selected for upgradation to 
Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) for which the funds have already been released. The facility survey reports 
have been received only from the States of West Bengal, Tripura and Pondicherry. The reminders have been issued 
to furnish facility survey reports on 06.07.06 from Secretary (Health and Fami ly Welfare), on 19.09.05 and 09.12.05 
from Additional Secretary (J) and at the level of JS (AS) on 07.04.06, 12.06.06 and on 12.07.06. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee takes serious note of the nonchalant attitude shown by States in furnishing facility 
survey reports despite so many reminders  issued to them in this regard. At the same time, it is also amazed to 
note that the Government has shown helplessness in this  regard. Apprehensions of the Committee seem to be 
coming out true. Already the second year since the laun ch of NRHM is nearing its end, and the base level 
work of facility survey regarding CHCs has not been completed by the States. The Committee has been given 
to understand that upgradation of CHCs to IPHS standards occupies centrality in providing adequate 
healthcare service across the country under NRHM. Und er these circumstances, the planned targets which  
the Government has envisaged to achiev e by end of each year under NRHM is sure to remain on paper only. 
The Committee would impress upon the Department to go beyond sending reminders to respective State 
Governments and get completed the over-due preparatory exercise so that a beginning could finally be made 
for effective implementation of NRHM. 
Recommendations/Observations 
28.5 The Committee has been observing that Sub-Centres, PH Cs and CHCs continue to suffer from the perennial 
problem of shortage of required Staff. As per the latest pos ition available, against the re quired number of 1,69,261 
Multipurpose Workers (female)/ANMs, sanctioned number of posts is 1,39,840 with number of ANMs in position 
being 1,33,232 as on September, 2005. Status of ANMs appointe d on contract basis is no better. Out of total 14,101 
ANMs appointed on contract basis, in-position are only 6096 with Bihar having not even one ANM against 1516 to 
be hired on contract. The Committee has also observed that State-wise details about ANMs reveals a more disturbing 
trend with some of the States sanctioning and recruiting more than the required number of ANMs, and in contrast, 
some States lagging far behind the target of even less than  required sanctioned posts. Position is the same in respect 
of the other key functionaries like Health Assistants (Mal e) at PHCs. The Committee has been constantly bringing 
this disturbing trend to the notice of Central Government. But it seems that the Central Government is helpless before 
the State Governments. The Committee can only conclude that all the planning at Central level, if not implemented 
by the State Governments in the right spirit as envisaged, will defeat the very objective for which the funds have been 
provided. It is high time that with the NRHM in its second year, the Central Government sits up and persuades the 
States to strengthen the health care infrastructure in rural areas. Constraint s/drawbacks of the existing as well as new 
programmes need to be eliminated at the earliest. 
Action Taken 
 The NRHM envisages the provision of an additional ANM at each Sub-Centre. Taking into account the 
vacancy of ANMs as per 1991 populati on norm and about 21983 new Sub-Centres needed to be established as per 
2001 population norm, in addition to provision of 142,655 additional ANMs under NRHM, about 2 lakhs ANMs 
would be required for strengthening the Sub-Centres. The salary of Health Assistant (Male) at PHCs is borne by State 
Government. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee expresses its seriou s dissatisfaction with the very vague and ambiguous reply given by 
the Department to a very specific reco mmendation made by it on a serious issue. Instead of enlightening the 
Committee about the factors responsible for acute shor tage of functionaries of Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs, the 
Department has indicated that position is going to wo rsen further. Instead of de vising means to check the 
anomalous appointment of ANMs and Health Workers, and taking initia tives to bridge the increasing gap 
between the required and in-position manpower of Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs, the Department has shown its 
disinclination to take any initiative and depend solely  on State Governments. Such distortions existed before 
the launch of NRHM and still continue even after the end of a year and half of its commencement. This is the 
position to which the Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department. The 
Committee, therefore, once again urges upon the Departme nt to take up the matter with the States and bring 
forth a satisfactory/visible result at the earliest so that the mission objectives are timely met.

Department. The MoHFW mainly relies on the monthly monitoring reports received from the State Governments 
with regard to physical achievements under various schemes including that for immunization. In addition, periodic 
surveys are also carried out to assess the change in pro cess indicators and the impact of the FW Programme in the 
field with the assistance of independent agencies. 
 The MoHFW also undertakes process monitoring of va rious interventions through special studies conducted 
by the Population Research Centres (PRCs) and other independent research organizations. 
 Similarly, Regional Evaluation Teams located at the Re gional offices of MoHFW at Delhi, Bangalore, Bhopal, 
Patna, Lucknow, Kolkata, and Chennai are undertaking sample verification of Family Welfare Programme 
beneficiaries both on qualitative an d quantitative parameters. The findings of these teams are regularly 
communicated to the State Governments and district authorities for taking necessary actions. 

 In addition, the MoHFW conducts large-scale sample surveys that also cover immunization data as given 
below: 
 National Family Health Survey (N FHS): For creating a comprehensive de mographic and health database in 
India at National and State level, National Family Health Surveys were conducted during the year 1992-93 and the 
Second Round was conducted in 1998-99. The results of both rounds of the survey have been published. The third 
round of National Family Health Survey 2006-07 is currently under progress. The International Institute for 
Population Sciences (UPS), Mumbai is the designated nodal agency for organising the survey. The final result is 
expected to be released in February-March, 2007. This survey covers various health and family welfare interventions 
including immunization. Under the NFHS-III, the survey covers 1.25 lakh households that would yield reliable 
estimates at the State level. 
Rapid Household Survey (RHS)/District Level Household Survey (DLHS): To assess the impact of the RCH 
Programme, utilization of services provided by Government h ealth facilities etc. at district level, RHS in all the 
districts of the country in two phases was initiated in the ye ar 1998-99. In the first round, 50 per cent of the districts 
were covered in the first phase of the project in 1998 and thereafter, the remaining 50 per cent districts were covered 
under second phase in 1999. The IIPS, Mumbai organised the survey. 
 The second round of the district level RHS was initiated in the year 2001. The survey was conducted in two 
phases. The sample size for the survey was fixed at 1000 households per district. 
 The comparative data for immunization, computed as the ratio of children in the age group of  
12-23 months who have received BCG, 3 doses of DPT, 3 doses of Polio, Measles for the DLHS-I (1998-99) and 
DLHS-II (2002-04) is at Annexure-II. Presently, preparatory work for the third round of the DLHS is in progress. 
 Thus there is a variation in the source and methodolog ies for data collection from the health administrative 
machinery (Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs etc.) and that collected through a Survey, which is essentially canvassed to the 
Households/recipients of the service. Consequently, the data from the two sources are not strictly comparable. The 
immunization data as given by surveys shows the percenta ge of children in the age group 12-23 months immunized 
for the particular antigen whereas the service data performance data sent by States/UTs is compiled and analyzed vis-
a-vis the estimated beneficiaries in that year for the particular antigen. 
 In addition, there is no mechanism at  present to independently verify the field level figures for any State. The 
data released through Surveys are essentially an impact assessment of the Family Welfare initiative. 
 The numbers of measures initiated by the Department to ensure better coverage of Routine Immunization 
Programme are as under: 
 (i) Downsizing Bacille Ca lmette Guerin (BCG) vial from 20 dose to 10 dose. 
 (ii) Use of auto disable syringes replacing the ex isting glass syringe in order to bring in improved 
injection safety and fidelity to the programme. 
 (iii) Alternate vaccine delivery-last storage point for vaccine in the country is PHC. In order to carry out 
the village session sites, vaccine w ill be delivered from the last stor age points to these village session 
sites. 
 (iv) Social mobilization of children -ASHA/Li nk worker will mobilize all children immunization to 
session site. 
 (v) Slum and underserved/unserved area will be supported by the alternate vaccinator. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee does not dispute the fact that there is a variation in the source and methodologies for 
data collection from the health administrative mach inery (Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs etc.) and that collected 
through a survey. The Committee would however, like  to point out that the objective of both the 
methodologies is to make the correct assessment of ground realities for taking corrective measures afterwards. 
The very fact that there is no mechanism at present to independently verify the field level figures for any State 
confirms that exact implementation status of various interventions under RCH programme is not  available. 

The Committee, therefore, reiterates that State figures ne ed to be verified by an independent agency. A pilot 
study can easily be initiated by the Department.

XXXII. DECLINING SEX RATIO  
Recommendations/Observations 
32.3 The Committee notes that there are as many as 27,2 28 bodies (Genetic Counseling Centers, clinics, labs, 
ultrasound, machines/ image centers et c.) registered in the country as on 31.07.2005. The Committee would, 
however, like to point out that there might be equal number of, if not more, unregistered clinics doing their business. 
Total number of 322 complaints filed in the courts/police st ations against the violators of law and sealing and seizure 
of 33 ultrasound machines during 2005-06 can only be termed  as a very small and insignificant attempt to solve a 
sensitive problem, which indi cates a dark future for our country. Th e Committee appreciates that the Govt has 
initiated a number of measures, at both State and Central le vel. The Committee, however, feels that these measures 
can only bring about a change if sustained initiatives are pu t into effect by all concerned. One should also not forget 
that social awareness about the implications of this probl em has to be built up. The Committee would also like to 
point out that our medical community is in need of sensitizing the public so that they start playing a pro-active role. 
The Committee understands that a survey of ultrasound centres was undertaken during 2004-05 in the most 
vulnerable states and findings of this survey have been sent to the concerned States for taking necessary action on 
30.03.2005. The Committee would like to be apprised about full details in this regard. 
Action Taken 
 Nine Population Research Centres were entrusted with  the task of carrying out a survey of clinics/centres 
registered under the Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnost ic Techniques Act, 1994 to know the extent of use of 
ultrasound machines by these centres and to know the opinion of AYUSH doctors regarding use of ultrasound 
machines. The States covered were Andhra Pradesh, Punjab , Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Prad esh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, 
Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu. The findings indicated that  the Appropriate Authorities are not aware about their 
functions, and not visiting the registered clinics and ex amining their records properly. The records maintenance by 
the registered clinics was poor and they were not aware of various violations and provisions of the Act. Reports of 
the findings were sent to the respective States for taking action on the findings. 
 Government of India has requested the States/UTs to organize sensitization of the Appropriate Authorities 
regularly with the funds available with them under RCH Programme. Indian Radiological and Imaging Association 
has been given financial assistance for organizing zonal wo rkshops to create aw areness about the provisions of the 
Act among its members. 
 Teams of National Inspection and Monitoring Committee (NIMC) also visit the States/UTs from time to time 
to see the implementation of the Act on the ground. During the past one year or so, the team has visited the States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Gujarat, Himachal  Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, 
Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal and West Bengal. The concerne d District Appropriate Authorities take action on all 

violations like non-registration of ultrasound centres a nd non-maintenance of records noticed during these visits. 
Reports of the visits are sent to the Chief Secretaries of the concerned States for taking action on the findings. 
 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare regularly monitors the implementation of the PC and PNDT Act in the 
States/UTs. As per the latest information (31.7.2006) available from the States/UTs, 28870 clinics have been 
registered under the Act and 395 court cases are filed in different courts for violating different provisions of the Act. 
Comments of the Committee 
 The Committee is happy to note that a number of initiatives have been taken by the Department in Co-
ordination with State Government for sensitizing all concerned about the declining Sex Ratio and also 
constant monitoring of implementation of the PC/PNDT Act in the States/UTs. It has been informed by the 
Department that as on 31.7.2006, 28870 clinics have been registered un der the Act and 395 Court cases have 
been filed in different courts for violations of differen t provisions of the Act. In this regard, the Committee 
would like to be further informed as to how many conv ictions have been made so  far. The Committee also 
feels that the efforts in this regard would be more result oriented if public at large is sensitized towards this 
social evil by involving the local bodies and focusing on districts showing an alarming sex-ratio.
