without specifying the efforts made and the level of correspondence entered into with the defaulting States is 
not sufficient. The Committee, would therefore, like to be enlightened about the precise steps taken 
subsequent to the Committee’s recommendation on making vigorous efforts for early submission of Utilization 
Certificates and subsequent judicious utilization of allocated funds. (Para 25.3.2) 
Japanese Encephalitis 

 The Committee is happy to note that steps have  been initiated to contain the spread of Japanese 
Encephalitis, in U.P, Assam, West Bengal and Karnataka. However, the Department has been silent as to 
whether any steps have been initiated to contain the disease in Haryana. The figures given by the Department 
for the year 2005 already show a rise in the number of reported cases as well as deaths in Haryana. 
Apprehending a similar trend in 20 06 also, the Committee would appreciat e if JE vaccination programme is 
made an integral component of Universal Immunization Programme in Haryana. (Para 25.4.1 and 25.4.2) 
XXVI. REVISED NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME  
 The Committee notes that the Depa rtment’s reply does not address the concerns raised by it with 
regard to under-achievement of targets by certain States /UTs in terms of examination of T.B. suspects among 
the new adult outpatients and in annualized total ca se detection rate. The Committee would like the  
Department to focus their attentio n on vulnerable States under RNTCP.  The Committee hopes that with 
NGOs and Private Practitioners being involved in IEC acti vities concerning awareness building among people 
spread of T.B. would be contained. (Para 26.2) 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that status of unspent balances under RNTCP shows no 
improvement in 2005-06. Against unspent balances amounting to Rs.298.12 lakhs as on 1.4.2005 availability of 
unspent balances has reached Rs.348.75 lakhs as on 1.4.2006. The Committee hopes that the impact of number 
of initiatives taken by the Department would have been evident in 2006-07. The Committee would also like to 
point out that availability of unspent balances and th eir being carried forward to the next year cannot be 
considered a positive sign. This can on ly mean that the implementing agenci es are facing some  constraints in 
optimum and judicious utilization of allocated funds. This aspect also needs to be taken care of. (Para 26.3) 
XXVII.  NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS  
 The Committee notes with concern that the Department has given ev asive response. The Committee is 
very much aware as to how many surgeons have been trained but the Committee’s concern was that the 
number is not adequate considering the higher percenta ge of blindness cases in the country. The Committee 
would like to emphasize once again that the Department should evaluate time bound plan for training for eye 
surgeons specially for those districts which suffer from  lack of good eye care. Th e Committee would also like 
to be enlightened on the suggestion made by the Planning Commission that quality of Intra-occular lenses 
needs to be improved. (Para 27.4) 
XXVIII. INFRASTRUCTURE 
 The Committee takes serious note of the nonchalant attitude shown by States in furnishing facility 
survey reports despite so many reminders  issued to them in this regard. At the same time, it is also amazed to 
note that the Government has shown helplessness in this  regard. Apprehensions of the Committee seem to be 
coming out true. Already the second year since the laun ch of NRHM is nearing its end, and the base level 
work of facility survey regarding CHCs has not been completed by the States. The Committee has been given 
to understand that upgradation of CHCs to IPHS standards occupies centrality in providing adequate 
healthcare service across the country under NRHM. Und er these circumstances, the planned targets which  
the Government has envisaged to achiev e by end of each year under NRHM is sure to remain on paper only. 
The Committee would impress upon the Department to go beyond sending reminders to respective State 
Governments and get completed the over-due preparatory exercise so that a beginning could finally be made 
for effective implementation of NRHM. (Para 28.2 and 28.3) 
 The Committee expresses its seriou s dissatisfaction with the very vague and ambiguous reply given by 
the Department to a very specific reco mmendation made by it on a serious issue. Instead of enlightening the 
Committee about the factors responsible for acute shor tage of functionaries of Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs, the 
Department has indicated that position is going to wo rsen further. Instead of de vising means to check the 
anomalous appointment of ANMs and Health Workers, and taking initia tives to bridge the increasing gap 
between the required and in-position manpower of Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs, the Department has shown its 
disinclination to take any initiative and depend solely  on State Governments. Such distortions existed before 
the launch of NRHM and still continue even after the end of a year and half of its commencement. This is the 

position to which the Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department. The 
Committee, therefore, once again urges upon the Departme nt to take up the matter with the States and bring 
forth a satisfactory/visible result at the earliest so that the mission objectives are timely met. (Para 28.5) 
XXX. ROUTINE IMMUNIZATION PROGRAMME  
 The Committee is constrained to observe that leve l of expenditure by the States under the Routine 
Immunization Programme during 2005-0 6 has been very discouraging. The Committee is not very convinced 
by the justification for slow pace of utilization of funds given by the Department. The very fact that States 
were facing difficulties in preparin g their plan as per the specific re quirement and implementation thereof 
indicates that there was lack of in teraction between the Centre and the State level implementation agencies. 
The Committee hopes that things might have improved in 2006-07 and utilization level reached a satisfactory 
level.  (Para 30.2) 
 The Committee does not dispute the fact that there is a variation in the source and methodologies for 
data collection from the health administrative machinery (Sub-Centres/PHCs/CHCs etc) and that collected 
through a survey. The Committee would however, like  to point out that the objective of both the 
methodologies is to make the correct assessment of ground realities for taking corrective measures afterwards. 
The very fact that there is no mechanism at present to independently verify the field level figures for any state 
confirms that exact implementation status of various interventions under RCH programme is not  available. 
The Committee, therefore, reiterates that State figures ne ed to be verified by an independent agency. A pilot 
study can easily be initiated by the Department. (Para 30.3) 
 The Committee is disappointed to note the ‘action’ taken by the Department. The view of the 
Committee cannot be considered as mere suggestion. The Committee was expecting the concrete plan from the 
Department to expedite the process of replacement of Cold Chain System. The Committee, therefore, directs 
the Department to indicate the mechanism adopted by it  to ensure early replacement of Cold Chain System 
and the progress made since the initiation of this process. (Para 30.4) 
XXXII. DECLINING SEX RATIO  
 The Committee is happy to note that a number of initiatives have been taken by the Department in Co-
ordination with State Government for sensitizing all concerned about the declining Sex Ratio and also 
constant monitoring of implementation of the PC/PNDT Act in the States/UTs. It has been informed by the 
Department that as on 31.7.2006, 28870 clinics have been registered un der the Act and 395 Court cases have 
been filed in different courts for violations of differen t provisions of the Act. In this regard, the Committee 
would like to be further informed as to how many conv ictions have been made so  far. The Committee also 
feels that the efforts in this regard would be more result oriented if public at large is sensitized towards this 
social evil by involving the local bodies and focusing on districts showing an alarming sex-ratio. (Para 32.3) 
XXXIII. MISCELLANEOUS 
 The Committee hopes that adequate funds would be provided during the Eleventh Plan period for 
improving the health care services available in Govern ment Medical Colleges. The Committee is of the view 
that pre-assessment of level of requirement in State G overnment Hospitals can be initiated by the Department 
by involving an independent agency. The Committee would also like to point out that a survey may be 
conducted through the existing monitoring mechanism at State/Centre level about the status of availability of 
cold-chain equipments at PHCs so that wherever required, necessary provision could be made. (Para 33.2)

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS / OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
V.  DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL
Recommendations/Observations
5.3       The Committee has been given to understand that fund constraint if any in the provision of Rs.11 crores in  
2006-07 will be overcome by re-appropriation of savings from other schemes at the RE stage, provided suitable
proposals are received from states.   The Committee strongly feels that quality control of AYUSH drugs   is required to
be maintained in view of the increasing demand for such drugs and also for checking circulation of spurious drugs in the
market. 
 
Action Taken
Department of AYUSH is taking necessary measures for the enforcement of Quality Control of AYUSH drugs
throughout the country.  The State Enforcement Mechanism are being supported and directed to implement the
provisions under Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules strictly. 
 
Recommendations/Observations
5.5       Assistance amounting to Rs.2.52 crores was provided to units obtaining GMP certificates.        The Committee
has been given to understand that a subsidy amount of 25% subject to a maximum of RS. 5 lakh being provided to
AYUSH units for becoming GMP compliant was not proving to be sufficient enough.    Keeping in view increasing
number of cases of spurious and fake drugs available in the market, the Committee feels that there is a need for  
increasing the quantum of financial assistance under this component.    This would enable individual units or a group of
units to set up a joint quality control lab and acquire requisite equipment for testing of heavy metals and raw materials
etc.  The Committee strongly recommends that a decision for  enhancing the funding for units obtaining GMP
certificates should be taken well before the beginning of XIth Plan.
 
Action Taken
            It is proposed to increase the assistance from Rs. 5 lacs to Rs. 50 lacs in the XI Plan.
 
Recommendations/Observations
5.6       The Committee has been given to understand that the implementation of the provisions of the Drugs and
Cosmetics Act and Rules made thereunder is the responsibility of the State Govt. licensing authority.    The Committee
would, however, like to emphasize that there is an urgent need for the Department for taking a pro-active role by
making persistent efforts for strengthening of drug testing labs and the other allied controlling authorities.     
 
 
Action Taken
Department has taken urgent action to strengthen State Drug Testing Laboratories by enhancing the grant-in-aid
upto Rs. 150.00 lakh to State Drug Testing Laboratories.   Apart from this Private Drug Testing Laboratories are also
being recognized for the testing of ASU drugs.

Recommendations/Observations
8.12     The Committee has been informed that independent third party evaluation of both the schemes has been assigned
to the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education, Dehradun and Indian Institute of Forest Management,
Bhopal. The Committee hopes that reports of these studies would provide critical input to the Board to modify and
recast the scheme accordingly. The Committee has a suggestion to make in this regard. Involvement of Forest
Department will not be helpful simply because they do not have any expertise in growing trees. The Committee is of the
firm opinion that agriculture universities like Pant Nagar need to be involved in the implementation of schemes like
Promotional and Contractual Farming. The Committee fails to understand the reason for not initiating the provision of
recovery of funds provided in the terms and conditions of both the schemes. The Committee strongly feels that a review

drawbacks being noticed in the two schemes.   
 
Action Taken
Reports of Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education, Dehradun and Indian Institute of Forest
Management, Bhopal have been received. Salient findings of Reports are below:
(i) The National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) promoted projects had a positive impact in terms of production of
medicinal plants, which has increased quantitatively. Performance of the projects implemented by some of the NGOs
was noteworthy.
(ii)
                            Under the Commercial Projects the emphasis has been on a few species like Safed Musli, Amla, Isabgol,
Senna and Ashwangandha. The other prioritized species have been cultivated over less than 30% of the total area
covered.
(iii)
                           Most of the farmers wanted the Contract Farming supported by National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)
to continue by better networking between corporate, retailers, manufacturers and the farmers.
(iv)
                          The average success rate of commercial projects is more than 77%. The average per acre production was
recorded as the highest in Chhatisgarh  and lowest in Rajasthan. The production in Rajasthan is lowest due to the harsh
soil and climate conditions.
(v)
                            The Commercial projects resulted in 36% of the cost being incurred on employment. More than 50% of the
cultivators were those with area more than 6 acres. In other words the beneficiaries were mostly medium and large
farmers. The average representation of women was 17%.
 
(vi)
                          MoU between the Buyer and Seller was a  weak link. More than 50% of the cultivators claimed to have
sold 100% of their production. Only less than 7% were not able to sell their products. 30% of the growers sold their
products after some processing. Marketing, therefore, remained a constraint. However, there were Farmers Federation in
some states which had taken the responsibility of marketing and such innovations were found useful and therefore,
needed to be replicated.
(vii)
                         Though the Quality Planting Material was raised under the Promotional projects, there was no proper
networking for its supply to the cultivators.
(viii)
                       Monitoring by the SMPBs was found to be either absent or weak except in some of the states like
Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh.
(ix)
                          Requirement of certification of UCs by a Chartered Accountant has been a cause of delay in submission of
UCs by farmers, affecting delay in release of next installment. This in turn delayed the project implementation.
(x)
                            There were isolated cases of SHGs providing linkage for implementation of Promotional projects. This had
a positive impact on the project implementation.
(xi)
                          The organizational structure of SMPBs is generally weak. Mostly the SMPBs are located in the ISM&H
Departments headed by ISM&H officials. There are also states where SMPBs are located in the Forest/Horticulture
Departments. In states where either the SMPBs are in the Forest Departments or where IFS officers are on deputation
with ISM&H Department, the functioning of SMPB is much more effective.
(xii)                         On the whole, the implementation and achievement of objectives present a mixed picture. There is,

XIII. STANDARDIZATION OF NATUROPATHY COURSES
Recommendations/Observations
13.4     The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for regulation of education of naturopathy. There are
ten-degree colleges of naturopathy in the country. But in the absence of any council having the power to regulate the
education of naturopathy, such colleges are running courses in a haphazard way, without any Central Standardization or
and any accountability whatsoever. The Committee is of the firm view that the Department should initiate immediate
action so that people are not put to any trouble. The Committee is happy to note that Department is reviewing the status
of both education and treatment aspects of naturopathy and would be coming out with a proper regulatory system in this
regard within a period of three months. The Committee would like to be apprised of the same.
 
Action Taken
               After consulting eminent practitioners and academics, the guidelines on the accreditation of Naturopathy
practitioners and institutions have been circulated to all the States and Union Territories. State Governments have also
been requested to enact comprehensive legislation at the State level covering the registration of practitioners, the
regulation of medical education and all related matters in due course and that till then a system for registration and
accreditation as suggested above should be put up in place immediately. A copy of the Department’s letter written to all
the Health Secretaries of the States and Union Territories dated 14.09.2006 is at Annexure-IV.
 
XVI.    MISCELLANEOUS
Recommendations/Observations
Tibetan Medicine has become quite popular amongst the people although it is not a recognized system in India. 
In states like Himachal Pradesh, Amchis are the medical practitioners in the Tibetan system of medicine.   There have
also been reports about violations concerning wildlife and usage of huge amount of bone material in this system of
medicine. The Committee has been given to understand that the Tibetan Medicine does not find any mention in our
existing legislation.  The Drugs and Cosmetic Act 1940 has a chapter on Indian Medicine but it does not mention
anything about the Tibetan medicine.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Tibetan system of medicine should be
brought within the ambit of law.  The Committee urges the Department to consider the inclusion of Tibetan system of
medicine in the legislation so as to regulate and recognize it for the benefit of the people.
 
Action Taken
            Department is undertaking research on Amchi (Tibbetian) system through RRI Leh a unit of CCRAS.
Department is developing the institute.   It also appears that Amchi system of medicine has originated from Ayurveda. 
Department is analyzing whether it should be developed as a separate system or as another specialty of Ayurveda. For
recognition of new medicinal systems, a bill is likely to the introduced by Department of Health and Family Welfare.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/Observations
2.1       The Committee observes that there has been massive enhancement in the allocation of plan funds for the
Department.   As compared to Ninth Plan allocation of Rs. 364.43 crores, funds provided to the Department in the Tenth
Plan were Rs. 1194.60 crores.   Department has   managed optimum utilisation of funds during both the plan periods,
massive enhancement of funds notwithstanding.    The Committee notes that the trend of allocation and utilisation of
funds during the last two years of both Ninth and Tenth Plan indicates interesting similarity.   The Department could not
match the substantive increase in allocation of plan funds in 2000-01 and 2001-02, the last two years of Ninth Plan. 
Committee notices the same position in 2005-06 where funds had to be reduced at the RE stage.  The Committee
apprehends the same position during      2006-07 also.
 
Action Taken
The administrative set up for AYUSH is very weak in most of the States.  Funds under Centrally Sponsored
Schemes are released through the State budget and in many cases there is inordinate delay in release of funds to the
implementing agencies by the States.   Most of the construction work at the State level is centralized at the level of State
P.W.D who take inordinate long time to complete the construction component of the Centrally Sponsored Scheme.   
Due to these reasons the absorption capacity of the State is low and they are not able to furnish Utilization Certificates
in time, which leads to reduction at RE stage.  Further, some projects relating to All India Institute of Ayurveda, New
Delhi and National Institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy, Arunachal Pradesh could not get administrative and
financial approval in time on account of various reasons.  This also resulted in reduction in R.E. 2005 – 2006.
 
Comments of the Committee
            Admission by the Department that the administrative set-up for AYUSH being very weak in most of the states
reveals the ground realities.   The Department has cited the inordinate delay in release of funds to the implementing
agencies by the State Govts as the main factor behind Central funds remaining under-utilised.   While appreciating the
constraints of the Central Govt., the Committee would like to point out that holding the State Govts. responsible would

AWAITED
-Nil-
OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS – AT A GLANCE
 
 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Comments of the Committee
            Admission by the Department that the administrative set-up for AYUSH being very weak in most of the states
reveals the ground realities.   The Department has cited the inordinate delay in release of funds to the implementing
agencies by the State Govts as the main factor behind Central funds remaining under-utilised.   While appreciating the
constraints of the Central Govt., the Committee would like to point out that holding the State Govts. responsible would
not serve the purpose.    The Committee is of the firm view that role of the Department should not continue to be
confined as a fund-distributing agency.    The Department has to play a more pro-active role by identifying the
procedural bottlenecks at both State and Central level and take effective measures for removal of the same. (Para 2.1)

21st Report of Committee On Health And Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/21streport.htm[29-06-2016 14:49:58]
 
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee observes that the vigorous efforts made by the Department at highest administrative levels for
obtaining the pending Utilization Certificates have not led to any significant improvement.   Apprehensions of the
Committee remain unchanged as number of 343 UCs amounting to Rs. 78.28 crores as on 31.3.2006 have reached to
663 UCs amounting to Rs. 263.25 crores.  Details made available by the Department indicate that maximum pendency
of Rs. 149.11 crores is under the scheme of hospitals and dispensaries.  The Committee strongly feels that alongwith
pursuing at the highest levels for clearance of pending UCs with the major defaulter States, the Department should also
make an assessment of its schemes so as to identify their inherent drawbacks / constraints and removal thereof.   The
Committee has been compelled to make such an observation as pendency of UCs has been noticed in respect of majority
of States. (Para 2.4)
 
 
III.  CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES
 
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee has been expressing its serious concern over the ever-increasing number of Utilization
Certificates under different Centrally sponsored schemes of the Department.   In its Seventeenth Report, the Committee
had dwelt at length on this aspect of the scheme of ‘Development and Upgradation of AYUSH Institutions / Colleges.   
The Committee views with serious concern the response received from the Department.   The Committee is not inclined
to believe the contention of the Ministry that further funds are being released on the basis of clearance of pending UCs. 
Last year the Committee had pointed out the example of a few states which continued to receive funds inspite of
pending UCs.  The Committee is disturbed to note that the position remains unchanged.   From the details made
available to the Committee, as on 30.9.2006 i.e. during 2006-07, these very States were released further funds.  The
Committee strongly feels that by the end of the financial year of 2006-07,  the position would have aggravated further. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should initiate concerted efforts without any further delay
so as to ensure maximum and judicious utilization of allocated funds. (Para 3.4, 3.5 & 3.6)
 
IV     HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
Comments of the Committee
           
The Committee was informed that out of 10,000 AYUSH dispensaries / units located in rural and backward
areas, only 7936 dispensary could be provided funds during 2005-06.  The Committee hopes that things must have
improved during 2006-07, and the changes proposed in the Scheme during the Eleventh Plan would also make the
Scheme more effective and useful for the targeted
beneficiaries.                                                                                                                 (Para 4.2)
 
VI     CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES
STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS
Comments of the Committee
In its Seventeenth Report, the Committee had noted that the Central Register of Homoeopathy was sent to the
Controller of Publication, Delhi on the 21
st June, 2004.  As per the latest feedback received from the Department, the
Register published in 2004 was received in October, 2006.  The Committee does not appreciate this misleading
information.  The Committee can only conclude that although the Registers are being received at a later date from the
Press, they are being shown as published w.e.f. the date of their being sent to the Press.   This must be true in respect of
earlier Registers also.   The Committee would like to point out that this inordinate delay in printing indirectly gives
undue benefit to those practitioners whose names had to be removed for justified reasons.  The Committee, therefore,
emphasizes that the Department should pursue with all concerned authorities, be it State Councils/ Boards, State
Governments or the Govt. Press for timely publication of the Central Register.   Suggestions made at the workshop held
in October, 2006 with State agencies could be used in expediting the
process.

The Committee is not satisfied with the reply given by the Department.   The Seventeenth Report of the
Committee on the Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the Department was presented to the Parliament on the 22 nd May,
2006.  Action Taken Note sent by the Department on the 30 th November, 2006; i.e. after six months, simply informs

            The Committee in its 11th Report on the Indian Medicine Central Council (Amendment) Bill, 2005, presented to

democratically elected body having eminent experts in their respective fields, its members cannot be substituted by the

that the Central Government should start the election process six months prior to the expiry of the term of an elected

All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi
           
Comments of the Committee

for the All India Institute of Ayurveda in the year 2006.  The Committee observes that observations with regard to the

rd

Comments of the Committee
            The Committee is happy to note that there is no indecisiveness in respect of status of the Board.  The Committee
would, however, like to point out that it is more than five years since the Board was set up, yet the phase of conducting
study on its status and organized structure has not ended.  Stopgap arrangement for carrying out the functions of the

affairs.  The Committee, therefore, reiterates that every possible effort needs to be made at the earliest to make the
Board fully functional.  (Para 8.5)
 
 
IX. STRENGTHENING OF PHARMACOPOEIAL LABORATORIES
 
Comments of the Committee
            Apprehensions of the Committee have proved to be true.  Tenth Plan would be over shortly and there would be
no regular Director for PLIM, Ghaziabad.  This is a classic example of making plans without having any prior
assessment.  The post of Director, PLIM, Ghaziabad was advertised.  Thereafter it was re-advertised in the lower scale. 
Then it was realized that for getting a well-qualified and experienced person, the upgradation of the post needed to be
done.  Present position is that the Department is striving hard to achieve the same.  The Committee expresses its deep
sense of unhappiness on this state of affairs.  The Committee once again emphasizes that the Post of Director, PLIM,
Ghaziabad may be filled up without any delay.   (Para 9.2)

Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that another Institute i.e. North Eastern Institute of Folk Medicine (NEIFM) will be
established at Passighat, Arunachal Pradesh.  The Committee would like to know the objectives of setting up of this
Institute for Folk Medicine.   Inordinate delay has already taken place in respect of the North Eastern Institute of
Ayurveda and Homoeopathy.  The Committee apprehends that the Institute of Folk Medicine might also meet the same
fate.   In order to obviate the possibility of further delay, the Committee reiterates its already expressed concern that
after the approval of CCEA is sought for both the Institutes, preparatory exercises should be started based on the
detailed project reports as early as possible and a deadline set for the completion of the projects so that these Institutes
benefiting the North Eastern region see the light of the day. (Para 10.2)
 
XI.     PERFORMANCE AUDIT OF DEPTT. OF AYUSH FOR THE PERIOD OF 2000-01 TO 2004 – 05 BY CAG
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee has taken note of the corrective measures taken by the Department on the observations made in
the CAG Report. Efficacy of Planning, Allocation and Utilization of funds (Para 5.1 to 5.1.8 of the CAG Report)
 
            The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has initiated measures for timely utilization of funds and
obtaining of UCs.  The Committee hopes that monitoring by the Secretary (AYUSH), in active co-ordination with State
Health Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, Programme Officers and State Health Societies will lead to maximum and
judicious utilization of allocated funds in future.   The decision to release the Department’s Centrally Sponsored
Schemes funds to states through the State Health Societies (SHSs) for onward release of funds to the implementing
agencies is a welcome step.  The Committee hopes that these steps will help break the vicious circle of ill planning,
misallocation and underutilization of funds.  The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that concerted efforts
also need to be made for recovery / adjustment of unspent balances without any further delay.    (para 11.3)
Medical Education
            The Committee is dismayed to note the response of the Department to very specific and serious discrepancies
pointed out by the CAG.  Department’s contention that there being no question of any student passing out from any
college obtaining the degree from a college continuing without recognition does not nullify the fact that as on March,

21st Report of Committee On Health And Family Welfare

2005, medical qualifications awarded by 69 out of 444 colleges were yet to be recognized.
 
            The Committee understands that it is a difficult job to monitor the functioning of 458 AYUSH Colleges spread
over in different parts of the Country.  All the 142 Colleges inspected during 2000-05 failing to fulfill the minimum
requirement of prescribed infrastructural and teaching standards is indeed a serious matter.    However, Ministry’s
attempt to wash its hands off by stating that the onus of creating the required infrastructure and making provision for
teaching faculty lies with the college   is more disturbing.  The Committee would like to point out that this was only a
test check by CAG.  Position would not be different in respect of the remaining colleges also.  Being the administrative
Department, the Department of AYUSH cannot escape its responsibility of ensuring compliance of prescribed
standards.  It would have been better if the defaulting institutions were approached for taking corrective measures.
 
The Committee fails to comprehend the justification given by the Department for giving permission for
admission in the next session on the basis of previous year’s inspection.   Absence of complaint does not confirm that
minimum standards of infrastructure and teaching are being maintained by a particular college.  Annual inspection is all
the more required in the cases of colleges getting permission for admission on year-to-year basis.   The Committee is of
the firm view that this practice should be discontinued forthwith.   (Para 5.2.1 to 5.2.10)
 Updation of Central Registers
The Committee has been reiterating on timely updation of Registers so that elections are held in time in CCIM
and CCH. Organizing a workshop of Registrars of all State Councils is a step in the right direction.  Concerted effort
should be made by the CCIM/CCH so as to evolve a mechanism to hold the State Councils / Boards responsible.  The
Committee recommends that feedback from the State Boards/Councils should be taken so as to help them in removing
procedural difficulties, if faced any.  (Para 5.2.11 to 13 of the CAG Report)
National /Apex Level Institutes                                                                                                                                     
 
            Audit Remarks on the functioning of two well-established institutions, i.e. National Institute of Homoeopathy,
Kolkata and the National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur and response of the Department thereto clearly establishes that
all is not well with these two premier institutions.   Continuance of vacancies for such a long period for want of suitable

these drawbacks.  The Committee is not inclined to agree with the contention of the Department that trainees of diploma
courses in Ayurvedic Course / Compounder in NIA, Jaipur can be easily engaged in hospital duties, thereby doing away

Comment of the Committee
The Committee has been given to understand that the Screening Committee of the Department recommends the
names of industries for incentives for participation in international fairs after examination of their eligibility criteria.

Action Taken
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is surprised to note that no acquisition of manuscripts has been done so far by the Department

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parlia mentary Standing Committee on Health and Family 
Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to pres ent the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this 
Twenty-second Report of the Committee on the Demands fo r Grants (Demand No.46) of the Department of

2. The Committee considered the vari ous documents and relevant papers received from the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard the Secretary  
and other officials of that Department on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on the  
10th April, 2007. 
3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted  the same in its meeting held on the 27th April, 
2007. 
  AMAR SINGH 
NEW DELHI ; Chairman, 
April 27, 2007 Department-related Parliamentary 
Vaisakha 7, 1929 (Saka) Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

REPORT 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instru mental and responsible for implementation of various 
programmes on a national scale in the areas of Health and Family Welfare, prevention and control of major 
communicable diseases and promotion of traditional and indigenous systems of medicine. The Ministry incurs 
expenditure either under Central Schemes through its two Departments i.e. Department of Health and Family 
Welfare and Department of AYUSH or by way of grants -in-aid to the autonomous/statutory bodies etc. and 
NGOs. In addition to the 100 per cent centrally sponsored Family Welfare Programme, the Ministry is 
implementing several World Bank assisted programmes for control of AIDS, Malaria, Tuberculosis, etc. in 
designated areas. Besides, States Health Systems Development Projects with World Bank assistance are under 
implementation in various States. The projects are im plemented by the respective State Governments and the 
Department of Health and Family Welfare only facilita tes the States in availing of external assistance. All 
these schemes aim at fulfilling the national commitment to  improve access to primary health care facilities 
keeping in view the needs of rural areas and where the incidence of disease is high. 
 Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare in his presentation before the Committee 
highlighted the following main objectives of the Department:— 
 — Enhance public spending on health 
 — Improve access to health care deli very and promote primary health care 
 — Move towards population stabilisation 
 — Attain targets set for communicable diseases 
 — Decentralised planning with  active community participation 
 — Develop availability of super-specialit y and tertiary care in deficient areas 
 — Address emerging concerns (lifestyle diseases, avian flu, deafness) 
 — Involve private sector through Public Private Partnership. 
1.2 Secretary emphasised that health was one of the thrust areas under the National Common Minimum 
Programme (NCMP), wherein the Government intended to  raise public spending on health from current 0.9 
per cent of GDP to at least 2-3 per cent of GDP over the next five years with focus on primary health care, 
introduction of a national scheme for health insurance for poor families and step up public investment in 
programmes to control communicable diseases. 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
2.1 The Ministry had proposed a total outlay of Rs. 18,281 crores for the Department of Health and Family 
Welfare for 2007-08 to the Planning Commission. The approved allocation against this projected requirement 
is Rs. 13,875 crores including North East. The Committee  was informed that against the projected requirement 
of Rs. 12,866 crore for NRHM, only Rs. 10,890 crore has been provided. Similarly, for Health Programmes 
outside NRHM, Plan allocation of Rs. 2985 crore has been made which was almost half of the projected 
requirement of Rs. 5415 crore. Under NRHM, activities  directly under the Mission  were allocated Rs. 9928 
crores against a proposed outlay of Rs. 11649.35 cror es and for Disease Control Programmes, the final 
allocation stood at Rs. 962 crores against the projection of approximately Rs. 1217.27 crores. 
2.2 It was clarified that the impact of this reductio n will be known during the cour se of the year depending 
on the absorptive capacity of the States. Ongoing health schemes were likely to be affected more severely. This 
is because, out of the approved outlay of Rs. 2985 cr ores, Rs. 600 crores was towards Oversight Committee 
and Rs. 150 crores towards PMSSY, leaving a balance of  Rs. 2235 crores to be spread across the various 
schemes, Hospitals and Dispensaries, Research and Medical Institutions etc. Due to the insufficient allocation, 

final scheme-wise outlays in some cases were  less than even the existing RE for 2006-07 e.g. ICMR. In the 
case of certain other schemes, the BE for 2007-08 was less than the BE for 2006-07. Major programmes likely 
to be affected by inadequate prov isioning included PMSSY, Assistance to States for Capacity Building, 
Hospitals and Dispensaries (Safdarj ung, Dr. RML, CIP, Ranchi, AIIS&H, Mysore), CGHS and institutions 
concerned with medical education and training like JIPMER, LHMC, NIMHANS etc. In some of the Hospitals 
like Dr. RML  and Safdarjung and Medical Instituti ons like JIPMER, LHMC, construction activities were on 
and under provisioning was likely to affect the completi on of these works and in th e process the Institutions 
adversely. Adequate provisioning had also not been possible for development of Nursing Services and 
institutions like AIIH and PH, Kolkata which are covere d under Public Health. NIB,  Noida, Central Research 
Institute, Kasauli, Central Drug Standard Control Orga nization, National Medical Library have all been given 
provisions lower than that had been projected for. On Health Sector, Disaster Preparedness, a token provision 
has been made against the projected requirement. Not only this, small institutions like LRSTB, Delhi falling 
under the Central Sector and set up for providing research support for existing national programmes and 
institutions concerned with medical education, training and research would be deprived of the required funds. 
2.3 Secretary informed the Committee that on receipt of  the final allocation, Planning Commission had been 
addressed regarding the insufficiency of outlays in respect of Health sector programmes. It has now been asked 
by the Planning Commission to indicate the schemes/pr ogrammes where the requirements were insufficient. 
Critical minimum requirement in all the affected schemes was being communicated to the Planning 
Commission so that the momentum in implementation of these programmes was not lost. Committee was also 
given to understand that the Ministry would be moving for additionalities in the first supplementary and 
subsequently, in some of the schemes, seek a higher allocation at the RE level, based on the pace of their 
expenditure. 
2.4 The Committee is dismayed to note that the Department at the initial stage has failed to project its 
budgetary requirements in an effective and prudent way, which is evident from the fact that the 
Planning Commission has requested the Department to indica te the schemes/programmes where the 
allocation is insufficient. The Committee would like the Department to process the matter with a sense 
of urgency so that the stumbling blocks in the allo cation of sufficient funds for a crucial sector like 
health are removed. 
2.5 Secretary, while justifying the projected requirements of the Department for 2007-08, informed the 
Committee that by the end of financial year 2006-07, Depa rtment was able to utilise Rs.9295.55 crore against 
RE allocation of Rs. 10,000 crore i.e. 93.5 per cent of allocated funds. The Committee, however, is not 
inclined to agree, simply because the detailed analysis of trend of allocation of plan funds and utilisation 
thereof during 2006-07 reveals a different position. Th e Committee would like to  draw the attention of 
the Department towards the fact th at BE allocation of  Rs. 11,305.00 crore had to be brought down to 
Rs. 10,000.00 crore at the RE stage. As per the information available with the Committee, actual 
expenditure figures as on the 15th February, 2007 in the Heath sector were Rs. 1435.78 crore against RE 
allocation of Rs. 2048.92 crore. Under NRHM, there was utilisation of Rs. 6047.30 crore as on 28th 
February, 2007 against RE provision of Rs. 7951.08 cror e. Even if total provisional expenditure of  Rs. 
9295.55 crore as on 31st March, 2007 turns out to be the final utilisation status, the fact remains that 
about Rs. 2000.00 crore were spent in the latter half of the last quarter of the financial year. During 
2005-06 also, allocated funds remained under-utilised . Against a total plan allocation of Rs. 9332.00 
crore, final expenditure figures were Rs. 7926.55 crore. 
2.6 Committee has been commenting on this discouraging utilizatio n trend year after year. However, 
there does not seem to be any noticeable improvement . This is all the more di sturbing as there was no 
significant enhancement in the plan allocation for 2006-07 when compared with 2005-06. Against this 
backdrop, total plan allocation of Rs. 13,875.00 crore  for the entire health s ector including NRHM for 
2007-08 is at an enhanced level when compared with the previous year. The Committee is well aware 
that health sector is the most vital sector for a va st country like ours where  majority of population 
remains deprived of even the minimum medical fac ilities. The Committee has been advocating higher 
allocation for health and family welfare and would continue to do the same this year too. 

2.7 The Committee is fully aware that health being a state subject, central funds are to be spent 
through the agencies of State  Gov ernments alone. It is also true th at absorption capacity varies from 
State to State. The Committee would like to emphasize once again that the Centre has to play a more 
pro-active role. The main priority for the Depart ment should be to extensively monitor both the 
implementation of all the schemes and functioning of  those premier institutions/ hospitals, constantly 
showing unsatisfactory performanc e level. The Committee wonders whether any exercise has been 
initiated so far so as to analyse their status duri ng the Tenth Plan. The Comm ittee strongly feels that 
with the Eleventh Plan al ready begun, such an analysis should be made, if not done already, without 
further delay, followed by remedial measures. 
2.8 The Committee views with serious concern very discouraging utilization status of major disease 
control programmes like National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, National Cancer Control 
Programme, National Mental Health Programme, Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, Rural 
Family Welfare Services, State Training Centres, Routine Immunisation, Inst itutes/Organisations like 
Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi, JIPMER, Po ndicherry, National T.B. Institute, Bangalore, 
Central Drug Standard and Contro l Organisation, Drug Control, De velopment of Nursing Sciences, 
Health Sector Disaster Preparedness and Management , Health Education. Performance under/of these 
schemes/institutions needs to be monitored all the more as their plan allocation for 2007-08 shows 
considerable enhancement. 
2.9 On a specific question regarding diversion of funds from plan to non-plan during the financial year 
2006-07, the Department informed that  Rs. 109.75 crores were likely to be diverted from plan to non-plan. 
This was on account of the fact that at BE stage th e projected requirements fo r non-plan were not fully 
provided for. Additional funds for non-plan had been al located at RE stage by di verting funds from plan to 
non-plan. It was felt that an internal exercise was n ecessary to look into the non-plan budget in respect of 
institutions like AIIMS for drawing up a strategy for the same so that transfer of funds from plan to non-plan 
was avoided. 
2.10 The Committee in this connection would like to ob serve that this unhealth y practice of diverting 
plan funds to meet the expenditure on the non-plan si de has been continuing for the last several years. 
The Committee in its 16th Report on Demands for Grants 2006-07 had recommended to curb this trend. 
The Committee, however, observes  that the trend has remained unabated during the financial year 
2006-07 also. In this regard, the response of the Department that it needs to do an internal exercise to 
look into the non-plan budget of institutions like AIIMS and draw a strategy is a much delayed but very 
much required action. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should complete 
whatever exercise proposed to ensure that adeq uate funds are available to meet the non-plan 
expenditure and unhealthy practice of diversion of funds from plan to non-plan is brought to an end. 
2.11 The Committee in this connection would also like to observe that non-plan expenditure in respect 
of Health and Family Welfare Sector has a slightly different character and impact as compared to non-
plan expenditure of other organizations and Depart ments. A large chunk of non-plan funds of the 
Department is spent on consumables, drugs and ma intenance of hospitals, machinery and equipment. 
Therefore, insufficient provision for meeting such vital recurring expenditure year after year will 
eventually paralyse the running of various Hospit als and Institutions. The Committee expects that the 
above mentioned concern would be shared and appr eciated by the Government while allocating non-
plan funds for the Department. 
2.12 Committee has been viewing with serious concern the pendency of Utilisation Certificates under 
various schemes of the Department. Committee was informed that the Department has been pursuing 
the clearance of pending Utilisation Certificates wi th State  Governments. However, the problem of 
pending UCs continues unabated. The Committee is co nstrained to observe that as on 1st March, 2007, 
there were as many as 2810 outstanding UCs amountin g to Rs. 1184.05 crore for the grants released 
upto 2004-05. The Committee finds that problem is more acute under Family Welfare Sector having 

outstanding UCs for Rs. 716.12 crore. By the close of  2006-07, total number of UCs which have become 
due is 4153 amounting to Rs. 5417.34 crores. 
2.13 The Committee was given to understand that und er the revised Finance Mi nistry guidelines, UCs 
become due after 12 months instead of earlier period  of 18 months. The Committee is of the view that 
under the new dispensation, this problem is bound to aggravate. It seems that the Department has so far 
failed to take any effective corrective measure in spite of the Committee rep eatedly making pointed 
references in this direction. The Committee does not have much fa ith in the Programme Management 
Units being set up at State level and District level and deputing of managerial experts to the States by 
the Department. Committee has been compelled to make such an observation in view of a serious 
shortfall in the accounting/audit system of the Mini stry itself, pointed out in the CAG Report on the 
functioning of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the period 2002-05 (Report No. 12 of 
2006). It has been noticed that audit of all the central and centrally sponsored health programmes, PSUs 
under the Department and autonomous bodies like AIIMS, PGI, Chandigarh are kept out of jurisdiction 
of Internal Audit. CAG was of th e opinion that in view of huge amount of funds involved, such a 
procedure defeated the very purpose of having an  Internal Audit Wing of  the Ministry. Committee 
views the proposed audit of autonomous bodies from 2007-08 by the Internal Audit Wing of the 
Ministry too late an exercise in the day. Committee finds the statemen t of the Department all the more 
disturbing that internal audit of all central and centrally sponsored schemes would require the 
Internal Audit Wing to be strengthened considerably. This clearly shows that there is not much hope of 
situation improving in the near fu ture. The Committee would, therefore, urge upon the Department to 
set its own House in order first without any further delay. The Committee also feels that vigorous efforts 
need to be made on priority basis to clear th e UCs pending for the last three decades or so. 
Simultaneously, the Department should pursue with the States showin g maximum pendency, if 
necessary at the highest level. 
2.14 During the course of deposition before the Comm ittee, under-utilization of the allocated funds for 
NRHM was brought to the notice of the Department by the Committee. When asked to identify the factors 
responsible for the under-utilization of the allocated fu nds and the specific steps, if any, initiated by the 
Department to ensure the optimum and judicious utilization of the allocated funds, the Secretary explained that 
in 2005-06, the Mission was just beginning. In 2006-07, most of the money was sanctioned to the States on the 
basis of State level Programme Implementation Plans (PIP s). But now, micro planning has been taken to the 
district level and district programme implementation plans are being made based on the specific requirement of 
each district. These plans are amalgamated into Stat e level Programme Implemented Plans and sanctions are 
now being made, on that basis. He also informed the Committee that management system is also being 
strengthened. The Secretary opined th at more micro plans and the releases  based on specific programmes and 
items in each district would enable the States to spend money faster and furnish utilization certificates timely. 
2.15 Dwelling further on the micro planning, the Join t Secretary of the Department stated that the 
Department’s emphasis is on decentralization and it has been decided to spend 70 per cent of the money at the 
block and below block levels, 20 per cent at the District level and only 10 per cent at the State and National 
level. He however brought to the notice of the Co mmittee a systemic constraint. Implementation of many 
components of NRHM involves the household, the village, the sub-centre, PHC, CHC, reporting to the State 
and then to the Central Government. This procedure takes time and also requires a large management structure 
to collect feedback for preparing the Utilization Certific ates. He stated that the fu nds are released to PHCs, 
CHCs, sub-centres and district hospitals  for the entire year and they are re quired to be spent over the entire 
year. As per the revised General Financial Rules, Utiliz ation Certificates have to be furnished within 12 
months of the end of the financial year. He further informed that the Government’s General Financial Rules till 
2005 provided for an 18-month period after the end of the financial year for th e submission of Utilization 
Certificates in respect of non-recurring grants. 
2.16 As regards recurring grants, it requires submission of the Utilization Certificate before applying for the 
second instalment. He pleaded that given the existing cons traints associated with dece ntralization as also with 

the fledgling management system, the old GFRs which provided for 18-month period for the submission of 
UCs for non-recurring grants should be restored. The Committee was given to understand that this 
dispensation was required for three years only as the existing constraints would be taken care of by then. 
2.17 The Committee takes note of the concerns regarding submission of utilization certificates within 
12 months, as required by the General Financial Rule s, as amended in 2005. The Committee is inclined 
to agree to the Department’s view that given the nature of decentralization and the mandate of the 
NRHM, the issue of submission of Utilization Certificates within a period of 12 months of the end of the 
Financial Year needs serious re -examination. The Committee theref ore recommends that applicability 
of revised GFR in the context of Health and Fa mily Welfare Programme may be reviewed and the 
Ministry of Finance may be approached in this regard. 

Part-A  
(HEALTH SECTOR) 
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME, (CGHS)  
3.1 The CGHS is a welfare scheme of Central Govern ment which takes care of the medical needs of the 
Central Government employees, pensioners, sitting MP s and Ex-MPs, sitting and retired Judges of Supreme 
Court/High Courts, Freedom Fighters, Ex-Governors, serving and pensioner employees of a few autonomous 
organisations in Delhi and the cities where CGHS is in  operation. There are at present 9.11 lakh CGHS card 
holders and 33.01 lakh beneficiaries. 
3.2 Plan Allocation of Rs. 35.00 crore for CGHS for 2006-07 was enhanced to Rs. 39.57 crore at the RE 
Stage. Committee has been given to understand that provisional expenditure as on 31st March, 2007 would be 
Rs. 34.42 crore. The Committee would,  however, like to point out that act ual utilization status as on 28th 
February, 2007 was only Rs. 28.36 crore which is even less than the BE allocation of  Rs. 35.00 crore. Not 
only this, Rs. 3.00 crore earmarked for N-E region have  remained unspent. The Co mmittee has also observed 
that during the Tenth Plan, while during the first three year s, utilization level remained satisfactory, in the last 
two years, enhanced provision has remained under utilised. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
every effort should be made for optimum and judicious utilization of Rs. 40.00 crore provided for CGHS 
in 2007-08. 
3.3 The Committee observes that a number of init iatives are proposed for CGHS which include 
delegation of enhanced financial powers to Minist ries and within CGHS, Local Advisory Committees at 
dispensary level, compilation of manual of rules and procedure, reduction in waiting time for 
registration and delivery of medicines. Welcomin g such initiatives, the Committee would like to 
emphasize that all the proposed in itiatives should be implemented in a time-bound manner with the 
ultimate objective of making CGHS more patient-friendly. 
3.4 The Committee observes that the target of Com puterisation of all CGHS dispensaries in Delhi 
during 2006-07 could not be accomplis hed. Only the Pilot Project of co mputerization of dispensaries in 
Laxmi Nagar, North Avenue, South Avenue and Parl iament House Annexe could be completed. On a 
specific query in this regard, Department has also submitted that the original programme of completion 
of computerization by the end of 2006-07 could not be achieved due to resource constraints as funds 
could be allocated only during February 2007. Sancti on order for the computerisation of dispensaries in 
Delhi has been conveyed to National Informatics Ce ntre and it is expected that the computerisation 
process would be completed by 17th August, 2007. 
3.5 The Committee would like to point that BE allocation of Rs. 35.00 crore was enhanced to Rs. 
39.57 crore at the RE stage. Provisional expenditure as on 31st March, 2007 as informed by the 
Department is Rs. 34.42 crore, leaving a gap of Rs. 5.00 crore. Hence the reply of the Department that 
due to resource constraints, funds could be alloca ted only during February , 2007 has raised more 
queries than it has answered. The Committee feels that delay must have occurred due to prolonged 
procedure involved while sanctioning a new project. The Commit tee, accordingly, recommends that 
computerization of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi should be completed by the revised target date of 17th 
August, 2007. 
3.6 In reply to a query, the Department has submitted th at “to be more realistic to the current attendance of 
beneficiaries in all dispensaries in CGHS, it has now been decided that the SIU report will be implemented on 
the basis of the norms fixed based on attendance data for 2005. All Additional Directors/Joint Directors in-
charge of CGHS cities have been requested to forwar d the average attendance deta ils for the year 2005. As 
soon the details are received, the SIU Report will be implemented and assessed strength of each dispensary 
will be calculated and fixed accordingly.” 

3.7 The Committee is constrained to observe that implementation of SIU Report has been kept 
postponed on one pretext or the other year after year. Upto last year, information on existing strength in 
the dispensaries was being sought from CGHS un its. Norms have changed since then and now SIU 
Report is to be implemented on the basis of norm s based on attendance data for 2005. The Committee, 
however, observes that details from all Addition al/ Joint Directors are yet to be received. The 
Committee apprehends that if there is a further delay in getting the average attendance details for the 
year 2005 as proposed by the Department, the data so received will again not match the ground realities 
which will again delay the implementation of the SIU Report. The Committee, therefore, recommends to 
the Department to complete all the procedural forma lities, paving the way for early implementation of 
the SIU Report. 
3.8 Committee observes that follow- up action on a number of recomm endations made in the Report 
given by M/s Ferguson and Company, sponsored by European Union has been taken by the 
Department. Committee would like to comment on some  aspects of action initiated by the Department. 
The reduction in the number of functional dispensaries to half, due to work-load being negligible during 
emergency hours cannot be considered a wise move . The Committee is not in clined to agree with the 
contention that in an emergency, the beneficiary ca n take treatment at any private hospital, whether 
empanelled or not. The Committee is of the strong view that for small emergencies, the patient should 
depend on the nearest dispensary which would be providin g free of cost treatment. It would be better if 
emergency service is made available in more and more dispensaries, specially in view of quite a few 
dispensaries, at least in Delhi, moving in buildings of their own. 
3.9 European Commission study has also pointed out that the present dispensary timings are inconvenient to 
serving employees. Committee has also been voicing its concern in this regard since long. The Committee 
is surprised to note that the Department continues to  indicate that operating dispensaries in two shifts 
was not possible due to resistance by the Em ployees’ Association. The Committee expresses  its strong 
reservation to this line of argument. The Committee reiterates that the Department has to play a more 
pro-active role in such matters. A beginning can be easily made by starting two shifts in a few 
dispensaries as a test case. After some time, an analys is about patient visits to dispensary can be easily 
made and a final decision taken in the end. 
3.10 Committee has been observing that CGHS continues to suffer from shortage of manpower. The latest 
status of cadre-wise vacancy position under the CGHS system as furnished by the Department is as under:-

 The Committee has been given to understand that pending implementation of SIU Report, large number 
of post continue to remain  vacant. Superannuation and Vo luntary retirement cases have also led to increase in 
vacancies. 
3.11 The Committee observes that si nce on the basis of its earlier recommendations, Ministry of 
Finance has already lifted the ban on filling up of technical posts, the responsibility for expediting the 
filling up of vacancies lies now on the Departme nt and any further delay in the matter cannot be 
justified. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to expedite the filling up of 
vacancies at the earliest. 

3.12 The Department has informed that in respect of  non technical posts, the Screening Committee in 
its meeting held on December, 2006, has cleared 136 posts in CGHS for being filled up and action to fill 
them up has been initiated. The Committee would like to be informed about the progress made in this 
regard. 
3.13 The Committee notes that the empanelment process for CGHS Delhi has been completed and the list of 
empanelled hospitals and diagnostic centres with effect from 1st November, 2006, has been placed on the 
website of the Ministry. 
3.14 The Committee was given to understand that one significant change has been made in the new 
system. Now empanelment of hospitals/diagnostic centers is a continuous process, option being available 
to join the CGHS at any time. The Committee would, however, like to point out that there are inherent 
drawbacks under such a system. Beneficiaries will have to keep a track of empanelled hospitals which is 
not always possible under such a flexible system, clerical errors may sometime occur, putting the 
patients to inconvenience. The Committee, therefore,  feels that it would be appropriate if a minimum 
period of empanelment is also la id down for private hospitals/diagnostic centres and labs, as done 
earlier. 
3.15 The Committee has another very strong obje ction in respect of the new procedure. The 
Committee is of the firm opinion that inclusion in th e list of empanelled hospitals/diagnostic centres on 
the basis of lowest quotations cannot be considered to be based on a sound principle. The Committee 
feels that the mandate of the Government is to provide a fullsome and comprehensive medical care 
facility to the beneficiaries and not a piece-meal one. Private hospitals/diagnostic centres have been 
recognized throughout the countr y for specialist treatment/diagno sis, providing access of quality 
medical care to the beneficiaries on the one hand and relieving the Government Hospitals of the extra 
patient load on the other. Moreov er, there cannot be two opinions th at in almost al l the Government 
Hospitals, the infrastructure and other facilities are already overstretched. The Committee thinks that 
provision of private recognized hospitals and diagnostic centres should be logical and essential extension 
of the existing system and to hold that it is an additional facility is not in sync with the current buzzword 
of Public-Private-Partnership. 
3.16 The Committee feels that literally speaking, though the Department cannot force private 
hospitals/diagnostic centres to be empanelled, it can indirectly compel the quality private 
hospitals/diagnostic centre to opt ou t of empanelment, if the rates quo ted are very low. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the rates should be fixed realistically, taking into acco unt the market 
realities so as to encourage quality private hospitals and diagnostic centres to join the system. 
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI  
4.1 Safdarjung Hospital is the largest of the three Central Government, tertiary care multi-disciplinary 
hospitals in Delhi with a pre-independence history as it was established in 1942, during the Second World 
War. The Hospital presently has facilities in the 34 clinical and 45 special clinics. 
4.2 The BE plan allocation for Safdarjung Hospital for the year 2006-07 was Rs. 48.00 crores which was 
subsequently increased to Rs. 51.39 crores at the RE stage. The provisional expenditure figures till 31st March, 
2007 is Rs. 43.27 crores. With regard to the Vardhman  Mahaveer Medical College attached to the Safdarjung 
Hospital, against an allocation of Rs. 30.00 crore, provisional expenditure reported upto 31st March, 2007 is 
Rs. 29.09 crore. This clearly reflects that in case of VMMC though the utilization of funds has been optimum, 
the same is not the case fo r the Safdarj ung Hospital. The Committee also observes that trend of plan 
allocation and utilization thereof during the Tenth Pl an period shows that somehow the Hospital has 
failed to keep pace with the allocation of plan funds. 
4.3 The Committee notes that the Annual Plan proposed for Safdarjung Hospital for 2007-08 was Rs. 92.50 
crore. However, only Rs. 51.00 crore have been provided. Committee has be en informed that under-

provisioning is likely to adversely affect the completi on of ongoing construction act ivities and in the process 
the Hospital itself. 
4.4 The Committee has been observing that even thou gh the patient load in the Hospital has been 
showing a steady increase over the years, the bed st rength of 1531 of the Hospital, continues to remain 
unchanged. Appreciating that the ever- increasing patient load has al ready overstretched the Hospital 
services and infrastucture, the Committee has been st rongly advocating the need for increase in the bed 
strength of the Hospital. The Committee is happy to  note that a proposal for the redevelopment of 
Safdarjung Hospital has been prepared and submitted to Planning Commission for approval. The 
estimated cost of the whole project is Rs. 1400 crores to be spread over 15 years (within Three Five Year 
Plans). The first phase of this redevelopment plan is estimated to cost Rs. 700 crores. The Committee 
was, however, informed that the Pl anning Commission has refused to grant ‘in- principle’ approval for 
the proposal. 
4.5 During the course of discussions with the Department , the Committee sought clarifications in this regard 
from the Secretary. The Committee was then informed th at the Planning Commission was of the view that the 
health facilities of Delhi needed comprehensive redevelopment and accordingly, focus only on the 
redevelopment of a specific institution should not be th ere. Accordingly, the Department was asked to come 
back to the Planning Commission with a proposal for revamping the health services in the NCR, Delhi. The 
Department then clarified that health  services was primarily the responsibility of Delhi Government. Except 
Safdarjung Hospital, Planning Commission had already okayed the redevelopment plans of all the Central 
Institutions. Against this background, it would be unjus tified to leave Safdarjung Hospital, specially because 
the Hospital was serving not only the Delhi citizens bu t from the neighbouring States as well. The Committee 
was informed that the Department have now been asked to revise the redevelopment plan with a shorter period, 
preferably a plan period, taking care of cost containment also. 
4.6 The Committee notes that the redevelopment plan of Safdarjung Hospital is a phase-wise conversion 
from 1531 beds to 3000 beds, with full-fledged facility for medical and para-medical training alongwith tele-
connectivity with the Vardhman Medical College. The Committee was given to understand that planning was 
done in such a manner that the services of the Hospital, i.e., patient-care services and teaching and training 
services are not disturbed even for a single day. 
4.7 The Committee observes that the Hospital caters not only to the ordinary citizens of Delhi with 
meager means but also of the neighbouring States. The basic idea not to disturb the existing services and 
simultaneously go for redevelopment needs to be impl emented without any deviation and dilution in the 
original plan deserves to be implemented in the real sense. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends to the Department to approach the Pl anning Commission once again to convince the 
Commission of the necessity of  according approval for the  redevelopment plan of the Hospital as 
originally envisaged. At the same time, the Depa rtment should make ever y conceivable effort to 
complete the redevelopment plan with in the targeted date and also with out cost escalation to the extent 
possible. The Committee would appreciate if th e Department puts in place a joint monitoring 
Committee of Department and Hospital authorities so as to tie all the loose ends and work towards the 
redevelopment of the Safdarjung Hospital. The Committee also recommends that the required funds are 
made available for the project. 
4.8 Committee’s attention has been drawn by the fo llowing quantifiable deliverables/physical outputs 
identified for the hospital for the year 2006-07:- 
 (i) To initiate the establishment of Renal Transp lantation in Department of Surgery/Urology  and 
Invitro Fertilization (IVF) clinic in Obs and Gynae Deptt. 
 (ii) Construction of Vardhaman Ma havira Medical College building. 
 (iii) Filling up of 245 technical posts, which ar e under process of recruitment. Procurement of 
equipments and medicine. 

 Achievements made, as intimated by the De partment in this regard are given below:- 
 (i) Renal Transplantation unit is in the process of establishment,  
 (ii) Construction of V.M.M. Colle ge building is under progress,  
 (iii) Filling up of 245 technical po sts are under process of recruitment. 
4.9 The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has failed to achieve tangible 
achievements in respect of even one proposed target. More so, the eloquent silence in respect of progress made 
in the establishment of IVF clinic in Obs and Gynae Department is reflective of the fact that work has not even 
been started. The Committee notes that identi cal targets have been set for 2007-08 also. In view of the 
discouraging level of achievement, the Committee wo uld like to observe that merely defining targets 
without showing any achievement does not make out a very convincing case for allocation of additional 
funds. The Committee in this co nnection would like to emphasise that non-optimum utilization of 
planned funds would not help the hospital’s cause of getting an enhanced allocation for future expansion 
or development, thereby impacting adversely the health care delivery system and depriving a 
substantially large number of poor patients of basic health care facilities. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department, in coordination with the hospital authorities, should closely monitor 
the ongoing projects from the beginning of financial year 2007-08 itself. Only then, the Department can 
make out a case for additional funds at the RE stage.

below:—

level of utilization of plan funds will do no good to  the Department’s projection  of higher allocation for

of the allocated funds has accentuated over the years, no attempt se ems to have been made to arrest the 
trend. The Committee hopes that in the light of as surance given by the Secretary before the Committee 
that each Central Institute will be having a separa te Monitoring Committee, things will improve and 
ongoing projects will be completed as envisaged in a time-bound manner. 
5.5 The Committee observes that a number of projects and activities are planned for 2007-08. Following are 
the three major projects which have been going on for the last few years:— 
 — Strengthening of Accident and Emergency Department and setting up of Trauma Centre. 
 — Upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing. 
5.6 The Committee notes that the new building with separate trauma beds, emergency Operation Theatre 
and ICU is almost completed and likely to be commi ssioned very soon. The manpower is being selected for 

recruitment and sophisticated equipmen ts are being procured. PGIMER at the Hospital is also likely to be 
completed during 2007-08. The Committee observes that buil ding for Trauma Centre is to be handed over by 
HSCC and CPWD by June, 2007 and required equipment are likely to be procured shortly. 
5.7 The Committee would like to point out that this project has been going on for the last so many 
years. Committee’s experience has been that even after completion of construction work, process of 
obtaining of clearance from all the concerned authorities is a protracted and complicated exercise which 
is likely to take another one-two years. The Committe e would, therefore, imp ress upon the Department 
to expedite the completion of all required formalities in coordination with the hospital authorities. At the 
same time, the recruitment process for getting t echnical and non-technical manpower and obtaining 
required equipments should also begin at the earliest. 
5.8 Upgradation of School of Nursing into a College of Nursing is another project of the Hospital which has 
been in the implementation status since long. In the absence of any information about the progress made so far, 
the Committee is inclined to believe that this proj ect must be entangled in procedural formalities. The 
Committee would like to be apprised about the present status of this project.

also submitted that functioning of the PGIMER is not yet started. The structural construction upto 8th Floor is

drastically reduced mid-way through its completion. Since the Institute is near completion, cutting the

our country needs specialist doctors and that too in large numbers. To meet this burgeoning need the 
actual operationalization of this Institute is urgently required. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that allocation for the Institute be enhanced suitably.
