VIII. INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR), NEW DELHI  
8.1 The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) is the apex body for the planning, organization, 
implementation and coordination of medical research in the country. It promotes biomedical research through a 
network of its 21 permanent institutes and 6 Regional  Medical Research Centres distributed throughout the 
country and also through grants-in-aid given to projects in non-ICMR institutes. 
8.2 The plan allocation for the ICMR was Rs. 217.00 crore in 2006-07, against which an expenditure of Rs. 
210.00 crore has been reported upto 15th February, 2007. As per the information made available by the 
Department, provisional expenditure would be Rs. 307. 00 crore by 31st March, 2007. Against the projected 
requirement of Rs. 375.86 crore in 2007-08, provision of only Rs. 176.65 crore has been made. 
8.3 The Committee has noted that the ICMR’s reco rd in utilizing the allocated funds has been 
impressive and except for 2004-05, the ICMR’s ut ilization has either matched the allocated funds or 
exceeded the same. In view of the above, the Committee is at a loss to understand the basis for non-
provision of required provision to ICMR for 2007-08. The Committee feels that due to the reduction in 
allocation for this premier institut e of the country in the field of me dical research, not only a number of 
ongoing research projects will be affected adversely but it will  also be very difficult to undertake any 
new project. This, in the opinion of the Committee w ill prove to be detrimental for the medical research 
in the country, specially in the fi ercely competitive global scenario. The Committee is disturbed to note 
that its strong recommendation for higher allocation of funds for the Council for 2006-07 made last year 
which was based on the Performance Appraisal Board’s expert advocacy, failed to get additional funds 
released at the RE stage. The Committee, however, reiterates that the Depa rtment should vigorously 
pursue the matter with the Planning Commission to meet the requirements of medical research in the 
country and release adequate funds for this purpose. The Committee is of the firm view that funding for 
medical research should not be looked at the same level as funding for routine schemes/matters. Overall 
cut in the plan funds should not be made applicable to one and all. 
8.4 The Committee is happy to note that ICMR ha s undertaken a number of successful and path-
breaking studies on subjects like Viral Encephalitis. H. Pylori infection, improving the utilization of 
emergency contraception through paramedics, multi-centric study on genomics of male infertility, 
assessment of prevalence of osteoporosis in adult population etc. 
8.5 The Committee notes that there is unanimity in the Government on the issue of the creation of a new 
Department of Health Research within the Ministry  of Health and Family Welfare for the purpose of 
addressing the needs of specialized research and budgetary requirements more forcefully as is evident from the 
fact that the Committee of Secretaries at its meeting held on 9th August, 2006 has given its “in principle” 
approval to the proposal. The Committee in this connection would like to observe that what is needed for 
the upliftment of research in the country is more fu nds and greater autonomy and lesser control. In this 
connection, the Committee would like to recall the observations made by the five member Performance 
Appraisal Board having two international and three national experts. This Board was constituted by the 
Department in 2005 and had made valuable sugges tions about changes required in the authority, 
autonomy, financial support and restructuring. In th e opinion of the Committe e, bureaucratization of 
the research institutes is actual ly part of the problem and not th e remedy. The Committee feels that 
need of hour is to make massive investments in medi cal RandD and not to fasten it with a red tape. The 
Committee would like to be apprised about follow-up action, if any, initiated by the Department on 
PAB’s recommendations. 
IX. NATIONAL CANCER CONTROL PROGRAMME  

9.1 Cancer is an important public health problem in India with nearly 7-9 lakh new cases occurring every 
year in the country. It is estimated that there are 20-25 lakh cases of cancer in the country at any given point of 
time. With the objectives of prevention, early diagnosis and treatment, the National Cancer Control 
Programme (NCCP) was launched in 1975-76. The Progra mme was revised in 1984-85 and subsequently in 
December 2004. Under the National Cancer Control Programme there are 25 Regional Cancer Centres 
recognized in various parts of the country. It is proposed to recognize new RCCs in uncovered areas and 
additional RCCs in populous states and provide these cen tres a one time financial assistance of Rs. 5.00 crores 
for development of infrastructure to a certain level, based on action plan. 
9.2 The Committee is aware that cancer is a dreade d disease which can be cured, if detected early. 
The Committee is of the considered view that upgradation of existing  RCCs into Centres of Excellence 
and setting up of more RCCs, specially in unders erved and unserved areas is a step in the right 
direction. The Committee would, however, like to advise the Department to ensure that the targets set in 
this regard are invariably met. The Committee, theref ore, recommends to the De partment to inform it 
about the progress made in the matter of upgradation of existing RCCs into Centres of Excellence and 
setting up of more Regional Cancer Centres, specially in remote and backward areas of the country. 
9.3 The Committee observes that the trend of plan allocation and utilization thereof under the National 
Cancer Control Programme during the Tenth Plan remained satisfactory during the first four years of the Plan 
period. However, the Committee is constrained to observe that during the last year, i.e. 2006-07 plan allocation 
of Rs. 87.00 crores was reduced to 47.00 crores at the RE stage. Explaining the reasons for the decrease in 
allocation, the Department has informed that due to non initiation of the construction activity of the second 
campus of CNCI, Kolkata for want of allotment of land by West Bengal authorities, funds allocated for CNCI 
could not be utilized at all. Efforts are being made to  take up this activity in the right earnest. The Committee 
was also given to understand that in view of a number of mature proposals waiting for release of grants-in-aid 
on account of non-availa bility of funds, Budget Division has be en requested to restore the allocation. The 
Committee fails to comprehend the level of utilizatio n as by 15th February, 2007, only Rs. 16.88 crore 
could be spent. The Committee views with concern th e provisional expenditure of Rs. 42.98 crore as on 
31st March, 2007 with Rs. 8.70 crore earmarked for N-E region remaining almost unutilized. 
9.4 A look at the level of performance of Physical Targets set under the Programme for 2006-07 reveals a 
very disturbing scenario. Against the target of streng thening of 6 existing Regional Cancer Centres (RCCs) for 
equipments, only the strengthening of RCC at Cuttak could be completed Grant of Rs. 5 crore each for 
strengthening of another four RCCs located at Allaha bad, Trivendram, Ahmedabad and Banglore could only 
be approved. Details about the fifth RCC are not known. 
9.5 The Committee observes that an enhanced allocation of Rs. 180.00 crore has been made for 2007-
08 and targets have been set up under different co mponents of the programme. The Committee would 
like to emphasise that every effort should be made  to take the maximum benefit of the new scheme of 
Upgradation of existing RCCs into Centres of Excellence. All the existing 25 RCCs should be upgraded 
in a time-bound manner during the Eleventh Plan. The Committee also takes note of the fact that RCCs 
have been made the nodal agencies for implementati on of the NGO Scheme of ‘Health Camps’ with a 
view to provide guidance to the NGOs and also monitoring the implementation of the scheme. The 
Committee appreciates this initiative. 
9.6 The Committee also observes that the proposal of the Ministry for conducting the evaluation of 
the National Cancer Control Programme is at the final stage. The Committee is of the view that with the 
survey of cancer-prone areas, the programme in it s modified form would be implemented in a more 
effective manner. The Committee would appreciate if this survey is conducted at the earliest. 
9.7 The Health Secretary while making a power-point  presentation before the Committee informed the 
Committee that the funds are regularly released to Region al Cancer Centres. On a specific query as to whether 
the funds have been released to Mahavir Cancer Ins titute, Patna, the Health Secretary replied in the 
affirmative. However, it has been  brought to the notice of the Co mmittee that the Mahavir Cancer 

Institute, Patna is yet to receive the funds. The Committee is aware that th e Mahavir Cancer Institute, Patna is 
a reputed regional institute. The Committee therefore recommends that funds proposed for 2006-07 be 
released to the Institute, if not released so far.  The Committee also recommen ds that the details about 
the funds earmarked for the same for 2007-08 be supplied to the Committee.

XI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS), NEW DELHI  
11.1 AIIMS is a premier institute of the country engaged in under-graduate and post graduate medical 
education, research and training. The Institute lays major emphasis on medical research in the areas of national 
needs, besides providing patient care in specialties and s uper specialties. It is considered to be a centre of 
excellence in modern medicine. 
11.2 A plan allocation of Rs. 675.00 crores was made for the Tenth Plan in favour of the Institute. The trend 
of allocation and actual expenditure indicates that as compared to the first two years of the plan period, 
allocated funds during the last three years remained under-utilised. The Committee is constrained to observe 
that upto 15th February, 2007 only half of the Plan al location could be utlised. As per the latest details 
made available to the Committee, by the end of 31st March, 2007, provisional expenditure was Rs. 
160.07 crore. 
11.3 During the course of discussions, Director, AI IMS was asked by the Committee to specify the reasons 
for allocated funds remaining under-utilised during 2006-07.  Director clarified that against a plan allocation of 
Rs. 205.00 crore, the Institute was released only Rs. 100. 00 crore till March, 2007 inspite of the Department 
being approached every week for rele ase of balance funds. However, things remained unchanged as Rs. 75.00 
crores were already surrendered by the Department. It was only after vigorously pursuing the matter with the 

Department’ and the issue also being taken up with the Se cretary (Expenditure), that Rs. 33.55 crores could be 
released against the requirement of Rs. 53.55 crores. 
11.4 On being asked to clarify the position, Secretary informed the Commi ttee that first instalment of Rs. 
100.00 crore was released to AIIMS without asking for Utilisation Certificates, as  per the existing financial 
norms. However, in view of more stringent financial norms being brought into force by the Ministry of 
Finance which stipulate submission of Utilisation Certificates within 12 months against the earlier period of 18 
months, Ministry had to act accordingly. Secretary informed the Committee that the Institute had not submitted 
the required UCs. However, Financial Advisor of th e Institute who was also present in the meeting, 
categorically stated that not a single Utilization Certificate was pending. 
11.5 The Committee is disturbed by such a level of  communication gap between the premier Institute 
of the country and the administrative Ministry. The Committee is of the firm view that if things are 
allowed to continue in th is manner any further, it would not be  in the interest of the country and its 
people. The Committee can only emphasise that cons cious efforts need to be made to break this 
deadlock by all concerned and consequent return of the normalcy. 
11.6 The Committee was informed that the Institute has projected the requirement of Rs. 3080 crore for 
Eleventh Plan for construction of a number of projects and proposed centers. However, against the annual 
requirement of Rs. 500 crores, only Rs . 200 crores have been provided for 2007-08, which is the first year of 
Eleventh Plan. It was strongly advocated that additional funds were required to be provided to the Institute. On 
a specific query about the status of pending projects, the Committee was informed that the Jai Prakash Narayan 
Apex Trauma Centre had become functional and would be completely operational before the end of May. With 
regard to the Dental Education and Research Centre, things  were moving in the right direction, only difficulty 
being faced about re-appropriation of funds. The third project, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Institute and Rotary Cancer 
Hospital had also become functional and its services were being expanded. 
11.7 The Committee also notes that a number of steps have been taken for improving the patient care 
services at the Institute which include addition of 60 be ds in emergency ward, abolition of waiting list in the 
private ward, de-congestion of OPD, Medicine and Paed iatrics, setting up of new mortuary etc. Another 
positive development which has taken place is the covering of open drain to prevent the last year’s outbreak of 
dengue. Taking note of the status of various projects undertaken during the Tenth Plan and 
augmentation of existing health care services at the Institute and the projects planned for Eleventh Plan, 
the Committee recommends that required funds be made available to the Institute for 2007-08. It should 
not be forgotten that AIIMS is the most prestigious Institute of the country and its status should be 
maintained, present constraints notwithstanding. 
11.8 The Committee had recommended last year that th ere was a need for setting up of a Burns Unit 
in the AIIMS. The Committee is, however, surprised to note that so far it has not been possible to place 
the proposal before the Governing Body of the Instit ute. The Committee expresses its reservation to the 
casual approach adopted by the Department to  a recommendation made  by a Parliamentary 
Committee. The Committee would appreciate if the proposal for Burns Unit is placed before the 
Governing Body without any further delay. The Committee  strongly feels that with the proposed 
expansion of various facilities at the Institute, the proposal for Burns Unit can also easily be handled.

NEIGRIHMS. Accordingly, supporting staff in Group ‘C and ;D’ in these Departments are not being filled for

14.5 The Committee expresses its concern at the delay in  actual operationaization of the Institute. The 
Committee can understand the constraints faced by the Department in filling up the vacant posts due to 
shortage of specialists in NE Region, but the delay in procurement of equipment is beyond its 
comprehension. The Committee would also observe th at NE Region already lags behind in terms of 
health care and other infrastructure facilities as compared to other regions of the country. Delay in 
operationalization of the Institute amounts to denying quality and tertiary health care facilities to the 
people of the region which is very important strategically. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the 
Department to make more vigorous ef forts towards making the Institute fully functional at the earliest. 
The Committee also advises the Department to purs ue the matter with DG,AFMS for an expeditious 
decision in the matter. 
XV. PRADHAN MANTRI SWASTHYA SURAKSHA YOJNA (PMSSY)  
15.1 Government of India has launched Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojna (PMSSY) on 15th July, 
2003 with the objective of correcting regional imbalance in the availability of affordable/reliable tertiary 
healthcare services and also to au gment facilities for quality medical ed ucation in the country. The PMSSY 
Scheme has two components; (A) Establishment of six ne w AIIMS like institutions and (B) Upgradation of 13 
medical college institutions to the level of AIIMS. 
15.2 The PMSSY envisages the following:- 
 Establishment of six new AIIMS like institutions 
 • Under PMSSY, it is proposed to set up one AI IMS like institution each in  the States of Bihar 
(Patna), Chhattisgarh (Raipur), Madhya Prad esh (Bhopal), Orissa (Bhubaneshwar) Rajasthan 
(Jodhpur) and Uttaranchal (Rishikesh).

XVII. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME 
17.1 The AIDS epidemic has become a major health and development concern. Although India remains a 
low prevalence country with overall HIV prevalence of 0.9 per cent, the last few years have seen it moving 
from high risk groups to the general population with  women, youth and the rural population being highly 
vulnerable. 
17.2 According to the Sentinel Survey figures released in 2005, total number of HIV infected people 
amongst the adult population (15-49 years) numbered 5.206 million. Consequently a mere 0.1 per cent increase 
in prevalence, translates into 0.5 million new infectio ns. India accounts for nearly 13 per cent of the global 
HIV prevalence. The categorization of the country as a low prevalence country hides the large numbers of HIV 
infected people. 
17.3 Sexual transmission is driving India’s AIDS epidem ic, accounting for approximately 86 per cent of HIV 
infections. The remainder 14 per cent  are through, Parent-to-child transm ission, use of infected syringes and 
needles by Injecting Drug Users (IDU), and contaminated blood transfusion etc. 
17.4 Presently Phase-III of National AIDS Contro l Programme (2006-2011) is being implemented  
NACP-III seeks to implement the principle of a continuu m of care. Accordingly, prevention will go hand in 
hand with access to prophylaxis, management of opportunistic infections and ART. Given the spread of HIV 
infection into rural areas, NACP-III will further de centralize its organizational structure to implement 
programmes at the district level. The basic unit of implem entation will now be the district. Accordingly, based 
on the epidemiological and vulnerability criteria, all the 6 10 districts in the country ha ve been classified into 
four categories: Category A-141 districts - high prevalence;  Category B-46 districts - concentrated epidemic; 
Category C-309 districts - increased presence of vul nerable population and Category D-114 districts - 
low/unknown vulnerability. 
17.5 The categorization of districts based on vulnerability  is useful for enabling the Government to prepare 
plans that are need based. Accordingly, differential packages of services have been developed for each 
category of districts. Institutional arrangements and ca pacities of the SACS as well as the proposed District 

AIDS Prevention and Control Units (DAPCUs) will be st rengthened. To address spec ial vulnerabilities of the 
North-Eastern States, a Regional AIDS Control Unit (RACU) will be established as a sub-office 
of NACO but embedded in the governance structure of NRHM. NACP-III has also developed an HRD plan to 
continuously update and improve the competency and skills of the programme personnel. 
17.6 NACO has launched National Paediatric AIDS initiative on 30th November, 2006 to provide 
comprehensive care and support (including ART) to children infected and affected by HIV/AIDS. NACO, 
alongwith the Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP),  UNICEF, WHO and Clinton Foundation, has developed 
guidelines for paediatric ART including diagnosis in child ren. Paediatric drugs formulations as per weight 
bands for treating 10,000 children in the current year have been provided to the ART centres. Other 
activities under this initiative include establishment of seven regional Paediatric Centres, free CD4 monitoring, 
free DNA PCR test for children up to 18 months, liqu id formulations for babies weighing less than 5 kg, 
diagnosis and treatment of opportunistic infection and micro nutrient supplementation.. The initiative also 
includes training of paedia tricians and counsellors. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
achievements made vis-a-vis the targets fixed under National Paediatric AIDS Initiative. 
17.7 The Department in its Annual Report has informed that care and support for CLHA (Children Living 
with HIV/AIDS) orphans and vulnerab le children forms an integrat part of NACP-III. A comprehensive 
service package for these children will be funded under GFA-RD-VI and will be offered through home and 
foster based care and support services in 2007. The Committee recommends the Department to inform 
about the specific steps taken and the progress made in this regard. 
17.8 One of the most important components of the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP-II) is the 
Targeted Intervention (TI) projects that aim to interrupt HIV transmission  among highly vulnerable 
populations. These population groups are at a greater risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV infection due to 
more frequent exposure to HIV, higher levels of risk y behaviour and insufficient capacity or power to make 
decisions and take appropriate action to protect themselves. Such population groups include- commercial sex 
workers, injecting drug users, men who have sex with men (MSMs), truckers, and migrant workers. The 
following table reveals the estimated size and estimated coverage of these High Risk Groups.

17.9 The Committee is deeply disturbed to note that all the High Risk Groups have not yet been

17.10 Condom promotion has important role to HIV pr evention. Behavioural Surv eillance Survey (BSS) end 
line 2006 shows a significant increase in consistent con dom use from 32.4 per cent in 2001 to 49.7 per cent in 
2006 among those who had sex with any non-regular sex partners in the previous 12 months. Condom use 
reported during the last sexual intercourse with any non-regular from 40 per cent in 2001 to 58 per cent in 
2006. Awareness about condoms increased from 77 per cent to 82 per cent during the last five years. About 65 
per cent of respondents during the end line BSS were aware that consistent condom use could prevent 
transmission of HIV/AIDS, which is an increase of 15 per cent since 2001. Accessibility of condoms within 30 

minutes from the nearest source, which is one of the key determinants for condom use, increased from 46 per 
cent to 81 per cent. In 2001-02 fiscal year, the distribu tion of condoms under free supply and social marketing 
was 733 million pieces and 438.79 million pieces respec tively. In 2006-07, the dist ribution has increased to 
1250 million pieces and 593 million pieces under free su pply and social marketing, respectively. Under 
NACP-III, the objective is to increa se condom use to 3.5 billion pieces per annum by the year 2009 from the 
present level of about 1.8 billion per annum, through intensive demand generation and supply efforts with 
support from a Technical Support Group (TSG) to be constituted by NACO with support from the Bill  and 
Melinda Gates Foundation. 
17.11 The Committee is appreciative of the fact that use of condoms and its awareness as a preventive 
weapon to fight AIDS has increased over the years. The Committee, however, notes that use of condoms 
amongst those who had sex with any non-regular sex part ner is still 49.7 per cent which is considered to 
be low. Since having many sex partners or changing  sex partners frequently increases the vulnerability 
towards AIDS, the Committee recommends to the Department to ta ke effective steps to increase the use 
of condom amongst this group. 
17.12 The Department has informed that in order to reiterate the Government’s commitment to prevent the

Chief Ministers of select states, repr esentatives of the privat e sector, civil society and NGOs are members of

involvement and participation of the private sector , civil society and key Government Departments. The 
Committee recommends to the Department to finalize  the modalities of the proposed multi-sectoral 
response and inform the Committee accordingly.

17.14 The Committee appreciates that the Department has prioritised a number of activities for

17.15 As per media reports, out of 47000 patients receiv ing anti-retroviral treatment (ART) under the National 
AIDS Control Programme, about 3000-5000 patients have b ecome resistant to the treatment. Such patients 
need second-line treatment which is  too costly. In reply to a query whether, the Department/NACO has

technical issues. We had been able to roll out and st abilise the first line of ART treatment to 60,000 patients

been decided that the rollout of 2n line ART drugs would be considered only after the coverage of 1 lakh 
persons is reached”. 
17.16 The Committee feels that it is highly insensitiv e and in-human to delay th e availability of second

therefore, recommends to the Department to take some  initiative towards star ting the second line of

 • Provide services for early detection  and treatment of mental illnesses in the community

18.3 Plan allocation of Rs. 50.00 crores for 2006-07 under these programme had to be reduced to

Institute of Biologicals (NIB), Noida from Rs.34.40 crores in BE 2006-07 to  Rs. 19.65 crores in RE 2006-07. 
The reasons for this reduction are as follows:- 
 “A provision of Rs.14 crores had been made for pr ocuring movable scientific equipments for the newly 
constructed Lab and Animal House at NIB, Noida. Further, a provision of Rs.9.71 crores was made for 
electricity charges and various annual  maintenance contracts required for full functioning of the new Lab and 
Animal House. A provision of Rs. 2 crores was kept fo r fixed equipments and furnishings of the same Lab and 
Animal House building. However, there was a delay in handing over of the Lab and Animal House to NIB due 
to several reasons including rectification of faults in the construction. Due to the delay, a decision was taken to 
stagger the procurement of equipments and it was decided to reduce the provision in procurements of 
equipments from Rs.14 crores to Rs.9.85 crores.

undertaken due to administrative reasons which resulted in further savings.  
19.2 The Committee expresses its displeasure over the fa ct that in a premier scientific institution like 
NIB, the newly constructed animal house and lab coul d not be made operational due to defects in the 
construction of the building. The Committee feels that this delay would definitely have a damaging effect 
on the quality and quantity of various biological products that are manufactured in the Institute. The 
Committee, therefore, exho rts the Department with all powers at its command to make the lab  and 
animal house functional at the earliest.

the recommendations of UPSC, medical examination of  the candidates is co nducted and provisional 
letter of appointment given to the successful candidates straight  away without any verification. The 
other problem area highlighted was undue long time taken in conducting of combined medical services 
examination. Every candidate sitting for this exam also applies for admi ssion in post graduate courses. 
On getting admission, they are permitted to join on a later date after completion  of their post graduate 
studies. As a result, the present joining rate is below 40 per cent. Inspite of having enhanced panel of 
candidates, problem continues to be the same. The Committee understands that efforts are being made 
to resolve this genuine problem by giving incentive s for joining in difficult areas. The Committee hopes 
that with such initiatives, things would improve in 2007. 
XXV. CAG REPORT 
25.1 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by the CAG Report on the functioning of the Ministry for 
the period 2002-05 (Report No. 12 of 2006). While Committee has given its observations on the matter of 
schemes/PSUs being kept outside Internal Audit under the heading ‘Budgetary Allocation’ in the Report, the 
Committee makes the following observations on the other main Audit Objections. 
25.2 Audit Objection 
 Not more than 33 per cent of the budget should be utilized during the last quarter. However, between 40 
and 51 per cent of plan allocation was utilized only in the last quarter of the respective years during 2002-05.

 The reasons for utilization of funds more than 33 per cent of the budgeted allocation in the last quarter 
of years during 2002-05 may be mainly attributable to delay in receipt of approval of schemes/ programmes by 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC), CCEA etc., Non receipt of adequate proposals from the State 
implementing agencies in time, slow pace of implementati on of schemes/capital work and/ or non receipt of 
utilization certificates/audited accounts etc, delay in  procurement of major equipments due to delay in 
completion of procedural formalities (i.e. tendering technical and financial evaluation etc.)  

25.3 The Committee would like to be apprised ab out the corrective measur es initiated by the 
Department so as to ensure proper utilization of allocated funds in this regard. 
25.4 Audit Objection 
 A test check of stock registers of the Department an d its subordinate offices reve aled that the system of 
periodic physical verification of assets had not been instituted and implemented in the Department/ 
Subordinate Offices. As a result, actual status rega rding custody of stores, position of condemned and 
unserviceable items and losses, if any, could not be ascertained.

 A yearly physical verification of the assets of th e hospital are regularly conducted and actions taken 
accordingly. 
 The Committee would, however, like to point out that as per CAG Report, no record of previous 
physical verification of stock of assets of the Department of Health and Directorate-General, Health Services

25.5 The Committee would like to be apprised about th e remedial measures, if any, initiated by the

 Physical verification of CGHS not done since 1995 and of National Medical Library not done since

XXVI. MISCELLANEOUS 
26.1 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by the fa ct that State Government hospitals attached to the 
medical colleges at the district level which are in a precarious state. There is absence of ICUs and Cath Labs in 
most of them and most of the existing ICUs do not  have basic life saving equipments. Moreover, these 
hospitals lack basic laboratory facilities and diagnostic facilities like ultrasound. Financial ill health of the 
States also does not allow them to address these problems satisfactory. The Committee, 
therefore, is of the firm view that along with upgradation of State Government hospitals, it is high time 
that Government should take some initiative in  providing assistance to such hospitals which are 

attached with Medical Colleges and other district level hospitals. A beginning can perhaps be made by 
providing assistance to the hospital attached to the G.R. Medical College, Gwalior. 
26.2 The Health Secretary during the course of his de position before the Committe e, stated that the State 
Governments are not investing money in upgrading State Medical Colleges.  He also informed the Committee 
that in this Budget, the Government has kept mone y for the upgradation of State Medical Colleges. The 
Committee welcomes the initiative of the Department to allocate funds for the upgradation of the State 
Medical Colleges. The Committee is also aware that  the maintenance of district hospitals leaves 
much to be desired. The Committee welcomes the initiative of the Department to provide funds for the 
upgradation of State Medical Colleges. In this contex t, the Committee would also like to point out that 
the majority of the district hospit als are also in a very bad shape and need financial assistance. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that  besides allocating money for upgradation of State Medical 
Colleges, the Department also initiate steps to provid e maintenance grants to the districts hospitals, to 
the extent possible. 
26.3 The Committee has been given to understand that  the President while pr esiding in a function  
at Christian Medical College, Vellore had expressed the desire that for serious patients, there is a need  
for having Stem Pathology Lab in every Medical College/ Hospital in the country. Allahabad, M.L.N Medical 
College which was earlier under the State Government of U.P. had been provided some financial assistance by 
the State Government for this purpose. With the Allaha bad University becoming a Central University recently, 
the College has also come under the jurisdiction of Central Government. The Committee would appreciate 
if, funds are released to this Medical College for setting up of Stem Pathology Lab. 
26.4 During the course of the deposition of the Hea lth Secretary before the Committee, the Committee 
brought to the notice of the Secretary the issue of regi onal imbalance in the distribution of medical colleges in 
the country. It was pointed out by the Committee that wh ile in one part of the country, a number of medical 
colleges have come up, there are very few in the other parts. The Committee impressed upon the Secretary that 
it is the Government’s responsibility to take steps to  remove skewed distribution of medical colleges in the 
country. The Secretary informed the Committee that one of things the Government is considering in this regard 
is to permit district hospitals, which have the capacity to take clinical load, to attain synergy with private 
medical colleges. Explaining the background of the Government’s current thinking on the above lines the 
Secretary informed the Committee that it has been observed that private hospitals lack patient load while the in 
State Government hospitals, absenteeism arising of private practice is very rampant. 
26.5 The Secretary assured the Committee that his Depart ment will try to provide some incentives for the 
removal of regional imbalance in the development of medical colleges. 
26.6 The Committee views with serious concern the exis ting skewed distribution of medical colleges in 
the country. The Committee strongly feels that it is high time that the Department adopt a more pro-
active role in the setting up of medical colleges in uncovered areas. The Committee accordingly 
recommends that the Department finalize with fair amount of promptitude its policy on offering 
incentives for removal of regional imbalance in the development of medical colleges in the country. The 
Committee has also observed that there is a shortage of teaching staff in Medical Colleges. Standards of 
Medical Colleges are going down. To meet the shortage  of staff, the Committee strongly feels that the 
present age limit of 65 years may be relaxed. 
26.7 National Illness Assistance Funds was established/ set up during 1996-97. Under this scheme, Central 
Assistance in the form of Grants-in-Ai d towards expenditure on hospitalization of the poor is released to all 
such State Governments/UTs where the State Illness Assistance Funds/ Societies have been established. The 
assistance is limited to 50 per cent to the State G overnment contribution to the State funds/society to a 
maximum of Rs. 5.00 crores for bigger States and Rs. 2.00  crores for smaller States. Central assistance to the 
tune of Rs. 50 lakhs each is granted to Union Territ ories without Legislature where the Funds/Societies have 
been set up. State Government/UTs are empowered to sa nction upto Rs. 1.5 lakhs to each patient living below 
poverty line for treatment of life-threatening diseases, from the funds. Out of the Budget allocation of Rs. 5.00 

crores made to National Illness Assi stance Funds an advance of Rs. 10.00 lakhs each have been placed at the 
disposal of Medical Superintendent of AIIMS, Safdarjung Hospital, Dr. R.M.L.Hospital, LHMC  and Smt. 
S.K.Hospital, PGI, Chandigarh and JIPMER, Pondicher ry. These Institutions have been empowered to 
sanction upto Rs. 25,000 in each deserving cases from the Central Funds of NIFM. The Committee feels that 
the sum of Rs. 25,000 is perhaps too little a sum to provide any meaningful assistance to individuals 
suffering from life threatening diseases. The Committee also feels that since 1996, when the ceiling of Rs. 
25,000 was laid down, the cost of treatment has in creased substantially. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Department should increase the ceiling limit of Rs. 25,000 suitably.

1.1 The National Rural Health Mission was operationalis ed in April, 2005 throughout the country. Special 
focus of the Mission is on 18 States which have weak h ealth infrastructure and health indicators. These States 
include 8 Empowered Action Group States (Bihar, Jharkha nd, M.P., Chhattisgarh, U.P., Uttaranchal, Orissa 
and Rajasthan) 8 North-East States, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu  and Kashmir. The main objective under the 
Mission is to provide accessible, af fordable, accountable and effective healthcare delivery, especially to the 
poor and the vulnerable sections of the society, bridge gaps in healthcare, facilitate decentralized planning in 
the health sector, ensure population stabilization, gender  balance and bring about inter-sectoral convergence. 
The NRHM also provides an overarching umbrella to the existing programmes of Health  and Family Welfare 
including RCH-II, Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, TB, Leprosy, NPCB and the Integrated Disease 
Surveillance Project. It also addresses the issue of  health in the context of a sector-wise approach 
encompassing sanitation and hygiene, nutrition and safe  drinking water as basic determinants of good health 
and also advocates greater convergence with related social sector Departments like Women  and Child, 
Panchayati Raj etc. Mainstreaming of AYUSH is also one of the strategies under the Mission.

Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Prad esh, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Assam and Jammu 
and Kashmir. ASHA is envisaged as a trained women community health volunteer who will reinforce 
community action for universal immunization, saved delivery, new born care, prevention of water born disease 
and communicable disease, improved nutrition and promo tion of house hold toilets. She is required to inform, 
interact, mobilize and facilitate improved access to preventive and promotive healthcare and also provide basic 
curative care through her drug kits. She will assist in form ulation of village health plan by the village health 
and sanitation committee. ASHA will also promote awar eness and usage of ISM. The requirement for ASHA 
is one per thousand population with relaxation to this norm depending upon the workload and terrain. ASHA is 
envisaged to be a primary resident of the village who would be selected by the Gram Sabha following an 
intense community mobilization process. She will be fully accountable to the Panchayat.

Shortfall in the required manpower in Rural Health Services 
2.14 The Committee is disturbed to note that shorta ge of manpower more or less persists in all 
States/UTs. As on March, 2006, the overall shortfall (which excludes the existing surplus in some of the 
States) in the posts of ANM was 10.9 per cent of the total requirement. In case of Lady Health Visitors 
(LHVs), the shortfall was 26.9 per cent and that of Health Assistant Male was 32.5 per cent. For doctors 
at PHCs, there was a shortfall of 9.7 per cent of the total requirement. Even out of the sanctioned posts, 
a significant percentage of posts are vacant at all the levels. For example, about 8.1 per cent of the 
sanctioned posts of ANMs were vacant as compared to about 31 per cent of the sanctioned posts of 
MPW (M). At PHCs, about 14 per cent of the sanction ed posts of LHV, 24.7 per cent of Male Health 
Assistant and 20.8 per cent of the sanctioned posts of doctors were vacant. The Committee believes that 
ANMs/LHVs/MPW (F) are grassroot-level health func tionaries who are entrusted great responsibilities  
concerning IEC, awareness building, identification of diseases/cases of serious health hazards and 
carrying basic but vital primary heal thcare to the doorsteps of the peop le in rural areas. Vacancies and 
shortfall in their numbers speak of the improper programme implementation process leading to 
apathetic outcome reflected by the health indicators. 
2.15 The Committee notes that abou t 7.5 per cent of the PHCs were without a doctor, about 38.9  
per cent were without a lab technician and about 17.7 per cent were without a pharmacist. Not only this, the 

current position of specialists manpow er at CHCs reveals that out of the sanctioned posts, about 59.4 per cent 
of Surgeons, 45.0 per cent of Obstetricians  and Gynecologists, 61.1 per cent of Physicians and about 53.85 per 
cent of Pediatricians were vacant. Overall, about 54.4 per cent of the sanctioned posts of specialists at CHCs 
were vacant. Moreover, there was a shortfall of 70.2 per cent specialists at the CHCs as compared to the 
requirement for existing infrastructure on the basis of existing norms. The shortage of manpower, more or less, 
persists in all States/UTs. 
2.16 In reply to a specific query,  the Department has informed the Committee that the acute shortage of 
health functionaries ANMs/LHV/MPW (M) and(F)/HW (M) and (F) as well as poorly staffed primary 
healthcare centres is one of major causes of such bale ful condition of maternal and child health indicators in 
the EAG States. In its 16th and 21st Report, the Comm ittee had urged the Department to take appropriate 
measures in this regard so that year after year the same story is not repeated. The Department’s stock reply that 
every effort is made to realize the objective does not sound convincing to the Committee. 
2.17 The Committee is not satisfied with simply pur suing the matter of filling the vacancies with the 
State/UT Governments by the Department and subsequent display of helplessness on its part. Apathy on part 
of the States at the cost of jeopardizing Family Welfare Programmes ought to be treated on a serious note. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Department should review its policies and plan of action concerning 
this matter and take necessary steps towards filling up of the posts of various health 
functionaries lying vacant for a number of years within a time-bound framework during the Eleventh Plan 
period. The Department, should not confine its role to  that of fund-disbursing authority but play a more 
proactive role in overcoming the obstacles.

ensure services of doctors in rural areas. Some important suggestions are as follows:— 
 • increase in the retirement age to 65 years 
 • decentralization of recruitment at district level 
 • walk in interview and contractual appointment of doctors 
 • enhancing the salary for posting in the rural areas by l/3rd

Mobile Medical Units (MMUs)

600 districts in the country with MMUs, whereas, only 318 districts co uld be provided with such units. What 
makes it noteworthy of mention is the fact that th ese 318 districts are distributed among 18 States only 
and among which names of the bigger states like Bihar, Jharkhand, M.P., Maharashtra, U.P. find no

proposals at the earliest, so that MMUs can be provided with all districts. 
III. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)  
3.1 The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) is an umbrella programme for 
prevention and control of vector borne diseases viz., Malaria, Filariasis, Kala-azar, Dengue/Dengue 
Haemorrhagic Fever (DF/DHF) and Japanese Encephal itis. Under the programme, comprehensive and multi-
faceted public health activities are being implemente d in the country. These diseases pose immense public 
health concern and are major impediments in the path of socio-economic development. The high-risk areas are 
generally rural, tribal and urban slums inhabited by  the poor, marginalized and vulnerable sections. 
Remoteness and inaccessibility, socio-economic conditions , inappropriate health seeking behaviour, migration 
of population as well as emerging drug and insecticide resistance are the contributing factors to the problem of 
vector borne diseases in the country. 

3.2 The Directorate of NVBDCP is the nodal agency for planning, policymaking, technical guidance, and 
for monitoring and evaluation of programme implementation in respect of prevention and control of the vector 
borne diseases. The States are responsible for planning, implementation and supervision of the programme. 
3.3 The Committee observes that during the Tenth Pl an, funds allocated for the Programme remained 
under-utilized. Year 2006-07, the last year of the Tenth Plan was no exception. Against the plan allocation of 
Rs. 371.58 crore marginally increased to Rs. 381.56 cr ore at the RE stage, expenditure reported upto 28th 
February, 2007 is only Rs. 259.65 crore. The Committee has been given to understand that as on 31st March, 
2007, provisional expenditure was Rs. 306.91 crore. The Committee fails to unde rstand the reasons due to 
which inspite of funds being made available, impl ementing agencies have failed to make optimum 
utilization thereof.  
3.4 The Committee has also observed that physical ta rgets set under various co mponents of different 
vector-borne disease covered under the Programme during 2006-07 show unde r achievement. Similar 
targets have been set for 2007-08 also. The Committee would like to point out that with an enhanced 
provision of Rs. 400.00 crore being made for 2007-08 which marks the beginning of Eleventh Plan, it is 
all the more necessary that corrective measures were taken by the Department. If such an action is yet 
to be taken, the Committee would urge upon the Department to do so at the earliest.

Japanese Encephalitis 
3.16 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has been reported 
repeatedly from 15 States. There is no specific anti viral drug for JE and cases are managed symptomatically. 
Efforts have been directed to provide technical support and strengthen capabilities of State through training to 
tackle this disease. A vaccination programme for children between 1 and 15 years of age under the Universal 
immunization programme, using single dose live attenuated SA-14-14-2 vaccine has been launched in 2006. A 
total of 93.08 lakhs children were vaccinated against the target of 105.31 lakhs children achieving 88.39 per 
cent coverage. 
3.17 During the year 2006, 2832 cases due to suspected JE  were reported from ten States in the country, with 
Uttar Pradesh (2320 cases), Assam (392 cases), and Bihar (73 cases) leading the tally. During 2006, 658 deaths 
were reported against 1682 deaths reported during the previous year. 
3.18 The Committee has been given to  understand that till 31st December 2007, the number of cases 
reported and resultant deaths have shown a sign ificant decrease on a year-on-year basis. The 
Committee is happy to note that the number of cases reported and also deaths thereof are on the decline. 
However, the Committee would also like to draw th e attention of the Depart ment towards the rising 
death cases due to JE reported from Assam during 2006. While the cases detected and deaths were 145 
and 52 in 2005, the numbers for 2006 at 392 and 119 respectively, is more than double in cases reported 
and deaths thereof, over that of the previous year. No  doubt, in U.P. the number of cases detected and 
deaths have come down significantly, yet the Co mmittee asks the Department not to let down its 
vigilance and step up efforts in Assam as well as U.P. so that the dreaded disease is eliminated for good. 
The Committee urges the Department to step-up the ongoing IEC activities in the endemic States so that 
the desired objective is reached soon.

IV. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME  
4.1 T.B is a major health problem in India. India accounts for l/5th of the global incidence of T.B. cases. To 
control the problem of TB, Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), an application of WHO 
recommend Directly Observed Treatment short course with an objective of achieving cure rate of 85 per cent 
of new sputum positive cases and to detect at least 70 per cent of such cases, was launched in the country on 26 
March 1997. The Department has informed that the Programme was implemented in a phased manner and by 
March, 2006, the entire population of the country covering 632 districts has been covered. The Committee has 
been further informed that 2263 NGOs and 14674 Private Practitioners have been involved in RNTCP under 
various GoI approved schemes. As against a target of 70 per cent case detection of new sputum positive cases, 
65 per cent level could be achieved by December, 2006. Against the targeted cure ra te of 85 per cent of new 
sputum positive cases,  83 per cent cure rate was achieved upto December, 2006. 
4.2 The RNTCP project Phase-II has been approved by the Government for the period October, 2005 to 
September, 2011 for a total outlay of Rs. 1,156 Crore (USD 256.9 million) which includes credit from World 
Bank of Rs. 756 crores (USD 170 million) and commodity  assistance of anti-TB drugs from DFID through 

WHO for Rs.287 crores (USD 63.7 million) with balance of Rs.191 crores (USD 42.5 million) will be given by 
GoI. In addition, 427 crores through GFATM and USAID have also been provided.

rate of infection may increase per year. Moreover, it is likely that the virus may manifest resistant strains that 
may, in all likelihood, cause difficulties in treatment  in future. The Committee ther efore suggests that since 
records of T.B. cases are kept, the he lp of both NGOs and Private Practition ers should be taken for identifying 
defaulting patients and mainstreaming them into RNTCP. 
4.8 The Committee notes that one of the new initiative s proposed under the Prog ramme is the introduction 
of diagnostic and treatment services for Multi-Drug Resi stant T.B in a phased manner, starting with Gujarat 
and Maharashtra in the first quarter of 2007. Committee has been given to understand that anti-TB Drugs for 
MDR TB are over 400 times more expensive than re gular DOTS. The Committee is not aware whether any 
assessment about the estimated number of patients in the country needing such treatment has been made so far. 
The Committee strongly feels that such a survey should be carried out at the earliest both for identifying such 
patients and the factors responsible for this emerging problem. 
V. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME (NLEP)  
5.1 National Leprosy Eradication Programme was launched with the objective of eliminating Leprosy i.e. 
achieving prevalence rate of <1case/1 0,000 population from the country. National level elimination of leprosy 
has been achieved since 31st December, 2005 when the prevalence rate came down to 0.95 or less than 
1/10,000 population. Prevalence rate has further redu ced to 0.85/10,000 population in May, 2006 and to 
0.75/10,000 population in January 2007.  27 States/UTs ha ve achieved elimination level while States of Bihar, 
U.P., Jharkhand, West Bengal, Chha ttisgarh and UTs—Delhi, Dadra  a nd Nagar Haveli and Chandigarh are 
close to achieving the goal of elimination of leprosy. 
5.2 Rs. 38.63 crores was allocated at RE 2006-07 while  an allocation of Rs.40 crores has been made for 
2007-08 towards this objective. Justifying the allocati on the Department has stated that although elimination 
has been achieved at Nationa l level, new cases will continue to come up for some time. These newly detected 
cases have to be provided quality leprosy services so th at they are diagnosed and treated early. Further, there 
are 29 districts and quite a number of blocks having prevalence rate of >2 per 10,000 population situated in 7 
States. Any relaxation at this stage may lead to accumu lation of large number of hidden cases thus requiring 
the existing services under the programme to be sustained.

VI. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS  
6.1 The National Programme For Control of Blindness was launched in the year 1976 as a 100  
per cent Centrally Sponsored scheme with the goal  to reduce the prevalence of blindness from 1.4  
per cent to 0.3 per cent. As per Survey in 2001-02, prevalence of blindness is estimated to be 1.1 per cent. 
Target for the Tenth Plan is to reduce prevalence of blindness to 0.8 per cent by 2007. The Committee would 
like to know the actual achievement made against th e target of reducing the prevalence of blindness to 
0.8 per cent during the Tenth Five Year Plan. The Comm ittee would also like to be informed of the time 
frame by which prevalence of blindness is targeted to be reduced from 1.4 per cent to 0.3 per cent. 
6.2 A total release of Rs. 110.44 crores was made during 2006-07 while the expenditure reported upto 28th 
February, 2007 is Rs. 94.7 crores. Out of Rs. 85.34 crores, 20 major States could spend a Rs. 15.68 crores. 
Himachal Pradesh is the only State that has been able to utilize the allocated funds fully while Bihar, 
Chhattisgarh, Goa, J&K, Maharashtra and Uttaranchal reporting nil expenditure. The programme has not taken 
off properly in the other States, with Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh reporting 
very meagre spending. A total amount of Rs. 10.68 crores were released to 8 NE States while the provisional 

expenditure reported has been only Rs. 4.57 crores during 2006-07. Among the NE States, poor utilization has 
been reported from Tripura, Mizoram, Meghalaya and Assam. 
6.3 The Committee is disturbed to note that the st atus of utilisation of allocated funds during

been monitored properly. The Committee would like to be apprised about the sub- optimal utilization of the 
allocated funds and also the steps taken to streamline the monitoring of the Programme.

VIII. INTEGRATED DISEASE SURVEILLANCE PROJECT (IDSP)  

8.1 Integrated Disease Surveillance Project is a de centralized, State based Surveillance programme 
launched in the country in November, 2004. It is intended to detect early warning signals of impending 
outbreak and help initiate an effective response in a time ly manner it is also expected to provide essential data 
to monitor progress of ongoing disease control programmes and help allocate health resources more 
effectively. Malaria, Acute Diarrhoeal Disease (Cholera), Typhoid, Tuberculosis, Measles, Polio, Road Traffic 
Accidents, Plague, Yellow Fever, Meningo-encephalitis, respiratory Distress, Haemorrhagic fevers, HIV/HBV, 
HCV, water quality, outdoor air quality, Obesity, Blood pr essure, Tobacco use etc. ha ve been included in the 
core list for surveillan ce. The States can identify up to five States  specific diseases that require surveillance 
based on disease burden and availability of public health action. 9 States in Phase-I (Andhra Pradesh, 
Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya  Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttarancha l, Tamilnadu, Mizoram and Kerala) 
and 14 States/UTs in Phase-II (Chha ttisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan, West Bengal, Manipur, 
Meghalaya, Orissa, Tripura, Chandigarh, Pondicherry, Delhi, Nagaland) have been covered. The programme is 
being initiated in remaining 12 States/UTs in Phas e-III (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jammu  and Kashmir, 
Jharkhand, Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Sikkim, A&N Islands, D  and N Haveli, Daman  and Diu, 
Lakshadweep) after the pre-requisites are met, for which the process is already going on. The progress made 
includes: 
 • In most districts of Phase-I and II States , Rapid Response Teams have been identified and 
trained. 
 • In Phase-I States, 927 Programme Officers /RPT and in Phase-II States, 605 Programme 
Officers/RPT have been trained at 9 identified National Level Institutions. 
 • In Phase-I States, 9596 Medical Officers, 341 82 MPWs,  and 241 Laboratory Technicians and 
in Phase-II States, 4086 Medical Officers, 19166 MPWs  and 731 Laboratory Technicians have 
further been trained in IDSP. 
 • IDSP has developed specific training manuals, operation manuals, standard operating protocols 
and guidelines for capacity building of IDSP officers and staff. 
 • NIC has been assigned the task to establish and manage Information Technology Network 
connecting about 800 States  and District He adquarters, as well as Government Medical 
Colleges. NIC would be developing specific software to facilitate data transfer and analysis. 
 • IDSP has developed and distributed reporting formats and guidelines in 23 Phase-I  and Phase-
II States. CSU presently receives weekly diseas e surveillance reports from about 63 per cent 
(250/394) districts. Respective districts are taking data analysis and action. 
 • Strengthening of the district level, State level and referral laboratories for diagnosis of 
epidemic prone diseases in Phase-I  and Phase-II States.

10.8 The Committee observes that huge unspent balances have begun to pile up in the High Focus states. Not

10.9 The Committee has noted that under the Janani Suraksha Yojana an amount of Rs.1400/- is given as

to keep a check on IMR and MMR and to encourage In stitutional Delivery leading to safe Motherhood.

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 The Committee is dismayed to note that the Depart ment at the initial stage has failed to project its 
budgetary requirements in an effective and prudent way, which is evident from the fact that the 
Planning Commission has requested the Department to indica te the schemes/programmes where the 
allocation is insufficient. The Committee would like the Department to process the matter with a sense 
of urgency so that the stumbling blocks in the allo cation of sufficient funds for a crucial sector like 
health are removed. (Para 2.4) 
 The Committee, however, is not inclined to agree, simply because the detailed analysis of trend of 
allocation of plan funds and utilisation thereof during 2006-07 reveals a different position. The 
Committee would like to draw the attention of the De partment towards the fact that BE allocation of  
Rs. 11,305.00 crore had to be brought down to Rs. 10,000.00 crore at the RE stage. As per the 
information available with the Committee, actual ex penditure figure as on the 15th February, 2007 in 
the Heath sector were Rs. 1435.78 crore against RE allocation of Rs. 2048.92 crore. Under NRHM, there 
was utilisation of Rs. 6047.30 crore as on 28th February, 2007 against RE provision of Rs. 7951.08 crore. 
Even if total provisional expenditu re of  Rs. 9295.55 crore as on 31st March, 2007 turns out to be the 
final utilisation status, the fact remains that about  Rs. 2000.00 crore were spent in the latter half of the 
last quarter of the financial year. During 2005-06 al so, allocated funds remained under-utilised. Against 
a total plan allocation of  Rs. 9332.00 crore, final expenditure figures were Rs. 7926.55 crore. (Para 2.5) 
 Committee has been commenting on this discouraging utilizatio n trend year after year. However, 
there does not seem to be any noticeable improvement . This is all the more di sturbing as there was no 
significant enhancement in the plan allocation for 2006-07 when compared with 2005-06. Against this 
backdrop, total plan allocation of Rs. 13,875.00 crore  for the entire health s ector including NRHM for 
2007-08 is at an enhanced level when compared wi th the previous year. The Committee is well aware 
that health sector is the most vital sector for a va st country like ours where  majority of population 
remains deprived of even the minimum medical fac ilities. The Committee has been advocating higher 
allocation for health and family welfare and would continue to do the same this year too. (Para 2.6) 
 The Committee is fully aware that health being a state subject, Central funds are to be spent 
through the agencies of State  Govern ments alone. It is also true that  absorption capacity varies from 
State to State. The Committee would like to emphasize once again that the Centre has to play a more 
pro-active role. The main priority for the Depart ment should be to extensively monitor both the 
implementation of all the schemes and functioning of  those premier institutions/ hospitals, constantly 
showing unsatisfactory performanc e level. The Committee wonders whether any exercise has been 
initiated so far so as to analyse their status duri ng the Tenth Plan. The Comm ittee strongly feels that 
with the Eleventh Plan al ready begun, such an analysis should be made, if not done already, without 
further delay, followed by remedial measures. (Para 2.7) 
 The Committee views with serious concern very discouraging utilization status of major disease 
control programmes like National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, National Cancer Control 
Programme, National Mental Health Programme, Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, Rural 
Family Welfare Services, State Training Centres, Ro utine Immunisation, Institutes/Organisations like 
Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi, JIPMER, Po ndicherry, National T.B. Institute, Bangalore, 
Central Drug Standard and Contro l Organisation, Drug Control, De velopment of Nursing Sciences, 
Health Sector Disaster Preparedness and Management , Health Education. Performance under/of these 
schemes/institutions needs to be monitored all the more as their plan allocation for 2007-08 shows 
considerable enhancement. (Para 2.8) 
 The Committee in this connection would like to ob serve that this unhealth y practice of diverting 
plan funds to meet the expenditure on the non-plan si de has been continuing for the last several years. 
The Committee in its 16th Report on Demands for Grants 2006-07 had recommended to curb this trend. 

The Committee, however, observes  that the trend has remained unabated during the financial year 
2006-07 also. In this regard, the response of the Department that it needs to do an internal exercise to 
look into the non-plan budget of institutions like AIIMS and draw a strategy is a much delayed but very 
much required action. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should complete 
whatever exercise proposed to ensure that adeq uate funds are available to meet the non-plan 
expenditure and unhealthy practice of diversion of funds from plan to non-plan is brought to an end.  
  (Para 2.10) 
 The Committee in this connection would also like to observe that non-plan expenditure in respect 
of Health and Family Welfare Sector has a slightly different character and impact as compared to non-
plan expenditure of other organizations and Departments. A large chunk of  non-plan funds of the 
Department is spent on consumables, drugs and ma intenance of hospitals, machinery and equipment. 
Therefore, insufficient provision for meeting such vital recurring expenditure year after year will 
eventually paralyse the running of various Hospit als and Institutions. The Committee expects that the 
above mentioned concern would be shared and appr eciated by the Government while allocating non-
plan funds for the Department. (Para 2.11) 
 Committee has been viewing with serious concern the pendency of Utilisation Certificates under 
various schemes of the Department. Committee was informed that the Department has been pursuing 
the clearance of pending Utilisation Certificates wi th State  Governments. However, the problem of 
pending UCs continues unabated. The Committee is co nstrained to observe that as on 1st March, 2007, 
there were as many as 2810 outstanding UCs amountin g to Rs. 1184.05 crore for the grants released 
upto 2004-05. The Committee finds that problem is  more acute under Family Welfare Sector having 
outstanding UCs for Rs. 716.12 crore. By the close of  2006-07, total number of UCs which have become 
due is 4153 amounting to Rs. 5417.34 crores. (Para 2.12) 
 The Committee was given to understand that und er the revised Finance Mi nistry guidelines, UCs 
become due after 12 months instead of earlier period  of 18 months. The Committee is of the view that 
under the new dispensation, this problem is bound to aggravate. It seems that the Department has so far 
failed to take any effective corrective measure in spite of the Committee rep eatedly making pointed 
references in this direction. The Committee does not have much fa ith in the Programme Management 
Units being set up at State level and District level and deputing of managerial experts to the States by 
the Department. Committee has been compelled to make such an observation in view of a serious 
shortfall in the accounting/audit system of the Mini stry itself, pointed out in the CAG Report on the 
functioning of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the period 2002-05 (Report No. 12 of 
2006). It has been noticed that audit of all the central and centrally sponsored health programmes, PSUs 
under the Department and autonomous bodies like AIIMS, PGI, Chandigarh are kept out of jurisdiction 
of Internal Audit. CAG was of th e opinion that in view of huge amount of funds involved, such a 
procedure defeated the very purpose of having an  Internal Audit Wing of  the Ministry. Committee 
views the proposed audit of autonomous bodies from 2007-08 by the Internal Audit Wing of the 
Ministry too late an exercise in the day. Committee finds the statemen t of the Department all the more 
disturbing that internal audit of all central and centrally sponsored schemes would require the 
Internal Audit Wing to be strengthened considerably. This clearly shows that there is not much hope of 
situation improving in the near fu ture. The Committee would, therefore, urge upon the Department to 
set its own House in order first without any further delay. The Committee also feels that vigorous efforts 
need to be made on priority basis to clear th e UCs pending for the last three decades or so. 
Simultaneously, the Department should pursue with the States showin g maximum pendency, if 
necessary at the highest level. (Para 2.13) 
 The Committee takes note of the concerns regarding submission of utilization certificates within 
12 months, as required by the General Financial Rule s, as amended in 2005. The Committee is inclined 
to agree to the Department’s view that given the nature of decentralizatio n and the mandate of the 
NRHM, the issue of submission of Utilization Certificates within a period of  12 months of the end of the 

Financial Year needs serious re -examination. The Committee theref ore recommends that applicability 
of revised GFR in the context of Health and Fa mily Welfare Programme may be reviewed and the 
Ministry of Finance may be approached in this regard. (Para 2.17)

III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)  
 The Committee observes that a number of init iatives are proposed for CGHS which include 
delegation of enhanced financial powers to Minist ries and within CGHS, Local Advisory Committees at 
dispensary level, compilation of manual of rules and procedure, reduction in waiting time for 
registration and delivery of medicines. Welcomin g such initiatives, the Committee would like to 
emphasize that all the proposed in itiatives should be implemented in a time-bound manner with the 
ultimate objective of making CGHS more patient-friendly. (Para 3.3) 
 The Committee observes that the target of Com puterisation of all CGHS dispensaries in Delhi 
during 2006-07 could not be accomplis hed. Only the Pilot Project of co mputerization of dispensaries in 
Laxmi Nagar, North Avenue, South Avenue and Parl iament House Annexe could be completed. On a 
specific query in this regard, Department has also submitted that the original programme of completion 
of computerization by the end of 2006-07 could not be achieved due to resource constraints as funds 
could be allocated only during February, 2007. Sanction order for the computerisation of dispensaries in 
Delhi has been conveyed to National Informatics Ce ntre and it is expected that the computerisation 
process would be completed by 17th August, 2007. (Para 3.4) 
 The Committee would like to point that BE allocation of Rs. 35.00 crore was enhanced to Rs. 
39.57 crore at the RE stage. Provisional expenditure as on 31st March, 2007 as informed by the 
Department is Rs. 34.42 crore, leaving a gap of Rs. 5.00 crore. Hence the reply of the Department that 
due to resource constraints, funds could be alloca ted only during February , 2007 has raised more 
queries than it has answered. The Committee feels that delay must have occurred due to prolonged 
procedure involved while sanctioning a new project. The Commit tee, accordingly, recommends that 
computerization of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi should be completed by the revised target date of 17th 
August, 2007. (Para 3.5) 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that implementation of SIU Report has been kept 
postponed on one pretext or the other year after year. Upto last year, information on existing strength in 
the dispensaries was being sought from CGHS un its. Norms have changed since then and now SIU 
Report is to be implemented on the basis of norm s based on attendance data for 2005. The Committee, 
however, observes that details from all Addition al/ Joint Directors are yet to be received. The 
Committee apprehends that if there is a further delay in getting the average attendance details for the 
year 2005 as proposed by the Department, the data so received will again not match the ground realities 
which will again delay the implementation of the SIU Report. The Committee, therefore, recommends to 
the Department to complete all the procedural forma lities, paving the way for early implementation of 
the SIU Report. (Para 3.7) 
 Committee observes that follow- up action on a number of recomm endations made in the Report 
given by M/s. Ferguson and Company, sponsored  by European Union has been taken by the 
Department. Committee would like to comment on some  aspects of action initiated by the Department. 
The reduction in the number of functional dispensaries to half, due to work-load being negligible during 
emergency hours cannot be considered a wise move . The Committee is not in clined to agree with the 
contention that in an emergency, the beneficiary can take treatment at any private hospital, whether 
empanelled or not. The Committee is of the strong view that for small emergencies, the patient should 
depend on the nearest dispensary which would be providin g free of cost treatment. It would be better if 

emergency service is made available in more and more dispensaries, specially in view of quite a few 
dispensaries, at least in Delhi, moving in buildings of their own. (Para 3.8) 
 Committee has also been voicing its concern in this  regard since long. The Committee is surprised 
to note that the Department continues to indicate that operating dispensaries in two shifts was not 
possible due to resistance by the Employee s’ Association. The Committee expresses  its strong 
reservation to this line of argument. The Committee reiterates that the Department has to play a more 
pro-active role in such matters. A beginning can be easily made by starting two shifts in a few 
dispensaries as a test case. After some time, an analys is about patient visits to dispensary can be easily 
made and a final decision taken in the end. (Para 3.9) 
 The Committee observes that si nce on the basis of its earlier recommendations, Ministry of 
Finance has already lifted the ban on filling up of technical posts, the responsibility for expediting the 
filling up of vacancies lies now on the Departme nt and any further delay in the matter cannot be 
justified. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department to expedite the filling up of 
vacancies at the earliest. (Para 3.11) 
 The Department has informed that in respect of  non technical posts, the Screening Committee in 
its meeting held on December, 2006, has cleared 136 posts in CGHS for being filled up and action to fill 
them up has been initiated. The Committee would like to be informed about the progress made in this 
regard. (Para 3.12) 
 The Committee was given to understand that one significant change has been made in the new 
system. Now empanelment of hospitals/diagnostic centers is a continuous process, option being available 
to join the CGHS at any time. The Committee would, however, like to point out that there are inherent 
drawbacks under such a system. Beneficiaries will have  to keep a track of empanelled hospitals which is 
not always possible under such a flexible system, clerical errors may sometime occur, putting the 
patients to inconvenience. The Co mmittee, therefore, feels that it would be appropriate if a minimum 
period of empanelment is also la id down for private hospitals/diagnostic centres and labs, as done 
earlier. (Para 3.14) 
 The Committee has another very strong obje ction in respect of the new procedure. The 
Committee is of the firm opinion that inclusion in th e list of empanelled hospitals/diagnostic centres on 
the basis of lowest quotations cannot be considered to be based on a sound principle. The Committee 
feels that the mandate of the Government is to provide a fullsome and comprehensive medical care 
facility to the beneficiaries and not a piece-meal one. Private hospitals/diagnostic centres have been 
recognized throughout the countr y for specialist treatment/diagno sis, providing access of quality 
medical care to the beneficiaries on the one hand and relieving the Government Hospitals of the extra 
patient load on the other. Moreov er, there cannot be two opinions th at in almost al l the Government 
Hospitals, the infrastructure and other facilities are already overstretched. The Committee thinks that 
provision of private recognized hospitals and diagnostic centres should be logical and essential extension 
of the existing system and to hold that it is an additional facility is not in sync with the current buzzword 
of Public-Private-Partnership. (Para 3.15) 
 The Committee feels that literally speaking, though the Department cannot force private 
hospitals/diagnostic centres to be empanelled, it can indirectly compel the quality private 
hospitals/diagnostic centre to opt ou t of empanelment, if the rates quo ted are very low. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the rates should be fixed realistically, taking into acco unt the market 
realities so as to encourage quality private hospitals and diagnostic centres to join the system. 
  (Para 3.16) 
IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI  

 The Committee also observes that  trend of plan allocation and utilization thereof during the 
Tenth Plan period shows that someho w the Hospital has failed to keep pace with the allocation of plan 
funds. (Para 4.2) 
 The Committee has been observin g that even though the patient load in the Hospital has been 
showing a steady increase over the years, the bed st rength of 1531 of the Hospital, continues to remain 
unchanged. Appreciating that the ever-increasing patient load has al ready overstretched the Hospital 
services and infrastucture, the Committee has been st rongly advocating the need for increase in the bed 
strength of the Hospital. The Committee is happy to  note that a proposal for the redevelopment of 
Safdarjung Hospital has been prepared and submitted to Planning Commission for approval. The 
estimated cost of the whole project is Rs. 1400 crores to be spread over 15 years (within Three Five Year 
Plans). The first phase of this red evelopment plan is estimated to cost Rs.700 crores. The Committee 
was, however, informed that the Pl anning Commission has refused to grant ‘in- principle’ approval for 
the proposal. (Para 4.4) 
 The Committee observes that the Hospital caters not only to the ordinary citizens of Delhi with 
meager means but also of the neighbouring states. The basic idea not to disturb the existing services and 
simultaneously go for redevelopment needs to be impl emented without any deviation and dilution in the 
original plan deserves to be implemented in the real sense. The Committee, therefore, strongly 
recommends to the Department to approach the Pl anning Commission once again to convince the 
Commission of the necessity of  according approval for the  redevelopment plan of the Hospital as 
originally envisaged. At the same time, the Depa rtment should make ever y conceivable effort to 
complete the redevelopment plan with in the targeted date and also with out cost escalation to the extent 
possible. The Committee would appreciate if th e Department puts in place a joint monitoring 
Committee of Department and Hospital authorities so as to tie all the loose ends and work towards the

should closely monitor the ongoing projects from the beginning of financial year 2007-08 itself. Only 
then, the Department can make out a case for additional funds at the RE stage. (Para 4.9)

 The Committee has noted that the ICMR’s record in utilizing the allocated funds has been 
impressive and except for 2004-05, the ICMR’s ut ilization has either matched the allocated funds or

ongoing research projects will be affected adversely but it will  also be very difficult to undertake any 
new project. This, in the opinion of the Committee w ill prove to be detrimental for the medical research 
in the country, specially in the fi ercely competitive global scenario. The Committee is disturbed to note 
that its strong recommendation for higher allocation of funds for the Council for 2006-07 made last year 
which was based on the Performance Appraisal Board’s expert advocacy, failed to get additional funds 
released at the RE stage. The Committee, however, reiterates that the Department should vigorously 
pursue the matter with the Planning Commission to meet the requirements of medical research in the 
country and release adequate funds for this purpose. The Committee is of the firm view that funding for 
medical research should not be looked at the same level as funding for routine schemes/matters. Overall 
cut in the plan funds should not be made applicable to one and all. (Para 8.3)

breaking studies on subjects like Viral Encephalitis. H. Pylori infection, improving the utilization of 
emergency contraception through paramedics, multi-centric study on genomics of male infertility, 
assessment of prevalence of osteoporosis in adult population etc. (Para 8.4) 
 The Committee in this connection would like to obs erve that what is needed for the upliftment of 
research in the country is more funds and greater au tonomy and lesser control. In this connection, the 
Committee would like to recall the observations ma de by the five member Performance Appraisal 
Board having two international an d three national experts. This Board was constituted by the 
Department in 2005 and had made valuable sugges tions about changes required in the authority, 
autonomy, financial support and restructuring. In th e opinion of the Committe e, bureaucratization of 
the research institutes is actual ly part of the problem and not th e remedy. The Committee feels that 
need of hour is to make massive investments in medical R and D and not to fasten it with a red tape. The 
Committee would like to be apprised about follow-up action, if any, initiated by the Department on 
PAB’s recommendations. (Para 8.5)

 The Committee would like to be ap prised of the achievements made vis-a-vis the targets fixed
