Directorates and matter is also being taken up at the highest administrative level, as and when required. 
The Committee hopes that with such co-ordinated meas ures, the Department will be able to contain the 
number of outstanding UCs, increase in the fund allocation notwithstanding. (Para 2.8) 
III. EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS  
National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur 
 The Committee is hopeful that thes e set targets would be achieved by the Institute and there would 
be optimum and judicious utilizations of funds for the above-mentioned purposes. (Para 3.2) 
 The Committee expresses its serious concern on th e status of vacancies in teaching posts in a 
premier Institute of Ayurveda. Inspite of CAG observations, situation has not improved, rather 
worsened. The Committee has been observing that due to court cases, vacancies continue to exist for a 
very long period. The Committee would like to point out that prolonged vacancies, that too of as many as 
23 posts cannot be considered satisfactory at any co st for a teaching institution. The Committee hopes 
that selection process for 7 posts of Professor and A ssociate Professor must have been over and selected 
candidates must have joined. For th e remaining 16 posts, concerted effo rts need to be made for getting 
the High Court stay vacated, wherever applicab le and expedite the recruitment procedure. The 
Committee is also of the view that  there is a need for review of exis ting selection process/recruitment 

procedure so as to make the same foolproof and expeditious. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department should take up this matter with the Institute authority. (Para 3.5) 
RASHTRIYA AYURVEDA VIDYAPEETH, DELHI 
 The Committee takes note of the observation ma de in the Performance Audit of Department of 
AYUSH of 2000-01 to 2004-05 by CAG that CCIM did not recognize the courses run by the RAV. 
  (Para 3.7) 
 The Committee is of the opinion that imparting traditional Ayurvedic knowledge is the end goal of 
RAV and imparting this knowledge through the trad itional method of Guru-Shishya Parampara is the 
means to that end. The Committee opines that RAV m ay not confer degree but this exercise can be made 
more authentic if the courses run by RAV are rec ognized by CCIM leading to systematic, orderly and 
authentic dissemination of Traditional Ayurvedic knowledge through its Guru-Shishya Parampara. The 
Committee does not understand th e reluctance of the Department in recognizing RAV courses which 
would not in any way dilute the objectives of the RAV. (Para 3.8) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF HOMOEOPATHY (NIH), KOLKATA 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the phy sical target for Tenth plan for this Institute to 
increase the bed capacity from 60 to 100 has not been completed. The Committee has been given to 
understand that this 60 bedded hospital is now proposed to be expanded to 250 bedded hospital in view of 
the additional requirements for increase in seats on account of 27 pe r centreservations for OBC, creation 
of new PG faculties and provision of seats for BIMSTEC countries.  
 The Committee is doubtful about the timely completi on of these projects, as  even after the end of 
the Tenth Plan, the 60-hedded hospital could not be expanded to 100-bedded one. The Committee 
however, hopes that during the Eleventh plan, this long pending project would be completed in a time-
bound manner, under close monitoring by the Department as well as the Institute authorities. (Para 3.10) 
 The Committee is perturbed regarding the way the selection of Director of NIH has been handled so 
far.  (Para 3.11) 
 The Committee is specially disturbed by the fact that there was a CBI case against the  
Ex-Director also which led to his suspension. The Committee does not understand the basis for selecting a 
candidate against whom a vigilance case is pendin g. The Committee wonders whether the appointing 
authority was aware of these details of the candidate or not. Moreover, the Committee would like to 
know the reasons for undue delay in the disposal of Inquiry Report. The Committee hopes that the case is 
expedited soon so that the post of Director is filled  to avoid a situation which allows running of a premier 
Institute like NIH, Kolkata without the supervision of Institutional head. (Para 3.12) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF UNANI MEDICINE, BANGALORE 
 The Committee is, however, constrained to obs erve that the enhanced provision remained under 
utilized. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon th e Department to make concerted efforts to get the 
2nd phase of construction completed during 2007- 08. Whatever bottleneck, have  been experienced in 
getting the works completed in time, should be got removed, in close coordination with the Institute 
authorities. At no cost, allocated funds remaining unutilized like in 2005-06 and 2006-07, should be 
allowed to be repeated in 2007-08. It is high time that NIUM moves towards it s objective of becoming a 
center of excellence for the development and propagation of Unani system of medicine. (Para 3.14) 
IV. STATUTORY INSTITUTIONS  
CENTRAL COUNCIL OF INDIAN MEDICINE 
 The Committee is constrained that this work does not find any place under the physical targets set 
for the Council for 2007-08. Report on modernization of Under Graduate education including restricting 
of syllabus is to be taken up during 2007-08 in stead. The Committee can only recommend that the 
process of modernization/review of both Under Grad uate and Post Graduate AYUSH courses should be 

completed in a time- bound manner. This is required to  be accomplished on an urgent basis, keeping in 
view increasing acceptance of AYUSH system of medicine both in the country and aboard. (Para 4.2) 
 Committee has been continuously expressing its co ncern on the undue delay in updation of Central 
Register of Indian Medicine. Latest status made av ailable to the Committee reveals that position is 
deteriorating with the pass age of each year. This is indeed a sorry state of affairs. The Department 
cannot escape by taking the plea that maintenance and updating of Central Register of Indian Medicine 
is the statutory responsibility of the Central Council. (Para 4.3) 
 The Committee is happy to note that all the Chie f Secretaries have been asked to get a regular 
fulltime Registrar posted in all the State Boards wi th minimum complementary staff. One time financial 
assistance is also to be given on the condition that State Boards are made functioning. The Committee 
feels that the steps initiated by the Department we re long overdue. The Committ ee would appreciate if 
the process started by the Department is brought to its logical end. (Para 4.4) 
CENTRAL COUNCIL OF HOMOEOPATHY, NEW DELHI 
 The Committee had been reiterating on timely updation of Central Register by identifying the 
bottlenecks in the process. (Para 4.6) 
 The Committee appreciates the pro-active role adopted by the Departme nt. The Committee hopes 
that things will now improve. Howev er, constant monitoring will have to be done by the Department in 
close co-ordination with State Govts./Councils/Boards.  The Committee would appreciate if a status note 
on the progress made during 1st quarter of 2007-08 is forwarded to it. (Para 4.10) 
 The Committee understands that names of about 43500 practitioners published in 1993 are to be 
removed from the Central Register of Homoeopathy. The Committee would like to be apprised about the 
progress made in this regard. (Para 4.11) 
V.  RESEARCH COUNCILS  
 The Committee appreciates the extensive research wo rk carried out by all the four Councils during 
the Tenth Plan period. The Committee observes that  a number of research projects when completed 
would make meaningful contribution in providing health care facilities to our people. The Committee 
supports the proposed enhanced allocation of Rs.424.50 crore fo r these Research Councils for the 
Eleventh Plan Period and hopes that all the research projects at present under implementation will be 
brought to a logical end and also new projects will be undertaken during this period. (Para 5.3) 
VI. YOGA AND NATUROPATHY  
 The Committee expresses its concern regarding:— 
 • regulation of education of Naturopathy 
 • regulation of training, propagation and treatment by yoga and Naturopathy 
   (Para 6.1) 
 The Committee was given to understand that Mo rarji Desai National Institute of Yoga was 
preparing draft curriculum for various courses and norms for accreditation of Yoga institutions. The 
National Institute of Naturopathy, Pune was also preparing similar gu idelines. These guidelines were to 
be circulated to the States for their guidance and enforcement. 
 The Committee would like to know whether any State has brought out any legislation with regard 
to guidelines on the accreditation of Naturopathy practitioners and institutions. The Committee also 
urges the Department to rethink s eriously about the establishment of a regulatory Council for Yoga and 
Naturopathy. The Committee is of the opinion that the setting up of a Council would help in 
standardization of education and practice of Yoga a nd Naturopathy and benefit the public at large. The 
Committee also feels that there is a need for wider publicity of yoga and naturopathy so that the public at 
large benefit from it. (Para 6.3) 

VII. HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES  
NATIONAL AYURVEDA HOSPITAL, DELHI 
 The Committee would like to point out that one plan period is over and another has started. 
However, it is not known whether final approval from  EFC could be obtained by the Department. The 
Committee is of the firm opinion that had there been better  coordination between the Department and 
the Ministry of Finance, such a situation would not have continued for so long. The Committee would like 
to point out that at the initial stage only, had th e ground-work been done properly, the complication 
arising due to DDA demanding commercial cost of land  in view of there being public-private partnership 
could not have been there. The Committee fails to understand the rationale of going for private 
partnership on public land. The Committee would like to point out that such confusion at the initial stage 
has resulted in a delay of three years. The Committee ca n only emphasize that a ll the loose ends may be 
tied now and formal approval obtained from all co ncerned so that construction work starts at the 
earliest. The Committee would also ap preciate if Department closely mo nitors the progress made in this 
project. (Para 7.3) 
EXPANSION OF AYUSH DISPENSARIES IN CGHS 
 The Committee observes that again st 7 dispensaries for Ayurveda, 7 for Homoeopathy, 3 for Unani, 
2 for Siddha and 1 Yoga Centre dispensaries to be  opened, only 1 for Ayurve da, 2 for Homoeopathy and 
1 each for Unani, Siddha and Yoga Centre could be  opened so far. The Committee would like to 
emphasize that there is need for better co-ordination between the two authorities if creation and filling up 
of posts leading to opening and functioning of more AYUSH dispensaries under CGHS has to be effected.  
  (Para 7.6) 
 Committee is of the view that an Ayurveda Dispensary under the existing scheme may also be set up 
in Kerela, preferably in Trivandrum. Hence, the Committee recommends that new dispensaries of ASU 
and H should be opened in the Southern region so as to promot e AYUSH all over the Country and 
benefit the people at large. (Para 7.7) 
AYURVEDA HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI 
 The Committee has been given to understand that the work of upgradation involving civil 
construction work is on the verge of completion. Also, work of repair and renovation of the hospital is 
also in the process and Rs. 15.28 lakhs has been sanc tioned. Hence, the Committee hopes that it starts 
functioning as soon as possible. (Para 7.8) 
 The Committee has been given to  understand that major problem affecting the functioning of 
CGHS Ayurveda hospital, is the fact that there is dual control over the functioning of the Hospital.  
 The Committee is of the view that the Department is merely shifting all the blame for non-fulfilment 
of posts on the DGHS. Since the Department has the administrative control over the Hospital, matter of 
filling up of vacant posts and outsourcing should have  been taken up with the DGHS and the urgency of 
the matter explained. Non-filling of posts of the Hospital affects the efficient functioning of the Hospital in 
delivering treatment facilities to CGHS beneficiaries. Hence, concerted efforts should be made by the 
Department in filling up of the vacant posts without playing the blame game. (Para 7.9) 
VIII. NATIONAL MEDICINAL PLANTS BOARD 
 The Committee believes that these elaborate quanti fiable deliverables outlined by the Department 
for the Eleventh Plan are overwhelming. 
 The Committee observes that th ese quantifiable deliverable given by the Department should be 
divided in five groups to be achieved in the five years of the Eleventh Plan. The Committee is unclear 
about what all is expected to be achieved in the current year 2007-08. Further, the Committee 
recommends that:  
 (i) A detailed examination of all projects along with its feasibility or viability studies should be 
undertaken. 

 (ii) Allocation for each project should be earmarked.  
 (iii) Proposals for various projects should be invited early so that the Board does not come with 
the excuse that lack of suitable proposals rece ived led to non-utilization of funds and non-
completion of projects on time. 
 (iv) Identification of States in which seed cent res for QPM are to be set up, Medicinal Plants 
processing zones are to be set up, documentation and threat assessment to be done etc. 
 (v) Concepts like Good Harvesting Practices, Good Agricultural Practices need to be 
elaborated upon so as to make the farmers aware of them leading to cultivation and  
availability of good quality medicines. 
   (Para 8.3) 
 Hence, the Committee wants to impress upon the Department that  preparatory exercises for the 
high-sounding targets must be done beforehand for the timely completion of projects and judicious and 
optimum utilization of funds. (Para 8.4) 
 The Committee without any pessimism hopes that the NMPB would be able to accomplish its target 
so that sustainability and availability of Good Qu ality Medicines is assured. The Committee hence 
expects that the enhanced budgetary allocation for the NMPB stands ju stified in view of the expected 
accomplishments of tasks outlined for the NMPB. (Para 8.5) 
 The Committee also takes into consideration the rec ommendations entailed in the Report of Indian 
Council of Forestry Research and Education, Dehradun and Indian Institute of Forest Management, 
Bhopal in strengthening the NMPB . The Committee believes that these recommended measures should 
be adhered to by the NMPB and SMPB for strengthening the Board in the various areas like linkage 
between buyers and sellers, networking for the supply of  quality Planting material to cultivators, better 
organization structure of SMPBs and effective monitoring mechanism of SMPBs. (Para 8.6) 
 The Committee is dismayed to find that the problem of pendency of Utilization Certificates (UCs) 
still persists. The Committee had urged the Department to make concerted effort in this regard and the 
Department in order to tackle this problem had come up with steps like:- 
 • Monitoring by the Secretary (AYUSH) in ac tive co-ordination with State Health 
Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, Programme offi cers and State Health societies for proper 
utilization of funds. 
 • Release of funds of CSS to States through th e State Health Societies (SHSs) for onward 
release of funds to the implementing agencies. 
 However, there has only been slight improveme nt in the reduction in the pendency of UCs. 
  (Para 8.7)

         (Para 8.8) 
 The Committee fails to understand the reason for the pendency of  UCs. The Committee emphasizes 
the need to accelerate the process of reduction of pendency of UCs.  
 The Committee believes that ad-hocism of such ki nd is a hindrance. The state of poor infrastructure 
at State and Central level also poses problems.  
 The Committee expects the Department to start th e preparatory exercises for ensuring State Health 
Society in each State and a monitoring mechanism to be  put into practice for better results. Due to new 
measures adopted by the Department, the Committee hopes that these sanctioned projects would be 
completed well in time with no pendency of UCs involved herein.  
 The Committee would appreciate if  the report is submitted without any delay so as to make clear 
the status and organizational structure of the Board. (Para 8.9) 
IX. STRENGTHENING OF PLIM  
 However, the Committee is dismayed to point out that the post of Direct or, PLIM which became 
vacant on 28.2.04 is still vacant. The Committee expre sses its serious concern on the process followed in 
filling up the post of Director. The post had to be adve rtised twice but still no suitable candidate could be 
selected.  (Para 9.2) 
 The Committee finds it very disturbing at the manner in which such an important matter of filling 
up the post of Director, PLIM was handled. One should not target the fact that PLIM is the nodal agency 
in the country which handles the sensitive issue of quality control of AYUSH drug. The Committee would 
like to point out that unless and until the post of Director is filled by a suitable and well- qualified person, 
one cannot hope for developing this laboratory as an  institute of international standards. The Committee 
has also been given to understand that 12 additional  posts in the grade of Sc ientists and others got 
created with the approval of the Ministry of Fina nce. The Committee urges the Department to make 
efforts to fill these 12 posts soon and not follow th e way the post of Director, PLIM which is still lying 
vacant. (Para 9.3) 
X. ACQUISITION OF MANUSCRIPTS AND PUBLICATION OF TEXT-BOOK/OUT POINT 
BOOKS 
 The Committee takes note of the fact that actual expenditure as on 28.2.07 has been nil. Rs. 1.25 
crore have been provided for 2007-08. The Committee is unclear about how this allocation of  Rs. 1.25 
crore would be  spent in the current year when one takes note of the trend of non-utilization of funds in 
the last year. (Para 10.2) 
 On a specific inquiry in this re gard, the Committee was given to und erstand that no time frame is 
given to complete the proposals under this scheme. The Committee finds that giving no time frame for 
any project is uncalled for and would lead to non-completion of projects, as there would not be any hurry 
or seriousness to complete the task. The Committee is of  the opinion that this re vision of gu idelines for 
having a time frame for completion of projects sh ould be expedited to avoid pending and incomplete 
tasks defeating the very purpose and objective of the Scheme. (Para 10.3) 
 The Committee is not impressed with these tempor ary arrangements of th e Department. However, 
collaboration with National Manuscripts Mission would be a fruitful step. The Committee opines that the 
very objective of the Scheme would be defeated if  these rare manuscripts are ac quired but not preserved 
properly. The Committee emphasizes the importance of these rare manuscripts and books which, if 
preserved properly, would really benefit the students, teachers and research scholars of ISM. (Para 10.4) 
XI. NORTH-EASTERN INSTITUTE OF AYUSH / FOLK MEDICINE  

 The Committee had recommended in its earlier Report that preparatory exercises should be started 
based on the Detailed Project Report (DPR). The Comm ittee is interested in knowing what preparatory 
exercises have been done by the De partment for setting up of these two Institutes. The Committee hopes 
the construction activities of both the Institutes would start in full swing once they get the required 
approval. (Para 11) 
CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES 
XII. DEVELOPMENT OF AYUSH INSTITUTIONS  
 However, the Committee takes into cognizance the result of clearing of pending UCs. Uptill 28.2.07, 
130 UCs worth  Rs. 1942.04 lakhs have been cleared. This means that there are still 211 pending UCs 
worth  Rs. 4362.93 lakhs. The Committee reiterates that  the pending UCs be cleared as soon as possible 
taking into consideration the Department’s initiative s of online monitoring of funds and pending UCs so 
that there is optimum utilization of funds and completion of projects in time. (Para 12.2) 
 The Committee observes that when achievement of physical targets set for the Tenth Plan are 
considered as a whole, the results are not satisfactory for schemes like ROTP, Renovation and 
Strengthening of hospital wards of Government/Government aided teaching hospitals of ISM i&H and 
establishment of computer laboratories in ISM&H Colleges as mentioned below:-

 The Committee is of the opinion that the outcome or accomplishment of the physical targets when 
taken for the entire 10th Plan gives a mixed picture, the level of achievement of targets set for the various 
components within the scheme for the year 2006-07 is highly dissatisfactory. The Committee was under 
the impression that the components in their re vised form was being closely monitored. However,  instead 
of the expected improvement in the achievement level, the results have been otherwise. (Para 12.5) 
 The Committee has been informed about the proble ms identified by the Fe rguson Commission but 
not about the recommendations given by it. The Committee has been given to understand that from 2007-
08, funds would now be released through State Health  Societies. An effective area Officer System and 
online monitoring of Central Grants and Pending UCs is to be introduced soon. The Committee however, 
wonders about the preliminary exerci ses initiated for having State Heal th Societies. The Committee is 
hopeful that these preliminary exercises are done before hand to avoid delays in release of funds and lead 
to better implementation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes like Development of AYUSH institutions. 
  (Para 12.6) 
XIII. AYUSH HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES AND NRHM 
 The Committee notes that apart from these achiev ements of the Department in 2006-07, utilization 
of funds has been more or less satisfactory during the entire Tenth Plan. (Para 13.5) 
 The Committee expects that these quantifiable de liverable are achieved by the Department by 
March end 2008 as promised. Subsuming these schemes into NRHM will make available the treatment 
facilities to the several public in th e allopathic hospitals thereby giving an alternative choice to patients. 
This will also provide financial assistance to Stat e Governments for essential drugs which will help in 
ameliorating the situation of short supply of drugs of ISM&H dispensaries in States thereby benefiting 
the people at large. The Committee has been given to  understand that the sub-scheme for the supply of 
drugs to AYUSH dispensaries has been found to be useful and beneficial for the people but the financial 
assistance of Rs. 25,000 per dispensary has been found to be inadequate and in proposed to be revised. 
The Committee recommends this revision of financial a ssistance for this sub-scheme be done soon so that 
enhanced funds can be allocated for the utmost success of this scheme. (Para 13.8) 
 The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department in clearing of pending UCs and hopes that 
pendency of UCs would not be a hindrance in the successful implementation of these schemes.  (Para 13.9) 
XIV. DRUGS QUALITY CONTROL 
 The Committee has been reiterating  the need for increasing the quantum of financial assistance 
under this component so that GMP compliant manufacturing units have their own quality control lab for 
testing of heavy metals. The Committee appreciates this proposal of the Department in enhancing 
assistance to GMP compliant units. However, the Committee recommends for enhanced budgetary outlay 
for this Scheme, as the present allocation of Rs. 10.00 crore seems inadequate. (Para 14.2) 
 The Committee observes that as on 31.12.2006, 150 UCs were pending for this Scheme involving a 
sum of Rs. 4856.95 lakhs. The Committee however, a ppreciates the Department for substantial clearance 
of UCs in the next two months and as per the records on 28.02.2007, only 33 UCs were pending involving 
a sum of Rs. 1394.28 lakhs. (Para 14.3) 
 The Committee has observed that the physical targets of Tenth Plan for this Scheme has been 
satisfactory but the Committee is of the opinion that due to the critical importance of this scheme, special 
focus of the Department on this Scheme is required  to ensure Drug Quality Control and prevent the 
usage of spurious drugs. The Committee has been given to understand that out of 9000 units, 
approximately 4000 units are GMP compliant. The Committee believes that seri ous efforts are to be 
continued for making all remaining 5000 units GMP compliant. The Committee hopes that the 
Department is able to achieve these within the stipulated time period. 
  (Para 14.4) 

 The Committee would like to know about the feedback if r eceived during 2006 after the 
introduction of mandatory testing to heavy metals for AYUSH drugs for export purposes. The 
Committee believes that the Department should move ca utiously as the same Council was entrusted with 
the job of quality control for marine products for export purposes and resu lt was not positive. The 
Committee is also unclear about the role of Pharmexcel for the promotion of ASU drug exports. (Para 14.7) 
 The Committee is still awaiting the decision of the Department regarding introduction of 
mandatory testing for heavy metals for AYUSH drug s for domestic consumption. The Committee would 
like to know the reason for delay in introducing such a mechanism for domestic usage of AYUSH drugs.  
  (Para 14.8) 
 The Committee opines that in view of the fact that State and private drugs testing labs are provided 
financial assistance by the Central Government, it would be proper if the Central Government along with 
the State Government monitors the proper functionin g of these labs. Further, Committee would also like 
to know whether any Inspection Reports of insp ectors conducted were received by the Central 
Government during 2006-07. (Para 14.9) 
XV. MISCELLANEOUS  
 The Committee would like to emphasize that Tibetan System of Medicine is practiced at many 
places and is not confined to J&K or Leh and a Region al Institute for it at Leh will not address the issue 
properly. The Committee recommends that the Institutes like this sh ould be given due importance and 
funds allocated for proper development and promotion of Tibetan System of Medicine. (Para 15.2)

The Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry Bill, 2007 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha
on the 7th March, 2007 and referred to the Committee for examination and report on the 14 th March, 2007. The Statement of Objects
and Reasons appended to the Bill reproduced below gives the background justifying the need for bringing a new Bill-
      “The Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research, Pondicherry was established in 1964
primarily with the objectives to develop patterns of teaching in undergraduate and postgraduate medical education so as to
establish and demonstrate high standards of education. The Institute has been providing quality education and excellent patient
care delivery services. Over the years, however; it could not grow due to constraints in the process of manpower selection,
lack of academic autonomy, lack of flexibility in administrative and financial powers, commensurate with other institutions
like, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi and Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research,
Chandigarh.
 It is proposed to make the Institute a statutory body corporate and declare as an institution of national importance
under entry 64 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution so that it may develop as a high level institution of
medical education and research on the pattern of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi and the Post-Graduate
Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh.
      This Bill will empower the Institute with academic autonomy to develop its own curriculum, set new trends in medical
education and research and award its own degrees and also enable it to have appropriate delegated administrative and financial
powers. The conferring of statutory status on this Institute will enable it to grow into a model centre of excellence.”
 
2.         The Committee initiated the process of consideration of the Bill by having the benefit of the views of the Secretary of Ministry
of Health and Family Welfare in its meeting held on the 8
th June, 2007. The Secretary gave the background that necessitated the
formulation of this legislation. At the time of setting up of the Institute, it was envisaged that JIPMER, Puducherry will develop as an
Institute at par with premier institutions in North India, namely, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi and Post-
Graduate Institute of Medical Education & Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.  However, it was noticed that while AIIMS and
PGIMER have shown substantial growth both in medical education as well as research, the progress of JIPMER, Puducherry has not
been commensurate with the aims and objectives for which it was set up. 
3.         Elaborating upon the main reasons for the restricted growth of JIPMER, the Secretary stated that being a subordinate office of
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, directly under the administrative control of DGHS, the Institute is governed by
rules/instructions as applicable to any other subordinate office of the Ministry.  Lack of financial/administrative autonomy coupled
with distance from Delhi resulted in undue delay in clearance of even routine matters.   Not only this, JIPMER is at present subject to
the regulation of statutory bodies like Medical Council of India, Dental Council of India, and Nursing Council etc. As a result it can
neither set its own curriculum, nor can it increase the number of seats or post-graduate programmes.   In contrast, AIIMS and
PGIMER set up by statutes are free from the control of these regulatory bodies.  They are free to prescribe their own curriculum and
decide which discipline they want to start and how many seats should be there. 
4.         The Secretary reiterated that through the Bill an effort has been made to overcome the present plethora of problems and
convert JIPMER into a statutory body on the pattern of AIIMS/PGIMER so that an environment for developing high standard of
medical education and also to undertake research of highest order may evolve. It will also grant the Institute a ‘University’ status
which will provide the necessary flexibility to frame its own regulations and pursue the task of setting standards of medical education
independent of Medical Council of India and also of Puducherry University. Besides that, JIPMER will also have its own policy for
manpower selection and retention.
5.         Subsequently, a number of representations from different associations/ unions of JIPMER were received by the Committee.  
Quite a few political parties also approached the Committee.   The Committee observed that all these representations indicated grave
apprehensions not only about different provisions of the Bill but also about the very basis for bringing out such a legislation. The
Committee also felt that a number of provisions proposed in the Bill have grave ramifications as far as the autonomy of the JIPMER
is concerned. Against this backdrop and keeping in view the far-reaching implications of the Bill on the future of JIPMER, the
Committee decided to have detailed interactions with all concerned so as to ensure better understanding of the subject.
 6.        The Committee, accordingly, visited JIPMER, Puducherry from 1
st to 4th July 2007 and held extensive discussions with a
large number of witnesses representing the management and faculty members of the Institute, various associations/unions of the
Institute and Hospital, representatives of various political parties, the State Government of Puducherry and the state branch of Indian
Medical Association.

7.         Keeping in view the fact that the present Bill was broadly based on Acts governing AIIMS and PGIMER, the Committee also
had useful discussions with the Director, PGI Chandigarh, and the Director, AIIMS, besides some ex-Directors of JIPMER. On the
basis of the feedback received by the Committee during the course of its interactions with various individuals/associations and experts
who appeared before it, the Committee sought further clarifications from the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on
certain aspects of the Bill at its meeting held on the 27th July 2007. 
8.         All these interactions proved to be very useful and helped the Committee to a great extent in formulating its opinion on
different provisions of the Bill. The Committee would like to emphasize here that during the entire exercise, its efforts were directed
towards putting forth an objective assessment of the Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research
Puducherry Bill 2007 and report thereon.
9.         The Committee has been given to understand that the proposed Bill is broadly based on the lines of PGIMER Chandigarh Act
and the AIIMS Act.   However, given the special requirements relating to the prior existence of JIPMER as a Central Government
Institute, suitable changes have been made, wherever necessary, in the interest of effectiveness.  The Committee would like to point
out that, difference in the origin of the Institutes notwithstanding, a comparative analysis of the PGIMER Chandigarh Act, the AIIMS
Act and the proposed Bill reveals that there are basic differences in some provisions which needed a close scrutiny before arriving at a
final viewpoint. The Committee would be highlighting the same while reporting on such Clauses.
 
The Clauses where the Committee has suggested amendments are discussed in the succeeding paragraphs. 
Clause 3
10.       Clause 3 provides for definitions of certain words/terms used in the Bill.   The Committee observes that whereas in both
AIIMS and PGIMER Act, specific definition of words ‘regulation’ and ‘rule’ has been given, in the present Bill, there is no such
definition. Instead it has been proposed to define the words ‘prescribed’ and ‘specified’ with reference to rules and regulations
respectively.  The Committee fails to understand the rationale for giving the definition of ‘regulation’ and ‘rule’ in a roundabout
manner.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that in place of definition of ‘prescribed’ and ‘specified’ as given in the Clause 3
(e) and (f), following definition of ‘rule’ and ‘regulation’ may be given
(e)
                ‘rule’ means a rule made by the Central Government;
(f)                 ‘regulation’ means a regulation made by the Institute.
 
The Committee also recommends that consequential amendments may be carried out in the relevant provisions of the Bill by
suitably substituting the words ‘prescribed’ and ‘specified’ by the words prescribed/specified by rules or regulations.
 
Clause 5
11.       Clause 5 of the Bill relates to the composition of the Institute Body.
            The Committee has been given to understand that the JIPMER Bill has been largely modeled on the lines of the AIIMS Act
and the PGIMER Chandigarh Act.  However, a detailed perusal and comparison of the composition of the Institute Body, as provided
in the aforesaid Acts and the Bill reveals very significant differences, the first being reflected in the strength of the three Institute
Bodies.  The Committee observes that JIPMER will be a 22 member Institute as compared to 20 Members of PGIMER, Chandigarh
and 17 Members of AIIMS.  As per JIPMER Puducherry Bill-2007 out of total 22 members, 8 will be ex-officio members and 11
shall be Govt. nominees.  During the course of discussion with different witnesses, it was constantly emphasised that the inclusion of
so many ex-officio members and nominees of the Government to the Institute Body would affect the autonomous character of the
Institute.  Strong apprehensions were voiced that the proposed composition of the Institute Body would lead to undue governmental
interference.
11.1     The Committee strongly feels that these apprehensions seem to be very true, especially due to a striking departure, i.e.
proposed inclusion of the Minister-in-charge of Health and Family Welfare as the President, and, Secretary, Department of Health and
Family Welfare as ex-officio members in the Institute Body. On a specific query in this regard, Secretary, during the course of his
deposition before the Committee on the 27
th July, 2007, stated that autonomy should not be confused with lack of accountability.  
AIIMS, PGIMER and JIPMER are all Central Government Institutions and therefore, are accountable to the Central Government
through the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and through the Government to the Parliament.    The Secretary clarified that in
both AIIMS and PGIMER, the Minister is nominated as a member of the Institute Body and then by convention he becomes the
President.  The Secretary justified the proposed explicit provision in the JIPMER Bill, drawing the attention of the Committee to the
following observations made by the Supreme Court in the B. Shankaranand versus Common Cause and Others case: -

   “Government appears to have nominated the Minister of Health and Family Welfare and the Secretary of the
Department of Health as Chairman and Member, respectively, so that in the ultimate management of the supreme body
constituted under the Act, the Government also will protect the interests of the institution.   Otherwise, it would appear
that the Government does not seem to have any say or control in the management of the AIIMS.  Considered from this
pragmatic background and from the point of view of the importance of the institution and public interest, we are of the
considered view that the Central Government is justified to nominate four persons other than Scientists, the fifth being a
non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association”.
 
11.2    The Secretary clarified that the Health Minister and the Health Secretary have been made ex-officio members of JIPMER,
keeping in view the above observations of the Supreme Court. The Committee has its reservations on this crucial issue.   The
Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that the observation of Supreme Court was made in the
context of inclusion of the Minister and the Secretary in the ex-officio nominated category in the Institute Body of AIIMS. By no
stretch of imagination it can be said that the Apex Court has approved the separate nomination of the Minister and the Secretary to the
Institute Body. The Committee would also like to point out that the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the said judgment delivered in 1996
had also observed that there should be no undue interference by the Government in the autonomous management of the AIIMS and it
should not be treated as any other Department of the Government.
11.3     During the course of deliberations on the composition of the Institute Body, Committee’s attention was also drawn to the
reported observation endorsing the inclusion of the Minister and Secretary as ex-officio members in AIIMS made by the Rajya Sabha
Committee on Subordinate Legislation in its meeting held on 27
th September, 2006. The Committee is very surprised by the kind of
intervention made by the representative of the Ministry. It is very disturbing to note that deliberations of a Parliamentary Committee,
not conclusive with the Report yet to be presented to the House, have been placed before another Parliamentary Committee. It is a
well-established convention to maintain the confidentiality of Parliamentary Committee deliberations which is supposed to be strictly
adhered to by all concerned. Expressing its serious reservations on such a development, the Committee refuses to take cognizance of
the submission (both verbal and written) made by the representative of the Ministry.
11.4     The Committee is disturbed to note that the proposed nomination of the Minister and the Secretary, no doubt in ex-officio
capacity, is in addition to seven persons to be nominated under Clause 5(1) (i). This has virtually resulted in increasing the strength of
ex-officio members, which cannot be considered appropriate, if autonomy of the Institute is sought to be maintained.
11.5     The Committee would like to point out that during the Parliament debate at the time of consideration of AIIMS Bill in 1956, it
was emphasised that having a majority of non-officials was always a healthy convention. Only that could ensure that the people who
were there will not be persons who will act according to orders given, written or otherwise.
            The Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the following observations made by the standing Committee on Human
Resource Development in its 31
st Report:-
The AIIMS was set up as an autonomous Institute by an Act of Parliament. The Act had envisaged an
Institute Body and a Governing Body at its apex and there was a tradition of Government nominating the Minster of
Health as its President. The Committee would like to note that the advantage and disadvantages of this tradition have
been debated from time to time but there has been no departure from the traditional practice, nor could the argument
be clinched either way.
The Committee has given serious thought to the conflicting views available on the utility and propriety of
continuing with the practice of the Health Minister being nominated as the President of the Institute. This has been
stretched so far that even after demitting office, the ex-Minister continues to remain the Institute’s President. The
arguments in favour briefly appear to be that this was initiated in the past so that such Ministerial presence may
increase the influence of the Institute in Governmental circles. It has also been argued that there is nothing in the Act
to prohibit the Minister from being nominated as President.
It may be pointed out that the Act does not, at the same time, provide that the Minister would be ex-officio
President of the Institute, which could easily have been done had such been the intention. On the other hand, there is
much evidence, to the contrary, particularly from eminent witnesses closely associated with the growth of AIIMS.
They are of the firm opinion that neither the Health Minister nor the Health Secretary should be nominated as a
member of the Institute Body. Instead, the only ex-officio members should be the Director-General of Health
Services and the Finance Advisor in their official capacities and the Minister and the Secretary should keep out of
any direct involvement in bodies charged with manning of the AIIMS and its day to day working. The advantage
would be that not being directly  involved and thus becoming party to the Institute Body’s decision, the Minister and
the Secretary would be able to assess matters objectively and hold the Institute body accountable to performance.

11.6     The Committee would like to emphasise that the above line of thinking continues to remain relevant, and has rather become
more relevant in the present circumstances.  The Committee has been compelled to make such a statement as there have been several
unsavory developments in the recent past that have cast their shadow on the autonomy of AIIMS.  A host of issues involving AIIMS
and Ministry of Health & Family Welfare are again before the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi.  The Committee is not averse to the idea
of Government having a say in the management of Central Government Institutions.  But if the intervention of the Government proves
baneful for the autonomy of institutions of excellence, the issue of the nomination of the Health Minister and the Health Secretary as
ex-officio members therein clearly needs to be revisited. The Committee apprehends that being a sister Institute, JIPMER may meet
the same fate and fall prey to the same problems as are plaguing AIIMS.
 11.7    The Committee notes that under Clause 5 (1) (e), (g), (h) and (i) four Government nominees have been made members of the
Institute.  Besides, the Government is also empowered to nominate seven persons to the Institute Body under Clause 5 (j).  The
Committee is reasonably hopeful that the Bill leaves enough scope to the Government to wield control and influence for the
implementation of Government policies in JIPMER.
            The Committee favours the views held by eminent witnesses and the stakeholders of JIPMER and concurs that for objective
assessment of the work of the Institute, the Minister and the Secretary of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should remain
out of any form of direct involvement in any of the Institute bodies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Clause 5(1) (a)
and (b) be deleted.
 
Clause 5(1) (c ), (d) and (g)
 
11.8     The Committee observes that Vice-Chancellor of Puducherry University (ex-officio), Vice-Chancellor of the Tamil Nadu Dr.
M.G.R. Medical University (ex-officio) and Chief Secretary, Government of Puducherry (ex-officio) are proposed to be members of
the Institute. On a comparison of relevant provisions of AIIMS Act and PGIMER, Chandigarh Act, the Committee finds that only
Vice-Chancellor of Delhi University and Punjab University are represented in these two Institute Bodies.
11.9     During the course of its deliberations at Puducherry, it was impressed upon the Committee by some witnesses, that the
following should also find place in the Institute Body:-
*          Health Minister of Puducherry
*          One/three MLA(s) of Puducherry Legislative Assembly
*          Secretary to Government (Health), Govt. of Puducherry
*          Director of Health and Family Welfare Services, Puducherry
 
11.10   The Committee is not inclined to concur with these suggestions, simply because   state representation in the JIPMER Institute
is already more when compared with AIIMS and PGIMER, Chandigarh Institute Body. One should not forget that JIPMER is sought
to be declared as an institution of national importance. It would be in the fitness of things if regional imbalance is not reflected in an
institute having an all India status.
 
11.11   Clause 5(1)(j) of the Bill provides that: -
“(j) seven persons of whom one shall be a non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association, to be
nominated by the Central Government in such manner as may be prescribed;”
 
 
11.12   Serious doubts on the above category of members were raised by eminent witnesses and the stakeholders of the Institute
during their interaction with the Committee. It was stated that the membership, as laid down under the above sub-clauses does not
specify any criteria as to who can be nominated to the above mentioned category thereby, leaving ample scope for the Government to
nominate any person of its choice which will ultimately affect the decision-making of the Institute Body. It was also suggested by the
witnesses that in order to avoid ambiguity, nominated members under sub-clause (1) (j) of Clause 5 should be ex-officio.
 
11.13   The Committee notes that the sub-clause (1)(j) of Clause 5, in its present form, leaves   room for ambiguity and interpretation
and may lead to nepotism and favoritism. The Committee observes that the criteria as to who can qualify for such membership under

Clause 5 (1) (j) of the Bill should be categorically mentioned.
11.14   The Committee deliberated the issue at length and sought opinion of the various experts who appeared before the Committee.  
Based on the feedback received, the Committee observes that excellence is all about processes and all care needs to be taken to ensure
that processes get precedence over predilections.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the six members who should find place
in the Institute Body, (other than a non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association as provided under
Clause 5(1)(j) ), should be persons of eminence and should be nominated from  a panel of 14 fellows half of whom shall be from
Medical  Faculties of Indian Universities and Health Science Universities  suggested by the Indian National Science Association, New
Delhi, Indian Academy of Sciences, Bangalore and National Academy of Sciences, Allahabad.
 
The said sub-clause (1)  (j) of Clause 5 should, therefore, read as follows-
“(j) seven persons, of whom one shall be a non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association
and the other six members shall be persons of eminence and shall be nominated from  a panel of 14 “fellows” half of
whom shall be from medical faculties of Indian Universities and Health Science Universities as suggested by Indian
National Science Association, New Delhi, Indian Academy of Sciences, Bangalore and National Academy of Sciences,
Allahabad, to be nominated by the Central Government in such manner as may be prescribed;
 
Clause 5(1)(k)
            Clause 5(1)(k) of the Bill provides that: -
“(k) Four representatives of the medical faculties of Indian Universities to be  nominated by the Central Government in such
manner as may be prescribed;
11.15   During its study visit to Puducherry, the stakeholders and witnesses suggested that the four representatives of the medical
faculties of Indian Universities to be nominated by the Central Government under Clause 5(1) (k) of the Bill should be in active
service, should also be practitioners of allopathic medicine, and must be ex-officio members and not otherwise. A view point which
emerged was that the four representatives should be the Director AIIMS, Director PGIMER, Chandigarh, Director Sree Chitra Tirunal
Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology, Thiruvananthapuram and Director, National Institute of Mental Health and
Neurological Sciences, Bangalore.
11.16   The Committee agrees that clear mention of who should be the four representatives from the medical faculties of Indian
Universities needed to be provided in the Bill itself. This would ensure that eminent persons from medical fraternity would find place
in the Institute Body. On the basis of the submissions made before the Committee and also the inputs made available to it, the
Committee is of the view that the four representatives proposed under this category, should be the Director, AIIMS, New Delhi, the
Director, National Institute of Mental Health and Neurological Sciences, Bangalore, Director PGIMER, Chandigarh and Director Sree
Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences & Technology, Thiruvananthapuram.
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that sub-clause (1) (k) of Clause 5 be modified on the above lines.
Clause 5 (1) (l)
11.17   The Committee notes that AIIMS Act and the PGIMER Chandigarh Act  provide that three  Members  of  Parliament of 
whom  two  shall  be elected from among themselves by Members of the House  of the  People (Lok Sabha) and one from among
themselves by    members of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) should be in the Institute Body.  The Committee is, however,
surprised to note that a distinction is sought to be made in the JIPMER Bill which provides that two Members of Parliament from the

14.       Clause 10 deals with Governing Body and other Committees of the Institute. Clause 10 (1) reads as follows:-

Provided that the number of persons who are not members of the Institute shall not exceed one-third of the total

14.1     On a comparative analysis of relevant provision in AIIMS and PGIMER Act, the Committee observed a slight variation.  
Provision of having not more than one-third of total membership of the Governing Body from persons not being members of the
Institute proposed in the JIPMER Bill is based on PGIMER Act.  AIIMS Act has only members of the Institute as members of the
Governing Body.  When asked to justify the basis for having such a provision, the Committee was informed that it would facilitate
nominating members from Tech/ Management and such specialized fields.
 
14.2           During its interaction with different witnesses, divergent views emerged on this aspect.   It was emphasized by the
various associations connected with the Institute that the Governing Body should have only members of the Institute as its
members. The other viewpoint voiced by experts/ ex-Directors was that only medical scientists from Indian Science Congress and
Medical Universities should be included in the Governing Body from outside.
 
14.3           The Committee agrees that mere reference to one-third members who are non-members of the Institute leaves a wide
scope as to who can be or cannot be nominated by the Central Government to the Governing body of the Institute. The Committee
fails to understand the rationale for having non-members in the Governing Body.  The Committee is of the firm view that Clause
10 can be easily based on the relevant Clause of the AIIMS Act. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that proviso to Clause
10(1) may be deleted.
 
14.4     Sub-clause (5) of Clause 10 deals with the constitution of Standing Committees and ad-hoc Committees by the Institute.
The witnesses and the various stakeholders of JIPMER who appeared before the Committee were of the view that the details
of Standing Committees to be constituted should be specified. It was further stated by some of them that the Faculty of JIPMER
should be given adequate representation in Standing Committees and ad-hoc Committees. The Central Government nominees who
were to be nominated to the Standing/ad-hoc Committees may be specified in the Bill (though it is not done so in AIIMS / PGIMER
Acts) and that these nominees should be drawn from Universities of excellence, Department of Science and Technology and Teaching
Institutions.
 
14.5     The Committee is also of firm opinion that the number of Standing Committees, which the Institute may form, should be
provided in detail. It feels that the membership of the Standing Committees should be formed from among the members of the
Institute. The Committee therefore recommends that a new sub- Clause may be inserted in the Clause 10 of the Bill on the lines of the
sub-clause (6) of Clause 10 of the AIIMS Act.
 The new sub-clause may now read as: -
 
“A Standing Committee shall consist exclusively of members of the Institute, but an ad hoc Committee may
include persons who are not members of the Institute but the number of such persons shall not exceed one- half
of its total membership”
 
 
14.6     The Committee’s attention was drawn to several suggestions given by the witnesses and stakeholders regarding the
composition of the Governing Body. It was stated that the Students’ Body, the Resident Doctors Association, the CHS Officers’
Welfare Association, and the employees’ union should be adequately represented in the Governing Body.
 
14.7     The Committee observes that an autonomous institute of learning should have at least one representative each representing the
students’ body and the employees and the staff of the Institute in the Governing Body. This would not only provide them a platform
to voice out their sentiments and opinions but also act as a necessary balance to the policy-making and decision-making processes and
representative nature of the Governing Body. The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable modification be made to Clause 10

“If in, or in connection with, the exercise of its powers and discharge of its functions by the Institute under this

16.1     Perusal of similar Clauses of the AIIMS Act and the PGIMER Chandigarh Act reveals that the said Clauses speak only of the
matter of resolution of any dispute arising between the Institute and the Central Government. However, unlike in the case of the

16.2     The Committee observes that the connotation of the word ‘dispute’ varies from that of the word ‘difference’ in degree or

21.   Miscellaneous Comments/Suggestions made by the Committee.
 
 
21.1           During its interaction with the various witnesses representing student associations, employees’ union, political parties
and Ex-Directors of JIPMER, it was unanimously opined that the present status of reservation of certain percentage of medical
seats for undergraduates hailing from Puducherry should be continued even after the conferment of autonomy to JIPMER and that
any increase in the overall number of seats should result in a proportionate increase in the reserved seats for the people of
Puducherry.

provision for reservation of certain percentage of medical seats for undergraduate courses for the residents of Puducherry was
made when there was no other medical college in Puducherry.   The Ministry further stated that since a number of medical
colleges (seven already established and 2 or 3 including one from the State Government) are under process with projected
undergraduate medical seats numbering almost around 1000, adequate number of seats is available for the residents of
Puducherry. Under the circumstances such reservation may not be appropriate if JIPMER was to maintain status of being an
Institute of national importance.
The Ministry went on to clarify further that at present there is no proposal for withdrawing the facilities given to the residents of
Puducherry in admission to undergraduate medical courses.  As regards the PG courses the principle laid down by Supreme Court
in Saurav Chaudhary i.e. number of seats to be reserved for those students passing out from JIPMER, would hold good. 
 
The Committee is satisfied with the explanation of the Ministry and recommends that the above assurance on reservation of
seats be incorporated in the Bill for the sake of clarity.

already more when compared with AIIMS and PGIMER, Chandigarh Institute Body. One should not forget that JIPMER is
sought to be declared as an institution of national importance. It would be in the fitness of things if regional imbalance is not
reflected in an institute having an all India status. (Para 11.10)
 
The Committee notes that the sub-clause (1)(j) of Clause 5, in its present form, leaves  room for ambiguity and interpretation and
may lead to nepotism and favoritism. The Committee observes that the criteria as to who can qualify for such membership under
Clause 5 (1) (j) of the Bill should be categorically mentioned.  (Para 11.13)
 
The Committee deliberated the issue at length and sought opinion of the various experts who appeared before the Committee. 
Based on the feedback received, the Committee observes that excellence is all about processes and all care needs to be taken to
ensure that processes get precedence over predilections.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the six members who should
find place in the Institute Body, (other than a non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association as
provided under Clause 5(1)(j) ), should be persons of eminence and should be nominated from  a panel of 14 fellows half of
whom shall be from Medical  Faculties of Indian Universities and Health Science Universities   suggested by the Indian National
Science Association, New Delhi, Indian Academy of Sciences, Bangalore and National Academy of Sciences, Allahabad.  
The said sub-clause(1)  (j) of Clause 5 should, therefore, read as follows-
“(j) seven persons, of whom one shall be a non-medical scientist representing the Indian Science Congress Association
and the other six members shall be persons of eminence and shall be nominated from  a panel of 14 “fellows” half of
whom shall be from medical faculties of Indian Universities and Health Science Universities as suggested by Indian
National Science Association, New Delhi, Indian Academy of Sciences, Bangalore and National Academy of Sciences,

themselves by    members of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) should be in the Institute Body.  The Committee is, however,

nominated by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. The Committee observes that JIPMER being an Institute of national importance
should be nationally representative in character and spirit; hence, regional representation should be avoided. The Committee holds the

clause (1) (l) of Clause 5 should read as follows: -
“three Members of Parliament of whom two shall  be elected from among themselves by Members of the House  of the  People
(Lok Sabha) and one from among themselves by Members of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)” (Para 11.17)
 
            In view of the amendment suggested by the Committee to sub-clause (1) (l) of Clause 5, the above sub-clause should be
suitably amended to allow for the election of the members of the Parliament to the Institute Body. The said sub-clause should now
read as follows: -
“Save as otherwise provided in this section, the term of office of a member shall be five years from the date of his
nomination or election.”

(6)                 of Clause 6.                                                                                                                     (Para 12.1)

should be modified to read now as:-

      The Committee observes that an autonomous institute of learning should have at least one representative each representing the
students’ body and the employees and the staff of the Institute in the Governing Body. This would not only provide them a
platform to voice out their sentiments and opinions but also act as a necessary balance to the policy-making and decision-making
processes and representative nature of the Governing Body. The Committee, therefore, recommends that suitable modification be
made to Clause 10 in order to provide the above-mentioned bodies adequate representation in the Governing Body.  (Para 14.7)

insulate the said Committee from extraneous influence the Chairmanship of the Committee should be institutionalized. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the three-member Selection Committee should consist of the Vice-Chancellor of
Puducherry University who shall be the Chairman, the DGHS and the Director of the Institute.  (Para 14.9)
 
            Representatives of several Associations/ Unions of JIPMER hospital and Institute raised apprehensions that non-specification
of rules of recruitment would lead to manipulation in filling up of posts in various grades in the Institute. To a query regarding
Gazette notification of recruitment rules in AIIMS, the representatives of AIIMS, during the course of their deposition before the
Committee on 27
th July 2007, replied that none of the recruitment Rules have ever been Gazette notified. The Committee is appalled
to note that in this era of e-governance, when there is almost universal practice of bringing out all relevant details and posting the
same on the Internet for the sake of fairness and transparency, the Recruitment Rules of AIIMS are yet to be Gazette notified. The
Committee is of the firm view that such a state of affairs makes the selection process prone to manipulation and extraneous
considerations.
      Taking a cue from the above state of affairs, and also on the basis of the feedback made available, the Committee recommends
that the Recruitment Rules of JIPMER be Gazette notified from the date of operation of JIPMER Act and the same be posted on
the Internet for the sake of transparency and fair play.  (Para 15.1)
 
The Committee observes that the connotation of the word ‘dispute’ varies from that of the word ‘difference’ in degree or amount
by which there is disagreement on an issue or matter between two parties, in this instance the parties being the Institute and the
Central Government. The Committee believes that if any difference on any issue arises between the Institute and the Central
Government, then such a difference can always be resolved amicably at the earliest.   On a specific query about the basis for
adding the word ‘difference’, the representative of the Department failed to give a convincing reply. The Committee strongly feels

Institute and the Central Government would tantamount to arbitration by the Central Government. Hence it recommends that the
word  “differences” may be deleted from the said Clause.                                        (Para 16.3)
 
 One of the apprehensions expressed by the various Employees’ Union was that Clause 28 (1) merely states that those who have
not opted to be an employee of the JIPMER shall continue to be treated as Government employee for a period of six months only
and that nothing had been mentioned about redeployment after six months.               (Para 17.2)
 
 
 
Asked to clarify the matter, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in a written submission informed the Committee that the

the Surplus Cell as per rule 37-A (6) of CCS (Pension) Rules.

amended to reflect the above position with a view to dispel misgivings of the Employees’ Union. (Para 17.3)

option to remain an employee of the CHS or to join the JIPMER Institute should be extended to one year after the notification of
the terms and conditions of service by the autonomous Institute. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the word “six-
months” may be replaced with the word “one year from the date of notification of the terms and conditions of service by the
autonomous Institute” in sub-clause (1) of Clause 28. (Para 17.6)

recommends that the above assurance be incorporated in the Bill for the sake of clarity.

Asked to comment on this, the Ministry had replied in the affirmative stating that allowing the employees’ of JIPMER after

The Committee notes that although sub-clause (1) (a) speaks of the summoning and holding of meetings, other than the first

provision for reservation of certain percentage of medical seats for undergraduate courses for the residents of Puducherry was
made when there was no other medical college in Puducherry.   The Ministry further stated that since a number of medical
colleges (seven already established and 2 or 3 including one from the State Government) are under process with projected
undergraduate medical seats numbering almost around 1000, adequate number of seats is available for the residents of

The Ministry went on to clarify further that at present there is no proposal for withdrawing the facilities given to the residents of

proposals.                                                                                             (Para 21.3)
 
The Committee has observed that the medical institutions like AIIMS, PGIMER, JIPMER, apart from the academic activity, have
a major mandate of providing specialised services to the public at large.   Often, these institutions are the final destination of a
large segment of the society to seek quality care at affordable cost.  Against such a backdrop, the need for having a prompt and
proper mechanism is required to solve the genuine grievances of all categories of employees. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends that initiative should be taken by the Govt. for evolving such a mechanism.                                  (Para 21.4)
 
Though the Committee was happy with the provision for according status of national importance to JIPMER, it felt that
infrastructure and health facilities in a number of hospitals across the country leave much to be desired. The Committee

which are catering to far larger number of people than the JIPMER, Puducherry for the purpose of improvement of infrastructure
and patient care facilities and allocate additional funds to them. The Committee would like the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare to appraise it on the progress made on this matter at the time of examination of Demand for Grants 2008-
09.                                                              (Para 21.5)

Sabha and member of the Committee during 2006-07, on 1st August 2007.  The Committee expressed its profound grief at the

2.
                              Thereafter, the Committee suo moto took cognizance of non-issuance of degree certificates to the Resident Doctors of
AIIMS and the resultant strike by Doctors of AIIMS, thereby paralyzing the patient care services there and subjecting the common
people to great sufferings.  The Committee felt that, as a watchdog, it cannot remain a mute spectator to the happenings in AIIMS and
hence passed the following resolution to be forwarded to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
“The Committee expresses its deep concern over the non-issuance of degree certificates to the Resident Doctors of AIIMS and
the resultant strike which has severely paralyzed the patient care services at the premier Institute.   The Committee urges upon
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to take immediate remedial measures for the issuance of degree certificates to the
eligible Doctors of AIIMS without further loss of time and also to put in place a mechanism to ensure that such a situation
does not recur in future.”

th Report on the Jawaharlal Institute of Post Graduate Medical Education

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
The Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research, 
Pondicherry was established in 1964 primarily with the objectives to develop patterns of 
teaching in undergraduate and postgraduate medical education so as to establish and 
demonstrate high standards of education. The Institute has been providing quality education 
and excellent patient care delivery services over the years, however; it could not grow due 
to constraints in the process of manpower selection, lack of academic autonomy, lack of 
flexibility in administrative and financial powers, commensurate with other institutions like, 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi and Post-Graduate Institute of Medical 
Education and Research, Chandigarh.
2. It is proposed to make the Institute a statutory body corporate and declare as an
institution of national importance under entry 64 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the
Constitution so that it may develop as a high level institution of medical education and research
on the pattern of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi and the Post-Graduate
Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh.
3. This Bill will empower the Institute with academic autonomy to develop its own 
curriculum, set new trends in medical education and research and award its own degrees 
and also enable it to have appropriate delegated administrative and financial powers. The 
conferring of statutory status on this Institute will enable it to grow into a model centre of 
excellence.
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

INTRODUCTION
1.         The Committee in its examination of the Jawaharlal Institute of Post-Graduate Medical Education and Research Bill 2007
(hereinafter referred to as Bill) undertook a study visit to the Union Territory of Puducherry from 1 st to 4th July 2007.   During its
study visit the Committee had interacted with Management of JIPMER, Experts, various associations / unions of the Institute and
Hospital and other stakeholders who approached the Committee on the various provisions of the Bill as well constraints being faced
in the functioning of JIPMER.  The List of witnesses who appeared before the Committee at Puducherry on the JIPMER Bill-2007 is
appended as Appendix.  The views and suggestions expressed by different stakeholders are enumerated in succeeding paragraphs. 
 
MANAGEMENT OF INSTITUTE AND FACULTY OF JIPMER AND EXPERTS
 
Management of Institute
 
            On 2
nd July 2007 the Committee heard the views of Management of the Institute. While presenting the viewpoint of
management, Director, JIPMER gave an overview of the Institute, to the Committee.   JIPMER is a premier medical institute offering
a variety of undergraduate and postgraduate courses.  With bed strength of 1050, the Institute also provides patient-care and hospital
services.  
The Committee was informed that over the years, budget allocation for the Institute has shown a steady increase.   As
compared to 9th plan allocation of Rs. 70.00 crore, 10 th Plan allocation stood at Rs. 150.00 crore.  However, when compared with
Plan provision for AIIMS and PGIMER, funds provided to JIPMER cannot be considered sufficient enough.  Committee’s attention
was also drawn towards the shortage of required staff strength.  Against 3007 total sanctioned posts, only 2395 posts were in position,
with 612 vacancies.   Position was very discouraging in respect of Group A posts, where almost half (123) of the sanctioned (249)
posts were lying vacant.   The Committee was given to understand that staff position in AIIMS and PGIMER was quite different,
where the sanctioned staff strength was higher with the number of vacant posts being lesser.  Director, JIPMER highlighted the
following main constraints being faced by the Institute-
·
        Enormous increase in patient load
·        No increase in staff strength.
·        Recruitment for Group A and B (Gazetted) through UPSC not done in the last 4 years.
·        Selected candidates do not join or leave.
·                    Within 2 to 3 years, 47 candidates appointed by UPSC did not join. 
·        Enormous delay in implementing the expansion programmes for want of clearances.
·        Lack of educational autonomy and administrative flexibility
·        Distance from administrative authority.
 
Representatives of the faculty of JIPMER
The Faculty of JIPMER supported the change of status of the institute into an autonomous institute of national importance by
an act of Parliament, due to the fact that only such a change could bring about a marked improvement in its functioning, health care
delivery, teaching, research and national status.  The Committee was given an idea about the difficulties being faced in the
functioning of the Institute. The faculty expressed the following reservations about accepting the Bill in its present form. 
            It was pointed out that despite nearly 50% of the faculty posts lying vacant, JIPMER was being consistently rated among the
first five medical colleges in India.   Indicating the reasons as to why faculty do not join JIPMER or if they do, they leave quickly or
get transferred back to Delhi, the faculty stated that UPSC interviews had not been conducted for a long time.  If at all they were
conducted, the interviews were being held in Delhi, with the local experts from the region.  In the process, doctors hailing from those
regions only were filling the posts.  Even after selection, it took a very long time for the appointment orders to be issued.  Faculties
selected on contract basis were not issued their appointment orders for nearly three months or more resulting in many of the selected
candidates not joining due to a long waiting period.

24th Report of Committee On Haelth And Family Welfare
