The Committee was given to understand that despite having the basic infrastructure, clinical material, equipment and the
know-how to start different courses in super specialties, para-medical courses; it has not been possible to do the same. They have also
stated that lack of Faculty, non-fulfillment of requirements / stipulations of various professional bodies were the main factors
responsible for such a situation. The Institute was facing shortage of Faculty also due to unattractive pay scales and other incentives
being offered by it when compared with the service conditions of Faculty members of eight medical colleges located in Puducherry. 
The representatives further informed the Committee that the faculties of JIPMER were not able to conduct cutting edge
research mainly due to good equipment meant purely for research not being purchased for want of required funds.  Secondly, very
high teaching and clinical load left little time for research. The time lag in getting permission for funds for industry-academia
collaborative projects and for international collaborative research project, in getting permission from the ministry to leave the country
for conferences, workshops or training courses were the other de-motivating factors.
The faculty members made the following suggestions in various provisions of the Bill: -
·
        Politicization of the Institute Body should be avoided and no political person should be given the post of Chairman or the
membership.
·        The bill should be very explicit in the constituent members of the institute, governing body and standing committees.
·        Governing body and the Standing Committee of the Institute should be constituted by the institute from among its members
only as is existing in AIIMS / PGI Act.  No members to be included from outside the Institute.
·        Transfer of service of existing employees needs to be elaborated.   The notification on regulations including the designation,
pay scales, perks, conferences, benefits, allowances etc should be notified along with the Act.
·        Due consideration should be given to the faculty who have served for long years in the same post and due to be promoted to
the higher post.
·        On conversion to autonomous institute at par with AIIMS, the faculty should be absorbed at a higher pay scale with all the
perks.
·        Puducherry being a small city lacks the educational facilities as well as the social and recreational milieu of larger cities like
Chennai, Mumbai or Delhi. Therefore, additional special allowances should be granted to the faculty of JIPMER to
compensate for the inconveniences of working in a place like Puducherry.
·        The time duration given for an employee to exercise his/her option to remain an employee of the CHS or to join the JIPMER
Institute should be extended to three years and not six months as given in the proposed Bill.
·        In case officers of the Medical Officer grade opt to join the institute (as an autonomous organization) they should be suitably
absorbed with full protection of pay, all perks and allowances in the teaching cadre as lecturer/ reader/professor / administrator
and their such appointment should be given preference as they are already rendering service in the respective areas.
·        Existing health care and CGHS dispensary benefits should continue to all the officers even if one opts for institute cadre. 
Health care benefits should be continued even after retirement.   Besides, all those who move to other stations should be
covered by the CGHS and receive the benefits at those stations.
·        Well furnished quarters and recreational amenities should be provided to all consultants appropriate to their scale of pay.
·        To attract more faculties and simultaneously to retain them and maintain their interest in the institute, a well-regulated paid
clinic system should be started. 
·        The Faculty of JIPMER should be given adequate representation in Standing Committees and Adhoc Committees. The
Central Government nominees should be specified in the Bill (though it is not done so in AIIMS / PGI Acts).  These nominees
should be drawn from Universities of excellence, Department of Science and Technology and Teaching Institutions.  This is
especially important because the faculty believe that having more number of political persons nominated in the institute may
not be advantageous to the growth of the institute.
·
        The four (4) members from the medical universities should also be spelt in the Bill (though it is not done so in AIIMS / PGI
Acts).
·        The meetings of the Institute, Governing Body and other committees should be held at Puducherry.
·        There are a number of non-medical faculty openings in addition to existing ones in medical institutions of national eminence
in departments like Anatomy, Physiology, Biochemistry, Pharmacology, Microbiology, Statistics, radiotherapy (Physicist),

EXPERTS
The Committee had also heard the views of the former Directors of JIPMER and other Experts who are well conversant with
the functioning of JIPMER.
 
Prof. D.S. Dubey, Adviser, Mahatma Gandhi Medical College And Research Institute, Ex-Director, JIPMER, Puducherry
The Committee noted that Prof. Dubey had a long association with the Institute from 1984 onwards till his retirement as Director in
1997. Based on his experience of the day-to-day functioning of the Institute, Prof Dubey made the following observations: -
JIPMER as a medical Institute of reputation in our country has got lot of potential to grow as a national Institute of eminence in
the Medical field. The proposal for making it an autonomous Institute at par with AIIMS and PGIMER is a welcome proposal
which will definitely potentate and build up the capabilities of this Institution in that direction.
Many hurdles and bottlenecks are experienced locally in the smooth functioning and development of the Institute such as,
unsatisfactory budget allocation, filling of teaching and other group (A) posts through UPSC/Ad-hoc/Deputation from Delhi.
Lot of time is taken for these and in the bargain the Institute suffers. Unduly delayed process for Framing of recruitment
rules/change-modification of recruitment rules, disciplinary action, procurement of equipment were the other problem areas.
The response of the faculty after their regular or ad-hoc appointment has been very poor particularly those joining from
Northern part of the country being always interested to go back to Delhi on transfer.
Prof Dubey has also given following suggestions on the proposed Bill:
Clause 5(1) (j) lacks clarity, whereas it has been stated that seven persons of whom one shall be a Non-Medical Scientist
representing ISC will be nominated by Central Government. The question is as to who will be the remaining six persons from
which class of activity such as eminent medical people, eminent academicians/scientists or persons of academic and social
eminence etc. Clause should be suitably modified so as to allay the apprehensions in constituting the Institute body.
In the constitution of the Governing Body, in respect of clause No. 10(1), one third of the members (who are not members of
the Institute) should also be clarified and proper representation should be given to academic and medical people.
As regards the resolution of differences and transfer of service of existing employees, the same may be suitably drafted keeping
the interests and welfare of the employees particularly their retirement benefits, pension, gratuity and other facilities and
provision of a CGHS dispensary in JIPMER, Puducherry.
As far as the existing faculty is concerned, their option conditions and their absorption in autonomous status should also be
carefully drafted, so that their services interests are not compromised. The case of JIPMER autonomy at this stage is different
from AIIMS and PGIMER (these Institutes were raised as autonomous Institutes right from the beginning but in case of
JIPMER, it is a transition from existing Central Government status to an autonomous status after a gap of fifty years or so).
 
DR. N.ANANTHAKRISHNAN, Director, Peruthalaivar Kamaraj Medical College & Research Institute,
 
Dr. N. Ananthakrishnan who had served in various capacities in JIPMER for a period of nearly 30 years from Feb, 1977 to July, 2006,
made following observations / suggestions:
 
Faculty: Nearly 30-50 per cent of faculty posts remain unfilled in JIPMER at any time. The reasons for these are:
Undue delay in the posts being advertised by the UPSC.
The UPSC interviews are held almost always in Delhi with experts being mostly from Institutions based in Delhi or near
about. Hence candidates who are selected are also generally from these Institutions.
The candidates selected by UPSC either do not join or try to leave within a short time of joining.
There are hardly any incentives for faculty in the form of encouragement for research.

24th Report of Committee On Haelth And Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/24threport.htm[29-06-2016 14:53:05]
The pay scales are very poor compared to other private institutions. In Puducherry where there are seven private medical
colleges at present, the difference varies from 15,000-20,000 for each category, with private practice being additionally
allowed by these institutions unlike JIPMER. Hence there is a gradual outflow of staff form JIPMER.
The system of automatic promotion in the Central Health Services leaves no incentives to excellence.
Administrative issues: In the current system of control in JIPMER, it is impossible to create posts or create departments.
Starting of a new areas of patient care are nearly impossible.
Research: The research output of JIPMER is negligible when compared to All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) or
PGIMER for the following reasons.
There is minimal fund for research activity for faculty.
Although there are many requests, due to administrative delays, we are not able to accept invitations to join international
clinical or drug trials.
There are no incentives for research output.
The research equipment gets least priority in the budget earmarked for equipments after patient care and teaching-
learning activities.
Even scientific papers or reprints have to be sent at the author’s own expenses for want of funds.
 
 
Student related issues:
Although JIPMER was set up with the idea of establishing newer patterns of teaching, because of the restrictions imposed by
the MCI regulations, no curricular experiments outside the MCI norms are permissible. For example, Problems based learning,
modular learning, competency based curriculum are all the norms in leading educational institutions around the world.
However, the subject-oriented curriculum with all its deficiencies is still being followed in JIPMER because it is the only one
permitted under MCI norms.
JIPMER which ranks third in All India amongst medical institutions providing Under Graduate studies and seven other private
institutions with minimal facilities, clinical material and faculty, get the same degree from the University with no distinction or
mention of the Institute of training. Thus JIPMER students get no recognition when they apply for outside posts.
Administrative constraints do not permit liberal exchange of students, because the sanction which has to come from Delhi often
gets delayed.
Students are admitted late to other institutions whereas in JIPMER students are admitted in July itself.  Hence examinations get
delayed, results get delayed leading to delay in postings and curtailments of clinical time.
Due to difficulties in getting administrative approval, starting new paramedical courses, which are the need of the country, is a
Herculean task.
 
Patients’ care: Modern medicine is a costly affair requiring constant procurement of equipment and consumables. Due to
paucity of funds, even supply of all the required medicines leave alone consumables to deserving patients who are exceedingly
poor has not been possible. Equipment procuring process is very lengthy and because of this, even if one initiates the purchase
procedures early, often the financial year passes without successfully being able to procure the equipments.
 
Employee related issues: JIPMER, which is now fifty years old, has an ageing population of employees. The previous
Recruitment Rules have been based by and large on offering promotional opportunities without leaving any scope for lateral
entry. Because of large vacancies in the feeding cadre promotional posts like operation theatre assistants, operation theatre
technicians etc., do not get filled thus affecting patients’ care services. The process of modification and re-notifying of
Recruitment Rules is so tedious and cumbersome that years pass before any success can be achieved or expected in this area.
 
·        Suggestions on the Bill: -
 
There are serious apprehensions in the minds of some of the employees regarding what is involved by this change. It is
necessary to take all of them into confidence since they constitute the vast bulk of the employees, so that they become willing
partners in this welcome change. The Bill seems to be a verbatim copy of the AIIMS Bill. It must be remembered that AIIMS
started de-novo with no existing employees, whereas in the current instance, the status of a 50-year-old Institute with all its
existing employees is sought to be altered. Hence there is a great need of co-operation from everybody to make this change
meaningful and functional.
 
Governing Body of the proposed Institute: Looking across the nation it would be obvious that whatever be the field, whether
it is Engineering, Law, Management or Medicine, the top ranking institutions are only those which have a considerable degree
of autonomy in functioning. Perusal of the Institute Body of the Institute shows that out of twenty-one members, ten are ex-
officio and of the remaining eleven, seven are nominees of the Central Government. It is not clear who these nominees will be.
Autonomy must mean freedom to act and take decisions and must not remain only in name. Hence great care has to be given in
deciding the composition of the Institute Body as also the Governing Body.
 
Dr. D. Nagaraja, Director, NIMHANS, Bangalore

Clause does not specifically state that Government would guarantee the retirement benefits to those who opt to be governed by
Government Rules for retirement benefits. The word ‘to be governed by retirement or other terminal benefits admissible to the
employees of the Central Government, as amended from time to time’ does not give an assurance that the Government would
meet the retirement benefits. As per the Rule, Government assures the monthly pension and other retirement benefits for the
absorbed employees, in case the Institute is not in a position to pay it.
Clause 28 (5) (a): As per Rule, the dismissal order for the absorbed employee shall not be operated unless it is confirmed by
the Secretary to the Ministry
Clause 28 (5) (b): As per Rule, 15 days notice should be given before imposing penalty even though reasonable opportunity
was given and proposed penalty is on the basis of evidence adduced during enquiry and the Authority should not proceed
further till the disposal of the representation to be made by the employee in this regard.
Clause 28 (6): Why there is a word that ‘subject to provisions of sub-section (3)’?  This sub-section (3) states that absorbed
employees shall be governed by the regulations of the Institute for retirement benefits. Further, the regulations of the Institute
will be framed only after incorporation of Institute. So, whether it is applicable to the absorbed staff who opted to be governed
by the Government Rules for retirement benefits? The word ‘subject to provision of sub-section (3) should be deleted. As per
Rule, the compassionate allowance (equivalent to compensation pension) may be paid to the dismissed employee.
 
Along with the above, the JIPMER Staff Struggle Committee made the following suggestions to be incorporated in this Clause
in the Bill.
 
The existing staff that opted for pro rata retirement benefits for their services under Central Government should be placed in
the same scale of pay and in the same Basic Pay and in the same position in the seniority list.
Up-to-date amendments of Rule 37-A of CCS (Pension) Rules should be followed for the absorbed employee for pension from
the Government. This gives protection for retirement benefits to all the existing regular staff whether they have completed 10
years of service or not.
Absorbed staff should not be asked to contribute to the Pension Fund for getting pension from the Institute at the time of
retirement.
Family pension should be paid from Government for those staff who opt for pro rata retirement benefit for the services rendered
from the Government.   In addition to it, they should also be eligible for Family Pension from the Institute as per O.M.
No.4/10/2006-P & PW (D), dt, 14.5.2007, issued by DOPT, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions.
No promotional posts should be abolished. All promotional posts should be filled up with the in-service staff. Relaxations in
respect of number of years of service in the feeder cadre, should be relaxed, if vacancies arise due to VRS opted by existing
staff in the event of conversion of JIPMER as autonomous Institute. Promotion should be strictly on seniority-cum-fitness basis.
CGHS facility should be extended to the absorbed staff (including their dependents) who opt pro rata retirement benefits for
the services under the Government.

24th Report of Committee On Haelth And Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/24threport.htm[29-06-2016 14:53:05]
Provisions should be made in the Act that, absorbed staff may prefer appeal before the CAT against the dismissal or any other
order of Secretary of Ministry.
Reservation for certain percentage of vacancy in Group C and D posts should be made available for the heirs of existing Staff
who opt for voluntary retirement in the event of conversion of JIPMER as autonomous Institute.
No one should be victimized in any way for their anti-autonomy agitations so far. Their dies non period for 22 days for not attending
the office on account of threat by political parties in September 2006 should be treated as Earned Leave. A Forum consisting of staff
and administration should be made, and it should meet bimonthly to hear the grievances of staff and to set it right. Unions /
Associations should be recognized. They should be consulted for the formation / amendment of Recruitment Rules, in case it goes
against the interest of absorbed. Staff indulging in union activities should be not victimized for the democratic acts and other acts
permissible under law.
 
POLITICAL PARTIES
 
Views of the representatives of Puducherry State unit of AIADMK Party and CPI (M)
 
The representatives of AIADMK and CPI (M) party had identical views as expressed by the JIPMER Employees Union and JIPMER
Anti Autonomy People’s Action Committee.   Both the parties opposed the move for granting autonomy to JIPMER.  They also felt
that it is prima-facie a step to make JIPMER a private institute.
 
 
Views of the representatives of Puducherry State unit of DMK Party and Nationalist Congress Party (NCP)
 
The representatives of DMK and NCP parties welcomed JIPMER, Puducherry Bill 2007 as in their opinion it would improve the
status and development of JIPMER. Besides upgrading its status, the Bill would confer a number of advantages on the Institute such
as powers of decision making with regard to its education and medical service. This would avoid delay and accelerate the phase of
development of JIPMER. This process would help the poor patients and enable the students of Puducherry to get qualitative medical
education. After passing this Bill the Institute would get more funds for development.
 
Views of representatives of Puducherry State unit of PMK Party
 
Professor M. Ramadass, M.P. (Lok Sabha) led the delegation of PMK Party and made the following observation on behalf of the
PMK party:
 
JIPMER has received more resources in recent times and can grow with the present status. It can create infrastructure with the
added resources. But these facilities cannot be optimally used until and unless quality manpower is available. At present, the
recruitment being done through UPSC and the faculty being part of CHS cadre, there has been difficulties in people joining the
Institute. Even if suitable candidates are selected through UPSC they do not join the Institute. Consequently in many of the
departments, the positions of faculty remain vacant for many years, as a result of which the teaching activities in the Institution
have suffered a great deal. The appointment of specialists and experts in various specialties is much worse and the Institute is
unable to invite this valued human resource on its own since it has no authority to do so.
With the present status, the decision making in JIPMER has become highly cumbersome and complicated. For every activity,
whether it is medical education or health service, the Director of JIPMER will have to wait for the orders of the Ministry of
Health which is highly time consuming. These delays have created an uncongenial environment in the Institution. Most of the
developmental activities have been impaired because of centralization of decision-making at New Delhi. 
PMK party has analyzed the Bill clause by clause and noticed that the Bill in totality would help to confer the status of national
importance to JIPMER. and it wholeheartedly welcomes this Bill. 
The Bill, spread over 32 clauses, provides for an Institute Committee with 22 Members, a Governing body, many Standing
Committees and Adhoc Committees. This organizational set up envisaged by the Bill would provide sufficient freedom and
independence for the Institute for manpower selection, infrastructure development diversification of courses, financial powers
commensurate with other Institutions like AIIMS and PGI.
Another advantage of JIPMER becoming a national Institute is that it would enable it to overcome its present financial crunch. 
Section 15 of the Bill provides for a separate Budget to JIPMER. This would be a great relief to the Institute as it would enable
it to receive at least 3 to 4 times more than the present allocation of financial resources by the Government of India.
The Institute would be relieved form the clutches of Puducherry University and would emerge as an University by itself. It can
have academic freedom to design its courses in conformity with the needs of the society and the Country. 
The proposed National Institute would be able to determine better conditions of service to its employees, faculties and others.
The Bill primarily upgrades the status of JIPMER from an ordinary medical college into an Institution of national importance
like Central University, Puducherry. That Institute would be vested with academic, administrative and financial powers to take
decisions on its own through Institute Body, Governing Body, and Sub-Committees etc. Granting powers to the Institute is
incidental to its becoming a National Institute and autonomy is not the direct objective of the proposed Bill. 
The Institute would not affect the interest of any employees as the Bill makes it abundantly clear in section 28. 
The following modifications or amendments have also been suggested in the proposed Bill:

24th Report of Committee On Haelth And Family Welfare

The Bill should clearly state that the present system of user charges in JIPMER will not alter and more particularly the patients
below poverty line would be exempted from any of the charges.
The Bill should make it clear that the present reservation of seats to Puducherry students would continue, even after it becomes
the National Institute. The present reservation of twenty seats may be increased to thirty and correspondingly the total number
of seats may be increased.
·        Necessary rules should be framed in accordance with the Provisions of the Bill.
 
Views of Communist Party of India (CPI) Puducherry State Council
 
The representatives of CPI stated that they had gone through the JIPMER Bill-2007 and welcomed the declaration of the Institute
to be an institution of national importance as provided under the constitution of India provided; the following obligatory steps are
taken along with revamping the Institute:
 
o
       In the composition of the Institute, Health Minister of the Puducherry should be an ex-officio member of the Governing Body
of the Institute. Besides, three local MLAs of Puducherry should be in the Governing Body to facilitate a better access to the
local Public.
o       Free service of the JIPMER should continue to the poor.
o       The payment system or charging the affordable should not exceed the charges fixed by the local Government.
o       The retirement age, pension, General provident Fund system etc. hitherto available to its employees should be continued to its
employees recruited prior to the date of passing of the Bill. 
o       The student enrolment for Medical education should be enhanced.  50% student admission should be from Puducherry origin. 
Misuse of college admission against the local Government norms should be curtailed.
o       The employees should not be compelled to exercise option as provided in section 28 (4) of the Bill.
o       In Section (4) (a) the last word shall be substitute as “of the scale applicable to the post under the Institute to which he is
“lastly appointed” and should not be based on his initial appointment.
o       Filling up of all Groups – ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts as also the Daily rated, casual and Part-time engagements of staff in JIPMER
should be done with the Union Territory of Puducherry origin persons only.
 
In short, the representatives of the CPI welcomed & supported the declaration of the Institute as an Institution of national importance
as proposed by the Bill, subject to the condition that the steps that they indicated above are fulfilled and its implementation, assured
through the proposed Act.
 
Views of the representatives of Puducherry State unit of Indian National Congress
 
The representatives supported the Bill with the following suggested incorporations: -
o
       The services rendered by JIPMER should not be to the disadvantage of the poor people.  It should continue to provide free
treatment to people over after autonomy.
o       The cost of MBBS course currently makes it affordable for the poor students.  The same should continue after autonomy
and no change should be effected in the existing fee structure.
o       The Bill should provide job security for the present employees of the JIPMER Institute.
 
 
Views of the representatives of Puducherry State unit of Lok Janshakti Party (LJP), MDMK AND BJP
 
The representatives of LJP, MDMK and BJP were totally opposed to the autonomy of the JIPMER Institute.  They opined that the
institute should continue to enjoy benefit of Central Govt. status. They also opined that the Group C and D category employees of the
Institute should be recruited from Puducherry.
 
 
Views of the representatives of Puducherry State unit of CPI (ML)
           
            The representatives were of the view that the status quo should be maintained in the present Administrative set up of the
JIPMER Institute to function directly as Subordinate Office of the DGHS under the Government of India for the following reasons:
 
If JIPMER is granted Autonomous, in the context of financial crunch, this Institute also. Like other Autonomous Institutions viz
AIIMS at Delhi and PGIMER at Chandigarh, etc. will be left with no other option but o mobilize the funds on its own by way
of charging the Patients for everything.
From the objective of the proposed Bill for JIPMER, it can be rightly observed that the Status of Autonomy for JIPMER will
eventually make the Institution an elitist one and take the Hospital and the College beyond the reach of the poor and middle
class people in and around Puducherry. The students who can now prosecute the studies for M.B.B.S., P.G. Degree Courses and
other allied courses with a few. Thousand Rupees will be compelled to pay exorbitant fees. The Employees of this Institution

24th Report of Committee On Haelth And Family Welfare
file:///D/health_family/24threport.htm[29-06-2016 14:53:05]
will have also to suffer in many ways in the process of conversion of the JIPMER Institution into an Autonomous Body.
In this context, it is the considered view of this Party that conferment of Autonomy is not the panacea for all the ills that afflict
the JIPMER Institute, nor will it aid the Development of the JIPMER Institute at Puducherry on par with other Autonomous
entities like the AIIMS, New Delhi and the PGIMER, Chandigarh etc.
This CPI (ML) is also of the considered view that adequate allocation of funds required for the maintenance, expansion,
Research and Development Activities of the JIPMER Hospital & College with the introduction of more specialties, the number
of beds in different Wards and above all, given more powers to this Institute by way of decentralization of Powers from the
Department “DGHS” through its Ministry “Health & Family Welfare”, of course, after restructuring / reorganization of the
present set up for quicker clearance of the proposals emanated from JIPMER etc., will go a long way in further developing and
strengthening of the JIPMER as a premier Institute of excellence in the services of Patient Care, Hospital Treatment and
Medical Education & Research in India.
Further it is not out of place to mention here that the move of Autonomy to JIPMER is only an attempt of certain vested interest
Political Parties / Leaders who would like to control this prestigious Institute for their Political vested interests at the cost of
Public Interests / Exchequer.
If autonomy is granted and elevated to the status of ‘National Institute of Excellence’ the fruits of reservation so far permitted in
appointments and in others will be denied, because normally reservation is not allowed in Autonomous Research Institute.
Hence Autonomy to JIPMER is detrimental to the Public.
Moreover, there are strong apprehensions in the minds of people of Puducherry that if the status of the JIPMER is altered from
its present status to that of autonomous body, rights of their wards to consideration fro appointment / recruitment to different
posts in the JIPMER on the basis of quota system will completely be taken away and as such their right to job and livelihood
will be infringed upon. 
 
 
OTHER ORGANISATIONS
Views of Bharathiya Labour Union
 
Bharathiya Labour union opposed the proposed move of granting autonomy to JIPMER.  However, the Union was in favour of
allotting more funds and taking other appropriate measures including filling up of all the existing vacancies of Doctors, Faculties and
Staff Members for the allround development of JIPMER in the existing pattern and status.  The Union was also in favour of granting
some extra powers by decentralization of certain powers from DGHS.  The Union stressed the need to allow JIPMER to function as a
“subordinate office “directly under the control of the Department of Health and Family Welfare of the Government of India in the
interest of the Public, the Student Community and the Employees of the JIPMER.
 
VIEWS OF THE GOVERNMENT OF PUDUCHERRY
           
The Government of Puducherry was in agreement with all the 32 Clauses proposed in the above Bill.  However, a few
modifications were suggested in the proposed Bill:
 
·
        Following three members may be included in the Governing Body from the Union Territory of Puducherry:
o       One Member of the Legislative Assembly of Puducherry to be nominated by the Hon’ble Speaker of the Assembly.
o       Secretary to Government (Health), Govt. of Puducherry.
o       Director of Health & Family Welfare Services, Puducherry.
·        The inclusion of these three members will facilitate the expression of views and concerns of the public of the Union Territory
in the Governing Body and also pave way for better cooperation from various Government Departments of Union Territory of
Puducherry in the functioning of the Institute.  It is all the more important in view of the Clause No. 13 (f) (i), (ii), (iii) & (iv)
which provides for establishment and maintenance of more Medical Colleges, Hospitals, Dental College, and Nursing College
etc by the Institute. 
·
        Clause 10 (3): Provides that the President of the Institute shall be the Chairperson of the Governing Body and as Chairperson
thereof he shall exercise such powers and discharge such functions as may be specified.
·        It is proposed that Hon’ble Minister for Health, Government of India shall be the President of the Institute as well as the
Chairperson of the Governing Body.  It is felt that Hon’ble Minister for Health and Family Welfare, Government of India may
or may not be in a position to attend the regular and extra-ordinary meetings of the Governing Body on a consistent basis.
 Hence, it is desirable that a Vice-Chairperson to the Governing Body be nominated who would be in a position to attend the
Governing Body meetings regularly.   This will ensure that the decisions of the Governing Body are taken with the full
involvement of the Chairperson/ Vice-Chairperson.  The Hon’ble Minister for Health, Government of Puducherry may be
designated as Vice-Chairperson of the Governing Body.
 
Views of Indian Medical Association-Puducherry State Branch
 
The representatives of Indian Medical Association endorsed the views expressed by the State Government and were in favour of
according autonomy to JIPMER. However, they made following suggestions:

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1 The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible for
implementation of various programmes at the national level in the areas of Health and Family
Welfare, prevention and control of major communicable diseases and promotion of traditional and
indigenous system of medicines. It also assists the States in preventing and controlling the spread
of seasonal disease outbreaks and epidemics through technical assistance.
1.2 The Ministry incurs expenditure either directly under Central Schemes through its three
Departments i.e. Department of Health and Family Welfare, Department of AYUSH and Department
of Health Research (Swasthya Anusandhan Vibhag), including the attached offices of DGHS and its
various subordinate offices, or by way of grants-in-aids to the autonomous/ statutory bodies and
NGOs. In addition to the fully funded Centrally Sponsored Family Welfare Programmes, the
Ministry is implementing several World Bank assisted programmes for control of AIDS, Malaria,
Tuberculosis, Disease Surveillance etc. in designated areas. Besides, State Health Systems
Development Projects with World Bank assistance are under implementation in various states. The
projects are implemented by the respective State Governments and the Department of Health and
Family Welfare only facilitates the States in availing of external assistance. All these schemes aim
at fulfilling the national commitment to improve access to Primary health care facilities keeping in
view the needs of rural areas and where the incidence of disease is high.
1.3 Explaining the trend of growth of healthcare in the country, the Secretary informed that
Health Sector has witnessed significant changes over the last decade. Health indicators showed a
discernible improvement with the Maternal Mortality Ratio, which was 327 per 1,00,000 live births
in 1999-2001 improving to 301 during 2001-2003 (SRS, 2005). Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)
recorded an improvement from 68 (SRS-2000) to 57 (SRS-2006). Total Fertility Rate showed some
progress, declining from 3.2 (SRS 2000) to 2.9 (SRS 2004).The latest National Family Health
Survey 2005-06 (NFHS-III) and District Level Household Surveys 2003-04 reveal that there is
upward movement in the provision of ante-natal care, institutional deliveries and post-natal care.
The percentage of pregnant women who received antenatal care was 76.9 in 2005-06 as against
65.8% in 1998-99. The NFHS-III survey indicates that 50.7 per cent of the pregnant women
had visited health care institutions for at least three antenatal care visits in 2005-06 as against
44.2 per cent in 1998-99. The State wise picture, however, shows that the developments in the
health indicators do not show a uniform pattern. During 2001-03, MMR was highest in Uttar
Pradesh including Uttaranchal (517) and lowest in Kerala (110). Two out of three maternal deaths
are reported from 8 EAG States and Assam. In comparison with SRS 1990-01, SRS 2001-03
indicates that the MMR has declined in all the States except Assam where it has shown an increase
from 398 to 490 per 1,00,000 live births. However, only 40.8 per cent of deliveries took place in
health facilities during the period.
1.4 The National Common Minimum Programme (NCMP) recognized healthcare as one of the
seven thrust areas for development and mandated the need for enhancing public health expenditure
to atleast 2-3% of GDP. The proposed outlay in the Eleventh Five-year plan for Health sector in
the Central sector is Rs.1,36,147 crores, against an expenditure of Rs.41,262 crores during Tenth
plan, registering an astounding increase of 229%. For the year 2008-09, the total outlay of the

2
Department of Health and Family Welfare increased by 14% to Rs.16,000 crores out of which the
NRHM component is 74.56% at Rs.11,930 crores. The balance outlay of Rs.4070 crores is
towards Health (Rs.3650 crores) and Health Research (Rs.420 crores). Under NRHM, the
major schemes in terms of allocations are Mission Flexipool (Rs.2285 crores), RCH Flexipool
(Rs.2535 crores), Maintenance of Infrastructure (Rs.3088 crores) and Disease Control Programmes
(Rs.1146.25 crores). In the Health Sector, an allocation of Rs.1100 crores has been made for HIV/
AIDS, Rs.373 crores for Human Resources, Rs. 490 crores for Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha
Yojana and for Redevelopment of Hospitals and Institutions, Rs.550 crores.
1.5 The financial envelop provided under the flexible pool will enable the States to develop the
required capacities in deficit areas and provide funds on the basis of needs rather than a strict
schematic format in terms of programme implementation. This would also provide the States
operational support for institutional strengthening and effectively designing programmes relating to
maternal and child health with clear pro-outcome and pro-poor focus. On the. health side, the
emphasis will be on developing human resources and evolving national programmes for healthcare
of the elderly and prevention and control of diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and stroke etc.
Another important initiative would be the National Urban Health Mission for the benefit of urban
poor families, slum dwellers, migrant workers and extremely vulnerable population who would be
identified by the Urban Local Bodies. Synergies are envisioned with schemes within and outside
health sector for maximizing benefits. A number of initiatives on specific programmes like National
Organ Transplant Programme, Oral Health, Prevention and Control of Fluorosis, National Advisory
Boards for standards, National programme for Blood and Blood Products etc. are proposed to
be taken up during the Eleventh Five Year Plan. Some of these schemes will be initiated during
2008-09.

HEALTH SECTOR
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1 The Ministry had projected a demand for Rs.21210.05 crores for the Department of Health
and Family Welfare for the Annual Plan 2008-09 to the Planning Commission. As against the
proposed outlay, Planning Commission approved an outlay of Rs.15580.00 crores for the
Department out of which the NRHM component is Rs.11930.00 crores. For Health Programmes
outside NRHM, the approved outlay is Rs.3650.00 crores, which is about 63% of the projected
outlay requirement of Rs.5761.49 crores. Out of this amount, Rs.1592.00 crores have been
allocated to the Central Sector Schemes and Rs.2058 crores to Centrally Sponsored Programmes.
2.2 The Committee is informed that this reduction in outlay is likely to affect implementation
of a number of ongoing schemes like Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY),
Redevelopment of Hospitals and Institutions etc. Some new initiatives like Urban Health Mission and
Health Care for Elderly may also require additional funds during the current year.
2.3 The Committee observes that Oversight Committee has been granted only Rs.100.00
crores against last year’s approved outlay of Rs. 600 crores, which, however, could not be
utilized. In the light of the recent Supreme Court’s judgment and the Government’s
propensity towards implementing it from this year itself, the Committee opines that
the funds would not be sufficient. Similarly against proposal of Rs.453.00 crores, only
Rs.329.00 have been provided to CGHS; against projected requirement of Rs.87.88 crores,
Safdarjung Hospital has received Rs.50.00 crores; Dr. RML Hospital has been allocated
Rs.59.20 crores against projected Plan requirement of Rs. 72.11 crores and Rs.68.95 crores
against Non-Plan requirement of Rs.71.88 crores; AIIMS has been granted Rs.452.00 crores
in Grant-in-Aids against projected requirement of Rs.753.00 crores and against the projected
total requirement of JIPMER for Rs.150.80 crores, it has received only Rs.98.00 crores. The
Committee observes that under provisioning in many of the Institutes is likely to adversely
affect the completion of construction and developmental activities undertaken by them and
in the process of the Institutions.
2.4 The Committee notes that the overall allocation for the health sector (outside
NRHM) has been on the higher side. Still, the Committee is constrained to note that the
Department has failed to project its budgetary requirements in an effective way for the
simple reason that the utilization of funds during the Tenth Plan is far from satisfactory
which is evident from the fact that the sanctioned BE for 2005-06 and 2006-07
was Rs.4253.84 crores and Rs.3564.95 crores, respectively, which was reduced to
Rs.4096.25 crores and Rs.3433.02 crores, respectively at the RE stage. The actual
expenditure figures of Rs.2907.96 crores and Rs.3377.34 crores were even less than the
budgeted allocations at the RE stage. The Committee notes that this trend has continued
during 2007-08 also. This goes to illustrate that the Department’s record in utilization of the
allocated funds is below par. The Committee would, therefore, recommend the Department
to first ensure optimum and judicious utilization of the funds allocated instead of
highlighting the reduced budgetary allocation. The Committee also recommends to the
Department to take substantive steps so that the stumbling blocks in the utilization of
sanctioned funds for 2008-09 for a crucial sector like health, are removed.

activities of these schemes/institutions under constant monitoring so as to arrest this trend
of under utilization.
2.9 The pendency level of Utilization Certificates has been engaging the attention of the
Committee for the last few years. According to latest figures as on 1st March, 2008, there

plans of the Department to reach a justifiable level of pendency, the Committee is given

to all the States through Resident Commissioners on this issue giving full details of pending
UCs in respect of the Department of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee is
dismayed to note that in the name of efforts; only a letter has been issued. The Committee
feels that spirited efforts, which are apparently lacking, need to be made on priority basis
to clear the UCs which are pending for the last three decades or so. The Committee also

2.10 In response to another specific query regarding audit of various Programmes/Bodies, the

all centrally sponsored programmes, PSUs and autonomous bodies under the Department. As per
GFR 211 (1), the Grantee Bodies like autonomous bodies, PSU etc. receiving Grant-in-aid are to
be audited by Principal Accounts Office of the Ministry and C and AG and for this purpose a
provision is being incorporated in the Sanction. The Committee has been informed by the
Department that it has taken steps to strengthen its Internal Audit Wing also.
2.11 The Committee welcomes the proposal of the Department to introduce a provision in
the Sanction itself regarding audit of all centrally sponsored programmes, PSUs under the
Department and autonomous bodies which are receiving Grant-in-Aid. The Committee
recommends to the Department to expedite the same and intimate the progress made in
this regard.
2.12 The Committee is given to understand that the Department proposes to undertake the audit
of more centrally sponsored health programmes and PSUs and autonomous bodies during the
Financial Year 2008-09. Besides the names of Bodies/Programmes which would be covered
during 2008-09, the Committee would like to be informed about the centrally sponsored
health programmes, PSUs and autonomous bodies which were audited during 2007-08 along
with the adverse audit findings and the action taken by the Department thereon.
2.13 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by high level of pendency of Audit paras
contained in CAG Report and Internal Audit on matters relating to the Department. The
Committee is surprised to note that there are 62 pending Audit paras dating back from
CAG Report No.2 of 1998 to the latest CAG Report No. 20 of 2007 on the Performance Audit
of procurement of medicines and medical equipment. The Committee fails to understand the
reasons for such high level of pendency. The very fact that such a large number of Audit
paras remain to be reconciled indicates that internal financial management of the Ministry
is weak. The Committee would like to be apprised about the corrective measures taken in
the light of the pending Audit paras.
III. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME (CGHS)
3.1 CGHS, a welfare scheme of the Central Government, was started in 1954 and takes care
of the medical needs of the Central Government employees (serving and pensioners), sitting and
Ex-MPs, Judges of the Supreme Court/High Court (sitting and retired), Freedom Fighters (free of
cost), Ex-Governors, Ex-Vice Presidents of India, employees of the semi autonomous bodies/semi
Government Organisations, Accredited Journalists, serving and pensioner employees of a few
autonomous organisations in Delhi and the cities where CGHS is in operation. It provides medical
services-both inpatient and outpatient care including diagnostic and investigations at the level of
dispensaries, Central/State Government Hospitals, recognised private hospitals/diagnostic centres,
dispensaries/units under ISM and H, regional cancer centre, polyclinics to its beneficiaries. As per
the latest figures, there are 9.11 lakh CGHS cardholders and 33.01 lakh beneficiaries.
3.2 Plan allocation of Rs.50.00 crores and Non-Plan allocation of Rs.329.00 crores has been
made for CGHS for 2008-09. The Committee notes that Plan allocation for 2008-09 is at an
enhanced level when compared with provision of Rs.40.00 crores made for 2007-08. As per
the Outcome Budget (2008-09), against a Plan allocation of Rs.40.00.crores for 2007-08
under CGHS; expenditure reported upto 29.02.2008 is only Rs.19.08 crores. The Committee
is, however, surprised to note that in response to a specific query made by it, utilization of

6
Rs.32.16 crores was reported upto February, 2008. The Committee is unhappy with the
conflicting figures of utilization of Plan funds. Either the information published in the
Outcome Budget is incorrect or inaccurate status report has been furnished to the
Committee, that too on a specific query made by it. Both the positions compel the
Committee to conclude that there is a need for better management at the Department
level. The Committee apprehends that chances are there that major utilization under CGHS
has taken place during the last quarter of the year. If it is true, this indicates improper
handling of the funds. The trend of utilization of major chunk of funds during the last
quarter is not a healthy sign. The Committee would like to be apprised about utilization of
Plan and Non-Plan funds (quarter-wise) during 2007-08. In the light of last year’s experience
of utilization of funds, the Committee recommends that concerted efforts need to be made
for optimum and judicious utilization of enhanced allocation made for 2008-09.
3.3 The Committee has been given to understand that against a proposal for allocation of
Rs.453 crores submitted under Non-Plan in BE 2008-09, an allocation of Rs. 329 crores has been
made, which is lower when compared to provision of Rs. 368.00 crores in RE 2007-08. The
Committee has been given to understand that additional Non-Plan funds were meant for salary for
vacant posts likely to be filled up during the year and also for payments to the MSDs, local
chemists etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation of funds under Non-
Plan be enhanced adequately so that the services available to the CGHS beneficiaries are
not affected.
3.4 The computerization of CGHS dispensaries and offices in Delhi was taken up at an
expenditure of Rs.8.74 crores. The Committee was informed that as on 26.3.2008, 83
dispensaries in Delhi have been fully computerized and the process of computerization of
remaining 4 dispensaries was under way. The Committee would like to point out that
computerization process of CGHS dispensaries in Delhi could not be completed as scheduled.
Originally targeted to be completed by 2006-07, revised date of 17th August, 2007 could also
not be adhered to. By the end of financial year, 2007-08, 4 dispensaries in Delhi still
remained to be computerized. Computerization of CGHS dispensaries located in Mumbai,
Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Nagpur and Pune to be taken up in 2007-08 as scheduled, is
yet to start. The Committee can imagine the status of third phase slated to be completed
in 2008-09. The Committee, keeping in view the past experience in respect of Delhi
dispensaries, can only emphasize that all steps need to be taken to complete the
computerization of dispensaries outside Delhi at the earliest. Corrective measures based on
the problem areas noticed in the computerization of dispensaries in Delhi need to be taken.
3.5 The Committee is given to understand that the feedback received from the officials
regarding computerization is very encouraging while there has been a mixed reaction from the
beneficiaries. The Committee would like to point out that situation is some what different.
Problems are being faced both by the CGHS functionaries and beneficiaries. Technicians,
junior staff manning counters in dispensaries and attending doctors need to be fully trained.
Practical problems like internet and electricity failure have to be tackled by having an
alternative arrangement. These initial teething problems should not be allowed to be
prolonged. At present, beneficiaries which include senior citizens also are being made to
wait for hours at the dispensaries. Their ordeal starts right from the registration counter
and continues upto delivery of medicines. The Committee would appreciate if all the
measures including training, smooth running of computers with full connectivity, backup for
power failure are taken at the earliest and also closely monitored.
3.6 The Committee has been emphasizing for long for introduction of two shift system
in CGHS. The Committee does not appreciate the contention of the Ministry that a large

7
number of private hospitals and diagnostic centres have been empanelled under the CGHS
and in case of emergency, beneficiaries can go there for treatment and claim re-
imbursement later. The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Ministry once
again to the fact that idea behind having two shifts in CGGS dispensaries is the
inconvenience being faced by the CGHS beneficiaries, majority of them office goers in going
to the dispensaries in the morning hours. The Committee is disturbed by the element of
helplessness shown by the Ministry in their candid admission of staff side vehemently
opposing the move. In this era where the service providers like banks etc. are opting for
flexible timings to give their customers maximum possible services, at least the Ministry
could have come forward with a positive and proactive approach. The Committee would
reiterate its recommendation made last year for starting two shifts in a few dispensaries as
a test case. One must not forget that CGHS is a service oriented scheme, supposedly
providing health care mainly to our serving employees and pensioners. It is the
responsibility of the Ministry to make the CGHS employees understand and not to be
pressurized by them.
3.7 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the problems being faced by a very large
number of CGHS beneficiaries residing in Dwarka sub-city in Delhi. At present, these beneficiaries
have to travel 10-12 Kms. for medical treatment at the nearest dispensary located in Manglapuri,
Palam. For pathological tests they have to travel even further to Janakpuri Dispensary. The
Committee was informed that approval for opening of CGHS dispensary in Dwarka has been
received and work would start soon. The Committee recommends that construction of
dispensary in Dwarka where land is already available should start at the earliest. All
procedural formalities should be expedited and completion of project strictly monitored.
3.8 The Committee finds that in-principle approval for opening of new CGHS dispensaries
in Sector 82, Noida and Gurgaon was given by the Planning Commission way back on
14th March, 2006.  The Committee is surprised to note that even after two years, suitable
accommodation for housing the dispensary in Sector 82, Noida and Gurgaon could not be
managed. Secretary (Health) Government of Haryana is now being requested to allot a
building for CGHS Dispensary in Gurgaon. Proposal for housing the CGHS Dispensary in
Community Centre, Sector 82, Noida on rent-basis is under consideration. The Committee
strongly feels that the Ministry should pursue the two proposals in hand so that large
number of CGHS beneficiaries residing in these two areas do not continue to remain
deprived of health care any more.
3.9 The Committee notes that CGHS continues to suffer from manpower shortage. Against 84
sanctioned SAG posts, 74 posts are lying vacant. The latest figures supplied by the Department
show that 495 vacancies are there in the grade of GDMO alone. The Committee has been given
to understand that on the basis of CMSE 2006, 125 candidates had been offered appointment and
pre-appointment formalities for 175 candidates were under different stages of process. Based on
CMSE 2007 , dossiers of 176 candidates had been received and were being processed. As regards
vacancies in technical posts, after necessary approval, advertisement has been issued. Requisition
for stenographers and LDCs had been placed with SSC. Action for vacant promotional posts had
been initiated through DPCs. Further after a long but avoidable delay, the Department had finally
started implementing the SIU report. Accordingly, all surplus posts identified in cities outside Delhi
have been abolished and action for creation of posts has been initiated for obtaining approval of
the Ministry of Finance. The Committee recommends to the Department to take the issue on
priority with the Ministry of Finance to complete all the procedural formalities so that
necessary posts are created and subsequently filled up. The Committee would also like to
be apprised about the cadre strength created as a result of implementation of SIU report
and the efforts taken so far to fill up the vacant posts.

8
3.10 The Committee’s attention has also been drawn by a very large number of vacancies in
Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ categories. Out of 3022 category ‘C’ sanctioned posts, 568 posts were vacant,
with Delhi alone having the maximum vacancies of 292. Similarly, there were 550  vacant posts
against 2934 sanctioned Group ‘D’ posts, with Delhi having the maximum vacancies of 325.
Besides that, staff other than medical officers was being out sourced/engaged on contract basis in
Dehradun, Bhubaneswar, Ranchi, Chandigarh, Shillong and Bhopal. The Committee understands

to be introduced. The Committee has been given to understand that as recommended by
SIU, Department of Expenditure, vacancies arising in Group ‘D’ posts are to be

3.11 The Committee views with serious concern the growing number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in CGHS dispensaries. The Committee understands that all
surplus posts identified in cities outside Delhi have been abolished. It has also been
informed that the staff strength in the dispensaries is decided as per the workload. The
very fact that at the present juncture, no CGHS city can be stated to have full complement
of the staff strength as per the SID norms establishes that the existing dispensaries are not
functioning as envisaged. The Committee also strongly feels that outsourcing/hiring of staff
on contract-basis on a big scale is a remedy worse than the disease. The concept of public
private partnership cannot be applied across the board specially in a set-up meant for
providing health care. The Committee would like to have a status note on the sanctioned
posts and vacancies, category-wise and region-wise in CGHS dispensaries.
3.12 To a specific query of the Committee as to payment of consultation fees to other agencies
owing to new fulfillment of needs of various indenters by Medical Stores Organization (M.S.O.),
it was informed that M/S HSCC alone was paid Rs.9.03 crores towards consultancy fees. The
Committee recommends that all out efforts be made for reduction in the consultation fees
to 2% for procurement of drugs/medicines for CGHS as assured by the Ministry and the
Committee be informed accordingly.
3.13 The Committee notes that as there is no private hospital empanelled under CGHS for
treatment of cancer patients in Delhi only adhoc arrangements are in place. Accordingly, cancer
patients could get treatment from Apollo Hospital, New Delhi, Batra Hospital, New Delhi,
Dharamshila Cancer Hospital, Delhi and Rajiv Gandhi Cancer and Research Institute, Delhi upto
31st March, 2008. The Committee is happy to note that these  adhoc  arrangements would
continue until further orders. The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that
empanelment of these hospitals should be made on permanent basis, specially in view of
cancer patients undergoing prolonged and costly treatment. The Ministry has to play a
proactive role in such matters.
3.14 The Committee was informed that CGHS rules for various procedures, tests etc. in CGHS
empanelled private hospitals and diagnostic centres were fixed on the basis of lowest rates
quoted for a group of CGHS cities, depending on the classification of the cities for purposes of
City Compensatory Allowance. Subsequently, on objections being raised on clubbing of cities for
fixing of rates, it was decided to issue rate list for each CGHS city separately, based on the lowest
rates quoted by hospitals/diagnostic centres for that city. The Committee notes that under the
revised exercise, rates in respect of Bangalore, Chennai, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kolkata,
Lucknow, Mumbai, Nagpur and Pune have been issued. The Committee hopes that rates for
the remaining cities would be issued at the earliest. The Committee would like to be
apprised about the level of difference in the rates for major hospitals/diagnostic centres in
the metro cities.

IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL AND V ARDHMAN MAHAVEER MEDICAL COLLEGE,
NEW DELHI
4.1 Safdarjung Hospital, established in 1942, is the largest of the three Central Government
Tertiary Care Multi-disciplinary Hospitals in Delhi with a pre-independence history. The Hospital has
total bed strength of 1531 including bassinets. The hospital presently has facilities in the 34 clinical
and 45 special clinics.
4.2 Plan allocation of Rs.51.00 crores for 2007-08 for the Hospital was raised to Rs.73.50
crores at the RE stage, keeping in view funds required for procurement of equipment, medicines
etc. and completion of ongoing projects. The Committee, however, notes that upto 29.02.2008
expenditure of only Rs.53.77 crores could be reported.
4.3 Against projected Plan requirement for the Safdarjung hospital (excluding VMMC) of
Rs.87.88 crores for the current year, allocation of Rs.50.00 crores has been made. The
Committee apprehends that the present allocation of funds to the Hospital might adversely
affect its services and in the process, the large number of patients. While cautioning the
Hospital to utilize its allocated funds judiciously and optimally, the Committee recommends
that it should be granted adequate funds to meet its functional requirements.
4.4 To a specific query on whether the Department proposes to work out a monitoring
mechanism in co-ordination with hospital authorities to ensure procurement of medical equipments
within the prescribed time limit and thereby result in reversing the trend of under utilization of
allocated funds, the Department came out with the often repeated rhetoric of ‘laid down
procedures’ that are to be followed. The Committee observes that procedures and rules are
made to streamline, strengthen and facilitate a process and not create hurdles and
bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends that effective coordination between the
Department and the Hospital authorities is required in this regard. If required, suitable
steps for improvement in the procedural aspect may be initiated so as to provide better
health care delivery system.
4.5 The Committee is happy to note that scheme of redevelopments of hospitals
including redevelopment of Safdarjung Hospital with the proposal to increase its bed
strength from 1531 to 3000 has finally been included in the approved schemes for the
Eleventh Plan. HSCC has submitted a final report on ‘Redevelopment Plan of Safdarjung
Hospital’ to the Department for consideration. The Department has started work for
engaging consultants for preparation of DPR for the detailed redevelopment plan. The
Committee would like to point out that ‘in-principle’ approval by the Planning Commission
has already taken considerable time. The Committee therefore, urges the Department to
make wholehearted efforts to expedite the procedural formalities at the earliest. The
redevelopment plan is required to be started without any further delay, keeping in view the
ever-increasing patient load on the Safdarjung Hospital. The Committee recommends that
scarcity of funds and lack of coordination should not come in the way of its timely
completion and the Department should make every conceivable effort in this regard.
4.6 The Committee has been monitoring the progress made in the projects relating to
establishment of Renal Transplantation Unit in the Department of Surgery/Urology and Invitro
Fertilization (IVF) clinic in Obs. and Gynae Department for the last two-three years. As per the
latest information furnished by the Department:—
“The space has been identified and funds allocated. Rs.98.48 lakhs for the purpose have
been placed at the disposal of CPWD for the renovation work. Equipments are under
process of procurement and likely to be completely procured within next quarter of
2008-09. Two Surgeons, one Pathologist and 15 Nurses have already under-gone training

10
in Renal Transplant at AIIMS. As regards IVF Unit, a proposal has been submitted by the
HOD, Obs. and Gynae for approval in principle.”
4.7 The Committee expresses its serious concern on the slow progress made with regard
to setting up of Renal Transplantation Unit. Status of the project for IVF unit is more
discouraging as ‘in-principle’ approval is yet to come. The Committee can only emphasize
that the Renal Transplantation Unit should be made functional by the year end by closely
monitoring the progress of the same. Procedural formalities with regard to IVF unit also
need to be completed at the earliest.
4.8 The Committee’s attention has been drawn by a large number of vacancies in
different categories of posts in Safdarjung Hospital. Out of the total sanctioned staff
strength of 4781, there were 1054 vacant posts in different categories as on July, 2007. The
Committee has been given to understand that workload of the Hospital has progressively
increased manifold in the past few years. The doctor-patient ratio has inversely grown, there
is an acute need of more doctors per patient and related infrastructure including sub-staff.
In such a scenario, with the redevelopment project of Safdarjung Hospital likely to take off
at the earliest, additional staff strength of all the categories would be required. The
Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department in co-ordination with hospital
authorities should chalk out an action-plan for acquiring the required manpower.
V. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL, NEW DELHI
5.1 Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital is one of the main public tertiary level hospitals in New
Delhi which was set up in 1954. Over the years, RML Hospital has grown to become a 1000-bed
hospital providing services in almost all major specialities and many super-specialties. Chosen by
the WHO to be developed as a model health promoting hospital, the first of its kind in India, RML
Hospital caters to two-lakh emergency patients and l2-lakh outdoor patients annually. The hospital
had been actively involved in information education communication activities. It had conducted
various training programme of HIV/AIDS, Hospital Waste Management, Leptospirosis, etc. It is
actively participating in National Programmes like Blindness Control, Leprosy, Family Welfare,
Immunizations, and Drug De-Addiction Programmes. It is a designated hospital for training of
Dengue and AIDS by WHO.
5.2 The Committee notes that an approved outlay of Rs.36.00 crores (including PGIMER) was
revised to Rs. 71.95 crores in 2007-08. However, upto 29.02.2008, expenditure reported is only
Rs. 56.60 crores. The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of an assurance that
each Central Institute will have a separate monitoring Committee, given by the Secretary,
H
 and FW before the Committee last year, no action seems to have been taken. The
Committee, therefore, reiterates that a proper monitoring mechanism needs to be put in
place so as to arrest this trend of sub-optimal utilization of the funds.
5.3 The Committee has been observing that a number of projects-big and small,
envisaged for strengthening and augmenting the existing services in the premier Hospital,
continue to remain in the implementation status with very little progress being made. The
Committee has been constrained to point out that the year 2007-08 was also no exception.
Funds allocated remained under-utilized with the following three major projects running
behind schedule:—
• Strengthening of Accidents and Emergency Department and setting up of Trauma Care
Centre.
• Setting up of PGIMER at Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital.
• Upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing.

11
All these projects were to be completed in 2007-08 only. The Committee notes that
academic session for PG courses in Medicine, Paediatrics and Anesthesia is to begin in 2008-
09. While welcoming the starting of PGIMER at Dr. RML hospital, the Committee would
appreciate if the PGI becomes fully operational running all the courses with the required
infrastructure and regular staff in place. The Committee apprehends that there is little
chance of Trauma Care Centre becoming operational in 2008-09 with appointment of 178
additional staff yet to be made and process of purchase of equipment and consumable going
on. The Committee also finds that not much progress seems to have been made in the
upgradation of School of Nursing into College of Nursing. The target remains the same in
2008-09 also as in the previous year.
VI. ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
6.1 AIIMS was established in 1956 as an institution of national importance. It continues to be
a leader in the field of medical education, research and patient-care in keeping with the mandate
of the Parliament.
6.2 Against annual requirement of Rs.500.00 crores, Plan allocation of Rs.200.00 crores was
made for AIIMS, out of which only Rs.160.00 crores were provided by the Planning Commission/
Ministry of Finance at the RE stage in 2007-08. Again, against a projected requirement of
Rs.733.00 crores of Grant-in-Aids in 2008-09 only Rs.452.00 crores have been allocated out of
which the Plan component is Rs.162.00 crores and Non-Plan component is Rs.290.00 crores. The
Committee was informed that the allocated funds would not be sufficient for maintaining
the infrastructure and patient care services of the Institute. The Committee feels that the
decrease in Non-plan from Rs.310.00 crores in 2007-08 to Rs.290.00 crores is surely going
to affect the patient care services offered by the Institute. The Committee apprehends
return of the ‘user charges regime’ in AIIMS because consumables are the only negotiable
component of the Non-Plan budget as salary and bills have to be paid any way.
6.3 The Committee notes that approved outlay for AIIMS for the Eleventh Plan is Rs.1461.00
crores which is more than double of the T enth Plan allocation of Rs.631.12 crores. The Committee
finds that the Institute could not keep pace with the enhanced provision being made in the last
three years of the Tenth Plan period. The Committee has been informed that full utilization of Plan
funds during 2002-03 (Rs.105.00 crores) and 2003-04 (Rs.105.00 crores) the first two years of
the Tenth Plan was made possible only by diversion of Plan allocation to Non-plan to the tune of
Rs.61.45 crores and Rs.32.25 crores for 2002-03 and 2003-04 respectively. During the next two
years of the Tenth Plan, i.e. 2004-05 and 2005-06 Plan funds remained under utilized. For the last
year of the Tenth Plan, out of Plan provision of Rs.205.86 crores, expenditure reported
was Rs.160.00 crores, with Rs.30.00 crores being released as late as on 15.03.2007 and
Rs.30.33 crores on 31.03.2007.
6.4 The Committee is constrained to observe that enhanced outlay for the Eleventh Plan
period does not seem to have any visible impact. Plan provision of Rs.200.00 crores for
2007-08 not only remains at the same level as in the previous Plan period but has also been
brought down to Rs.160.00 crores at the RE stage with actual expenditure reported up to
29.02.2008 being only Rs.113.33 crores. The Committee is not able to comprehend the
reasons for under-utilization of funds duly allocated for specific purposes. Failure on the
part of a premier institute like AIIMS to utilize the funds as targeted indicates that
problem areas continue to persist both in the co-ordination between the administrative
Ministry and the Institute and its functioning.
6.5 The Committee in its last year’s report had called for making conscious effort to break the
deadlock between the premier institute of the country and the administrative Ministry which had

12
affected the quality of services of the Institute badly. The Committee has been informed that on
17.03.2008, Minister of Health and Family Welfare along with officials of the Ministry had a one
to one dialogue with the heads of all the Departments of the Institute to try and find out the areas
to be focused in the days to come regarding creation of adequate manpower and allocation of
resources. The Committee hopes that position would improve now.
6.6 The Committee has been given to understand that the Centre for Dental Research at the
Institute has become fully functional in February, 2008. The Committee hopes that all the necessary
posts created for the centre have been filled up. The Committee notes that EFC has been submitted
for the project of Surgical Block with an estimate of Rs.42.00 crore to be commissioned by
2009-10. The Committee would emphasize that procedural formalities for the centre should
be expedited so as to complete it by the targeted date.
6.7 The Committee also takes note of major new initiatives for which plans were under
preparation during 2007-08 as listed below:—
➢ Construction of new PC Block.
➢ Advance facilities for Paediatrics (Medical) and (Surgery).
➢ Advance facilities for Geriatrics.
➢ Facility for Family Medicine and Public Health.
6.8 The Committee finds that another set of new projects has been listed to be taken
during 2008-09. The Committee strongly feels that new initiatives should be taken up with
priority being fixed for the most needed ones. The Committee would appreciate if these
initiatives do not continue to be on paper during 2008-09. The Committee recommends that
funds provided for the AIIMS in the Eleventh Plan show both optimum and judicious
utilization as per the action plan with additional provision as and when required. The
Committee is of the view that an effective monitoring mechanism to be effected by all
concerned both at the institute and the Ministry level needs to be in place for the purpose
at the earliest.

The Department needs to devise a strategy immediately to arrest this trend. The Committee
would like to be informed of the remedial steps taken in this regard.
6.11 Committee’s attention has also been drawn to a recent report of WHO according to which
out of 428 students of AIIMS (studying between 1989 and 2000), 233 (54%) are residing abroad.
The Committee is deeply concerned about the matter as the Institute is one of the best
training grounds for the doctors and that too at highly subsidized rates involving precious
tax payers’ money. The Committee is of the view that this brain drain is on two counts -
higher studies and lucrative assignments. At the same time, the Committee is also of the
opinion that some policy or enactment should be made so that tendency of leaving the
Institute by doctors/nurses can be minimized. This could be in the form of a monetary bond
or post qualification compulsory service. The Committee strongly feels that urgent steps are
required to be taken so as to ensure an ideal working environment for our young talented
doctors along with all the incentives comparable to those enjoyed by private sector doctors
to the extent possible. The Committee would like to be apprised of the steps taken in this
regard which should not be only AIIMS specific but should also cover all the Government
medical institutions.
6.12 The Committee is given to understand that the Valiathan Committee had submitted its
report on the functioning of AIIMS more than a year ago. The Committee is surprised to note
that only follow up action taken so far is a meeting held under the Chairmanship of Secretary
(Health and Family Welfare) with Director, AIIMS on the 1st March, 2008. The Committee was
informed that the matter was now under Government’s consideration. The Committee is not
happy with the undue delay in the implementation of Valiathan Committee recommendations.
Any further delay would simply negate the very purpose of setting up such a Committee, that
too at the directive of the Prime Minister. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the
Department to expedite the implementation of the Valiathan Committee Report.
6.13 The Committee in its last year’s Report had expressed its reservation to the casual approach
adopted by the Department to its earlier recommendation of setting up of a Burns Unit in AIIMS.
The Secretary, during the course of deposing before the Committee informed that the proposal for
setting up the same in the JPNA Trauma Centre, AIIMS could not be placed before the Standing
Finance Committee of the Institute on the 31st March, 2008, as scheduled and the same will be
done on the 17th April, 2008. The Committee can only hope that the Burns Unit, duly
approved, will be made operational by the targeted date.
