VIII. NORTH EASTERN INDIRA GANDHI REGIONAL INSTITUTE OF HEALTH AND
MEDICAL SCIENCES (NEIGRIHMS), SHILLONG
8.1 The main objective of the Institute is to provide advanced specialized health care to
the people of the North Eastern Region including those of Sikkim, to serve as a regional
referral services centre and to promote a programme of health manpower development and
training in identified fields of super-specialization. The Institute is fully funded by the Government
of India.
8.2 Though originally slated for completion in March, 2005, at a cost of Rs.422.60 crores, the
project has been delayed time and again due to various reasons. In view of the slippages, the
Institute (500 bedded hospital) is likely to be fully operational by 2008-09.
8.3 The Committee has been monitoring the progress being made, specially in the procurement
of equipments required for operationalizing various Departments and recruitment of manpower. The
Committee notes that like in previous years, allocated funds remained under-utilized in 2007-08
also. Provision of Rs.75.00 crores at the beginning of the year had to be brought down to
Rs.42.00 crores at the RE stage and by 29.2.2008 expenditure reported was only Rs.30.00 crores.
The Committee has, however, been informed that all the major equipments required for
operationalizing various Departments have already been procured and installation is going on at
present. The Institute has been operationalized as 365 bedded hospital as of March, 2008.
8.4 The Committee also observes that the Institute is successfully running a Nursing College
since 2006 with 50 seats capacity. Now, the third batch is being admitted to the Nursing College.
The process of expanding the Nursing College by increasing the number of seats to 100 is going
on at present and already SFC Note has been circulated for the purpose. MBBS and PG courses
are slated to be started during this year. Approvals are being obtained from various Government
Bodies/Departments for the same.
8.5 The Committee is happy to note that considerable progress has been made in
operationalization of NEIGRIHMS during 2007-08. The Committee is, however, perturbed to
note that no improvement could be made so far as manpower required for the Institute is
concerned. Like 2006-07, position remained unchanged during 2007-08 also. The Committee
has been informed that a total of 95 faculty members, including 31 senior faculty, 28 senior
residents and 36 junior residents have joined so far. For senior faculty positions, 31 out of 79 posts
are already filled in. To overcome the difficulty faced in attracting qualified faculty for
operationalizing various speciality and super-speciality Departments in the institute, the Ministry has
invited eminent institutes of India to collaborate with NEIGRIHMS and operationalize the
departments. The Institute has already entered into an understanding with NIMHANS for
operationalizing the Department of Neurology and Neuro-Surgery by transferring and operating the
faculty posts from NIMHANS. The Institute has also entered into MoA with Dr. Cherian’s Frontier
Lifeline, International Institute of Cardiology, Cardio-Thoracic and V ascular Surgery for outsourcing
the services of the Departments of Cardiology and Cardiothoracic Surgery. Efforts are on to clinch
similar agreements with other eminent institutes including CMC-Vellore, CMC-Ludhiana, Amrita
Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Kochi and efforts are on to take the expertise of other GoI
institutes like AIIMS, PGIMER.

17
8.6 The Committee would like to point out that efforts made by the Department for
getting the teaching/specialists faculty posted/deputed fr om Armed Forces Medical Services
have not been successful due to shortage of senior faculty in the AFMS cadre also. The
Committee would again emphasize that it does not have much faith in the collaboration
measures reported to be made with Institutions like NIMHANS and Dr. Cherian’s Frontier
Lifeline. The Committee is not aware how far the efforts for clinching similar agreements
with CMC-Vellore, CMC-Ludhiana, Amrita Institute of Medical Sciences, Kochi, AIIMS and
PGIMER would prove to be successful. The Committee fails to comprehend how the
Departments of Neurology, Neuro-Surgery and Cardiology could be made operational at the
Institute located at Shillong by hiring the services of faculty of NIMHANS located at the
other corner of the country. Same would be the position with the proposed tie-up with other
Institutes. The Committee would also like to point out that the Department must be fully
aware about the shortage of faculty at these premier Institutes also. The Committee
strongly feels that such stop-gap arrangements, even if made, cannot make the Institute
fully functional. Target of making 500 bedded hospital and teaching Institute at Shillong is
thus likely to remain on paper only for considerable time. The Committee reiterates that
the Department has to make all conceivable efforts for having permanent faculty at the
Institute. Special incentives and extra facilities have to be worked out for attracting the
required manpower to the Institute. Collaboration with leading Institutes/public-private
partnership can be feasible for limited number of posts and period only. The Committee
would also like to be apprised about the present status of phase-I of filling up of 725 posts
and phase-II of filling up of 794 posts.

9.1 Central Institute of Psychiatry is a premier Institute in the field of mental health in India.

out various research programmes. During 2007-08, 14 orientation courses for visiting nurses of
psychiatry, 9 continuing education programmes, 2 service programmes for ward attendants, 28
seminars, 17 journal clubs, 27 case conferences were conducted. Besides, 48 students were
enrolled for mental health education programmes.
9.2 The Committee notes that against a provision of Rs.10.00 crores in 2007-08 only an
amount of Rs.3.86 crores could be spent upto 29.02.2008. The Committee is constrained to

provision of Rs.62.20 crores, utilization of only Rs. 30.17 crores could be reported by the
end of the Plan period.

adequate infrastructure for patient care, various PF Training and Research in the field of Mental
Health and Neurosciences. The deficiencies are in the areas of manpower, capital construction
work and machineries and equipments. The Committee is disturbed by the continuance of such
a position that too in a pr emier Institute of the country,  inspite of availability of funds. The

development of the Institute during the Eleventh Plan is under consideration which includes
additional manpower requirement, construction of OPD, Neurology Block, Casualty and

work would be completed within the targeted date of 20 months. The Committee is,
however, worried about the fate of upgradation of Grants Medical College and JJ hospital,
Mumbai due to a court case pending in Nagpur High Court in the matter. The Committee
is of the view that the Department should take up other linked activities like arranging for
the faculty and requisite infrastructure simultaneously so that no delay takes place in
operationalization of the Institutions once the construction activity is completed.
11.7 The Committee also recommends that funds as and when required should be made
available to the Department. The Committee would however like to point out that though
funds have never been a problem for this ambitious project of national importance,
utilization thereof has been far from satisfactory level. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends setting up of a joint mechanism of Centre and the concerned States so that
greater coordination is achieved and effective monitoring of the ongoing projects is done.
The Committee also calls for greater emphasis on adhering to the time lines so that the
overall cost of the project is not escalated further.
11.8 The Committee, during the oral evidence of the Secretary had taken a serious view
of the delay in implementation of the project. The Committee, therefore, desires the
Department to apprise it of the progress made in implementation of the project, after every
two months.
XII. IMPROVEMENT OF NURSING SERVICES
12.1 During the Tenth Plan, a provision of Rs.102.00 crores was made for Development of
Nursing Services. The Committee has been emphasizing the urgent need for expansion and
strengthening of Nursing Services in the country. The Committee notes that enhanced allocation of
Rs.280.65 crores for Development of Nursing Services for Eleventh Plan can be considered a step
in the right direction. Another encouraging sign is a new initiative proposed for the Eleventh Plan

21
is provision of Rs.2900.00 crores for upgradation/strengthening of Nursing Services. Provision of
Rs.18.00 crores and Rs.198.00 crores has accordingly been made under these two components for

a provision of Rs15.00 crores with likely expenditure of Rs.1.80 crores during March, 2008.
However, the Committee is surprised to observe unsatisfactory level of achievement under
the quantifiable deliverables/physical outputs set for 2007-08. The first target set was
training of 8000 nursing personnel through 48 identified Nursing Institutions. By the end
of the year, no progress seems to have been made from the details made available to the
Committee. Proposal for conducting 78 courses for training of 2340 nurses was under
process. Training of additional 1600 nurses depended upon proposals to be received from the
Institutions. The Committee has been informed that out of 30 institutions, funds could be

of Nursing at Dr. R.M.L. Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and Lady Harding Medical College

at Lady Harding Medical College reported to have started functioning in 2007. The
Committee hopes that required manpower and infrastructure has been made available there.

Hospital will start functioning from the session, 2008. The Committee is not very hopeful as
upgradation of School of Nursing at Dr. R.M.L. Hospital has also been listed as one of the
targets to be achieved during 2008-09. The Committee would like to reiterate that all these
projects need to be closely monitored so as to ensure their completion within the time
schedule without any cost escalation in the original estimate. The Department should not
be a mere spectator, it should devise some mechanism for proper utilization of the funds
and its repeated contention that the utilization/grants of funds depends upon receipt of
SOE/UCs is not acceptable to the Committee. The Department has to play a more proactive
role in co-ordination with the hospital/college authorities. The problem areas, wherever

such projects. The Committee is of the view that such a mechanism will prove to be very

12 Centres of Excellence, opening of 73 ANM Schools, and 69 GNM Schools, strengthening of

the enhancement in the assistance to be provided to Nursing Institutions from Rs.10.00
lakhs to Rs.25.00 lakhs. Such a move was overdue. The Committee, however, wonders
whether any exercise has been initiated for identification of locations of all the proposed
Centres/Schools/Colleges so far. The Committee would appreciate if implementation of all
these projects is carried out in a time-bound manner. The Committee is not aware about
any assessment/review made recently about the (training both pre and in-service)
programmes for Nurses and also functioning of Training Institutions for Nurses. The
Committee is of the view that such an exercise is necessary for strengthening the Nursing
Services which is a very crucial component of health care.

mark of highest recognition for the meritorious services of the nurses and nursing
profession in the country, that continued up to 1989, have been revived and named as the

22
National Florence Nightingale Award from 2007 with the consent of the President of

2007.

of total nursing strength of 3015 in Central Government Hospitals in Delhi, only 795

are in Delhi, the Committee can well imagine the conditions in State Government Hospitals.
The Committee strongly feels that residential facilities for Nurses need to be augmented at
the earliest. The Committee recommends to the Department to formulate a comprehensive
policy to stop exodus of nurses as also to offer more incentives so as to make the

XIV . RASHTRIYA AROGYA NIDHI
14.1 R ashtriya Arogya Nidhi was set up under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 1997
to provide financial assistance to patients living below poverty line, who are suffering from major
life threatening diseases to receive medical treatment in Government Hospitals. Under the scheme
of Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi, grants-in-aid is also provided to State Governments for setting up State
Illness Assistance Funds. Such funds have been set up by the Governments of Andhra Pradesh,
Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pardesh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra,
Mizoram, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, West Bengal, Uttarakhand, Haryana, Punjab,
NCT of Delhi and Puducherry. Other States/Union Territories have been requested to set up the
fund, as soon as possible.
14.2 In order to provide immediate financial assistance to the extent of Rs.50,000/-per case, to
critically ill, poor patients who are living below the poverty line and undergoing treatment, the
Medical Superintendents of Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital, Smt. Sucheta
Kriplani Hospital, All India Institute of Medical Sciences New Delhi, PGIMER Chandigarh, JIPMER
Pondicherry, NIMHANS Bangalore, CNCI Kolkata, Sanjay Gandhi Post Graduate Institute of
Medical Lucknow, and CIP Ranchi have been provided with a revolving fund of Rs.10-20 lakhs.
The revolving fund is replenished after its utilization. For cases requiring financial assistance above
Rs.50000/- per case, the applications are processed in the Department of Health and Family Welfare
through a Technical Committee headed by Director General, Health Services before being
considered for approval by a duly constituted Managing Committee with Minister of Health and
Family Welfare as the Chairman. During the year 2006-07, financial assistance to the tune of
Rs. 305.35 lakhs was given directly to 234 patients under Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi.
14.3 The Committee observes that even after more than a decade of setting up of the
Fund with 50% of the contribution made by the State/UT to be provided by Central
Government, there are still several States/UTs which have not set up the State Illness

24
Assistance Fund. Every State/UTs should have such a fund. The Committee would appreciate
if this matter is taken up at the highest level in all such States/UTs.
14.4 The Committee feels that in order to facilitate easy access to quality health care to
the poor and downtrodden strata of our society, the limit of Rs.50,000 under immediate
financial assistance fund, per case, for which funds are placed at the disposal of Medical
Superintendents of above hospitals, need to be enhanced realistically for treatment of
dreaded diseases like AIDS, Cancer etc. Some of the major States like U.P., Assam,
Karnataka, Kerala and Jammu and Kashmir do not have such a fund. With only a very few
major hospitals located in metros having extended facility under the fund, people of such
States/UTs are being deprived of medical care for no fault of theirs. From the details of
funds released to States/UTs during 2005-08, it is very clear that such States are having
negligible funds at their disposal. The Committee wonders about the adequacy of such State
Funds. The Committee is of the view that with the increasing rate of inflation and also
increasing number of patients suffering from major diseases, an assessment of the
Rashtriya Arogya Nidhi should be made at the earliest. Necessary changes may be made
thereafter. The facility of financial assistance should be extended to more hospitals so as
to cover the geographical limits of the country. The Committee also recommends to the
Department to give wide publicity to the scheme specially in the hospital campuses to
generate awareness so that the same can be utilized by the needy and poor patients.
XV. NATIONAL URBAN HEALTH MISSION (NUHM)
15.1 As per 2001 census, 28.6 crores people live in urban areas, out of which 3.26 crores live
in slum areas of the cities/towns having a population of 1 lakh and above, which is expected to
reach 5.01 crores by 2007-08, thus putting greater strain on urban health infrastructure which
already has serious deficiencies. For urban poor, access to Urban Health facilities is severely
restricted due to their being ‘crowded out’ because of the inadequacy of the public health delivery
system; lack of economic resources inhibits/restricts their access to private facilities and lack of
standards and norms for urban health delivery, illegal status, poor environmental condition, over
crowding and environmental pollution makes the urban poor more vulnerable and worse off than
his rural counterpart. During 2008-09, it is proposed to launch the National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM) to address primarily health needs of these segments of population. This will complement
the activities undertaken by NRHM in rural areas. The Programme will be on Public-Private
Partnership mode.
15.2 All Cities with population above 1 lakh and State Capitals would be covered under it. 430
cities with a population of 22 crores with focus on 6.25 crores slum population would benefit.
Duration of the Mission is Eleventh Plan (2008-2012). Urban Poor families living in listed and
unlisted slums, un-authorized colonies and all other vulnerable population such as homeless, rag-
pickers, street children, rickshaw pullers, construction and brick kiln workers, sex workers and
any other temporary migrants would be identified by the Urban Local Body (ULB) concerned or
any other State specific mechanism and shall be issued a photo Family Health Card. Though, no
person would be denied service in the public health facilities, marginalized urban families identified
under the scheme would receive service on concession terms under National Urban Health Mission
(NUHM). Synergies are envisioned with Jawaharlal Nehru Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM),
SJSRY , Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) Swarna Jayanti Sharkari Rozgar Yojana
(SJSRY), etc. and with the ongoing National Health Programmes for maximizing benefits.
15.3 The Committee notes that the programme has been assigned an approved outlay of
Rs. 4495.00 crores during the Eleventh Plan out of which Rs.50.00 crores are earmarked for
2008-09.

25
15.4 The Committee observes that NUHM is one of the most ambitious Projects after
National Rural Health Mission (NRHM). Objectives of the Mission are laudable and are
according to the requirements of the present scenario. The Committee cautions the
Department to take all necessary steps so that the problems afflicting the implementation
of NRHM like those related to ground level healthcare functionaries, availability of doctors,
paramedics and infrastructure do not recur and interfere in the implementation of this
parallel scheme meant for urban areas. For achieving the targets proposed under mission,
the Department should do proper homework and work out modalities for their
implementation. The Department should start coordinating with the States right from the
beginning of the project. The Committee would like to be apprised about the progress made
in this regard.
XVI. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME (NACP)
16.1 The AIDS epidemic has emerged as one of the communicable diseases of immediate
concern. Based on the estimated prevalence rate of 0.36% (0.27% - 0.47%) it is presumed that
there are 2 to 3.1 million HIV infected persons in the country. Adult HIV prevalence is greater than
1 in Manipur (1.68%), Nagaland (1.27%) and Andhra Pradesh (1.06%). Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka,
Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu contribute 63% of the HIV infected persons in the country. Around
39% of the infections are in women and 3.8% in children. Out of the reported AIDS cases in 2007
(Jan-Oct 2007), 87.4% of the infections were transmitted through the sexual route and peri-natal
transmission accounted for 4.7% of infections. 1.8% and 1.7% of infections were acquired through
injecting drug use and contaminated blood and blood products respectively. The HIV prevalence
among high risk groups continues to be nearly 6 to 8 times greater than that among the general
population.
16.2 The National AIDS Control Programme accounts for about 9% of our national health
budget. NACO is scaling up its programmes through Targeted Interventions (TI) for High Risk
Groups, strategizing comprehensive Information, Education and Communication (lEC) packages for
specific segments and scaling up of the service delivery component.
16.3 The Committee was informed that the States of Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra have shown
a decline over a period of time and have recorded less than 1 % HIV prevalence in ANC clinic
attendees. There is decline in the HIV prevalence among ANC clinic attendees in most of the high
burden states, reflecting the impact of interventions. Similar trends are seen in Female Sex Workers
also. However, there are indications of increase in HIV prevalence among ANC population in some
of the low prevalence States. New pockets of HIV infection among ID users have been detected
in States like West Bengal, Punjab, Orissa and Tamil Nadu. The dual mode of transmission has been
observed in North Eastern States. Based on HIV/AIDS prevalence, 156 districts have been classified
in Category ‘A’ and 39 districts in Category ‘B’, which are focus of the programme interventions.
16.4 Currently, there are 571 SACS-funded TIs for FSWs/MSMs/IDUs with a coverage of 42%
and 165 TIs covering bridge populations (migrants/truckers), resulting in a total of 736 TIs. In
addition, by March 2008, it is expected to put in place 284 new TIs. During 2008-09 there will
be a scale up of 53% of core TIs which will ensure 85% coverage as per the present estimates
for core population. The scale up for Non-core TIs will be 58% during 2008-09 which would entail
the setting up of 308 TIs for Commercial sex workers and MSMs, 46 for Injecting Drug Users,
100 for Migrants and 106 for the Truckers totaling 506 interventions.
16.5 The Committee is constrained to note that against a Plan provision of Rs.815.00
crores which was increased to Rs.953.89 cror es at the RE stage during 2007-08 for NACP,
expenditure reported upto 13th March, 2008 was only Rs.767.34 crores. The Committee
observes that optimum utilization has not been achieved in any of the components of

26
NACO. The Committee notes that the Department has not been able to achieve optimum
utilization of funds during 2006-07 also. The Committee was given to understand that
procedural delays in the procurement of equipment and non-utilization of funds placed at

Information and Broadcasting were the main factors for under-utilization of allocated funds

16.9 The Committee in its last year’s report  had recommended to the Department to take some
initiative towards starting the second line of treatment so that the sufferings of patients, who have
been receiving Anti-Retroviral Treatment (ART) under the National AIDS Control Programme and
have become drug resistant, can be lessened to some extent. The Committee is given to understand
that NACO has developed a regulatory framework to implement the 2nd line treatment of drug
resistant PLHAs. A Technical Resource Group (TRG) on ART was set up in 2006 at NACO. The
TRG recommended that upfront introduction of second line treatment would be counter productive
as there are several operational issues that need to be addressed in the first instance namely,
training of doctors on second line treatment; establishing laboratories for viral load estimation which
is central to facilitate second line therapy; developing technical and operational guidelines for
providing second line treatment and clinical diagnosis and monitoring tools. The TRG further
recommended that above protocols must be in place before the rollout as drug resistance to second
line therapy has no further recourse and therefore great care needs to be taken to ensure that
patients, to the extent possible, are delayed being put on second line therapy. Complete adherence
to the second line is a must in order to prevent progression of the disease. The necessary
preparatory activities for roll out have now been done such as preparation of technical documents,
monitoring tools and handouts, counselling mat erial, job aids and patient education material. A team
of doctors from two centres was sent to Bangkok for hands-on experience on second line ART.
Drugs for second line ART are being supplied by Clinton Foundation which has an agreement with
UNIT AID, an international non-profit organization which raises funds by collecting tax on airlines
for funding HIV/AIDS treatment. As per regulatory mechanism developed, the patient selection for
second line will be done by a special panel of experts constituted by NACO. A SACEP (S tate AIDS
Clinical Expert Panel) has been established at state level. The panel consists of ART centre in
charge, another expert from outside the centre and programme person from the SACs. The panel
will meet periodically to review the records of patients failing on first line and decide on second
line drugs for these patients. The panel shall ensure that a very strict adherence protocol is
maintained for patients on second line ART and shall monitor them closely for adverse effects.
Hence, the second line roll out has been done at two sites initially-GHTM, Chennai and JJ Hospital,
Mumbai on a pilot basis and it shall be expanded later to other centres based on the experience
gained. The patients will be followed up very strictly and home visit shall also be made in case
of default to treatment. At NACO, the data from both centres is being collected about patient
evaluated for second line, tested for viral load and actually initiated on second line at these two
centres.
16.10 The Committee is happy to note that though delayed, the Department has taken the
desired step towards starting the second line of treatment to lessen the sufferings of drug
resistant patients. The Committee would like to recommend to the Department to put in
place an effective mechanism so that no patient in need of second line ART is deprived of
it.

XX. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR PREVENTION AND CONTROL OF DIABETES,
CARDIOV ASCULAR DISEASES STROKE (NPDCS)
20.1 India is experiencing a rapid health transition, with large and rising burdens of chronic Non-
Communicable Diseases especially Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD), Diabetes Mellitus, Cancer,
Stroke and Chronic Lung Diseases. It is estimated that in 2005 NCDs accounted for 5,466,000
(53%) of all deaths (10,362,000). Considering the fact that Non-Communicable diseases are
surpassing the burden of communicable diseases in the country and the existing health system is
mainly focused on communicable diseases, the National Programme on Prevention and Control of
Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke was envisaged.
20.2 The pilot programme for prevention and control of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and
stroke, has been planned with the objectives of providing effective promotion, prevention and
control strategies to provide an integrated action plan for these chronic diseases. The pilot
programme was launched on 4th January, 2008 in 7 St ates with one district each namely Assam
(district-Kamrup), Punjab (district-Jalandhar), Rajasthan (district-Bhilwara), Karnataka (district-
Shimoga), Tamilnadu (district-Kancheepuram), Kerala (Thiruvanathapuram) and Andhra Pradesh
(Nellore {tentatively}). Financial outlay for the pilot phase is Rs.5 crores.
20.3 Programme interventions have been grouped into three components i.e. Health Promotion
for the General Population, Disease Prevention for the High Risk Population and Assessment of
Prevalence of Risk Factors. At the state level, a State Non-Communicable Disease Cell with a nodal
officer will be established. The programme will be run through the District NCD Cell Society set
up under the NRHM. A nodal officer will be assisted by 2 contractual consultants with
competencies to manage two separate units of Health Promotion and Health Prevention/Surveillance
aspects which will constitute the District NCD Cell.
20.4 The Committee is happy to note that the pilot phase of the programme has finally
taken off during 2007-08. The Committee observes that the following targets have been set for
2008-09:—
➢ District Health promotion programme in 50 districts.
➢ Establishment of 20 Dedicated units of CVD/ Diabetes/Stroke Prevention Centers.
➢ Establishment of State NCD cells are proposed to be established at all States and UTs
and also Central level.

35
➢ Setting up of National Institute for Non-Communicable Diseases (NINCD) and Health
Promotion council of India.
20.5 The Committee notes that out of an approved outlay of Rs.1660.50 crores for the
Eleventh Five Y ear Plan, only Rs.30.00 crores have been earmarked for 2008-09. This, when
taken into account along with last year’s utilization of Rs.4.42 crores, leaves behind a
whopping amount of Rs.1625.50 crores for the last three years of the plan. The Committee
is given to understand that a steering Committee has been established to review and
expedite the Programme. A meeting of the States participating in the pilot project was held
on 17th October, 2007. Appreciating this initiative, the Committee recommends to the
Department to carry forward the  p rogramme vigorously during the remaining period of the
Plan so that the set targets are achieved with the optimum utilization of funds available for
the programme.
XXI. MEDICAL EDUCATION
21.1 The State Governments have the main responsibility for providing proper public health care
delivery system and also setting up of teaching institutions in the medical as well as para medical
spheres. The Central Government is involved in regulating the standards of medical and para
medical education. Under the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, regulations have been framed
containing norms for setting up of new medical colleges and also prescribing the medical
curriculum. In the context of severe shortage of manpower resources in the country, the
Government is in the process of updating these regulations so as to increase the seat capacity of
medical students and to improve the standards of the institutions including the medical curriculum,
provide relaxation in regulations for encouraging promotion of new colleges in hilly areas in various
deficient States and facilitate public-private partnership in setting up of these colleges.
21.2 The Committee is informed that out of an yearly requirement of about 60,000 MBBS
doctors only about 32,000 are passing out of the Medical Institutions. Further only about 3500 post
graduate level seats are available to them, which is a big gap.
21.3 Committee takes note of the following initiatives of the Department regarding the reforms
in medical education particularly in the under served areas and high focus States under the NRHM
as well as the North Eastern States:—
➢ Compulsory rural posting for doctors for one year for availing PG admission.
➢ To enhance PG seats and establish new PG Disciplines, Central funding to be given to
State Government Medical Colleges.
➢ MCI regulation under modification.
(i) UG medical educational regulation
(ii) PG medical educational regulation
(iii) Starting of new medical college
(iv) Minimum qualification of medical teachers education
➢ Relaxation of MCI norms in setting up medical colleges in NE States and high focus
States under NRHM.
➢ Allowing corporate entities to set up Medical Colleges.
➢ Allowing public private partnerships with Government/District Hospitals.

36
➢ Allowing private promoters to have land in 2 pieces within 10 Kms. of each other.
➢ Recognition of foreign PG Degrees.
➢ Up-dating UG and PG Curriculum.
21.4 The Committee is aware that keeping in view the shortage of doctors and existing
medical institutions not being adequate enough, MCI norms for opening of colleges/increase
of seats need to be reviewed. The Committee, however, feels that this exercise should be
undertaken with extreme caution so that objective of imparting quality medical education
remains intact. Relaxing norms by allowing private promoters to have land in two pieces
within 10 Kms. of each other and allowing corporate entities to setup medical colleges are
initiatives which should be implemented after examining all pros and cons. The Committee
is of the opinion that in the exercise of relaxation of existing norms, assessment of those
experts having the experience of this field should be given due weightage.
21.5 The Committee also takes note of the suggestion of the Department to MCI for
relaxing the age of retirement of staff of Private Medical Educational Institutes from 65 to
70 years, subject to their physical ability, in order to fill-up the acute shortage of teaching
staff in that sector. Secretary, Department of Health and Family Welfare has also informed
the Committee that a Cabinet Note has been prepared for increasing the age of retirement
to 65 years in Government Medical Educational Institutes. Committee is also given to
understand that PG degrees of USA, UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada have been
recognized and for other countries like Germany and France the matter is under
consideration. The idea is that they can come and settle here or they can come as visiting
faculties. The Committee welcomes these steps.
21.6 The Comm ittee has been informed that on a request of the Indian Ambassador in China, a
14 Member delegation visited China during 3rd June- 16th June, 2007 to assess the standard of
medical education available for Indian students in China. As per the report of the delegation, the
medical curriculum, medium of instruction, examination system and standard of medical education
imparted in China is different from the one prescribed in India. The Committee had a strong
apprehension that this would have a bearing on the quality of Indian healthcare when the doctors
educated in China practice medicine after their return to India. On being asked as to whether
any mechanism was in place to check this, the Secretary, Department of Health and Family
Welfare stated that at present there is no mechanism to prevent Indian students from going
abroad to study. The Committee is of the view that the Department needs to devise an
effective mechanism, which could include legislation, so that Indian medical students can be
prevented from going to such places whose educational system does not match with ours.
The Committee would like to be informed about the steps taken by the Department in this
regard.
21.7 On a specific query, the Committee is given to understand that at present there are 271
medical colleges in the country, out of which MBBS degree of 79 medical colleges are yet to be
recognized and 192 medical colleges in the country are already recognized under IMC Act 1956
and included in the First Schedule to the Act. There are 27 medical colleges where the first batch
of MBBS students has appeared for final examination but are yet to be recognized. Out of these
27 medical colleges, Medical Council of India has sent its recommendations to the Central
Government for recognition of MBBS degree in respect of 9 medical colleges, which is under
consideration of the Ministry. The Committee is anguished to note that the fate of so many
students of the remaining 18 medical colleges, who have already appeared in their final
examination, remains undecided. The Committee is of the view that the students should not
suffer due to such technicalities and bureaucratic hurdles. A decision without any further

37
delay may be taken in the matter. A Status Note on such colleges may also be submitted
to the Committee.
21.8 The Committee notes that the National Knowledge Commission has submitted a number of
recommendations with respect to areas of improvement in medical education in India, as indicated
below:—
• System of regulation of medical education by MCI is neither adequate nor appropriate.
A standing committee within the structure of the Independent Regulatory Authority for
Higher Education (IRAHE) may be constituted. MCI should function only as a
professional association with power to conduct nationwide exams and to give licenses
to prospective doctors.
• There should be only one All India Common Entrance Test including both Government
and Private medical colleges.
• An independent and standardized National Exit Exam immediately after the University
Exam to serve also as a postgraduate entrance exam.
• Continuing medical Education should be revamped based on distance learning. Research
centers should be set up at medical colleges with Central Assistance.
• Five regional centers for teacher training/faculty development should be set up.
• A list of priority sites for establishing medical colleges should be made by Central
Government for taking necessary follow up action.
• One institution should be identified in each State that can serve as a Centre of
excellence and role model for the other institutions of the State.
• Every district hospital should have an attached nursing school.
• A three tiered structure consisting of a one year diploma course, a three year B.Sc.
course and a three year Master’s Course may be introduced.
21.9 The Committee opines that if implemented, the recommendations of the Commission would
be a milestone in improving the standards and quality of medical education in India. The Committee
recommends that action may be initiated in this regard and Committee apprised accordingly.

22.4 The Committee has been receiving a large number of representations, particularly from the
GDMO cadre regarding very bleak chances of their career progression. The Committee is given to
understand that SAG level promotions to the GDMOs in Central Health Services is not at par with
other All India services. On a specific query regarding this, the Committee was informed by the

40
Secretary that the Department is aware that in GDMO cadre there are doctors who have PG
degrees and in many cases they are working as specialists also, but still they are not on the fast
track of career progression like specialists. The reason cited by the Secretary for this was that
while they are offered GDMO post after selection by UPSC on the basis of their MBBS degree,
they apply for PG courses and seek joining time till they complete their PG degree, which is usually
granted to them. But after two years they still join as GDMO and not as specialists. The Committee
is informed that the Department is looking into the demands of such GDMOs positively. As regards
their demand for enhancing the age of superannuation to 62 years, the Committee was assured that
the Department is going to take the issue to the Cabinet very soon. The Committee is further given
to understand that the recommendation of the Fifth Pay Commission that SAG level positions in
All India service should be 17% of total cadre strength could not be implemented. The Department
had initiated for up gradation of these posts and creation of extra posts at SAG and HAG level
to plug the gap arising due to Fifth Pay Commission recommendations. However, due to a stay in
a court case no fresh appointment could be made in SAG. Further, now the Sixth Pay Commission
has recommended that if additional posts are to be created to fulfill any gap, these should be
created in such a manner that they are filled up by direct recruitment. Further the Department has
expressed its practical difficulty in identifying supervisory level posts in approximately 40
participating units under Central Health Services so as to justify higher level of promotions. The
Committee is informed that due to this practical difficulty, they are moving for a proposal for one
time in-situ promotion which means that though they will be at dispensary level, they will get one
time promotional benefit of SAG grade.
22.5 The Committee views with serious concern the grave injustice done to the GDMO
cadre for no fault of theirs. Inspite of their being eligible for specialist post, continuance
of such doctors in GDMO cadre is indeed against all principles of natural justice. Non-
implementation of Fifth Pay Commission recommendation of SAG level positions in All
India Service to be 17% of total cadre has created another hurdle in their career
progression. The Committee finds that Sixth Pay Commission’s recommendation of filling
up the additional posts to be created for fulfilling any gap, by direct recruitment, will make
the position of GDMOs very vulnerable. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the
Department should take up this issue immediately with the Ministry of Finance. Every
attempt should be made to remove the grave injustice done to the GDMO cadre so that this
sub-cadre of professionals gets due recognition and morale boost like others in All India
Services.

PART-B
NATIONAL RURAL HEALTH MISSION (NRHM)
AND FAMILY WELFARE PROGRAMMES
1. The National Rural Health Mission was operationalised in April 2005 throughout the country.
The Mission covers the rural areas of the entire country with special focus on 18 States viz.
8 Empowered Action Group States (Bihar, Jharkhand, M.P., Chhattisgarh, U.P., Uttarakhand, Orissa
and Rajasthan) 8 North-East States, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir. The main objective
under the Mission is to provide universal access to equitable, affordable and quality healthcare
delivery, especially to the poor and the vulnerable sections of the society, bridge gaps in healthcare,
facilitate decentralized planning in the health sector, ensure population stabilization, gender balance
and bring about inter-sectoral convergence. The NRHM also provides an overarching umbrella to
the existing programmes of Health and Family Welfare including RCH-II, V ector Borne Disease
Control Programme, TB, Leprosy, NPCB and the Integrated Disease Surveillance Project.
Mainstreaming of AYUSH is also one of the strategies under the Mission.
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION (NRHM)
2.1 Time Bound Goals set by Planning Commission for the Eleventh Five Year Plan are given
below:
➢ Reducing Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to 1 per 1000 live births.
➢ Reducing Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) to 28 per 1000 live Births against the target of
30 per 1000 live berth fixed under NRHM.
➢ Reducing Total Fertility Rate to 2.1.
➢ Raising the sex ratio for age group 0-6 to 935 by 2011-12 and 950 by 2016-17.
➢ Providing clean drinking water for all by 2009 and ensuring no slip-backs.
➢ Reducing malnutrition among children of age group 0-3 to half its present level.
➢ Reducing anemia among women and girls by 50%.

III. INFRASTRUCTURE STRENTHENING
3.1 NRHM aims at strengthening of Primary Health Infrastructure and improving effective
service delivery across the country. Sub-centers, Primary Healthcare Centers and Community
Health Centres are the three pillars on which rural infrastructure is built upon. As on March. 2007,
there are 1,45,272 Sub-Centers, 22,370 PHCs and 4045 CHCs in the country. There is a shortfall
of 20,855 Sub-Centres, 6491 PHCs and 2525 CHCs in the country based on the 2001 population
norms. The Committee has been constantly drawing the attention of the Department to the uneven
spread of these centres across the country with prominent gaps in the High Focus States. The
Committee finds that there is no marked improvement in this regard.
The Committee has been expressing its serious concern on the continuance of lack of rural
health infrastructure, especially in the High Focus States where the need is the most. On being
asked to identify the problem areas, the Committee has been informed that health infrastructure and
allocation of health workers under NRHM is planned on the population, workload and distance
norms. Shortages on the basis of 2001 population are quantified as the difference between the
required number of facilities/providers as per the norms and those that are functioning or in
position. This method of determining norms and shortage does not take into account the varying
epidemiological, geographical and socio-demographic patterns across the different States!
Communities and between rural and urban areas within States. The actual availability of different
types of providers or the extent of private/voluntary sector involvement in health care delivery at
the community level is also not taken into account. The Committee notes that against the backdrop
of these very visible deficiencies, norms for setting up of the Sub-Centres and PHCs have been
modified by the Steering Committee of the Planning Commission. These norms to be adopted
during the Eleventh Plan have been duly approved by the Planning Commission also. The
Committee has been given to understand that population-centric norms are replaced with
flexible norms comprising habitation-based needs, community based needs and disease-pattern
based needs.
3.2 The Committee welcomes the modification in the criteria for assessing the
requirement of health infrastructure in the country. In a vast country like ours, rigid
norms based on population only and made uniformly applicable were perhaps not proving to
be justified and not based on ground realities. The Committee is also of the view that
change in the norms for health infrastructure proposed by the Planning Commission was
called for. The Committee is, however, not aware whether any preparatory exercise has been
initiated for conducting surveys as per the revised norms. The Committee is afraid that if
this issue is allowed to linger on for long, the very objective of NRHM of bridging gaps in
the health care will continue to be a distant dream. The Committee, accordingly, impresses
upon the Department to initiate action at the earliest.

ASHA
3.11 One of the most important strategic interventions under the National Rural Health Mission
is ASHA—a social health activist. ASHA is envisaged as a trained woman community health
volunteer who will reinforce community action for universal immunization, safe delivery, new born
care, prevention of water borne disease and communicable disease, improved nutrition and
promotion of household toilets. She is required to inform, interact, mobilize and facilitate improved
access to preventive and promotive healthcare and also provide basic curative care through her
drug kits. She will assist in formulation of village health plan by the Village Health and Sanitation
Committee. ASHA will also promote awareness and usage of ISM. The requirement for ASHA is
one per thousand population with relaxation to this norm depending upon the workload and terrain.
ASHA is envisaged to be a primary resident of the village who would be selected by the Gram
Sabha following an intense community mobilization process. She will be fully accountable to the
Panchayats. ASHA has been a major intervention for the ten high focus States namely Uttar
Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Assam
and Jammu and Kashmir.

51
3.12 Capacity building of ASHA is critical in enhancing her effectiveness as a link between the
community and the health facility. The initial orientation training is for a period of 23 days spread
in 5 rounds over a period of 12 months and followed by periodic re-training for about 2 days once
every alternate month, apart from the on-the-job training she would be getting. Training modules
for this purpose have been developed based on a thematic approach and States have also
constituted district and block training teams for this purpose. The Department has informed the
Committee, during its discussion on demand for grants, that selection of 5,87,512 ASHA has been
completed, 4,90,000 ASHA have completed their first round training and 2,18,339 ASHA have been
provided with drug kits.
The Committee is happy to note the progress made by the Department on the ASHA
initiative under NRHM. It is also happy to note that 86.41% ASHA have been trained in
their first module post induction training till 12th March, 2008. The Committee observes
that ASHAs have to undergo three more rounds of training. So far, only 27% ASHAs have
undergone 2nd round of training. The Committee is of the view that every effort needs to
be made to ensure that second round of training of all the ASHAs is completed at the
earliest.
The Committee has its apprehensions regarding the effectivity of ASHA as a multi-
purpose social health activist, as envisaged under the NRHM. The Committee observes that
job responsibilities of ASHA are manifold as indicated below :—
– awareness generation- Health, RCH, HIV/AIDS.
– advising newly married couples for their special needs.
– guiding pregnant women for availing of institutional facilities for Ante-Natal,
Natal and Post-Natal needs.
– counselling on nutrition, pregnancy, breast-feeding, immunization and family
planning.
– establishing link with PHCs, private providers and others for service requirement
of beneficiaries.
– mobilising parents for child survival interventions.
– promoting basic sanitization.
– provision of non-clinical spacing contraceptives.
– surveillance of communicable diseases.
3.13 ASHA is also the primary provider for National Health Programme. She is the Depot
Holder for health commodities like Vitamin A, Impregnated bed nets, ORS etc. She is also
supposed to handle treatment of minor ailments. Another  major task assigned to ASHA is
to provide escort services for women seeking delivery services at institutions, requiring
emergency care and MTP services, women and men for clinical contraception services and
VCTC. The Committee has been given to understand that States have also taken up the
training of ASHAs on diagnosis of malaria cases. For being eligible for ASHA, a woman has
to be 25 to 35 years of age, married, resident of the village, acceptable to the village and
community and proficient in reading and writing. The Committee fails to understand as to
how a single woman, who is a simple villager can take care of one thousand population by
performing such wide-ranging tasks. Situation becomes more complex and well away from
ground realities, when one finds that only remuneration payable to ASHA is for providing
Escort Services. Instances of Escort Services may not be very frequent some times. The
Committee strongly feels that ASHA is supposed to play a very challenging role.

52
3.14 The Committee is of the view that with the passage of time, the number of
responsibilities of ASHA will itself become a challenge for her to cope up with. This will not
only reflect in the quality of her work and performance but ultimately fail in fulfilling the
very objectives with which the initiative was initially conceptualized. As the initiative is still
in the early stages, the Committee suggests that the Department should review the
responsibilities entrusted to the ASHA. Committee’s attention has been drawn by the
findings of Common Review Mission which conducted appraisal of NRHM in November,
2007,16 months after NRHM got final Cabinet approval in July, 2006. Appraisal was based
on one-two districts in A.P., Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, M.P., Gujarat, J&K,
Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P. and West Bengal. The Committee notes that
performance assessment of ASHA has led to mixed findings in different States. Non-
payment against activities/conflicts regarding compensation money and lack of role clarity
between ASHAs and AWWs are two major  problem ar eas identified. The Committee
apprehends that situation may worsen with more complexities arising in future. The
Committee is, therefore, of the view that role of ASHA needs to be reassessed and
reformulated.

Mobile Medical Units (MMUs)
3.16 During 2006-07, though the target set was for providing MMUs to all 600 districts in the
country, only 318 districts could be provided with such units. As a result operationalisation of those
318 MMUs sanctioned in 2006-07, was set as the target to be achieved during 2007-08 under the
scheme. However, as informed by the Department, while 319 districts have been funded for
MMUs, operationalisation of only 198 MMUs could be achieved. The Committee had pointed out
to the Department last year that the names of bigger States like Bihar, Jharkhand, M.P.,
Maharashtra, U.P. did not register among those that had disbursed funds for providing MMUs in
the States. The Committee had also pointed out that these 318 districts are distributed among 18
States only. The Department, in its action taken note, had replied that these States had incorporated
and provided funds for MMUs in their Programme Implementation Plan (PIP-2007-08) under
NRHM. It seems that incorporation and provision of funds for MMUs in the Programme
Implementation Plan (2007-08), of Bihar, Maharashtra and U.P. has not been followed by
procurement of MMUs in these States. The Committee notes that MMUs were to be operationalised
in 400 districts by March, 2008. However, as per the latest figures there is no increase in the
number of 198 functional MMUs.
Against such a backdrop, chances of improvement do not seem to be possible in the
near future. The Committee understands that many States are having their own set-up of
ambulances which seem to be functioning well. There are also States where NGOs are
involved in providing this service. The Committee feels that based on the findings of
Common Review Mission in respect of some States, steps may be taken for strengthening
the facility of MMUs.
The Committee had the opportunity to apprise itself about the key findings of the
appraisal conducted by the Common Review Mission in November, 2007. The study is based
on team visits made to one or two districts in Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh,
Orissa, M.P., Gujarat, J&K, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, U.P. and West Bengal. The
Committee finds that assessment of NRHM on 24 parameters has been made through this
appraisal. The Committee takes note of the constraints being faced by these States in the
implementation of NRHM and the recommendations on the areas that need strengthening
and course correction. While appreciating this initiative, the Committee is of the view that
such an appraisal needs to be followed by intensive interaction with all the implementing
agencies in the States at the earliest. Otherwise the very purpose of undertaking such an
exercise will be defeated. The Committee also strongly feels that such Common Review
Missions should be conducted in all the States, with one region being taken at a time. It
would also be a good idea if two-three performing and non-performing districts in each State
are taken together for making an comparative analysis. Incorporation of surprise visits will
make the assessment more realistic.
IV. NATIONAL VECTOR BORNE DISEASE CONTROL PROGRAMME (NVBDCP)
4.1 The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) is an umbrella
programme for prevention and control of vector borne diseases viz., Malaria, Filariasis, Kala-azar,

54
Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (DF/DHF) and Japanese Encephalitis and Chikungunia. Under
the programme, comprehensive and multi-faceted public health activities are being implemented in
the country. The prevention and control of vector-borne diseases is complex as their transmission
depends on interaction of numerous ecological, biological, social and economic factors including
migration. The Directorate of NVBDCP is the nodal agency for planning, policy making, technical
guidance and for monitoring and evaluation of programme implementation in respect of prevention
and control of the vector borne diseases. The States are responsible for planning, implementation
and supervision of the programmes.

4.3 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by the following anticipated constraints/ problem

– Filling up of vacant posts of Health Workers

4.4 As per the information furnished in the Outcome Budget, the annual incidence of Malaria

impact indicator Annual Parasite Incidence (API) i.e., the number of malaria cases per year per

Committee is that the number of Pf-positive cases has been steady between 40-50 per cent over
the last four years and during 2007, the number of Pf-positive cases that were reported till
December is more than 50%. Not only this, in many pockets in the highly endemic States, the
disease has developed resistance to Chloroquine—the chief malarial drug.

4.7 The Committee notes that increased supervision and monitoring is one of the main
strategies adopted for effective control of malaria. The latest figures made available to the
Committee reveal continuance of shortage of surveillance and supervisory staff in NE
States. In Assam, the biggest State of NE Region, against the sanctioned posts of 694 Health
Supervisor (Male) only 570 were in position, against 343 Health Supervisor (Female), there
were 316 and only 1647 MPW(M) against 3080 sanctioned posts. What is more disturbing is
that while Tripura failed to furnish the data, Meghalaya and Nagaland have provided
incomplete information. The primary role of MPW (M) and MPW(F) is door to door
surveillance and detection of communicable diseases and it’s reporting. The fact that these
functionaries play a vital role in disease detection and surveillance cannot be ignored. By
not appointing these functionaries, the States leave a big gap at the field-level disease
surveillance, detection and treatment. This vital issue needs to be pursued at the highest
level in the concerned States. The other strategy adopted is use of Rapid Diagnostic Kits
by ASHAs. The Committee does not have high expectation from this initiative as firstly
required number of ASHAs have to be in place in malaria endemic States and even if they
are there, they would be over-burdened with the various tasks already assigned to them.
The Committee fails to comprehend the continuance of such a discouraging situation inspite
of special dispensation for NE States. The Committee can only reiterate that there is need
for drastic measures and extensive monitoring under the supervision of State Nodal
Officers.
Kala-azar
4.8 Kala-azar is a slow progressing indigenous the disease caused by protozoan parasite
leishmania donovani and spread by its vector—the Sandfly. The National Health Policy (2002) has
set the goal for elimination of Kala-azar from the country by 2010. An amount of Rs.20.86 crores
was earmarked in 2007-08 for combating the disease and which has been enhanced to Rs. 29.51
crores in 2008-09. Kala-azar is endemic in 33 districts in Bihar, 4 districts in Jharkhand, 5 districts
of Uttar Pradesh and 11 districts of West Bengal (total 53 districts) besides sporadically occurring
in a few other areas.
4.9 The Committee has been observing increasing trend of Kala-azar cases. In 2006, 39178
cases and 187 deaths were reported with 162 deaths occurring in Bihar alone. Position seems to
have worsened further in 2007. Upto November, 2007, already 35,638 cases with 158 deaths have
been reported. State-wise figures upto May, 2007 indicate that out of 79 deaths reported till then,
64 deaths have occurred in Bihar. While the Committee would not dispute the Department’s stand
that intensive surveillance has led to reporting of increased number of cases, the fact remains that
treatment compliance of Kala-azar cases detected is far from satisfactory in view of alarming rate
of deaths being reported. A number of initiatives undertaken for Kala-azar elimination seem to have
made no impact with ground reality continuing to be as discouraging as before. The Committee
understands that 200 villages of 9 districts reporting large number of Kala-azar cases have been
selected for focused interventions. The Committee strongly feels that effective surveillance,
timely treatment and compliance of treatment regimens in all PHCs would lead to better
reports in 2008. The Committee is of the view that only if intensive monitoring at all levels
is carried out, the goal of elimination of Kala-azar by 2010 can be made achievable.
Situation so far has not been very encouraging. All the quantifiable objectives listed in the
Action Plan for 2008-09 need to be closely monitored on monthly basis.

57
Japanese Encephalitis
4.10 Japanese Encephalitis (JE) is a viral disease with a tendency of seasonal outbreaks. JE has
been reported repeatedly from 15 States out of which, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana, Karnataka,
Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal have been reporting
repeated outbreaks. There is no specific anti-viral drug for JE and cases are managed
symptomatically. Efforts have been directed to provide technical support and strengthen capabilities
of State through training to tackle this disease. A vaccination programme for children between 1
and 15 years of age under the Universal Immunization Programme, using single dose live attenuated
SA-14-l4-2 vaccine has been launched in 2006. In 2006, 11 districts in 4 States were covered
which was expanded to 28 districts in 10 States during 2007. A total of 93.08 lakhs children were
vaccinated against the target of 105.31 lakhs children achieving 88.39% coverage. As per the
Annual Report, 2007-08, the vaccination campaign has so far been completed in Assam (89%),
Haryana (86%), West Bengal (61%) and in 7 districts of Uttar Pradesh (99.7%).
The Committee is dismayed to note that despite various methods adopted by the
Department over the past year to contain the disease, the number of cases reported to be
suffering from JE/ AES has shown an increase over the previous year figures. The fact is
even more disturbing that though the Department claims to have completed 99.97%
immunization in the past year in 7 worst affected districts in Uttar Pradesh, the situation
there has worsened with 2675 cases and 577 deaths in 2007 (till December) over the 2006
figures of 2320 cases and 528 deaths. The Committee fails to comprehend as to why inspite
of a number of preventive measures taken by the Central Government in co-ordination with
the State Government of Uttar Pradesh, the JE/AES related cases and deaths continue to
be high in the State. The Committee apprehends that the actual figures would increase the
tally much further. The Committee would like to take the opportunity to state that though
the data for Assam has not been made available by the Department, going by the fact sheet
of 2006, it is apprehensive that the situation in Assam would also show a similar trend as
that of U.P.
4.11 The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Department to the fact that
the year 2006 had reported a visible impact of preventive measures initiated by registering
a declining trend when compared with 2005 figures. Quantum jump in the first three
quarter of 2007 calls for a serious review with special focus on Assam and U.P., the two
main endemic States. The Committee would impress upon the Department that analysis of
epidemiological and entomological data for epidemic outbreak prediction and timely remedial
measures is required to be carried out on an urgent basis.
The Committee feels that perhaps the precautionary methods adopted by the
Department have not percolated properly to the affected population because of which the
disease has once again registered an increase. The Committee adds that lax monitoring of
the disease by the Central as well as the State Government could aggravate the situation
further unless it is dealt with a sense of urgency. It suggests the Department to undertake
on-the-spot review of the situation as to the possible causes for upsurge in the reported
cases. The Committee urges the Department to step-up the ongoing IEC activities in the
endemic States so that the desired objective is reached soon.
Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever/Chikungunya
4.12 Dengue/Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever is an acute viral infection transmitted by Aedes aegypti
mosquitoes that breed in man-made containers in which water stagnates for more than a week.
Dengue is endemic in 18 States/UTs with the population of about 450 million at risk. During 2005,
there were outbreaks in many parts of the country reporting 11985 cases and 157 deaths in 2005.

58
Year 2006 has also reported 12,317 cases and 184 deaths. In 2007 up to November 4574 cases
and 59 deaths have been reported.
4.13 Chikungunya is a debilitating, viral illness spread by the bite of infected mosquitoes. The
disease resemble dengue fever and is characterized by severe, sometimes persistent, joint pain
(arthritis) as well as fever and rash. Chikungunya fever has re-emerged in 16 States in the country
during 2006 in epidemic form after about three decades. The reported number of suspected
Chikungunya fever cases in the country in 2006 was 1.39 million. 15961 samples were tested out
of which 2001 were found positive for Chikungunya. During the year 2007 upto November, 56355
suspected Chikungunya fever cases have been reported. 7482 samples were tested, out of which
1876 were confirmed cases.
4.14 The overall strategies for prevention and control of Chikungunya are same as in Dengue
such as symptomatic management of cases, reduction of breeding sources, personal protection
and intensive IEC and capacity building. The Committee notes that against an allocation of
Rs.2.50 crores during 2007-08, the allocation for 2008-09 has been enhanced to Rs.14.59 crores.
The Committee has been given to understand that Dengue and Chikungunya are outbreak prone
viral diseases which require adequate IEC activities, capacity building, strengthening of sentinel and
Apex Laboratories and supply of diagnostic test kits.
4.15 Several steps were reported to have been taken during the last year to tackle Dengue and
Chikungunya, which include:
• Regional monitoring and identification of 13 Apex Referral Laboratories for advanced
diagnosis and regular surveillance of Dengue and Chikungunya fever cases and 110
sentinel surveillance hospitals for pro-active surveillance.
• States advised for intensive IEC activities through print, electronic media, Inter-personal
communication, outdoor publicity as well as Inter-sectoral collaboration with civil
society organizations (NGOs/CBOs/Self-Help Groups), Panchayati Raj Institutions
(PRIs), for taking community based measures.
The Committee also notes that an emergency package of Rs.21.60 crores was sanctioned
to the affected States for items like Fogging Machines, Pyrethrum Extract, Temephos and
Insecticide-treated bed nets and IEC activity.
4.16 State-wise analysis of suspected Chikungunya cases and number of confirmed cases during
2006 and 2007 reveals a very disturbing trend about the spread of this disease. In 2006, maximum
number of confirmed cases were reported from Maharashtra (804) followed by Karnataka (298)
and Gujarat (225). In contrast, Kerala reported the highest number of confirmed cases of 909 while
there are 347 confirmed cases occurring in West Bengal in 2007 uptil November. Another cause
of serious concern is overall increase in total number of confirmed Chikungunya cases from 2001
in 2006 to 1876 in 2007 (upto November).
4.17 Incidence of Chikungunya cases in the country during 2006 and 2007 has led the
Committee to the conclusion that various initiatives taken by the Department have so far
failed to yield any desired results. The Committee strongly feels that with the enhanced
allocation of Rs. 14.59 crore in 2008-09 for Dengue and Chikungunya, effective measures
are required to be undertaken in the affected States. Mere circulation of detailed guidelines
and advisories for prevention and control of these diseases to all affected States would not
serve any purpose. What is required is to identify the affected districts and go for regular
fever surveillance in such endemic areas to detect an unusual trend. The Committee is of
the view that if this analysis of ground reality is followed by IEC activities and
strengthening of apex Referral Institutions for diagnosis and treatment, number of Dengue/

59
Chikungunya cases would show a declining trend. The Committee apprehends that unless
adequate remedial measures are taken, sporadic outburst of these diseases would continue
to be reported from different States every year.
V. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME
5.1 T.B is a major health problem in India. India accounts for 1/5th of the global incidence of
T.B. cases. As per the latest estimates, there are approximately 18 lakh new cases every year in
the country. Two persons die from T.B. in India every three minutes, more than 1000 people every
day, and almost 3,70,000 every year.
5.2 To control this major health problem of the country, Revised National TB Control Programme
is being implemented. Phase-II of the project (period October, 2005 to September, 2011) has
a total outlay of Rs.1,156 crores which includes credit from World Bank of Rs.756 crores and
commodity assistance of anti-TB drugs from DFID through WHO for Rs. 287 crores with balance
of Rs.191 crores being given by GoI. In addition, Rs.385.5 crores through GFATM and USAID
have also been provided. Phase-II of RNTCP is a step towards achieving the TB related Millennium
Development Goal (MDG) targets. DOTS remain the core strategy. The Department has informed
that the total allocation under the Programme during 2007-08 was to the tune of Rs.267 crores
with expenditure of Rs.237.20 crores reported upto 29th February, 2008.
5.3 The Committee notes that around 4,03,917 patients have been put on treatment during 2nd
quarter of 2007 saving around 65,000 lives. More than 1,20,000 patients are being put on DOTS
every month. One of the major initiatives taken is the involvement of 2421 NGOs and 15,900
private practitioners working under the programme under Government approved NGO/ PP
Guidelines. Over 240 medical colleges are participating in the programme. Besides that, all the 16
centrally owned ESI Hospitals, Zonal Railway Hospitals, Coal, Steel and Mines Health Facilities,
Port Trust Hospitals, CGHS Hospitals and 150 Corporate Hospitals, BHEL, NTPC, Ranchi Armed
Forces Hospital are involved in RNTCP.
5.4 The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of RNTCP Phase-I and
ongoing Phase-II. Several initiatives/interventions taken at different levels and variety of
implementing agencies have contributed to the increasing population coverage and 85%
cure rate. However, India still contributes 20% of TB cases reported in the world. Out of
8.8 million cases per annum, 1.8 million cases are from India alone. New complex off shoots
of TB also keep on emerging, the most visible being worsening HIV epidemic increasing the
number of TB cases. The Committee notes that HIV is the most potent risk factor for
progression of TB infection to disease form. HIV-TB patients detected in 2005 were 12,062,
13,614 in 2006 and 18,559 in 2007. The Committee is aware that increase in number of
co-infected (HIV-TB) patients being detected over the last three years is a result of
innovative and co-ordinated measures taken by the Department. But the other dimension
of this trend is increasing complexities involved in the treatment of such cases. The
Committee hopes that the National Framework formulated by RNTCP and NACP for joint
TB/HIV collaborative activities will lead to better and effective control of this emerging
problem area.
5.5 The Committee observes that the other major challenge to TB control in the country
is increasing number of MDR- TB cases. The Committee is aware that such cases are bound
to increase the magnitude and severity of TB epidemic and pose a major threat to TB
control. The Committee in its earlier Report has pointed out that 7% defaulters in a year
is quite a significant number of cases remaining untreated or half-treated. With a single
TB patient infecting 10-15 persons in a year, rate of infection is bound to increase. The
Committee would like to point out that formulation of guidelines for management of MDR

60
TB cases and publication thereof will not prove to be sufficient enough. The Committee had
given a simple suggestion for identifying the defaulter TB patients from the records being
maintained at centres/ hospitals with the help of NGOs/Social Workers and Private
Practitioners. Intention of the Committee was to identify such cases at the first default
stage itself. The Committee finds that under a new initiative a total of 50 MDR- TB patients
were to be registered for treatment in Gujarat and Maharashtra during 2007-08 to be
doubled every year subsequently and ultimately in the entire country. While welcoming this
initiative, the Committee would also like to point out that cost of MDR- TB treatment is
300 times more than non-MDR TB. The Committee can only say that preventive measures
will be both cost-effective and helpful for the patients. The Committee is of the firm
opinion that through effective IEC activities and alertness of health workers regular intake
of medicines can be easily monitored. The Committee, therefore, suggests that monitoring
of TB patients the most vital aspect, should not be ignored at any cost.

5.8 Reacting to a query on the status of research by the Tuberculosis Research Centre, Chennai
that is currently involved in the designing stage of a new TB drug the Department has informed
that Johnson & Johnson pharmaceuticals approached Tuberculosis Research Centre, Chennai (TRC)

randomized trial to evaluate the anti-bacterial activity, safety and tolerability of TMC 207 in subjects
with sputum smear positive pulmonary infection with multi-drug resistant Mycobacterium
tuberculosis (MDR-TB). After extensive discussions with senior researchers at TRC followed by
the members of 35th Scientific Advisory Committee (SAC) of TRC in Nov 2007 as well as by a
Sub-Committee constituted by the SAC, the protocol now is ready to be presented to the
Institutional Ethics Committee (lEC) TRC in the month of March, 2008. In the meantime, the Drug
Controller of GoI has given clearance for the trial. It is likely to start in the month of May, 2008.
The Committee is happy to note that the pharma company Johnson & Johnson has
undertaken the responsibility for developing a drug for treatment of patients with Multi-
Drug Resistant TB. The Committee has been given to understand that the cost of treatment
of MDR- TB patients is very high. The Committee feels that the issue of cost effectiveness
of the drug needs to be examined simply because patients in India are generally poor and
lack means to afford the drugs. Under the circumstances, the affordability of the drug could
be construed as a blessing for the poor and downtrodden.
5.9 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by Studies like Social Assessment Study,
Institutional Assessment Study in respect of TB Control measures undertaken so far. The
Committee would like to point out that TB infection is no more confined to poor and
marginalise section of the society. Growing number of patients now belong to middle class
and also affluent population. There is an urgent need for making an analysis of basic
factors behind this emerging situation which can ultimately reach to alarming proportions.
The Committee hopes that with the availability of both funds and manpower, the
Department will take up such an exercise at the earliest.
VI. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME (NLEP)
6.1 National Leprosy Eradication Programme was launched with the objective of eliminating
Leprosy i.e. achieving prevalence rate of <1case/l0,000 population from the country. National level

62
elimination of Leprosy has been achieved since 31 December 2005 when the prevalence rate came
down to 0.95 or less than 1/10,000 population. 0.83 lakh cases were on record as on 1st April
2007 giving a Prevalence rate (PR) of 0.72 per 10,000 population. 31 States/ UTs have achieved
the level of elimination i.e. PR less than 1/10,000 population. 80% of districts and 75% of blocks
across the country have also achieved elimination. Four States, namely Bihar, Chhattisgarh,
Jharkhand and West Bengal having PR between 1 and 2 per 10,000 population with Chhattisgarh
having more than 2 per 10,000 population are yet to achieve elimination status.
6.2 The budget allocation was Rs.40.00 crores in 2007-08. As the States had unspent balances
with them, the BE 2007-08 was reduced to Rs.27.12 crores at RE stage. Expenditure reported upto
29.02.08 is only Rs.21.57 crore. Allocation of Rs.45.00 crore has been made for 2008-09. The
increased provision is meant for incentive to be given to leprosy affected persons undergoing re-
constructive surgery and institutions performing re-constructive surgery and performance based
incentive to ASHA in S tates with high leprosy burden such as Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand,
Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
The Committee in its 22nd Report, had voiced its serious concern for
under-utilisation of allocated funds in 2006-07 due to unspent balances in majority of
the States. The Committee takes note of detailed analysis of actual expenditure pattern in
2006-07 carried out by the Department. The Committee is surprised to observe that even
this detailed analysis indicates provisional figures of 77.59% of utilisation of allocated funds
by the States. The Committee’s concern is further deepened by the fact that the two major
States Bihar and Jharkhand could utilize only 33.9% and 30% of the allocated funds during
the year 2006-07. Creation of confusion due to merger of the leprosy society with the State
Health Society under NRHM has been cited as the main reason for this position. The
Committee has been given to understand that a number of measures like review of
programme performance and expenditure pattern in the quarterly review meetings of
district Leprosy Officers streamlining of procurement procedure and monitoring at the
central level were initiated during 2007-08. The Committee also notes that more focus was
given on implementation of Action Plan during annual meeting and quarterly review
meetings of State Programme Officers. Not only this the States were also instructed to
prepare a month-wise Action Plan of IEC and Training from July, 2007 onwards and
submitting the monthly implementation reports of these activities. The Committee is,
however, constrained to observe that these elaborate measures initiated by the Department
failed to make any visible impact as the ground realities continue to remain unchanged.
Drastic reduction of allocated funds had to be made at RE stage in 2007-08 with even that
provision remaining under-utilised upto 29.02.08.
6.3 The Committee is apprehensive that an enhanced allocation during 2008-09 may also
face similar outcomes. The Committee feels that though the plan of action under the
programme is well prepared, monitoring the timely and proper utilization of funds needs to
be taken on a more serious note. Mere advisories to State Implementing Agencies will not
serve the purpose. It, therefore, recommends that the Department take up the issue with
the State Programme Officers especially of Bihar and Jharkhand in an emphatic manner
during its quarterly review meetings.
